  "visuals": [
    {
      "path": "experiments/records/english-scorer-controls/comparison.svg",
      "caption": "Every language uses the same marks and axes. Original scores are blue; gray ranges contain all shuffles. The dashed threshold is fixed at -5.5."
    }
  ],
  "article": "## Would our scorer recognize a real answer?\n\nA search can recover meaningful text and still discard it if its scoring rule expects the wrong language. This experiment isolates that last step: give a fixed English four-letter scoring model known text in eight languages, then shuffle the same letters as a control. No cipher or decoder is involved.\n\nThe model accepts all English and French samples in this run, some German, Italian, Portuguese and Spanish samples, and none of the Finnish or Welsh samples. It accepts none of the 7,680 shuffled controls. That is useful separation from these shuffles, but **acceptance is neither English identification nor proof of a decryption**. Rejection also cannot rule out meaningful plaintext in another language.\n\n## Source and scope\n\nThe idea follows the scorer-language investigation in [Dukotah's repository](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/PAPER.md). We pin that revision and reuse its English quadgram count file and −5.5 threshold. We run a new, narrower control on our existing aligned FLORES translations; we do not reproduce the repository's full decoder benchmark or import its conclusions about the unsolved cipher.\n\nThe [language comparison experiments](#/experiments/parallel-languages) ask which reference profiles resemble manuscript statistics. This experiment instead asks what a candidate-selection tool accepts when the input is already known text. There are no unsolved-page inputs here.\n\n## Fixed procedure\n\nDivide each of the eight 1,012-sentence translations into the same eight consecutive sentence blocks: four of 127 sentences and four of 126. Join sentences with spaces. Apply each of two rules: uppercase and retain A–Z only; or uppercase, canonically decompose Unicode, remove combining marks, and then retain A–Z. The second rule folds many accented letters but is not a general transliteration system. Uppercasing can expand characters, such as ß to SS. The report records retained lengths and discarded alphabetic characters for each block.\n\nTake the first 120, 240 and 400 retained letters from every block. These are nested samples, not three independent passages. Aligned sentence blocks preserve source content boundaries, but equal character prefixes do not necessarily end at the same translated idea. Generate 20 deterministic shuffles of each excerpt, preserving its exact letter counts. Keep all 384 original cells and all 7,680 controls; there is no selection by score.\n\nFor each overlapping group of four letters, use log₁₀(count / total model count). An unseen group receives log₁₀(0.01 / total). Average over the length minus three groups. Accept a sample when this average is at least −5.5. This threshold belongs to this model and preprocessing; it is not portable to an arbitrary language scorer.\n\n## All conditions\n\nEach cell below is accepted originals out of eight blocks. Every condition also has 160 shuffles per language; all have zero accepted shuffles. The figure shows individual original scores and the full observed shuffled range, not a confidence interval.\n\n| Language | A–Z 120 | A–Z 240 | A–Z 400 | Folded 120 | Folded 240 | Folded 400 |\n| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |\n| English | 8/8 | 8/8 | 8/8 | 8/8 | 8/8 | 8/8 |\n| Finnish | 0/8 | 0/8 | 0/8 | 0/8 | 0/8 | 0/8 |\n| French | 8/8 | 8/8 | 8/8 | 8/8 | 8/8 | 8/8 |\n| German | 6/8 | 6/8 | 6/8 | 6/8 | 6/8 | 8/8 |\n| Italian | 7/8 | 8/8 | 8/8 | 7/8 | 8/8 | 8/8 |\n| Portuguese | 5/8 | 7/8 | 7/8 | 6/8 | 7/8 | 7/8 |\n| Spanish | 6/8 | 7/8 | 7/8 | 8/8 | 7/8 | 7/8 |\n| Welsh | 0/8 | 0/8 | 0/8 | 0/8 | 0/8 | 0/8 |\n\n## What this does and does not establish\n\nThis scorer can reject intact language while accepting a different non-English language. A successful candidate therefore needs more than crossing a threshold: a reproducible decoding rule, declared choices, coherent extended output and checks against controls appropriate to the whole search.\n\nThe shuffles preserve single-letter frequencies but destroy order. They are not wrong-key outputs from a specified cipher. Zero acceptances in this finite collection does not imply zero false positives, especially after searching millions of candidates and keeping the maximum. The overlapping sample lengths, reused translations and shared model also prevent treating these cells as independent trials or a general accuracy estimate. Model-training overlap with the benchmark has not been independently excluded.\n\nThis is not decoder recovery power: it bypasses decoding entirely. The completed [planted decoder controls](#/experiments/decoder-skip-controls) separately measure exact recovery and score acceptance under fixed encoder, key and skip rules. The [bounded search-maximum controls](#/experiments/search-maximum-controls) retain the maximum from each complete null search rather than treating individual null strings as equivalent to selected winners. These are separate experiments; neither retroactively turns this scorer-only test into a manuscript decryption test. The [newcomer control walkthrough](#/wiki/first-experiment?section=search-controls) explains how to read them together.\n\n## Reproduce and inspect\n\nDownload the experiment bundle and extract it with its directory structure. No network access, API key or third-party Python package is required.\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/english-scorer-controls/run.py --check\npython scripts/check_english_scorer_controls.py experiments/records/english-scorer-controls/results.json --receipt my-scorer-audit.json\npython experiments/records/english-scorer-controls/plot.py\n```\n\nThe producer checks every pinned input hash. The independent checker reconstructs the source excerpts and shuffles, calculates scores by counting four-letter groups rather than importing the producer, and checks every decision within an absolute numerical tolerance of 10⁻¹². Both computations passed; human review remains pending. The saved JSON includes excerpts, hashes, seeds, individual scores and normalization diagnostics, so every plotted mark can be traced back to its input.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/english-scorer-controls/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "bd7e40313e33f9098629450c74044c159dc1ea6a43dde32750e8285b52c97c9d",
  "record_type": {
    "id": "control",
    "label": "Control",
    "description": "Checks a search, decoder or scorer using synthetic inputs or reference text; it does not identify the cipher of an unsolved page."
  }
}

  "visuals": [

      "path": "experiments/records/f-delete-lag13/comparison.svg",
      "caption": "The F-deleted lag-13 count lies inside the shuffled reference range."
    }
  ],
  "reader_note": "An exact lag-13 block repeat remains ordinary under a fixed all-F deletion and page-preserving control.",
  "reader_limit": "Tests one F-deletion interpretation and one exact motif; it does not test the complete proposed stream cipher.",
  "scope_summary": "LP2-00–55 · delete all 458 F runes · lag 13 plus lags 2–28 · 499 shuffles.",
  "article": "## Finding\n\nDeleting every F rune does **not** reveal an unusual lag-13 two-rune repeat under this fixed test. The archived LP2-00–55 stream has **17** exact matching two-rune blocks at lag 13. After deleting all **458 F runes** within their pages and joining the retained neighbors, the count is **18**. In **499** page-preserving shuffle trials, the middle 95% of counts is **8–22**, and **104** trials reach at least 18.\n\n![Lag-13 exact two-rune matches before and after removing F, with the shuffled reference.](experiments/records/f-delete-lag13/comparison.svg)\n\nThe displayed counts have different numbers of opportunities: **12,186** before F deletion and **11,728** afterward. The fixed lag-13 result is therefore best read beside its own shuffled reference, not as a one-count improvement by itself.\n\n## Full lag search\n\nThe program also repeats the same exact-block test at every lag from **2 through 28**. It divides each observed count by that lag's mean under shuffled pages, then compares the largest ratio with the largest ratio from every shuffled trial. The observed best is **lag 5**, with a ratio of **1.707**; **109 of 499** shuffled searches do at least as well. Lag 13 was proposed in the discussion, but the broader scan guards against quietly choosing another attractive lag afterward.\n\n## Rule and limit\n\nThis test interprets an “F skip” as deleting **every** F (GP index 0) from the rune-only stream, independently on each page. It does not say that the source participant used this deletion rule. Their account did not specify whether F is copied, removed, or consumes a key slot. Nor does this test model collision-driven skips, I/M resynchronization or a key stream. It tests only whether this one removal operation exposes exact two-rune repeats at the proposed lag.\n\nRun `python experiments/records/f-delete-lag13/run.py --check` from the repository root. The [saved report](experiments/records/f-delete-lag13/results.json) retains per-lag counts, reference means, input hashes and the seed so the comparison can be reproduced.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/f-delete-lag13/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "69ef2705284f675410927975d7ffb3076686f72a0e04273a5bbd222b8fb82bc6",
  "record_type": {
    "id": "measurement",
    "label": "Manuscript measurement",
    "description": "Measures a stated feature or statistical comparison; it does not test a complete decoding rule."
  }
}

  "id": "feedback-opening-census",
  "status": "published",
  "title": "Feedback ciphers with fixed starting values",
  "question": "Do scalar-primed feedback rules recover a known 12-rune opening at an unsolved LP2 page start?",
  "summary": "Neither feedback rule recovers a known opening across 1,856 fixed configurations on 55 pages. Different openings and other starting sequences remain untested.",
  "reader_question": "Could an earlier ciphertext or plaintext rune supply the key for a familiar opening?",
  "reader_note": "This batch checks specific rules against specific opening words. It does not tell us whether the unsolved text begins with different words or uses another feedback rule.",
  "reader_limit": "Unknown openings, arbitrary primer vectors, another alphabet, extra key layers and matches later in a page are outside this batch.",
  "scope": {
    "pages": [],
    "artifacts": [
      "experiments/suites/feedback-opening-census/manifest.json"
    ],
    "representation": "Canonical GP indices from 12,956 runes on the 55 nonempty pages of LP2-00–55. Hyphen/period delimit words; slash/newline do not.",
    "procedure": "Subtract feedback modulo 29; before the chosen lag use a repeated scalar primer, then an earlier ciphertext or plaintext value. Test continuous-page and per-word initialization. Compare each output's first twelve runes with nine fixed known-reading openings.",
    "parameters": "2 feedback sources × 16 lags × 29 scalar primers × 2 boundary rules = 1,856 configurations; 55 pages and nine opening cribs = 918,720 exact comparisons.",
    "exclusions": "Unknown openings, later crib positions, arbitrary primer vectors, added key layers, symbol skipping, other arithmetic signs and other alphabets."
  },
  "outcome": "not-supported",
  "finding": "No tested configuration recovers any of the nine exact 12-rune openings. The longest matching prefix is three runes. All 1,856 synthetic recovery controls and the independent full-census checker pass.",
  "limitations": "This is an exact-crib census rather than a language or cipher-identification test. A correct plaintext with another opening would fail this acceptance rule. The proposed feedback rules are solver hypotheses, not established instructions from the manuscript.",
  "next_steps": "Test a source-specified starting sequence or added key layer against an independently chosen continuation. Keep every tried rule and opening in the comparison.",

  "batch": {
    "suite_id": "feedback-opening-census",
    "manifest_path": "experiments/suites/feedback-opening-census/manifest.json",
    "cases_path": "experiments/suites/feedback-opening-census/cases.json",
    "case_count": 1856,
    "scope_note": "Each configuration covers 55 nonempty LP2 pages and nine fixed 12-rune openings. A configuration is a parameter case, not an independently reported historical idea."
  },
  "article": "# Feedback ciphers with fixed starting values\n\n**None of these rules recovered any of nine known 12-rune openings at the beginning of an unsolved LP2 page.** We checked 1,856 configurations, each applied to 55 pages, for 918,720 exact comparisons. These are variations of two feedback rules, not 1,856 separate historical proposals.\n\nThe question is narrow: could these feedback rules reproduce an opening already seen in a documented reading? A different plaintext opening could still be correct. A failed crib match therefore closes this particular comparison, not the feedback-cipher family.\n\n## The rules\n\nEach decoded rune is its ciphertext index minus a feedback value, modulo 29. Before enough runes have been read, that value is the selected scalar primer. After the chosen lag, the feedback value comes from either an earlier ciphertext rune or an earlier decoded rune.\n\n| Choice | Tested values |\n| --- | --- |\n| Feedback source | Earlier ciphertext or earlier plaintext |\n| Lag | 1 through 16 runes |\n| Primer | Each index 0 through 28, repeated during initialization |\n| Word boundaries | Continue through the page, or restart after every hyphen and period |\n| Target | Each nonempty page on LP2-00–55, starting fresh at every page |\n| Acceptance | Exact equality with one of nine fixed 12-rune known-reading openings |\n\nSlashes and line breaks are layout marks in this parser. All 12,956 archived runes are retained; number-only LP2-50 supplies no rune stream. The nine openings are pinned to their original reproduction CSVs in the [manifest](experiments/suites/feedback-opening-census/manifest.json).\n\nThe longest matching prefix is **three runes**, attained by four configurations. No English-language score or statistical significance is assigned to those fragments. The [complete result file](experiments/suites/feedback-opening-census/cases.json) lists every tested rule and a digest of its full decoded output.\n\n## How the batch is checked\n\nThe producer encrypts a synthetic plaintext and recovers it under every configuration. A separate checker reads the structured page records, implements the recurrence independently and recomputes all case digests, opening comparisons and prefix ties. It also compares the relevant one-step results with the earlier [LP2-54 header experiment](#/experiments/lp2-54-header-feedback).\n\nThis batch does not test arbitrary primer vectors, another alphabet, adding rather than subtracting feedback, skipped symbols, unknown plaintext openings, a key layer, or cribs at later positions. Those choices belong in another explicit manifest or engine version.\n\n## Reproduce\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/feedback-opening-census/run.py --check\npython experiments/suites/feedback-opening-census/check.py\n```\n\nThe scripts use Python's standard library and run without a network connection. The declared rules and pinned input files are included in the experiment ZIP.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/feedback-opening-census/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "1d07b5d85d4c2f359b3f33c294d7f9c569163465714674f1398647ef0ee8ca0e",
  "record_type": {
    "id": "method",
    "label": "Bounded solving test",
    "description": "Applies a fixed decoding, extraction or payload-retrieval rule to declared unsolved material, or excludes a specific direct-generation rule. Its result covers only those bounds."
  }
}

  "article": "# A 59-Fehu coordinate triad in LP2\n\n**Finding.** A reported construction is arithmetically reproducible on Liber Primus part two (LP2). Of 350 eligible starting Fehu runes, one start—**F182**—produces the ordered sums **3001, 2819, 2579** under the source's fixed three-window rule. All 177 coordinate labels in the three supplied streams also agree with the archived rune data. This is a numerical match, not a decryption or a probability that Cicada intended the construction.\n\nThe proposal treats every F/Fehu rune as a position marker. First concatenate LP2-00 through LP2-57 in page order, keeping the 29 manuscript runes and dropping punctuation. Number the resulting Fehus F1, F2, and so on. This produces 13,136 runes and 466 Fehus. The count is **LP2-only**: adding LP1 changes every later Fehu number. F182 occurs at zero-based rune index 4,949 in this stream.\n\nFor each chosen Fehu, subtract an origin Fehu's rune index. Put that distance on a grid 29 columns wide: its remainder after division by 29 is X, and the quotient modulo 29 is Y. Read X or Y as a zero-based Gematria Primus rune index and add the corresponding prime values. For example, F182 has offset zero from itself, so its X value is 0, the F rune worth 2. F183 is 60 runes later: `60 mod 29 = 2`, the TH rune worth 5. The source writes V for the rune indexed 1; this archive labels it U. The indices and prime values are the same.\n\n| Window | Coordinate and origin | Recomputed GP sum | Reported target |\n| --- | --- | ---: | ---: |\n| F182–F240 | X, origin F182 | 3001 | 3001 |\n| F211–F269 | Y, origin F182 | 2819 | 2819 |\n| F240–F298 | X, origin F240 | 2579 | 2579 |\n\nThe starts are 29 Fehus apart. The middle window crosses the shared F240 seam; the last window resets its origin there. These details matter. Using F240 as the middle origin or keeping F182 as the last origin asks a different question. The archived [plan](experiments/records/fehu-coordinate-triad/plan.json) fixes all three choices before the replay. The [results](experiments/records/fehu-coordinate-triad/results.json) retain the three sums at every eligible start, not just the match.\n\n![Three stacked line plots show the coordinate-prime sums across all 350 eligible starts. Dashed horizontal lines mark the three reported targets and a vertical line marks F182.](experiments/records/fehu-coordinate-triad/coordinate-scan.svg)\n\nOnly F182 yields all three exact targets in order among the 350 complete start positions **under this one rule**. That does not make the chance of the reported finding 1 in 350. The source describes an exploratory sequence: a 59-Fehu window, a 29-column grid, X and Y choices, target message segments with F included or removed, and an origin reset were selected or refined while looking at the data. The number of tried alternatives is unknown. Many such choices can create a unique exact hit, especially when large prime sums are used as targets. We have not run a selection-aware maximum over that wider search family or checked a predicted key or plaintext on untouched LP2 material.\n\nThe three target numbers are presented in the supplied discussion as adjusted sums from a 2016 message. This record reproduces the **LP2-side coordinate arithmetic** and checks the source's supplied coordinate streams; it does not independently establish that those message adjustments were specified in advance. The reported 2017 value 2131 has no placement in this triad. Nor does a match explain how coordinate values would decode neighboring runes.\n\n## Reproduce the bounded check\n\nPython 3.12 and its standard library suffice, offline:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/fehu-coordinate-triad/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/fehu-coordinate-triad/check.py\npython experiments/records/fehu-coordinate-triad/plot.py --check\n```\n\nThe producer verifies the three full label streams from the supplied discussion and enumerates all 350 starts. The separate checker recounts Fehus from each stored page line, recalculates every start with a different loop, and checks the one exact ordered match. The plan and report identify the local source extract by SHA-256; the private discussion transcript is not a retrievable public citation. See the [F-interrupter guide](#/wiki/interruptions), [prime-sum guide](#/wiki/prime-sums), and [search-space guide](#/wiki/search-space) before treating a numerically precise fit as a cipher rule.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/fehu-coordinate-triad/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "677b493716d06c999fc43a438e2934b7e17542380a9adf40d109be0c47b93e19",

  "visuals": [
    {

  "reader_note": "Four alternating streams show ordinary rune concentration under a page-preserving shuffle. This does not test every four-way cipher.",
  "reader_limit": "A fixed positional split and a monogram statistic are narrower than the cited 185-operation sweep.",
  "scope_summary": "LP2-00–55 except LP2-50 · 12956 runes · four phases · two IoC measures · 1999 page shuffles.",
  "article": "## Finding\n\n**Splitting the unsolved rune stream into four alternating streams does not expose the concentration expected from four simple substitution alphabets.** The four measured collision rates lie within the middle 95% of page-preserving shuffled comparisons. A planted four-stream example is detected by the same measure. This says nothing decisive about four separate running keys, feedback ciphers or a different way to assign runes to streams.\n\n![Successive rune positions assigned to four phases, followed by each phase's observed collision rate and the shuffled reference interval.](experiments/records/four-phase-ioc/phase-comparison.svg)\n\nTake every fourth rune, starting with positions zero, one, two and three. For each resulting stream, the index of coincidence (IoC) is the chance that two different positions contain the same rune. A fixed substitution or a fixed additive shift changes rune labels but preserves that concentration. An independent keyed stream that continually changes its substitution need not preserve it. [How IoC works](#/wiki/index-of-coincidence).\n\n| Check | Manuscript | Page-shuffle comparison |\n| --- | ---: | ---: |\n| Mean IoC across four phases | 0.034511 | 0.034416–0.034551 middle 95%; 361 of 1,999 shuffles at least as high |\n| Highest phase IoC | 0.034564 | 0.034460–0.034697 middle 95%; 945 of 1,999 shuffles at least as high |\n\nThe two upper-tail estimates are **0.181** and **0.473**. Neither is unusual; correcting for checking both measures gives a smallest adjusted estimate of **0.362**. Each comparison shuffles rune order *within each page*, keeping its length and rune counts. It then repeats the four-way split from the start of the concatenated book. Thus the test asks whether the original order adds a four-phase concentration signal beyond the fixed page histograms.\n\n## What was actually tested\n\nThe source is the [published “literal imperatives” sweep](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round22/C-literal-imperatives/RESULTS.md), which includes decimation and four-way interleaving among 185 operations. **This is an independent, narrower test, not a replay of its decoder verdict.** Its public checkout omits the generated nine-register language model and at least one corpus needed to rebuild it, so a fresh clone cannot currently rerun that entire scorer. The present record uses only the archived runes and a fully specified statistical comparison.\n\nThe source's phrase “LP2 pages 0–54” hides a numbering detail. Its loader drops an all-number page before numbering rune-bearing segments. Its 12,956-rune stream matches the actual images **LP2-00 through LP2-55, excluding number-only LP2-50**. We use those actual page labels: 55 rune-bearing pages, with the phase count continuing across page breaks. [Manuscript reader](#/reader).\n\nAs a power check, we Atbash-decoded the 184-rune [LP1 warning page](#/reader/lp1-01), made four copies shifted by 0, 3, 7 and 11 rune places, and interleaved them. Their mean phase IoC was **0.0640**. None of 1,999 whole-stream shuffles reached it. This confirms that the measure can see a strong four-stream substitution signal; it is not a control for every plausible cipher.\n\n## Repeat the check\n\nDownload [this experiment](downloads/experiments/four-phase-ioc.zip) for the script, fixed plan, input text, results and figure. From the repository root run:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/four-phase-ioc/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/four-phase-ioc/check.py\n```\n\nThe [plan](experiments/records/four-phase-ioc/plan.json) fixes the page mapping, two measures, shuffling rule and 1,999 trials. The [results](experiments/records/four-phase-ioc/results.json) retain the observed scores and tail counts. An [independent arithmetic check](experiments/records/four-phase-ioc/check.json) repeats the mean-IoC comparison with another random seed. The result is conditional on this particular four-phase concentration model; it does not close the broader hint or the source's other operations.\n",

  "sources": [
    {
      "label": "Original 256-cell word-search proposal",
      "url": "https://github.com/o3rynn/cicada-faw"

  "article": "# Does the 256-cell grid layout change the missing primes?\n\nYes. In the manuscript’s **32 × 8** arrangement, the four-cell search misses 1033, 2213 and 3301. Reshape the *same ordered cells* into **16 × 16**, and all three appear twice. Restrict those 16 × 16 paths to their own **8 × 8 quadrant**, and the three still appear. The original missing set therefore depends on the grid layout.\n\n![Observed number of missing values for each layout, with central ranges from shuffled digits.](experiments/records/grid-alternative-layouts/layouts.svg)\n\n## Fixed search rule\n\nTake the first digit of each of the 256 two-character tokens on LP2-49–51. Read four adjacent cells in any of eight straight directions, without wrapping or turns. Reject a path containing 4; allow leading zeroes; retain the resulting decimal number only if it is prime. There are **49** possible four-digit spellings from 0–3 that pass this test. The [original-layout recount](#/experiments/grid-prime-paths) defines the baseline.\n\nThe 16 × 16 test changes only where row breaks fall. Its quadrant version also forbids paths crossing an 8 × 8 block boundary. No cells are reordered within the underlying 256-token sequence.\n\n| Layout | Directed paths | Prime occurrences | Distinct primes | Missing values |\n| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |\n| Original 32 × 8 | 1,364 | 191 | 46 | 1033, 2213, 3301 |\n| Reshaped 16 × 16 | 1,508 | 206 | 49 | None |\n| Four fixed 8 × 8 blocks | 1,040 | 148 | 45 | 2003, 2111, 3023, 3203 |\n\nThe three named values each have **two** directed hits in the 16 × 16 layout. In the quadrant search, 1033 and 3301 have two each and 2213 has one. Opposite reading directions can share cells, so these are occurrences, not necessarily independent locations.\n\n## Control and limit\n\nWe shuffled the 256 first digits **3,000** times, preserving their overall frequencies, and repeated each fixed layout. Missing-value counts in the observed grids fall within the central 95% ranges of these shuffles: 0–4 for 32 × 8, 0–3 for 16 × 16, and 0–7 for the quadrant layout. The figure shows those ranges, not a probability that the manuscript was made by shuffling.\n\nThese layouts and the names 1033, 2213 and 3301 were considered after the original pattern was noticed. The controls cannot turn their post-hoc selection into a prospective test. This experiment does **not** examine suffix letters, the five-dot artwork, alternate paths, or an LP2 decoding rule. It shows that an absence claimed for one geometry is not stable under two simple, explicitly stated alternatives.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nFrom the repository root, with Python 3.12 and no extra packages:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/grid-alternative-layouts/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/grid-alternative-layouts/check.py\n```\n\nThe first command rebuilds the table, controls and figure. The independent checker enumerates endpoint pairs to verify the observed counts. [Results and shuffle histogram](experiments/records/grid-alternative-layouts/results.json) give the exact values. The [source account](https://github.com/o3rynn/cicada-faw) motivated checking these layouts; the statistics and controls here are our scoped reproduction.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/grid-alternative-layouts/article.md",

  "article": "# LP2-49–51: does the fixed bit grid decode as a barcode?\n\n**No valid QR Code or Data Matrix payload was found in the declared bit rendering.** The decoder returned zero valid payloads from 64 fixed-grid scans. It did decode both generated positive controls, so the null result is not simply a nonworking decoder. This result applies to the rendering and transformations below; it does not settle every way to rearrange the grid.\n\nThe [LP2-49–51 grid](#/wiki/alphanumeric-grids) contains 256 two-character entries. A [reported exploration](#/wiki/reported-attempts) converted them to binary and looked for QR-like or Data Matrix-like images. Its referenced result pictures and complete final plotting parameters were not preserved in the supplied text. We therefore test a **new, fully specified version** of that idea, rather than claiming an exact replay of every historical image.\n\n## What went into the decoder\n\nThe pinned [grid-bit audit](exports/grid-binary-audit.json) reads each entry under the stated base-60 alphabet as one byte, then writes that byte as exactly eight bits, most significant first. Eight entries make a 64-bit manuscript row. We tested the complete 32-row grid and the original page groups separately: 10 rows from [LP2-49](#/reader/lp2-49), 13 from [LP2-50](#/reader/lp2-50), and 9 from [LP2-51](#/reader/lp2-51). The conditional base-60 and byte assumptions are explained in the grid guide; they are not an established cipher solution.\n\n![Four fixed-width bit canvases, each with zero valid barcode decodes after 16 declared transformations.](experiments/records/grid-barcode-fixed-render/bit-canvases.svg)\n\nFor each canvas we tried four right-angle rotations, each with and without a horizontal reflection, in both color polarities: **16 scans per canvas, 64 total**. Every bit was an 8×8-pixel square with a four-module white border. We allowed no crop, row reflow, page permutation, added finder pattern, or missing bit. The scan used `zxing-cpp` 3.1.1 and accepted only a valid, nonempty QR Code or Data Matrix decode.\n\nTwo synthetic barcodes—one QR Code and one Data Matrix—decoded to their exact known strings with the same software and scan settings. Eight fixed-seed bit shuffles per canvas retained each canvas's dimensions and number of black bits; their 512 scans also yielded no valid payload. Those shuffles illustrate the background behavior of this detector, **not** the probability that the manuscript encodes a barcode. The [JSON report](experiments/records/grid-barcode-fixed-render/results.json) lists all 64 original transformations, image hashes, control settings, and outcomes.\n\n## Reproduce and interpret\n\nFrom the repository root, install the pinned Python dependency, then run:\n\n```text\npython -m pip install zxing-cpp==3.1.1 numpy\npython experiments/records/grid-barcode-fixed-render/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/grid-barcode-fixed-render/check.py\npython experiments/records/grid-barcode-fixed-render/plot.py --check\n```\n\nThe main script pins the input and plan hashes and rescans every case. The checker independently converts the [grid CSV](exports/alphanumeric-grids.csv) back to 2,048 bits, verifies manuscript row boundaries, and checks the saved census and controls. The figure script rebuilds the four pictured canvases from the same pinned bits.\n\nThis is a **negative result for four fixed canvases under 16 planar transformations each**. It does not test other disputed glyph readings, bit order, alternate widths, subwindows, padding, decoder settings, or other barcode types. Any broader image search should declare those choices and count every image examined before treating one apparent pattern as evidence.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/grid-barcode-fixed-render/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "148862031632ade9f19f1055373abbd9e67956f4ddbb38174fc1f2e444106099",

  "article": "# LP2-49–51: do the grid entries directly form a text or file?\n\n**None of the 16,384 byte streams in this bounded test passed a whole-stream ASCII or UTF-8 screen or began with one of the four specified file headers.** This rules out a straightforward reading of the grid under these particular byte and traversal rules. It does not rule out a different encoding, a later transformation, or a file header elsewhere in a stream.\n\nThe [LP2-49–51 grid](#/wiki/alphanumeric-grids) has 256 two-character entries. If each is read as one byte using the declared base-60 digit order `0–9, A–Z, a–x`, the most immediate question is whether those bytes already say something. This test checks that question without choosing a route after seeing the output. Base 60 is **conditional** on the one-byte and digit-order assumptions; neither is established as the intended interpretation.\n\n## What was tested\n\nThe 10 rows on [LP2-49](#/reader/lp2-49), 13 on [LP2-50](#/reader/lp2-50), and 9 on [LP2-51](#/reader/lp2-51) are joined in that order into a 32 × 8 rectangle. Each pair becomes `60 × first digit + second digit`, with no wrapping or omitted entry. The [ten bare-stem audit](#/experiments/grid-stem-uncertainty) supplies the only transcription alternatives: `I` or `l` in ten fixed cells. All 1,024 settings are tested; the other 246 entries, including the separate `2S` cell, stay as in the wiki transcription.\n\nFor both row-wise and column-wise reading, the script varies the outer direction, initial inner direction, and whether the inner direction alternates after each row or column. Those three binary switches make eight routes per axis, or **16 complete routes**. Each visits every cell exactly once. The complete scope is therefore `16 × 1,024 = 16,384` streams of 256 bytes each.\n\n![Six direct-format screens across sixteen complete grid routes; all cells show zero matches among 1,024 stem settings per route.](experiments/records/grid-direct-bytes/route-screen.svg)\n\nThe labels in the chart encode the three switches: outer reverse, initial inner reverse, and alternation, with `0` for forward/constant and `1` for reverse/alternate. A cell counts how many of the 1,024 stem settings pass that screen. Its zeroes concern only the screen named at the column top.\n\n| Screen | Exact acceptance rule | Passing streams |\n| --- | --- | ---: |\n| ASCII text | Every byte is printable ASCII or tab, LF, or CR | 0 |\n| UTF-8 text | Strict UTF-8 decoding accepts all 256 bytes | 0 |\n| PNG | First eight bytes equal the [PNG signature](https://www.w3.org/TR/png-3/#5PNG-file-signature) | 0 |\n| gzip | First three bytes are `1f 8b 08`, including compression method 8 ([RFC 1952](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1952.html)) | 0 |\n| ZIP | First four bytes are the local-file signature `50 4b 03 04` ([PKWARE APPNOTE](https://pkware.cachefly.net/webdocs/casestudies/APPNOTE.TXT)) | 0 |\n| zlib | First two bytes satisfy CM=8, CINFO≤7 and the modulo-31 header check ([RFC 1950](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1950.html)) | 0 |\n\nA header match would have been a **candidate for further validation**, not proof of a working file. UTF-8 validity would not by itself establish meaningful language. No stream reached either threshold here. The two text screens require the *entire* stream to pass; they do not inspect short readable fragments.\n\n## Reproduce it\n\nDownload this experiment's ZIP from the record, or run these commands from the repository root:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/grid-direct-bytes/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/grid-direct-bytes/check.py\n```\n\nThe first script pins the SHA-256 hashes of the grid export and ten-stem register, then recomputes every case and the [JSON report](experiments/records/grid-direct-bytes/results.json). That report retains each route, ten-bit mask, stream hash, first eight bytes and six outcomes. The independent checker rebuilds the entries from the page records, replays every route and mask, and tests positive synthetic controls for all six screens. Both use only Python's standard library and make no network or AI calls.\n\nThis result says nothing about a 16 × 16 reflow, a different digit assignment, other glyph uncertainties, a header at a nonzero offset, XOR, compression without one of these headers, or bytes embedded in a larger construction. Those are distinct tests with their own search spaces. The useful stopping point here is narrower: **a direct 256-byte text or one of these four offset-zero file starts does not emerge from these 16 routes and ten stem choices**.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/grid-direct-bytes/article.md",

  "article": "# The grid's 4-prefix cells\n\n**Finding:** Seventeen of the 256 pairs on LP2-49–51 begin with `4`. Their suffixes are restricted, but that restriction follows from a byte-sized base-60 reading: `4 × 60 + digit` cannot exceed 255, so the suffix digit must be 0–15 (`0–9`, `A–F`). This does not make the cells a separate cipher channel. Their positions are less evenly spread than a simple random-placement control, which is an observation worth preserving without assigning it a decoding role.\n\n![Map of the seventeen 4-prefix cells across four consecutive eight-row blocks.](experiments/records/grid-high-digit-cells/cells.svg)\n\nThe suffixes, in manuscript order, are `97DEF756B98A80EB9`: **11 distinct symbols**, not five as stated in the source account. The five *missing* hexadecimal symbols are `1`, `2`, `3`, `4` and `C`. These counts use the archived [grid transcription](#/wiki/alphanumeric-grids); its five known disagreements with another quoted transcription do not affect these `4`-prefix cells.\n\n| Fixed measurement | Result |\n| --- | ---: |\n| `4`-prefix cells | 17 of 256 |\n| Cells in four consecutive 8×8 blocks | 4, 2, 9, 2 |\n| Horizontally or vertically touching pairs | 7 |\n\nFor a limited placement check, the script chose 17 of 256 positions uniformly in 20,000 seeded trials. **43 trials** had at least seven touching pairs; **804** had a block containing at least nine marked cells. A second control preserved the observed count in *each row* and randomized only columns: **464 of 20,000** trials had at least seven touching pairs. These are descriptive reference frequencies, not a probability that Cicada engineered a second layer. The positional statistics were selected after seeing the table, and a uniform-position model ignores other structure in its construction.\n\nNothing here specifies what to read from the 17 cells, in what order, or how to test that output on another page. A separate-channel proposal would need those rules before examining its result. The [base-59/base-60 record](#/experiments/grid-radix-reconciliation) checks the broader digit-alphabet question.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nFrom the repository root, run `python experiments/records/grid-high-digit-cells/run.py --check` and `python experiments/records/grid-high-digit-cells/check.py`. Both use only Python's standard library; the second independently recounts the deterministic cell and adjacency measures from the coordinate-bearing export. The [plan](experiments/records/grid-high-digit-cells/plan.json) fixes the two placement controls and seed; [results](experiments/records/grid-high-digit-cells/results.json) include their full histograms. The [pinned source account](https://github.com/o3rynn/cicada-faw/tree/72f92e7ac8acf9b2e660e23d654107652cb00fb0) describes the proposed distinct `d=4` group.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/grid-high-digit-cells/article.md",

  "reader_note": "The first byte can resemble an OpenPGP tag; complete packet framing fails.",
  "reader_limit": "This excludes only one complete untransformed literal-data packet at byte zero.",
  "scope_summary": "LP2-49–51 · 16,384 direct byte readings.",
  "article": "# Does the 256-byte grid form an OpenPGP literal packet?\n\nThe first grid byte in printed row order is `CB`. In OpenPGP, that byte can begin a **literal-data packet**. It is a suggestive one-byte match, but the complete packet has to parse. Across **16,384 fixed grid readings**, none is a complete literal-data packet.\n\n![Of 16,384 byte readings, 4,096 begin with the literal-data tag but fail the complete-packet test; 12,288 do not begin with that tag](experiments/records/grid-openpgp-literal/packet-screen.svg)\n\nThe 4,096 readings with `CB` at the start all leave bytes after the packet length says the packet ends. The other 12,288 do not start with a literal-data tag. This reproduces a narrow structural check motivated by the public repository's OpenPGP test; it does not mean the grid cannot encode some other kind of data.\n\n## What was counted\n\nThe 256 cells printed across LP2-49–51 were converted under the [specified conditional base-60 digit order](#/wiki/alphanumeric-grids). We used the same 16 complete row/column routes and 1,024 readings of ten disputed `I`/`L` stem cells as the direct-byte experiment. This experiment adds a different recognizer: a complete OpenPGP **new-format tag-11 literal-data packet at byte zero**. It checks definite and partial lengths, complete consumption of all 256 bytes, the literal format byte (`b`, `t`, or `u`), the filename-length field, and the timestamp's presence.\n\nThe script tests two constructed positive controls: a normal complete packet and a valid packet whose first 128 body bytes use partial-length encoding. A truncated partial packet is rejected. These controls matter because the baseline grid starts with `CB E7`; `E7` denotes a 128-byte partial segment, which cannot be interpreted correctly by looking at only the first two bytes.\n\n| Outcome | Readings |\n| --- | ---: |\n| Does not start with literal-data tag | 12,288 |\n| Starts with tag, then fails complete packet framing | 4,096 |\n| Complete literal-data packet | **0** |\n\n## Boundary of the finding\n\nThis test reads untransformed bytes at offset zero and requires **one packet occupying the entire 256-byte stream**. It does not test hidden packets at later offsets, added prefixes, different base/character readings, a sequence of multiple OpenPGP packets, encryption, or other data formats. A one-byte OpenPGP resemblance cannot establish a payload; a negative complete-packet result is not a verdict on every possible transform.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nExtract the experiment and reference-data ZIP files into one folder, then run:\n\n```sh\npython experiments/records/grid-openpgp-literal/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/grid-openpgp-literal/check.py\n```\n\nThe first script uses only Python's standard library, verifies the hashed grid and stem input files, reruns all 16,384 reads, and checks the saved [result table](experiments/records/grid-openpgp-literal/results.json). The independent check audits how many bytes the `CB` starts actually consume: they end at offsets 94 or 217, leaving the rest of the 256-byte stream. For the general text and file-header screen on the same readings, see the [direct-byte experiment](#/experiments/grid-direct-bytes).\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/grid-openpgp-literal/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "f17be222237da4536e060eacc42c8e893127ce71bd183e44bf1b04cb06c1ac00",

  }

  "question": "Does the LP2-49–51 256-byte grid contain a contiguous 56- or 57-byte permutation of page indices under its published source bytes or fixed grid readings?",
  "summary": "Neither the source 256-byte stream nor 16,384 fixed grid readings contain a contiguous 0–55 or 0–56 page permutation; the longest eligible run is only five bytes.",

  "sources": [
    {
      "label": "Published E-02A page-permutation test",
      "url": "https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round16/zeroFP/PREREG.md"
    },
    {
      "label": "Pinned source canon_256.bin",
      "url": "https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/pp49_51/canon_256.bin"
    },
    {
      "label": "Grid transcription and base-60 reading",
      "url": "https://jelliottdev.github.io/#/wiki/alphanumeric-grids"
    }
  ],
  "related": [
    "grid-direct-bytes",
    "grid-stem-uncertainty",
    "grid-openpgp-literal"
  ],
  "reader_note": "No contiguous 56/57-page index permutation occurs in 6.57 million direct windows.",
  "reader_limit": "Only literal contiguous page-index bytes under specified readings are excluded.",
  "scope_summary": "LP2-49–51 · 16,384 direct streams · 6,569,984 windows.",
  "article": "# Is the LP2 byte grid a page-order table?\n\nOne published proposal asks whether a consecutive part of the 256-byte LP2-49–51 grid is a permutation of page indices **0–55** or **0–56**. That is a precise test: every byte in such a window must be in range, and each page index must appear once. We found **no matching window** in the source's saved byte stream or in 16,384 fixed grid readings that account for ten disputed `I`/`L` stems.\n\n![The longest run of eligible page-index bytes is five, far shorter than the 56 or 57 needed](experiments/records/grid-page-order-permutations/page-order.svg)\n\nThe simpler reason for the null result is useful: the longest uninterrupted run containing only values 0–55 is **three bytes** across the tested readings; allowing value 56 raises the maximum to only **five bytes**. A 56- or 57-byte permutation cannot occur without a run at least that long. The source's own pinned 256-byte file has a maximum run of three under either range.\n\n## Fixed search\n\nThe original E-02A proposal scans every 56-byte window of its saved 256-byte `canon_256.bin`; it also reports a 57-byte 0–56 variant. We replayed both on that exact file, then used the current page transcription's conditional base-60 conversion and the same 16 row/column routes and 1,024 `I`/`L` stem readings as the [direct-byte study](#/experiments/grid-direct-bytes). The source file and current printed-order conversion differ at **three byte positions**; they are not silently treated as identical.\n\n| Input | 56-byte windows | 57-byte windows | Longest eligible run | Matches |\n| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |\n| Published source byte file | 201 | 200 | 3 | 0 |\n| 16,384 grid readings | 3,293,184 | 3,276,800 | 5 (for 0–56) | 0 |\n\nThe scanner first checks the necessary value range in every window, then checks for a one-of-each permutation. Synthetic streams with deliberately planted 0–55 and 0–56 windows are detected at their planted offset. An independent check reconstructs the readings and verifies the longest eligible runs without using the window scanner.\n\n## What the result means\n\nThis excludes a **literal contiguous page-index table** in the declared byte readings. It does not test arithmetic transforms, encryption, noncontiguous selections, a different page count or a different transcription. The quoted page-order interpretation is a hypothesis about how the grid might guide reading; no page route or decoded text was claimed by this result.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nExtract this experiment and the reference-data bundle together, then run:\n\n```sh\npython experiments/records/grid-page-order-permutations/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/grid-page-order-permutations/check.py\n```\n\nBoth use Python's standard library. The [complete results](experiments/records/grid-page-order-permutations/results.json) give route-level maximum runs and counts.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/grid-page-order-permutations/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "41c03727b2e19e59895add3551db04b5a7a35ab17608d1dc6a484ab5b4ea6048",

  "article": "## Finding\n\nThe number grid on pages 49–51 can be read as a 256-byte payload. Six byte positions have two documented readings. We tried **every combination of those readings** as the seed of a rune-by-rune key. Across the source's **3,840 decoder calls**, no candidate reached its predeclared English-score threshold. The best score was **−6.872**; the required score was **−5.5**. Higher is better.\n\n![The best payload-derived candidate, source shuffled-text reference, planted control and required threshold.](experiments/records/grid-payload-prf-contested-masks/result-score.svg)\n\nThis screen was able to find a key when one was planted. We extended the source's recovery control to all **15 generators with both byte-to-rune reductions**: all **30** met its four recovery gates. That supports the negative finding for this bounded test, not a claim about every possible use of the grid.\n\n## What the search covers\n\nEach of the six uncertain bytes took one of its two recorded values: **2⁶ = 64 payloads**. The [pinned B-05 source](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round13/B05/sweep.py) expanded each payload with 15 pseudorandom generators, two ways to turn bytes into rune values, and both addition signs. It used a skip-aware decoder on the **first 400 runes** of the unsolved text (LP2-00 and the beginning of LP2-01). The key ran forward from offset zero, without Atbash.\n\nThe 3,840 calls contain **2,596 distinct key/sign cases**. AES-128-CTR uses only the first 16 payload bytes, so none of the six contested positions can change its key. Four AES-256/ChaCha variants use only byte 25 among those six. The remaining ten generators respond to all 64 readings.\n\n![How many distinct keys each generator group produces from the 64 candidate payloads.](experiments/records/grid-payload-prf-contested-masks/key-sensitivity.svg)\n\nThe source's 200 shuffled-text scores provide a reference, but their maximum is **not** a chance threshold adjusted for choosing the best of 3,840 calls. The fixed −5.5 English-score requirement is the decisive boundary here. This record covers B-05's **Part 2a**, not its larger main grid, single-byte-all-values sweep, other offsets, full-page reruns, or non-English readings.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nThe [complete score list](experiments/records/grid-payload-prf-contested-masks/cases.json), [summary](experiments/records/grid-payload-prf-contested-masks/results.json), and [key-equivalence count](experiments/records/grid-payload-prf-contested-masks/key-equivalence.json) are saved. From the repository root, use Python 3 with `cryptography`:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/grid-payload-prf-contested-masks/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/grid-payload-prf-contested-masks/control-all.py --check\npython experiments/records/grid-payload-prf-contested-masks/key-equivalence.py --check\npython experiments/records/grid-payload-prf-contested-masks/check.py\n```\n\nThe first command replays all 3,840 source-defined calls and takes several minutes. The other commands check the 30 planted controls, the effective-key duplicates, complete case coverage, and the 32 scores that overlap the earlier raw-payload test. Source code and bytes are bundled from the pinned MIT-licensed repository.\n",

  "article": "## Finding\n\nWe tested whether the 256-byte number-grid payload could supply a **rune-by-rune key** for Liber Primus. In this fixed 32-case screen, **none passed** the source's English-score threshold. The best candidate scored **−7.105**, below both the required **−5.5** and the highest of 200 shuffled-text controls (**−7.001**). A higher score is better.\n\n![Scores for planted controls, the best manuscript candidate, the shuffled-text ceiling and the required threshold.](experiments/records/grid-payload-prf-seed-corner/score-comparison.svg)\n\nThe decoder was capable of recognizing a supplied key. Four planted controls, one per generator, recovered **98.9%** of characters and scored **−4.17**. This makes the negative result meaningful for the fixed cases below; it does not prove the payload has no role elsewhere.\n\n## What was tested\n\nThe [pinned B-05 source](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round13/B05/PREREG.md) supplies two 256-byte readings of the number grid. Each was used directly as a seed for SHA-256 counter mode, RC4, HMAC-DRBG-SHA256 or AES-256-CTR. For each generator we tried both byte-to-rune reductions and both addition signs: **2 × 4 × 2 × 2 = 32** keys. The source's skip-aware beam decoded the first 400 unsolved runes with a forward key starting at offset zero.\n\nThis is a deliberately small corner of B-05, whose published search also included transformed payloads, more generators, reverse keys, Atbash, offsets, and contested-byte variations. We did not revalidate that whole published sweep here. Nor does an English-scoring failure exclude non-English plaintext or a different way to use the grid.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nThe [saved result](experiments/records/grid-payload-prf-seed-corner/results.json) lists all 32 scores. From the repository root, install Python 3 and `cryptography`, then run:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/grid-payload-prf-seed-corner/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/grid-payload-prf-seed-corner/check.py\n```\n\nThe first command reruns the four planted controls, 200 shuffles and 32 candidates using bundled pinned source in a temporary folder. The second checks the case grid, threshold, payload hashes and independent PRF spot checks. The [source manifest](experiments/records/grid-payload-prf-seed-corner/source-manifest.json) pins each upstream file by Git blob and SHA-256; the source is bundled under its MIT license.\n",

  "article": "# Are three missing grid primes unusual under fixed shuffles?\n\nThe [directional prime-path reconstruction](#/experiments/grid-prime-paths) finds 191 prime-path occurrences and 46 of 49 possible decimal-prime values in the first characters of LP2-49–51's grid. Three values are absent. This experiment asks a narrower statistical question: **if the same first digits were rearranged without changing their counts, how often would at least three values be absent under the identical path rule?**\n\n![Histogram of missing prime values in two sets of 5,000 shuffled grids; the actual grid has three missing values.](experiments/records/grid-prime-path-null/missing-primes.svg)\n\nThe shaded column marks the observed count of three. It is not a fitted threshold or a third control.\n\n## Fixed rule and controls\n\nThe [plan](experiments/records/grid-prime-path-null/plan.json) was saved with the two controls, four statistics, replicate count and seed before running them. Stack 32 rows of eight first digits in page order. Enumerate all 1,364 four-cell straight directed paths in eight directions, allowing page crossings. Reject paths containing a `4`. Read the four remaining digits as a decimal integer, including leading-zero strings, and test primality. There are 49 possible prime values from four positions over digits 0–3.\n\nEach control repeats this entire fixed calculation 5,000 times:\n\n1. **Global shuffle:** permute all 256 first digits; preserve their overall counts.\n2. **Within-row shuffle:** shuffle the eight first digits independently in every manuscript row; preserve each row's composition and its page location.\n\nBoth destroy some spatial arrangement while retaining different amounts of local structure. Neither is a model of how the manuscript was actually made.\n\n## Results\n\n| Statistic | Observed grid | Global shuffle mean | Within-row mean |\n| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |\n| Eligible paths | 1,058 | 1,034.54 | 1,043.22 |\n| Prime-path occurrences | 191 | 189.62 | 191.42 |\n| Distinct prime values present | 46 | 47.75 | 47.75 |\n| Prime values absent | 3 | 1.25 | 1.25 |\n\nAt least three values were absent in **761 of 5,000** global shuffles and **763 of 5,000** within-row shuffles. The inclusive plus-one empirical upper-tail estimates are **15.24%** and **15.28%**. Three missing values are therefore not rare under either declared control. The complete [result file](experiments/records/grid-prime-path-null/results.json) retains the histogram and both empirical tails for every predeclared statistic, not just the favorable comparison.\n\nThis does **not** assign a chance probability to the particular names `1033`, `2213` and `3301`: those values were noticed before this test was designed. It does not account for trying other layouts, directions, path lengths, bases or visually selected patterns. It also does not test any decryption. The result weakens an argument from the *number* of missing values under these two nulls; it cannot rule out a construction based on a more specific independently predicted feature.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nDownload the [experiment bundle](downloads/experiments/grid-prime-path-null.zip), extract it with its directory structure, then run Python 3.12 or later:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/grid-prime-path-null/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/grid-prime-path-null/check.py\npython experiments/records/grid-prime-path-null/plot.py --check\n```\n\nThe first script reruns all 10,000 control grids from seed `33012026` and checks the saved JSON byte for byte. The second independently enumerates endpoint pairs with a sieve for the observed grid and 24 fixed shuffled examples; it also checks the histogram arithmetic. The chart script checks the SVG against the saved histograms. The bundled [grid export](exports/alphanumeric-grids.json) supplies the 256 first digits, and the report pins its hash. Since the five documented archive-versus-wiki transcription differences affect only **second** characters, the numeric path statistic is unchanged by those five differences. Other unreviewed first-digit errors would require a new sensitivity test.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/grid-prime-path-null/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "8fa798df618ea50bec5a60f3722ae5af7962900d967cf07d7fffd3afb9221ac9",

  "article": "# Directional prime paths: a reproduced count claim\n\nThis record checks a specific observation about the alphanumeric grids on LP2-49–51. It reproduces **191 occurrences of 46 distinct decimal primes**, with **1033, 2213 and 3301 absent** from a 49-value candidate set. “Supported” refers only to that scoped recount. It does not establish deliberate construction, statistical significance or a hidden message.\n\nThe [grid guide](#/wiki/alphanumeric-grids) shows the source pages and token conventions. The [prime-path guide](#/wiki/grid-prime-paths) explains the path rule and comparison with the published occurrence CSV. The files below preserve every hit and two independent implementations.\n\n## Fixed search rules\n\nStack the 32 original rows in page order 49, 50, 51, retaining eight columns. Read four consecutive cells in each of eight straight directions. Paths cannot turn or wrap around an edge, but may cross page boundaries. Reverse directions count separately.\n\nTake the first character of each token. Reject any path containing a 4; do not remove the cell and join its neighbors. Interpret the four-position string as a decimal integer, allowing leading zeroes, and retain it if prime. Then record the four suffix characters and, separately, the base-4 interpretation of the digit string.\n\nFor example, LP2-49 grid coordinates (row, column) `(7,2) → (6,3) → (5,4) → (4,5)` contain `0G → 0S → 0d → 2U`. The digit string is `0002`, the decimal value is 2, and the suffix extraction is `GSdU`. Retaining the path does not make those suffixes plaintext.\n\n## Complete result\n\nThere are 1,364 geometrically valid directed paths. Of these, 306 contain a 4 and are rejected, leaving 1,058 eligible paths. The decimal-prime filter retains 191 occurrences, including 60 with leading zeroes and 40 crossing a page boundary. These counts describe overlapping paths, not independent trials.\n\nThere are 256 possible four-position strings over digits 0–3. Their decimal values include 49 primes; 46 occur in the grid. The three missing strings become 79, 167 and 241 respectively when read in base 4. All three conversions are prime, but that is a separate observation: the original filter tests decimal primality. Only 147 of the 191 retained occurrences are prime under both interpretations.\n\nThe JSON contains every retained path, its tokens, original page coordinates, direction vector, digit string, suffix extraction and both numerical interpretations. Its frequency table includes all 49 candidate primes, including zero counts. No appealing suffix string was selected as a successful decryption.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nExtract this experiment’s ZIP with its directory structure intact. Python 3.12 and its standard library are sufficient.\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/grid-prime-paths/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/grid-prime-paths/check.py\n```\n\nThe producer uses the shared, included `grid_prime_paths.py` helper to enumerate starts and direction vectors from the coordinate-bearing export. Without `--check`, it prints a fresh JSON report.\n\nThe independent checker reads the original archived page records, reconstructs their grid tokens, and enumerates pairs of endpoints instead. It uses a sieve to identify primes rather than the producer’s trial division. It checks the complete set of hits, source coordinates, suffixes, base-4 values and frequency table. Agreement checks the implementations against the same archived transcription; it is not an independent visual reading of every glyph.\n\n## Limits and related variants\n\nChanging to a 16×16 layout, prohibiting page crossings, requiring four nonzero-leading decimal digits, searching longer paths, or requiring both bases to be prime changes the test. Keep such experiments in this family with their changed rules and results visible.\n\nA linked [shuffle-control experiment](#/experiments/grid-prime-path-null) now fixes the path rule and compares the *number* of absent prime values with global and within-row first-digit shuffles. Three or more values were absent in about 15% of each control set. This does not assign a confirmatory probability to the particular three names selected after observation. Shuffling entire tokens would preserve different relationships from shuffling only first characters, and this baseline still does not claim that other representations were exhaustively excluded.\n\nRead [search space and bounds](#/wiki/search-space) and [null models and selection](#/wiki/null-models) before turning this reproduced pattern into a claim about intention.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/grid-prime-paths/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "eecd104e27f08f7a110538b77a9f475179a6e2801806ced3ada77d911b851942",

  "article": "# Prime paths with manuscript page boundaries\n\nThis variant asks whether the baseline’s exact three-value missing set survives when every four-cell path must stay on a single manuscript page. It does not: **1103 and 3011 become absent as well**. The original absent values, 1033, 2213 and 3301, remain absent.\n\n“Not supported” applies to preserving the same three-value missing set under this change. It does not reject the baseline recount or rule out a cipher.\n\n## The one changed rule\n\nThe [baseline](#/experiments/grid-prime-paths) stacks all 32 rows from LP2-49–51 and permits paths to cross the two page joins. This variant keeps the same row order, columns and coordinate system but rejects a path unless all four cells belong to one page.\n\nEverything else stays fixed: four consecutive cells, eight straight directions, no wrapping or turns, reject any path containing a first character of 4, permit leading zeroes, test primality in decimal, and retain the suffix extraction and separate base-4 value. No cells are deleted or moved.\n\n## Results compared with the baseline\n\n| Measurement | Joined-page baseline | Within-page variant |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| Geometrically valid directed paths | 1,364 | 1,148 |\n| Eligible after rejecting digit 4 | 1,058 | 876 |\n| Decimal-prime occurrences | 191 | 151 |\n| Distinct decimal primes | 46 | 44 |\n| Candidate prime values | 49 | 49 |\n| Missing values | 1033, 2213, 3301 | 1033, 1103, 2213, 3011, 3301 |\n\nThe removed set contains 216 directed paths, of which 182 have no digit 4 and 40 pass the decimal-prime filter. The remaining 151 hits equal exactly the baseline’s within-page subset, including their complete source coordinates and extracted strings. The variant produces no new hits.\n\n## Why 1103 and 3011 disappear together\n\nThe baseline has one occurrence of 1103:\n\n```text\nLP2-49 row 10, column 8: 1M\n              page boundary\nLP2-50 row  1, column 8: 15\nLP2-50 row  2, column 8: 0Z\nLP2-50 row  3, column 8: 3Q\n\nForward first characters: 1103\nReverse first characters: 3011\n```\n\nReading those same four cells backward produces the sole occurrence of 3011. Forbidding the boundary crossing removes both. These are two directed hits on one undirected path, not independent locations. This illustrates why counting multiple related observations does not automatically multiply the evidence for an interpretation.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nExtract the experiment ZIP with its directory structure intact. No external packages or network access are required.\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/grid-prime-paths-page-boundaries/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/grid-prime-paths-page-boundaries/check.py\n```\n\nThe producer enumerates starts and direction vectors from the archived grid export. The checker instead rebuilds tokens directly from page records, enumerates endpoint pairs and uses a sieve for primality. Both enforce the same page barrier. The output retains every hit and all 49 candidate frequencies, including zeroes.\n\n## What this comparison establishes\n\nThe exact missing set depends on whether page joins are searchable. Neither convention is proved to be the intended one. Since this variant only removes paths, it cannot restore a value already absent from the baseline; continued absence of the original three is therefore not an independent confirmation.\n\nThis is a deterministic scope comparison, not a statistical test. A chance model would need to preserve or deliberately change the relevant page structure and account for the exploratory choice of statistic. Further changes to layout, path length, numeral base or allowed directions belong in separately declared variants of this family.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/grid-prime-paths-page-boundaries/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "6563dbbb499abaa1a5b7cb09de56335424d1a8d92ac853cdd597098bd7369e1d",
  "record_type": {
    "id": "measurement",
    "label": "Manuscript measurement",
    "description": "Measures a stated feature or statistical comparison; it does not test a complete decoding rule."
  }
}

  "article": "# Does the grid use base 59 or base 60?\n\n**Both are valid ways to number the 256 printed pairs, but they require different digit alphabets.** The archived grid transcription uses 59 of the 62 possible case-sensitive letters and digits: `f`, `y` and `z` do not occur. That count does not tell us the radix. A text can use fewer symbols than its alphabet permits.\n\nThe reported base-59 script explicitly deletes lowercase `f` from the candidate `0–9 A–Z a–x` alphabet and moves every later lowercase letter down one digit. Under that rule, `x` becomes 58, so base 59 is mathematically valid. Under the ordinary order without that deletion, `x` is digit 59 and **cannot** appear in a base-59 numeral. This is the difference between a custom alphabet and just changing 60 to 59 in a formula.\n\n![Two digit alphabets: deleting an unused f moves g from 42 to 41 and x from 59 to 58.](experiments/records/grid-radix-reconciliation/digit-map.svg)\n\n| Interpretation | `x` digit | `4F` value | Largest of 256 values | Fit in a byte? |\n| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |\n| Base 59, remove `f` and renumber | 58 | 251 | 251 | Yes |\n| Base 59, keep ordinary digit numbers | 59 | — | — | Invalid: `x` is out of range |\n| Base 60, ordinary digit order | 59 | 255 | 255 | Yes |\n| Base 62, ordinary digit order | 59 | 263 | 263 | No: 12 entries exceed 255 |\n\nThe **byte condition matters**. If each pair must be exactly one unsigned byte and the ordinary digit order is fixed, the presence of `x` requires a base of at least 60, while `4F` must be at most 255 and therefore requires a base of at most 60. That makes 60 the only base *under those two assumptions*. Deleting `f` changes the digit assignments, so the base-59 proposal falls outside that conditional proof. Dropping the byte condition permits base 62 as a positional representation, though not as one byte per pair.\n\nThe two valid byte conversions are materially different: **220 of 256 values change** between custom base 59 and ordinary base 60 on the wiki text. For example, the first pair `3N` is 200 in the custom base-59 scheme and 203 in base 60. The fact that both produce 256 bytes does not identify which, if either, was intended.\n\n## Which transcription was tested?\n\nThe pasted discussion includes a full 256-pair list. Its count of **59 observed characters** and **161 distinct pairs** reproduces, but that list differs from the wiki export at five coordinates: LP2-49 (6,6) `1L`/`1l` and (7,3) `0L`/`0l`; LP2-50 (11,6) `0l`/`0I` and (12,5) `2s`/`2S`; LP2-51 (8,7) `3i`/`3I`. These are the already documented [source transcription disagreements](#/wiki/seventh-onion-transcriptions?section=grid), not evidence for one base over another. They change the exact byte streams and their hashes under **both** encodings.\n\nThe more detailed transforms described later in the discussion are separate proposals. This audit does not replay those scripts, test routes through the grid or infer a plaintext. It fixes the elementary input and alphabet question so those experiments can state what they actually used. The [grid guide](#/wiki/alphanumeric-grids) explains the page layout and the conditional byte interpretation.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nRun `python experiments/records/grid-radix-reconciliation/run.py --check` from the repository or extracted experiment bundle. The [script](experiments/records/grid-radix-reconciliation/run.py) reads the coordinate-bearing [wiki grid export](exports/alphanumeric-grids.csv) and the [256 quoted tokens](experiments/records/grid-radix-reconciliation/source-tokens.txt), applies each declared alphabet and checks the saved [result table](experiments/records/grid-radix-reconciliation/results.json). It uses only the Python standard library. The quoted tokens came from the supplied September 2026 discussion; the original linked script files were not supplied, so this checks the displayed list and code excerpt, not an executable historical repository.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/grid-radix-reconciliation/article.md",

  "article": "# The zero and capital O characters in the LP2 grids\n\n**The current transcription has 65 digit zeroes and seven capital `O` characters in 70 grid cells.** Two cells contain `00`, so there are 72 round marks in total. The coordinate register below covers every cell written with either character in the 256-entry wiki grid. The source-pixel contact sheets make it practical to inspect the whole set, including cells where the two archived text sources agree.\n\nThis is an input audit for [LP2-49–51](#/wiki/alphanumeric-grids), not a decoding result. A numeral conversion, bit image, checksum, or path can change if even one of these two shapes is copied incorrectly.\n\n## Inspect the printed forms\n\nEach panel below arranges **unscaled pixel crops** from a pinned original 2400 × 3600 JPEG. The small label gives page, grid row and column; adjacent characters may appear to the left or right of the target cell. Open a panel at full size or consult the complete [LP2-49](#/reader/lp2-49), [LP2-50](#/reader/lp2-50), and [LP2-51](#/reader/lp2-51) images. These are navigation aids for a human review, not OCR output.\n\n![Seventeen LP2-49 grid cells with a zero or capital O, labeled by grid row and column.](experiments/records/grid-round-glyphs/round-glyphs-lp2-49.png)\n\n![Thirty LP2-50 grid cells with a zero or capital O, labeled by grid row and column.](experiments/records/grid-round-glyphs/round-glyphs-lp2-50.png)\n\n![Twenty-three LP2-51 grid cells with a zero or capital O, labeled by grid row and column.](experiments/records/grid-round-glyphs/round-glyphs-lp2-51.png)\n\nIn this manual pass, the seven entries transcribed with `O` have the broader, rounder form, while the numerous zeroes are narrower. The strongest nearby comparisons are LP2-50 row 2 (`1O` beside `0u`) and LP2-51 row 6 (`2O` beside `00`). I did not identify a definite conflict with the stored `0`/`O` readings. This is **not** independent human certification of all 72 shapes: the coordinates were selected from the transcription, and other characters mistaken for neither `0` nor `O` would be missed. The [JSON coordinate register](experiments/records/grid-round-glyphs/results.json) gives every original crop rectangle for further review.\n\n| Page | Grid row, column | Transcribed capital-O entry |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| LP2-49 | 6, 2 | `1O` |\n| LP2-49 | 10, 6 | `2O` |\n| LP2-50 | 2, 6 | `1O` |\n| LP2-50 | 13, 5 | `2O` |\n| LP2-51 | 4, 8 | `1O` |\n| LP2-51 | 6, 5 | `2O` |\n| LP2-51 | 8, 1 | `2O` |\n\nThe separate seventh-onion and wiki transcriptions differ at [five grid cells](#/wiki/seventh-onion-transcriptions?section=grid), but none is a `0`/`O` difference. Their agreement is useful for locating a mark; it is not a second photographic observation.\n\n## What the byte assumption adds—and does not add\n\nUnder the [conditional base-60 rule](#/wiki/alphanumeric-grids?section=unique-base), `0` has digit value 0 and `O` has value 24. Sixty of the zeroes are the **first** character of a pair. Replacing one of those with `O` gives a value of at least `24 × 60 = 1,440`, outside a byte. Five zeroes occur as the **second** character: swapping four of them to `O` still fits a byte, while `40 → 4O` would become 264. All seven printed `O` characters occur second, and swapping any of those to `0` remains byte-valued.\n\nThis arithmetic constrains readings **only if** every pair is meant to be one unsigned byte with that digit order. It must not be used as independent proof of the printed letter or the intended encoding. The [direct-byte experiment](#/experiments/grid-direct-bytes) kept the current `0`/`O` readings fixed; its negative result therefore does not cover all conceivable round-glyph changes.\n\n## Reproduce the register\n\nFrom the repository root, or with the experiment ZIP and the named image files extracted alongside it:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/grid-round-glyphs/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/grid-round-glyphs/check.py\n```\n\nThe first script verifies source SHA-256 hashes, produces the same three contact sheets, and records the 70 source coordinates and conditional byte alternatives. It needs Python 3 and Pillow; it makes no network or AI calls. The second script independently rebuilds the entire 256-entry grid from the structured page records and checks every coordinate, token and alternate value. Neither script identifies printed glyphs automatically. The [plan](experiments/records/grid-round-glyphs/plan.json) states the inclusion rule and limitations.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/grid-round-glyphs/article.md",
