  "article": "# The ten bare stems in the LP2-49–51 grids\n\n**Ten of the 256 grid entries contain a character shaped like a bare vertical stem.** The current wiki text writes that character as either uppercase `I` or lowercase `l`. The preserved page images show no dot or horizontal foot at these positions, so the shape alone does not settle the case. Six of the ten positions agree across the two preserved text transcriptions; agreement does not turn an indistinguishable shape into a verified character.\n\nThis is an **input audit**, not a proposed LP2 decryption. It supplies exact coordinates and a bounded sensitivity calculation for readers who convert the two-character entries into bytes. It does not change the published transcription silently.\n\n## Locate the marks\n\nGrid rows begin at the first alphanumeric row on each page, excluding any runic lines. Columns run left to right from 1 to 8. The diagram maps the ten stems and, in tan, the separate `2S`/`2s` transcription disagreement. Select it for the complete SVG, and inspect the [LP2-49](#/reader/lp2-49), [LP2-50](#/reader/lp2-50), and [LP2-51](#/reader/lp2-51) images before choosing a reading.\n\n![Ten bare-stem positions mapped across the three eight-column grids; one separate S/s disagreement is marked.](experiments/records/grid-stem-uncertainty/stem-map.svg)\n\n| Page | Row, column | Seventh-onion text | Wiki text | If `I` | If `l` |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- | ---: | ---: |\n| LP2-49 | 1, 3 | `2l` | `2l` | 138 | 167 |\n| LP2-49 | 4, 2 | `3I` | `3I` | 198 | 227 |\n| LP2-49 | 6, 6 | `1L` | `1l` | 78 | 107 |\n| LP2-49 | 7, 3 | `0L` | `0l` | 18 | 47 |\n| LP2-50 | 2, 3 | `3I` | `3I` | 198 | 227 |\n| LP2-50 | 11, 6 | `0l` | `0I` | 18 | 47 |\n| LP2-50 | 12, 8 | `0I` | `0I` | 18 | 47 |\n| LP2-50 | 13, 7 | `2l` | `2l` | 138 | 167 |\n| LP2-51 | 2, 8 | `0l` | `0l` | 18 | 47 |\n| LP2-51 | 8, 7 | `3i` | `3I` | 198 | 227 |\n\nThe last two columns use the **conditional** digit order `0–9`, `A–Z`, `a–x` and the rule `byte = 60 × first digit + second digit`. They are not a claim that the manuscript intended base 60 or bytes. Changing `I` to `l` adds 29 to the value at every listed cell, but the number of changed bits depends on the first digit. The [full JSON report](experiments/records/grid-stem-uncertainty/results.json) keeps all coordinates, both values and the bit differences.\n\nThe `1L` and `0L` readings in the seventh-onion text would require an uppercase L with a foot; that foot is not visible in these image locations. The `3i` reading would require a dot; none is visible there. These observations constrain the historic transcriptions without deciding between `I` and `l`. At LP2-50 row 12, column 5, the distinct `2s`/`2S` disagreement is **not** a bare-stem case. In a close view, both preserved JPEG versions appear to show uppercase `S`; this remains a visual judgment for human review. The [five-source-difference guide](#/wiki/seventh-onion-transcriptions?section=grid) retains both text readings.\n\n## What changes if the ten cases remain open?\n\nStarting from the wiki's 256 tokens, the script changes **only** these ten second characters. Each may be `I` or `l`, giving `2^10 = 1,024` complete inventories. The other 246 entries, including `2S`, remain fixed. This is a sensitivity envelope, not a claim that all 1,024 combinations are equally plausible. A consistent font or a future source could constrain several together.\n\n| Inventory measure | Current wiki text | Range across 1,024 variants |\n| --- | ---: | ---: |\n| Distinct two-character tokens | 161 | 160–163 |\n| Set bits in the 256 conditional bytes | 1,017 | 1,006–1,026 |\n| Even-valued conditional bytes | 134 | 129–139 |\n\nThe widely cited **161 distinct tokens** is therefore a property of one transcription, not an image-settled invariant. A later analysis that depends on exact token equality, a checksum, a bit image, or a route through these cells should specify its readings and rerun under relevant alternatives. This audit does not test any route or candidate plaintext.\n\n## Reproduce and review\n\nFrom the repository root, use Python 3's standard library. If using the experiment ZIP, also extract [original-images.zip](downloads/original-images.zip) into the same folder before running the scripts; the experiment ZIP names and hashes its required page JPEGs but keeps those large images in the shared download.\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/grid-stem-uncertainty/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/grid-stem-uncertainty/check.py\n```\n\nThe first script verifies SHA-256 hashes for the wiki grid export, archived text and both preserved JPEG copies for each page, then enumerates every one of the 1,024 variants. The second rebuilds the 256 entries from the structured page records and independently checks every saved variant and metric. These checks verify the arithmetic and provenance; a person must still inspect the image shapes. The image files are preserved at [wiki LP2-49](images/lp2-49.jpg), [LP2-50](images/lp2-50.jpg), [LP2-51](images/lp2-51.jpg), and the [seventh-onion source collection](#/wiki/2014-seventh-onion?section=download).\n\nThe enumeration does **not** cover `0`/`O` or all conceivable glyph ambiguities, changes in numeral base, or the separate `2S`/`2s` choice. It also does not establish that independently changing the ten cases is typographically natural. Its purpose is to prevent a downstream result from being reported as robust merely because two text sources agree at a visually ambiguous stem.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/grid-stem-uncertainty/article.md",

    "rsa-window-54-source-replay"

  "article": "## Finding\n\nThe 2012 closing message places **131 digits on three physical lines** after “P.S.” A proposed reading turns that ragged block by taking columns instead of lines. We replayed the six fixed readings of the digits alone and four more readings that preserve the **five-character “P.S. ” indent**. **None passes the amended 95% printable-pair screen or matches a pinned longer constant.**\n\n![Printable-pair scores for all ten fixed readings of the 2012 P.S. block.](experiments/records/h03-ps-layout-replay/readings.svg)\n\nThe often-mentioned short strings **“3301” and “1033” do not occur in any of the six bare-block readings**. When the visual indent is preserved, “3301” appears once in one column direction and “1033” once in another. They are separate four-digit matches, not a continuous decoded message. The surrounding pair-decoded text does not meet the screen: the indented readings range from **73.8% to 78.5%** printable, against the **95%** threshold. All ten derived 131-digit integers also have explicit compositeness witnesses; primality was a report-only observation, not a hit condition.\n\n## Why the 95% threshold matters\n\nThe source initially borrowed an **80% printable** cutoff from a test of arbitrary bytes. A pair of decimal digits can only be 00–99, and **68 of those 100 values** map to printable ASCII characters. The old cutoff therefore produced **37 route firings in 200 random blocks** in the source's own control, before the real P.S. block was tested. The source raised the threshold to **95%** and repeated its controls before examining the real readings. Our independent run also shows the problem: **61 old-cutoff route firings** across 200 newly generated random blocks, but **zero** at 95%. All **10 planted readable blocks** pass the amended gate.\n\nThe five-column indent was added as a disclosed extension **after** the six bare readings returned no hits. It is reasonable to inspect the physical layout, but a newly noticed four-digit match is not a predeclared success. We retain the observed strings as observations and apply the same fixed 95% gate to the extra four routes.\n\n## Exact scope and reproduction\n\nThe [pinned signed-message text](experiments/records/h03-ps-layout-replay/source/ky_2012-01-final-message.asc) supplies the three digit lines, of lengths **40, 45 and 46**. The source runner refers to a separate local corpus path absent from its pinned checkout; we used the pinned repository's `.asc` copy and verified that its extracted digits exactly match the source's saved results. The test covers only four directions of column reading, the joined lines and their reverse, plus the four indented column readings. It does not test arbitrary widths, rearranged digits, a different numeral encoding or an unknown running key.\n\nFrom the Liberpedia repository root, run:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/h03-ps-layout-replay/run.py\npython experiments/records/h03-ps-layout-replay/check.py\n```\n\nThe [result](experiments/records/h03-ps-layout-replay/results.json) and [source manifest](experiments/records/h03-ps-layout-replay/source-manifest.json) include the exact input provenance. A separate checker reconstructs all ten routes from the physical lines, checks their scores and short-string counts, and compares them with the pinned source result.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/h03-ps-layout-replay/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "7cf5bcc6df9a5a32dc15a7d74043afefa5bd2942165cc8918af97cde2f375e9b",

  }

  "title": "Can missing duplicate runes hide an autokey pattern?",
  "question": "Can twenty missed adjacent duplicate runes restore the nonzero difference-diagonal unevenness predicted by one ciphertext-autokey rule?",

  "summary": "For exact adjacent duplicate insertions, all 28 nonzero rune-difference counts are unchanged. Even an artificial 20-count allowance reaches CV 0.066 against the source's 0.40 signal bar.",
  "finding": "The pinned transcription yields 9,640 within-word pairs, 60 doublets and nonzero difference CV 0.0608. Physical duplicate restoration leaves that CV invariant for any number of insertions. An exact upper bound allowing 20 freely allocated nonzero-diagonal additions is 0.0656; at 40 it is 0.0717. A separate checker confirms every count and the insertion identity for all 29^3 three-rune contexts.",
  "limitations": "This bounds only exact adjacent-duplicate deletion/restoration and the specified ciphertext-autokey difference statistic. The source amended its chi-square clause after its first run; the physical invariance does not depend on that clause. Other feedback rules, correlated multi-rune errors and nearly flat plaintext distributions remain outside scope.",

  "related": [

  ],
  "article": "## Finding\n\n**A missed repeated rune cannot change the 28 nonzero difference counts tested here.** The source asks whether about 20 instances of *haplography*—writing a doubled rune once—could make a ciphertext-autokey pattern disappear from LP2. Restoring one duplicate changes `a → x → b` into `a → x → x → b`. The old `x → b` transition remains; only the new `x → x` transition is added. Its rune difference is zero.\n\n![A duplicate insertion leaves the observed nonzero difference unevenness at 0.061. Even an artificial twenty-count allowance reaches only 0.066, compared with the source threshold of 0.40.](experiments/records/haplography-diagonal-bound/diagonal-bound.svg)\n\nWe reconstructed the source's **9,640 within-word adjacent pairs** from its pinned rune transcription and counted **60 equal-rune pairs**. The unevenness (coefficient of variation, or CV) of the 28 *nonzero* difference counts is **0.0608**. Inserting any number of exact adjacent duplicates leaves that number unchanged. This is an algebraic result, not a sampled search over insertion sites.\n\nThe source also gave a deliberately stronger, nonphysical adversary permission to add 20 counts to *any* nonzero difference. We independently bounded every such allocation: its largest possible CV is **0.0656**, still far below the source's **0.40** autokey-signal bar. At 40 additions the bound is **0.0717**. Our independent checker reconstructs the page runs by a separate parser, verifies all 41 bounds, and checks the insertion identity for every **29³** three-rune context.\n\n## What the result means\n\nFor the specific relation `c[i] = p[i] + c[i−1] + K (mod 29)`, differences between consecutive ciphertext runes mirror plaintext-rune frequencies. A strongly uneven plaintext distribution would therefore produce uneven nonzero differences. Exact deletion or restoration of a duplicated ciphertext rune **cannot hide that particular difference pattern**. This says nothing about other feedback rules, other transcription errors, or a plaintext whose frequencies were already nearly flat.\n\nThe original source reports a positive control made from *Pride and Prejudice* rune frequencies, but its checkout does not include the `pride.txt` file that its script loads. We therefore **do not claim to reproduce its reported 0.842 control CV or 0.784 separation**. Our replacement control is explicitly synthetic and lumpy: a planted ciphertext-autokey stream scores **1.316** after 20 merges, while a uniform stream scores **0.050**. It checks that the statistic can distinguish those two constructed cases; it is not a model of every possible natural language.\n\nThe source's initially frozen no-error rule included `χ² < 40`. Its later addendum sets that clause aside because the artificial adversary crosses 40 while CV remains low. Our strongest conclusion—the exact physical-insertion invariance—does not depend on either threshold. The nonphysical 20-count comparison is reported against the source's unchanged CV bar, with that rule change visible in the bundled source documents.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nFrom the repository root, with Python 3 and no additional packages:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/haplography-diagonal-bound/run.py\npython experiments/records/haplography-diagonal-bound/check.py\npython experiments/records/haplography-diagonal-bound/plot.py\n```\n\nThe [result data](experiments/records/haplography-diagonal-bound/results.json), [pinned source transcription](experiments/records/haplography-diagonal-bound/source/krisyotam_runes.txt), and the source's original plan, code and report are bundled. The copied source is MIT-licensed. Our result covers the **single-rune duplicate insertion** mechanism and this one ciphertext-autokey diagnostic, not the whole autokey family.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/haplography-diagonal-bound/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "7ac4438194ca760f9a9aa7edea4561173253cf5d09220ab8b1e16b4e42593ea2",

  }
}

  "reader_note": "132 of 458 F runes have I or M within two positions; the count is near the upper edge of page-preserving shuffles, but the interpretation was selected after viewing the text.",
  "reader_limit": "The forum proposal gives no marker distance or direction. The chosen pair and radius are post hoc; this is not a cipher or resynchronization test.",
  "scope_summary": "LP2-00–55 · fixed rule and local control.",
  "article": "## Finding\n\nIf I and M act as local markers for F interruptions, one simple prediction is that they should occur close to F more often than page composition alone would suggest. Among **458 F runes** on LP2-00–55, **132** have an I or M within two rune positions on either side. Shuffling rune order separately within each page gives a middle 95% range of **96–133**, with **34 of 999** shuffles at or above 132.\n\n![Observed F neighborhoods against page-preserving shuffles.](experiments/records/im-near-f-markers/proximity.svg)\n\nThe observed count sits near the upper edge of this particular reference. It is **not evidence of a reset rule**. The proposed I/M pair and proximity radius were chosen after discussion of the manuscript, and the reported stream-skip idea did not specify a distance or direction. Testing other rune pairs, distances and sections would create more chances for a high count.\n\n## Exactly what was counted\n\nFor each F, the script looks up to two rune positions before and two after it, staying on the same page. It scores one exposure if any of those positions contains I or M. Punctuation and word breaks are omitted, just as they are in the rune-only stream. The 999 reference trials retain each page's length and exact counts of every rune, including F, I and M, while shuffling their order.\n\nThis does not insert or remove F, model skipped key slots, detect doublet avoidance, or decode a message. A proposed stream cipher needs a fixed key generator and a deterministic transition for F, collisions and I/M before its full output can be compared with a held-out page.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nRun `python experiments/records/im-near-f-markers/run.py --check` from the repository root. The [results](experiments/records/im-near-f-markers/results.json) preserve page counts, the shuffle seed and all 999 comparison counts.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/im-near-f-markers/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "4131eb8f4122700abbcac15e547ddccd024580132a4e0d526467d91a3d435824",
  "record_type": {
    "id": "measurement",
    "label": "Manuscript measurement",
    "description": "Measures a stated feature or statistical comparison; it does not test a complete decoding rule."
  }
}

  "visuals": [
    {
      "path": "experiments/records/image-row-coverage/summary.svg",
      "caption": "Matched and unmatched individual rune rows under the frozen interval rule. LP2-50 contains no reference rune rows; it is a non-runic control. The full account links all eight annotated page overlays."
    }
  ],
  "article": "# Can image-only detection find every rune row?\n\nThis fixed detector does not reliably recover individual rune rows across the eight selected page layouts. It proposes 83 image bands; 43 match the 65 manually annotated rune rows under the frozen one-to-one interval rule. This is a segmentation control, not evidence of an omitted line in the archive.\n\nThe computation, independent check and visual review are preserved with this experiment. They establish the behavior of this fixed detector on the selected images; they do not certify the transcription.\n\n## What was tested\n\nThe source lead is Dukotah/cicada3301 at revision `f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1`, specifically `liber-primus/analysis/transcription/linecrop.py`. Its row-detection helper operates on the image alone; the later command-line mapping uses canonical rows. We implemented the fixed image-only rule separately rather than executing downloaded code.\n\nThe protocol and manual image reference were frozen before detector execution. The detector examines the central 22–78% of each image. Pixels darker than grayscale 128 contribute to the horizontal projection. A scanline is active when more than 1% of the examined columns are dark. Contiguous active intervals shorter than 20 pixels are discarded before remaining intervals separated by fewer than 12 pixels are merged. No thresholds were tuned after seeing these results.\n\nA proposal matches a reference interval when their intersection divided by their union is at least 0.5. Maximum-cardinality one-to-one matching prevents a large band from counting as several recovered rows. The result retains all eligible edges, matching alternatives and omission controls.\n\n## Results and overlays\n\n| Page | Reference rune rows | Image proposals | Matched rune rows | Overlay |\n| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |\n| LP2-00 | 12 | 12 | 9 | [Inspect](experiments/records/image-row-coverage/overlays/lp2-00.svg) |\n| LP2-03 | 11 | 6 | 4 | [Inspect](experiments/records/image-row-coverage/overlays/lp2-03.svg) |\n| LP2-15 | 8 | 11 | 5 | [Inspect](experiments/records/image-row-coverage/overlays/lp2-15.svg) |\n| LP2-31 | 12 | 12 | 12 | [Inspect](experiments/records/image-row-coverage/overlays/lp2-31.svg) |\n| LP2-39 | 12 | 12 | 9 | [Inspect](experiments/records/image-row-coverage/overlays/lp2-39.svg) |\n| LP2-50 | 0 | 13 | Not applicable | [Inspect](experiments/records/image-row-coverage/overlays/lp2-50.svg) |\n| LP2-56 | 5 | 10 | 2 | [Inspect](experiments/records/image-row-coverage/overlays/lp2-56.svg) |\n| LP2-57 | 5 | 7 | 2 | [Inspect](experiments/records/image-row-coverage/overlays/lp2-57.svg) |\n\nLP2-50 contains alphanumeric rows in this inventory, not rune rows. It is a non-runic control, not a zero-percent rune-recovery result.\n\nEvery overlay preserves the source JPEG beneath the annotations. Orange R brackets identify reference rune rows, gray N brackets identify other text rows, and blue D rectangles identify image-only proposals. Visual inspection classified all 83 proposals: 43 individual rune rows, 24 non-runic text rows, seven bands spanning multiple rune rows, and nine artwork bands. No reference interval was changed after detection. These categories describe visible regions; they do not identify precisely which pixels caused a merge.\n\nThe numerical count alone is insufficient: LP2-00 has 12 proposals and 12 reference rune rows, yet only nine match. Artwork and merged rows can conceal each other's count discrepancy.\n\n## Omission controls and limits\n\nEach of the 65 reference rune rows is separately treated as absent from a hypothetical candidate inventory while the image and its proposals remain unchanged. The report records whether that row can or must receive a match across all maximum matchings. These are deterministic coverage checks on shared images, not 65 independent trials or 65 actual transcription errors.\n\nAn inventory-only comparison cannot visit a row omitted from that inventory by construction. That comparison illustrates a coverage restriction; it does not reproduce the source repository's classifier or measure its accuracy.\n\nThe pages were selected for different layouts, not randomly sampled. The reference intervals are approximate manual body intervals and prior familiarity with pages is disclosed. Human review remains pending. This experiment does not recognize rune identities, audit within-row insertions or deletions, certify all 75 pages, or show that an archive row is missing.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nExtract the reproduction bundle and original-images.zip into the same root, or use the repository. With Python 3 and Pillow 11.3.0, run `python experiments/records/image-row-coverage/run.py --check` from the root. This reproduces the saved results and all eight overlays in a temporary directory and runs the independent check. To retain new output, use `--output row-replay` instead.\n\nFor the individual stages, choose output paths that do not exist:\n\n```sh\npython scripts/test_image_row_matching.py\npython scripts/image_row_coverage.py --output row-results.json\npython scripts/check_image_row_coverage.py row-results.json --receipt row-audit.json\npython scripts/render_image_row_coverage.py row-results.json row-audit.json --output row-overlays\n```\n\nThe producer checks the frozen plan, reference and image hashes. The independent checker uses scalar pixel bytes, regular-expression active runs, rational interval arithmetic and exhaustive matching enumeration without importing the producer. Both use Pillow to decode the JPEGs, so decoding is a shared dependency. The matching unit controls exhaust all 512 bipartite graphs with three vertices on each side.\n\n`results.json` is the untouched first-run report; its status describes the state at computation time. `audit.json` supplies the subsequent independent computational check. `overlay-review.json` records the later visual review and hashes of all eight overlays. Do not edit the first report to imply that review occurred before it was produced.\n\nFuture variants should change one declared segmentation assumption at a time and retain this baseline. More permissive matching alone is not evidence of better row detection.\n\n## Related explanations\n\nSee [transcription checking](#/wiki/transcription-checking?section=coverage-limits) for the difference between a recorded correction and complete review, and [search spaces and bounds](#/wiki/search-space) for why a result applies only to the declared test.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/image-row-coverage/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "7b258ffe338acc11039736f852d4850eb5432f668b6c7b692d3af55644b6093c",
  "record_type": {
    "id": "audit",
    "label": "Source or input audit",
    "description": "Checks image provenance, extraction or input coverage against a declared reference; it does not establish a decryption."
  }
}

  "scope_summary": "Two archived Cicada MP3s · 50–70 Hz and 14–17 kHz.",
  "article": "# Instar's high-frequency line and low hum\n\nThe archived *Instar Emergence* has a narrow line at **15,645.89 Hz**. It rises **39.72 dB above the nearby median** in a fixed full-track spectrum and remains prominent in all eight nonoverlapping 20-second windows. A separate low-frequency peak appears at **59.22 Hz**, 14.89 dB above its nearby median. These measurements make the reported spectral features inspectable; they do not identify a recording device, geographic location, encoded message, or watermark.\n\n![Two pinned Cicada tracks compared in the 14–17 kHz band](experiments/records/instar-narrowband-lines/lines.svg)\n\n## What was tested\n\nA discussion of the music described an approximately 15 kHz “CRT hum” and 60 Hz hum in *Instar*. We checked the exact archived `761.mp3` and used the separately preserved *Interconnectedness* recording as a comparison. Both files are pinned by SHA-256 in the downloaded record. The *Interconnectedness* carrier already has a documented OpenPuff branch, so it is a comparison of frequency spectra, **not** a clean “no-hidden-content” control.\n\nWe averaged the stereo channels, measured a Hann-windowed Welch spectrum over the complete 44.1 kHz track, and selected the largest bin in two bands fixed from the report: 50–70 Hz and 14–17 kHz. The FFT segment length is 65,536 samples with 50% overlap. Each peak is compared with the median of a local band, excluding 3 Hz around that peak. The same peak frequencies were checked in consecutive 20-second windows.\n\n| Track | Peak in 14–17 kHz | Above nearby spectrum | 20-second windows above 10 dB |\n| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |\n| The Instar Emergence | 15,645.89 Hz | +39.72 dB | 8 of 8 |\n| Interconnectedness | 14,497.23 Hz | +8.93 dB | 3 of 13 |\n\nThe low band also has prominent peaks in both tracks, though at different frequencies: Instar at 59.22 Hz and Interconnectedness at 69.98 Hz under this rule. “Near 60 Hz” is a useful description of the first measured peak. It is **not** proof of North American mains pickup: instruments, processing and MP3 artifacts are not excluded by a spectral peak alone.\n\n## What this leaves open\n\nThe source did not specify a watermark algorithm, payload or detector. A narrow spectral line is a property of the sound file, not an extraction of hidden data. The proposed ~500 Hz time-localized gaps were not tested here; they need a fixed event interval and a defined gap statistic. A later watermark test should pin a detector and decision threshold, then measure false positives on matched audio.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nDownload this experiment ZIP and the reference-data bundle, extract both into one folder and run:\n\n```sh\npython -m pip install numpy scipy soundfile\npython experiments/records/instar-narrowband-lines/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/instar-narrowband-lines/check.py\n```\n\nThe first script checks the two MP3 hashes, recomputes the Welch measurements and checks the figure. The independent check uses a single FFT per 20-second window, without Welch, and confirms both Instar peaks persist. The saved [results](experiments/records/instar-narrowband-lines/results.json) include every window score. Decoding may vary in last-place floating-point digits across library versions; the archived output was produced with the versions stated in the record.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/instar-narrowband-lines/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "f7ad3976ba9d8c7725b7c9259f8465cbc4fbd784c89a2215d3cabab8ab344ba7",
  "record_type": {
    "id": "measurement",
    "label": "Manuscript measurement",
    "description": "Measures a stated feature or statistical comparison; it does not test a complete decoding rule."
  }
}

  "article": "# JPEG byte histograms: the four-page split\n\n**Finding:** The reported LP2 split is present in the archived JPEGs. Of 58 files, **54 have `00` as their most frequent byte**. The four exceptions—LP2-00, 04, 24 and 26—have `44` as their mode. Both groups contain one-component and three-component JPEGs, so component count does not explain the split. Nothing in this measurement extracts a hidden message or shows that any file is random.\n\n![LP2 modal bytes crossed with JPEG component counts, with a shorter LP1 comparison.](experiments/records/jpeg-byte-mode-replay/modes.svg)\n\nThe test counts the **stored file bytes**, including headers and compressed data. It does not count visible pixel values or the individual digits in a hexadecimal display. The source called the common group “null” and the exceptions “random”; here those terms are replaced with the exact byte modes. Even on the page with the most zeros, `00` is only 20.1% of the file, not a majority. Byte `44` is hexadecimal for decimal 68 (ASCII `D`), consistent with the source’s display label.\n\n| LP2 most frequent byte | One-component JPEG | Three-component JPEG |\n| --- | ---: | ---: |\n| `00` | 22 | 32 |\n| `44` | 1 | 3 |\n\nThe same fixed rule gives 15 `00`-mode files and two `28`-mode files in the 17 archived LP1 images. Those exceptions are LP1-00 and LP1-02, corresponding to the source’s one-based “Page 1” and “Page 3.” This extends its sixteen-page list to the full local archive; it does not recreate the missing historical histogram screenshots. In all 75 archived files, at least 92.6% of the zero bytes occur **after the first scan header**. This locates the bytes within the stored JPEG stream but does not isolate every later marker or explain how its encoder produced them.\n\nThe [fixed re-encoding control](#/experiments/jpeg-modal-reencode-control) tests whether the byte class survives different JPEG settings. The four page numbers alone do not specify a date, a cipher or a payload. For a fuller explanation of the byte-versus-pixel distinction, see the [JPEG distribution guide](#/wiki/jpeg-byte-distribution).\n\n## Reproduce\n\nDownload the [original images](#/downloads) alongside this experiment, then run `python experiments/records/jpeg-byte-mode-replay/run.py --check` from the repository root. The script checks all 75 image hashes and re-counts their byte modes and JPEG frame components using Python's standard library. [The plan](experiments/records/jpeg-byte-mode-replay/plan.json) fixes the rule; [the results](experiments/records/jpeg-byte-mode-replay/results.json) list every page's checksum, byte length, mode, zero count and component count. The historical [source file repository](https://github.com/rtkd/iddqd/tree/master/liber-primus__images--unsolved) is not pinned to its October 2023 revision, so equality with that exact historical input remains unverified.\n",

  "reader_note": "The four-page byte-histogram class changes after re-encoding the same images.",
  "reader_limit": "The encoding control cannot identify the original encoder or test a hidden-message extraction.",
  "scope_summary": "58 LP2 JPEGs · three fixed re-encodes per page.",
  "article": "# JPEG byte classes after re-encoding\n\n**Finding:** The four LP2 files singled out in the 2023 byte-histogram report have a nonzero most-frequent byte in our archived originals. That four-page grouping **does not survive a fixed JPEG re-encode**. The same decoded page images yield 23 nonzero-mode files at quality 75, 23 at quality 85, and five at quality 95. A file-byte mode is therefore sensitive to JPEG encoding choices; the grouping alone cannot identify a manuscript layer or hidden message.\n\n![Bar chart comparing the number of nonzero-modal-byte LP2 files in originals and three fixed re-encodes.](experiments/records/jpeg-modal-reencode-control/mode-control.svg)\n\n| File set | Nonzero-mode pages | Original four still nonzero-mode |\n| --- | ---: | ---: |\n| Archived originals | 4 of 58 | 4 of 4 |\n| Re-encode at quality 75 | 23 of 58 | 1 of 4 |\n| Re-encode at quality 85 | 23 of 58 | 1 of 4 |\n| Re-encode at quality 95 | 5 of 58 | 0 of 4 |\n\nThe original four are **LP2-00, 04, 24 and 26**. At qualities 75 and 85, only LP2-24 retains a nonzero mode. At quality 95, none does. Re-encoding introduces many different nonzero-mode pages at 75 and 85; it does not simply turn every page into a `00`-mode file.\n\n## What was compared\n\nFor each of the 58 archived LP2 JPEGs, the script counts all 256 possible *complete-file byte values* and records the unique most frequent one. It then decodes that original and saves it in memory as a new JPEG at each of three specified quality settings, with chroma subsampling disabled and no resizing. The re-encoded files are **derivatives**, never replacements for the original manuscript images. The [existing byte audit](#/wiki/jpeg-byte-distribution) gives the full original histograms and frame-header checks; this test asks whether their four-page class is stable under a change of JPEG representation.\n\nThis is a bounded sensitivity control, **not a randomness test**. The quality settings are illustrative and were not sampled from a model of how Cicada made the original files. Re-encoding can change compressed bytes and decoded pixels, so this result neither explains the original file-production process nor rules out steganography. A proposed extraction must specify its target bytes, algorithm and expected output separately.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nRun `python experiments/records/jpeg-modal-reencode-control/run.py --check` from the repository root with **Pillow 11.3.0**. The [saved report](experiments/records/jpeg-modal-reencode-control/results.json) lists the SHA-256, byte length and mode of every original and all 174 temporary re-encodes. The [plan](experiments/records/jpeg-modal-reencode-control/plan.json) fixes the measurement and settings. The source claim and its 58-page table are summarized in [Reported attempts](#/wiki/reported-attempts?section=jpeg-hex-distribution); the historically linked [image archive](https://github.com/rtkd/iddqd/tree/master/liber-primus__images--unsolved) identifies its earlier image collection, whose 2023 revision has not been pinned.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/jpeg-modal-reencode-control/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "ff21e54613305993e37b4ba33649ed47a4e8bb4c8c657280e63862e68b8e9bbb",
  "record_type": {
    "id": "control",
    "label": "Control",
    "description": "Checks a search, decoder or scorer using synthetic inputs or reference text; it does not identify the cipher of an unsolved page."
  }
}

    "representation": "All nine known reading sections; headings included; slash/CR/LF wraps removed within sections. Unfiltered literal labels retained as diagnostic; amended rune-derived labels and native rune lengths; sections pooled without boundary joining.",
    "procedure": "Replay fixed known readings exactly. Compare all section/pool length histograms with all eight FLORES dev language profiles under letter, folded and GP grouping models. Check independently using archived traces, regex tokenization and rational distances.",
    "parameters": "Nine sections, 17 pages; 10 targets including the pool; 70 profiles, 90 eight-language rankings; bins 1–15 and 16+; all 997 development sentences per language. Original plan plus post-diagnostic amendment.",
    "exclusions": "No blind decryption, posterior, accuracy inference from independent random trials, new language labels for solved sections, or authentication of source readings. No new unknown-page results. GP grouping is an orthographic sensitivity."
  },
  "outcome": "inconclusive",
  "finding": "The pooled 739 native rune tokens rank closest to English in every comparison, but some individual known-English sections do not. Removing 38 non-rune alphabetic characters from LP2-56 changes its literal-profile comparison; the hash had doubled its apparent word count from 25 to 50.",
  "limitations": "Sections contain 18–208 native tokens and are not independent random samples. The pool reuses the sections. Literal spelling, symbol units and embedded material affect rankings. The amendment followed inspection of the first run; human review pending.",
  "next_steps": "Review conversion/boundary choices; add a fixed genre-matched parallel corpus and exact target-size calibration. Do not infer plaintext language from a short-section nearest match.",

  "visuals": [
    {
      "path": "experiments/records/known-reading-languages/controls.svg",
      "caption": "Nearest profile for established English readings under three counting models. All language names have identical styling. A different nearest profile is a limitation of the comparison, not a revised reading."
    }
  ],
  "article": "## Why test readings whose language is already known?\n\nA language comparison should be checked on Liber Primus itself, not only on ordinary translated web text. This control uses **all nine documented reading sections, spanning 17 runic pages**. Their English readings are reproduced with the existing fixed cipher parameters before any statistical comparison. The method is not asked to discover their plaintext.\n\nThe result is useful precisely because it is imperfect: **the pooled readings rank closest to English in every tested representation, but several individual sections have a different nearest language profile.** A nearest statistical match is not a dependable language label for a short section.\n\n## What was fixed before scoring\n\nThe original plan selects every documented section and the pool, includes headings, and uses the same eight FLORES development-language profiles and length-distance definition as the [baseline](#/experiments/parallel-languages). Within each section, page text is concatenated in order and slash/newline wraps are removed. Sections remain separate when their token lists are pooled.\n\nWe compare the literal Latin rune labels using the three corpus representations: letters, accent-folded letters, and GP-style grouping. We also compare native rune-token lengths with each corpus representation. Expanding a rune label into letters changes the counting unit: TH can be two letters but one rune. GP grouping is still a mechanical orthographic sensitivity, not a validated phonetic conversion.\n\n## An input problem found in the first run\n\nLP2-56's published literal field includes its hexadecimal target. A general letter tokenizer interprets the hash's letter fragments as extra words. The unfiltered field produces **50 apparent tokens**, while the rune-derived prose has **25**. All **38 excluded non-rune alphabetic characters** in this control come from LP2-56. The other eight sections have none under the same rule.\n\nWe retained that first report and froze a separate amendment before calculating the amended results. For every section—not just LP2-56—the added comparison constructs Latin labels from the verified decoded rune trace, preserves nonalphabetic delimiters, and replaces any alphabetic source character that is not a GP rune with a separator. This gives a consistently defined rune-derived text profile. The original unfiltered results remain in the download as a diagnostic, not a clean prose-language control. The amendment was made after inspecting the first run and is not described as part of the original predeclared design.\n\n## Reading the results\n\nThe chart names the nearest language profile for each known-English section. Every language uses identical styling. Its first column compares rune-derived letter lengths with corpus letter lengths; the next uses GP grouping on those labels; the final compares native rune lengths with the GP-grouped corpus. The raw report also contains the accent-folded and additional unit-comparison results.\n\n- The pool contains **739 native rune tokens** and ranks closest to English in all nine comparisons. It is still much shorter than the 2,896-token unsolved target.\n- The second koan has 87 native tokens. Its letter profile ranks closest to English, but its GP-grouped and native-rune profiles rank closest to a different candidate. The established English reading has not changed; the counting model has.\n- The final parable has only 20 native tokens. Its nearest profile changes between letter, GP-label, and native-rune representations.\n- For LP2-56, removing hash fragments changes the literal-profile result. This illustrates an input-selection effect rather than new evidence about the plaintext language.\n\nThese results do not prove that the corpus method is useless. They show what its successful pooled comparison does and does not establish. None of the nine sections is a random draw, the pool reuses them, and the representations reuse the same text. Do not turn these outcomes into an independent-trial accuracy estimate or a posterior probability for the unsolved manuscript.\n\n## Reproduce and inspect\n\nDownload this experiment's bundle and extract the folder structure intact. It contains the corpus references, archived traces, source transcriptions, reading parameters, original plan, amendment, diagnostic report, current report and scripts. Python 3 standard library only; no API or network.\n\n```sh\npython experiments/records/known-reading-languages/run.py --check\npython scripts/check_known_reading_language_control.py experiments/records/known-reading-languages/results.json\n```\n\nThe replay first reproduces the literal readings exactly against the stored page records. The independent checker reconstructs profiles from the separately archived CSV traces and a regex tokenizer; it checks all **70 profiles and 90 rankings** using exact rational distances, and verifies the excluded-character counts. This is computational review, not human review or a new authentication of the readings.\n\n[Current results](experiments/records/known-reading-languages/results.json) · [Original diagnostic](experiments/records/known-reading-languages/diagnostic-original.json) · [Original plan](experiments/plans/known-reading-language-control.json) · [Amendment](experiments/plans/known-reading-language-control-amendment.json)\n\nSee [known readings](#/readings), [word-length conventions](#/wiki/word-lengths), and the [shorter aligned-passage controls](#/experiments/parallel-language-blocks). The [equal-token control](#/experiments/target-sized-languages) now checks reference samples of exactly 2,896 tokens. It does not lengthen these known-reading sections or turn them into independent trials. Genre-matched parallel material and per-section unsolved analysis remain separate work.\n\nFLORES translations and this derived account are provided under CC BY-SA 4.0; source attribution is included in the bundle.   "article": "# Do “big-gap” pages have larger JPEG files?\n\nAn earlier comparison named 16 pages with unusually wide line gaps and 15 comparison pages, then claimed a **74 KB** difference in their average JPEG size. The page lists are useful because they let us check the arithmetic without choosing a new sample.\n\n![The original size labels average 582.8 KiB for the reported big-gap pages and 542.9 KiB for the comparison pages, a difference of 39.9 KiB.](experiments/records/large-gap-file-size-replay/file-size-comparison.svg)\n\n## What we found\n\nThe 16 printed size labels total **9,325 KiB**, giving the reported mean of **582.8125 KiB**. The 15 comparison labels total **8,143 KiB**. Their mean is **542.8667 KiB**, not the post's **508.9375 KiB**. Correcting that arithmetic reduces the difference from roughly 74 to **39.9458 KiB**. This correction matters even before considering any statistical comparison.\n\nAll 31 printed size labels match the corresponding [archived JPEGs](#/downloads) when each byte length is divided by 1,024 and rounded **up** to an integer. Using the precise byte lengths gives a **39.83 KiB** difference. The two group medians are about 564.2 and 529.0 KiB, respectively. The [result file](experiments/records/large-gap-file-size-replay/results.json) lists every one of the 58 LP2 JPEG sizes and its SHA-256 hash, including the 27 pages not chosen in the original comparison.\n\nAs a scale check, we repeatedly split these same 31 files into groups of 16 and 15 at random. In 100,000 seeded splits, **17,278** had a mean difference at least as large as the observed one in the same direction. That is a *descriptive reference for these fixed files*, not a probability that the gap observation is false: the original groups were not randomly assigned and were selected after looking at the manuscript.\n\n## What remains untested\n\nThe supplied discussion names the pages and reports a typical **109-pixel** large gap, **73-pixel** ordinary gap, and **129-pixel** exception on the parable page. Its original screenshot coordinates are absent from the supplied text. This record therefore accepts the author's page labels **only as labels for the file-size replay**. It does not independently establish which pages have a large gap, which glyphs caused one, or whether the space encodes anything. JPEG size varies with page content and encoding; a size difference alone cannot identify a font or cipher mechanism.\n\nTo reproduce, run `python experiments/records/large-gap-file-size-replay/run.py --check`, `python experiments/records/large-gap-file-size-replay/check.py`, and `python experiments/records/large-gap-file-size-replay/plot.py --check` from the repository root. The independent checker recalculates the original sums and checks all 31 file-size labels against the archived originals.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/large-gap-file-size-replay/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "32d16f535e9d395a5feda7a5a08d48e0acd993c6d79f6ed11c68059caef99da7",
  "record_type": {
    "id": "audit",
    "label": "Source or input audit",
    "description": "Checks image provenance, extraction or input coverage against a declared reference; it does not establish a decryption."
  }
}

  "id": "large-gap-mark-alignment",
  "status": "published",
  "title": "Marked lines and the gaps below them",
  "question": "In fixed source-guided LP2 image regions, do apostrophes, quotation marks and digits occur on the lines immediately above unusually wide gaps?",
  "summary": "Six marked lines on five selected pages are followed by 108–110-pixel gaps; 28 unmarked lines in the same regions and one control have 73–75-pixel gaps. LP2-35 needs its reviewed apostrophe correction to register the observed mark.",
  "tags": [
    "line gaps",
    "punctuation",
    "quotation marks",
    "apostrophe",
    "numerals",
    "transcription",
    "image measurement",
    "LP2",
    "reported attempt"
  ],
  "scope": {
    "pages": [
      "lp2-04",
      "lp2-07",
      "lp2-10",
      "lp2-35",
      "lp2-42",
      "lp2-14"
    ],
    "representation": "Aligned rows from original 2400×3600 JPEG crops and the archived raw/reviewed text fields in their structured page records.",
    "procedure": "Predeclare six source-guided image rectangles; count fully blank horizontal rows between printed lines at three thresholds; align each gap with the raw and reviewed text line above; compare punctuation/digit marks with the following gap.",
    "parameters": "Six pages, 34 measured interline gaps, ASCII apostrophe/double-quote/digit markers, wide-gap descriptive cutoff 100 pixels, grayscale cutoffs 100/160/200, five dark pixels per row, merge across at most 14 blank rows.",
    "exclusions": "Whole-book mark/gap association, independent sampling, causality, original author screenshot coordinates, typesetting mechanism and binary decryption."
  },
  "outcome": "supported",
  "finding": "The six marked lines all have 108–110 blank pixels below; 28 unmarked measured lines have 73–75. Raw text detects only five marked wide gaps because its LP2-35 line 4 omits the apostrophe that the image and reviewed text contain.",

  "article": "# Do marked lines sit above the large gaps?\n\nOne report links unusually tall spaces between LP2 rune lines to an apostrophe, quotation mark or numeral on the line **above**. That is more specific than saying the marked pages have unusual spacing somewhere. We aligned text rows with measured image rows on five pages named by the report and one comparison page. The regions were fixed in the [plan](experiments/records/large-gap-mark-alignment/plan.json); this is a selected, local check rather than a whole-book survey.\n\n![Six source-guided marked lines are each followed by a 108–110 pixel gap; 28 unmarked lines in the measured regions have 73–75 pixel gaps.](experiments/records/large-gap-mark-alignment/mark-gap-alignment.svg)\n\nThe six marked lines in the reviewed page text are LP2-04 line 8 (apostrophe), LP2-07 line 1 (quotation mark), LP2-10 line 8 (the numeral 7), LP2-35 line 4 (apostrophe), and LP2-42 lines 3 and 6 (quotation marks). Each has a **108–110-pixel** blank interval directly below it. The other **28** measured gaps on those pages and the LP2-14 comparison are **73–75 pixels**. The same row boxes and widths reproduce at three grayscale thresholds: 100, 160 and 200. [Results](experiments/records/large-gap-mark-alignment/results.json) give every line and gap coordinate.\n\nLP2-35 shows why the text version matters. Its original image has a small upright punctuation mark on line 4, and the stored **reviewed** text records an apostrophe there. The archived **raw** text omits it. A literal search of the raw text would therefore find five of the six marked wide-gap lines and classify LP2-35 as an unexplained wide gap. The correction is already documented in the [transcription decisions](#/wiki/transcription-decisions?section=review-lp2-35); this experiment measures its effect on a concrete image/text alignment.\n\n![Original LP2-35 line-four crop showing the narrow upright punctuation mark among the runes.](experiments/records/large-gap-mark-alignment/lp2-35-apostrophe.png)\n\nThis alignment is strong **within the six selected regions**, but it does not establish why the extra space appears. The pages and marker lines came from a report proposing the association; they were not sampled blindly. Letter shapes, font fallback or manual layout could produce the same observation without encoding a message. The 129-pixel parable exception and number-panel spacing are outside this test, as are punctuation marks elsewhere in the book.\n\nReproduce from the repository root with `python experiments/records/large-gap-mark-alignment/run.py --check`, `python experiments/records/large-gap-mark-alignment/check.py`, and `python experiments/records/large-gap-mark-alignment/plot.py --check`. The checker independently reads the archived and reviewed page records and reduces flat grayscale pixel rows.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/large-gap-mark-alignment/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "a34c4320d1da4099a6b4142e38203e6f410f3ec4ef8bc51e90f940b67adb4a06",
  "record_type": {
    "id": "measurement",
    "label": "Manuscript measurement",
    "description": "Measures a stated feature or statistical comparison; it does not test a complete decoding rule."
  }
}

  "article": "# Measuring the reported large line gaps\n\nA supplied analysis reports **109 blank pixels** in a large gap between rune rows, against **73** in an ordinary gap, with a **129-pixel** exception on the parable page. We measured fixed rune-text regions on two of its listed large-gap pages (LP2-04 and LP2-35), the named exception (LP2-57), and one of its ordinary-gap comparison pages (LP2-14). This is a check of the visible spacing claim, not a whole-book census.\n\n![Gap widths in four fixed page regions; three listed large-gap pages each have one wide gap, while the comparison region does not.](experiments/records/large-gap-pixel-replay/gap-measurements.svg)\n\nThe [original LP2-04 image](#/reader/lp2-04) has one **109-pixel** clear gap among eleven measured gaps; the others are **73–75**. [LP2-35](#/reader/lp2-35) has one **110-pixel** gap among eleven, and [LP2-57](#/reader/lp2-57) has the reported **129-pixel** exception among four. The [LP2-14 comparison region](#/reader/lp2-14) has six gaps, all **73–75**. These are counts of wholly blank horizontal pixel rows, not baseline distances. The full [results](experiments/records/large-gap-pixel-replay/results.json) include every ink-row coordinate. Repeating the measurement at grayscale cutoffs 100, 160 and 200 leaves all four gap lists unchanged.\n\nThis supports the *existence and scale* of the exceptional spacing on the selected archived images. The one-pixel difference on LP2-35 shows why a single exact width should not be applied to every page. The forum text does not include the original screenshot coordinates, so our rectangles and pixel rule are a declared independent measurement, not a reconstruction of the author's Canva selections.\n\nThe reason for the extra space remains open. The selected pages have different content and layouts. This measurement neither verifies the post's full 16-page classification nor shows that punctuation, numbers, a particular font or a cipher caused the gap. It also supplies no bit-reading rule.\n\nReproduce from the repository root with `python experiments/records/large-gap-pixel-replay/run.py --check`, `python experiments/records/large-gap-pixel-replay/check.py`, and `python experiments/records/large-gap-pixel-replay/plot.py --check`. The second script independently reduces flat pixel rows and compares every box at all three thresholds.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/large-gap-pixel-replay/article.md",

  "article": "# Does omitting F make both later messages prime length?\n\n**Result.** Yes, under the declared Gematria Primus transliteration. The preserved 2016 and 2017 signed-message bodies encode to **177** and **45** rune indices. Each contains four F runes. Removing every F leaves **173** and **41**, both prime. This reproduces the reported counts, but it is an observation about two known messages, not a decoding rule for Liber Primus.\n\n![A compact comparison shows the original 2016 and 2017 message lengths and the lengths after omitting F or W.](experiments/records/later-message-f-omission/omission-counts.svg)\n\nThe messages are stored as **Latin-letter text**. This record uses the site's explicit GP encoding: split into letter runs, map V to U, then take each word's unique shortest encoding with the archived rune aliases. It counts the message body before PGP signature armor, including the sign-off and verification text. A different transliteration or a different body boundary could change the count; neither source message contains literal runes to count directly.\n\nTo see whether prime lengths are specific to F, the script applies the same one-symbol removal to **each of the 29 GP runes**. Two omissions leave prime lengths in both messages: F gives 173 and 41, while W gives 173 and 43. The full [result](experiments/records/later-message-f-omission/results.json) records all 29 pairs. This is a finite comparison, **not a p-value** for intent: F was already a salient symbol in the puzzle, and these two messages were selected from a larger history.\n\nThe [plan](experiments/records/later-message-f-omission/plan.json) fixes the body, encoding and one-symbol comparison. The script reads the preserved signed payloads and verifies their hashes through the existing [message manifest](data/evidence/later-messages.json). From the repository root, run `python experiments/records/later-message-f-omission/run.py --check`. The public [later-messages guide](#/wiki/later-messages) explains source preservation and signature verification. Prime lengths alone do not say which LP2 positions an F should skip, whether a key advances, or what plaintext should follow.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/later-message-f-omission/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "99b5d316b0c16d2fd12c433b54ca3865c99fac6bb97375a8b0332b4523e4fa4a",

  "article": "## Finding\n\nThree similar-looking feedback rules make different predictions. For **additive** feedback, `c[i] = p[i] + c[i−1]`, a ciphertext doublet requires `p[i] = 0`. For **Beaufort-style** feedback, `c[i] = c[i−1] − p[i]`, the same is true. Their literal inverse outputs are negatives of each other modulo 29, so they identify **exactly the same 86 zero positions** in LP2-00–55. Doublet placement alone cannot distinguish these two rules.\n\nFor the **subtractive** variant, `c[i] = p[i] − c[i−1]`, the inverse is `p[i] = c[i] + c[i−1]`. Its zero condition is a pair summing to zero, not a repeated pair. The archived stream yields **437 zero outputs** under that literal inverse, rather than 86.\n\n![Zero-output counts for additive, Beaufort and subtractive feedback.](experiments/records/linear-ciphertext-feedback/zero-outputs.svg)\n\nThese are structural statements about precisely written recurrences. Neither 86 nor 437 tells us that the corresponding inverse is readable plaintext. A key term, symbol remapping, zero skip, or interrupted clock would change the model. The [literal multiplication check](#/experiments/multiplicative-ciphertext-autokey) addresses another feedback rule with a stronger, absorbing-zero contradiction.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nPython 3.12 standard library, from the repository root:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/linear-ciphertext-feedback/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/linear-ciphertext-feedback/check.py\n```\n\nThe first command rebuilds the [29-bin output frequencies](experiments/records/linear-ciphertext-feedback/results.json), page-by-page zero counts and figure. The second independently recounts the three zero conditions from each transcription and checks the modular identity.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/linear-ciphertext-feedback/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "6b5b4951361c067812952c75111dc1857a0359e9795a33bbcfbeca10d363e354",

  }
}

      "caption": "Two anchor outputs reduce the infinite modulus range to one identity branch and finitely many divisibility candidates."

  "article": "## What was tested\n\nCan one fixed rule `(a × p + b) mod m` rearrange all 29 Gematria Primus prime values into a different ordering of the same values? Here p is the literal prime, not a rune index. Every output must belong to the same prime alphabet, and distinct inputs must give distinct outputs.\n\nFor **every integer modulus m greater than 109**, the only resulting permutation is the identity: each prime stays itself. This is a fresh reconstruction of the supplied research archive’s C07 claim, not a new discovery or a rerun of its original certificate. No manuscript page or proposed plaintext is used.\n\n## Results\n\n| Check | Result |\n| --- | --- |\n| Distinct images of inputs 2 and 3 | 29 × 28 = 812 choices |\n| Exact integer permutations without modular wrapping | One: a=1, b=0 |\n| Remaining anchor choices | 811 |\n| Candidate maps requiring modular checks | 13,212 |\n| Nonidentity full-alphabet permutations | None |\n\nThis does not exclude shifts modulo 29 on **rune indices**, prime-derived running keys, or position-dependent transformations. It is specifically about a single affine map of the full literal-prime alphabet.\n\n## Why the infinite range is finite to check\n\nLet u be the output of 2 and v the output of 3. Subtract their congruences:\n\n```text\n2a + b ≡ u (mod m)\n3a + b ≡ v (mod m)\na ≡ v − u (mod m)\nb ≡ 3u − 2v (mod m)\n```\n\nNo modular division is needed. Composite moduli and coefficients that are not invertible modulo m are included. For each u,v define the unreduced integer expression `L(p)=u+(p−2)(v−u)`.\n\nIf L sends every prime into the palette as ordinary integers, its nonzero slope makes it injective. Exhaustive anchor checking finds only L(p)=p in this branch. Otherwise choose a palette input p whose integer image L(p) is outside the palette. To obtain an allowed modular output y, **m must divide the nonzero integer L(p)−y**. Enumerating those divisors for all 29 possible targets gives every candidate modulus for that anchor pair.\n\nThe identity works for every m>109 because all primes are canonical residues. Every other branch has a nonzero divisibility witness, so it is finite. There is no unsearched large-modulus tail. The report lists every anchor, witness and candidate modulus.\n\n## A worked branch\n\nSuppose 2 maps to 3 and 3 maps to 5. Then L(p)=2p−1, so L(5)=9 is outside the palette. For any allowed output y from 2 through 109, the nonzero difference 9−y has absolute value at most 100. No modulus above 109 can divide it. This anchor pair therefore has no candidates.\n\nOther pairs have larger differences and require checks. The program applies the reduction to every pair; this example alone is not the proof of the complete result.\n\n## Where the conclusion stops\n\n| Relaxed assumption | Counterexample | Consequence |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| Drop injectivity | a=0, b=2, m=110 maps every prime to 2 | Output membership alone does not force identity |\n| Use a partial palette | a=109, b=5, m=110 swaps 2 and 3 | The subset {2,3} has a nonidentity permutation |\n\nThe subset example is not a result about any actual manuscript page. A page using fewer than all 29 symbols requires its own support-specific test. Neither counterexample recovers plaintext.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nExtract the experiment bundle with its folders intact:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/literal-prime-affine/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/literal-prime-affine/check.py\n```\n\nBoth commands use Python’s standard library and make no network or AI requests. The first reconstructs the full report. The second does not import the producer: it checks candidate completeness by scanning each witness’s bounded modulus range directly, then enumerates all coefficient pairs for moduli 110 through 125. Those sixteen controls check the implementation; coverage above them comes from the divisibility argument, not extrapolation. The checker also verifies the two counterexamples.\n\nBoth checks passed on 20 October 2026. The question, planned procedure and controls are in `plan.txt`. No search bounds, scoring rules or exceptions were changed after seeing the result. Source alphabet, scripts and output hashes are included in the record. Computational review is complete within this scope; human review is pending. No Lean or other proof-assistant build is claimed.\n\nSee [rune indices and prime values](#/wiki/rune-values), [prime indices](#/wiki/prime-indices), [cipher invariants](#/wiki/cipher-invariants), and [search space and bounds](#/wiki/search-space) before applying this result to another proposal.\n\nThe [completed page-support variant](#/experiments/literal-prime-affine-pages) checks the actual archived LP2 supports. It retains two additional LP2-55 maps, illustrating this distinction with manuscript data.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/literal-prime-affine/article.md",

    "description": "Studies a declared mathematical mapping over the alphabet, rather than decoding an unsolved page."
  }
}

  ],
  "article": "## What changes from the baseline?\n\nThe [baseline](#/experiments/literal-prime-affine) requires one affine map to permute the entire 29-prime alphabet. This variant uses the prime values actually present on each archived LP2-00–55 page. Outputs may be any of the 29 allowed primes, but distinct observed inputs must still have distinct outputs. A page may use its own fixed coefficients and modulus.\n\nThe modulus range remains **every integer m greater than 109**. We do not score English or select a proposed reading. The supplied archive’s C08 claim predicted two LP2-55 exceptions; the fresh calculation retained all survivors rather than filtering for that prediction.\n\n## Results\n\n| Archived page support | Pages | Candidate maps checked per distinct support | Nonidentity maps |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| All 29 prime values | 53 pages | 13,212 | None |\n| 28 values, missing 7 | LP2-49 | 14,901 | None |\n| 25 values, missing 7, 29, 59, 103 | LP2-55 | 14,901 | Two |\n| No rune values | LP2-50 | Not tested | No conclusion |\n\nThus **54 of the 55 nonempty rune pages allow only identity** under this exact model. LP2-55 has two additional maps. LP2-50 contains the alphanumeric panel rather than a rune stream; this procedure does not interpret its characters as GP runes.\n\nThe counts refer to distinct input supports, not a separate rerun for each of the 53 identical full-support cases. There are 43,014 candidate-map checks across the three supports. The all-modulus identity branch is handled separately.\n\n## The two LP2-55 exceptions\n\n| Coefficients (a, b, m) | Image of prime 2 | Images of observed odd primes |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| (58, 57, 114) | 59: rune label T | Unchanged |\n| (102, 101, 202) | 103: rune label Y | Unchanged |\n\nBoth have the form `a=m/2+1`, `b=m/2`. For an odd prime p,\n\n```text\nap+b = p + (m/2)(p+1) ≡ p (mod m)\n```\n\nbecause p+1 is even. At p=2, the result is `2+m/2`: 59 for m=114 and 103 for m=202. Each map therefore changes only F to T or Y on this page. It does not decode the remaining runes or recover word boundaries.\n\nNeither 59 nor 103 occurs in LP2-55’s observed input support. Sending 2 to either value therefore does not collide with another observed input. On the full alphabet, the odd input 59 or 103 is fixed too, so two inputs would have the same output. That is why these exceptions do not contradict the baseline.\n\nThe coefficients 58 and 102 are not units modulo 114 and 202 respectively: each gcd is 2. Requiring the affine map to be invertible on the entire residue ring would discard them. Our stated model requires injectivity only on the observed prime support, so they must be retained.\n\n## Complete enumeration without a modulus cutoff\n\nEvery nonempty page support contains primes 2 and 3. Assign distinct allowed images u and v to them, giving 812 anchor choices per support. These determine `a=v−u` and `b=3u−2v` modulo m.\n\nFor each pair, examine the unreduced expression `L(p)=u+(p−2)(v−u)` on the page’s support. If every integer output is already allowed, record that branch separately. In this dataset the only such branch is identity. Otherwise choose the first supported prime whose L(p) is outside the full palette. Every valid modulus must divide one of the nonzero differences `L(p)−y`, where y is an allowed target prime.\n\nThe script tests every resulting divisor above 109, requiring both allowed outputs and no collisions on the observed support. The complete report retains each anchor’s witness and candidate list, the two surviving maps and their full outputs, and every page’s source hash. There is no arbitrary upper modulus bound.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nExtract this variant’s bundle with its folders intact:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/literal-prime-affine-pages/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/literal-prime-affine-pages/check.py\n```\n\nPython’s standard library is sufficient. The bundle includes the baseline’s divisor helper and all 56 archived page texts. No network or AI requests are made.\n\nThe independent checker does not import the producer or divisor helper. It reconstructs page support by counting each alphabet symbol, verifies page hashes, enumerates the possible moduli directly within each witness’s mathematical bound, and checks every survivor. It also verifies that both LP2-55 exceptions fix all its odd input primes and move 2 to a previously absent value.\n\nBoth commands passed on 20 October 2026. The method and controls were recorded in `plan.txt`; no input boundaries, candidate criteria or modulus bounds were changed after inspecting the result. Human review is pending. This is an elementary calculation with a checked certificate, not a proof-assistant build or a new decipherment.\n\n## Limits\n\nThe result concerns the archived rune transcription and one fixed literal-prime affine map per page. It does not cover corrected symbol streams that change a page’s support, position-dependent transformations, noninjective maps, nonlinear rules, rune indices modulo 29, or prime-derived keystreams. A change in any of those assumptions requires a separate variant.\n\nSee [rune values](#/wiki/rune-values), [the full-alphabet baseline](#/experiments/literal-prime-affine), and [search space and bounds](#/wiki/search-space) for the distinction between checking a model completely and claiming a general decryption.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/literal-prime-affine-pages/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "2eebb404162dbcf25288e036dca2cd0cdfa3393d7a7eb9982437fd63d73f890f",

  "article": "## What was tested\n\nSuppose a rune is replaced by its Gematria Primus prime value: F becomes 2, U becomes 3, and so on through the 29-value alphabet ending at 109. Could one fixed quadratic formula rearrange that entire alphabet without producing any values outside it?\n\nWe tested `f(x) = ax² + bx + c (mod m)` for **every integer modulus m greater than 109**. A modulus sets the wraparound size: values that differ by a multiple of m count as the same output. We required the formula to send all 29 primes to **29 distinct primes from that same alphabet**. The result is identity only: under these assumptions, each prime must map back to itself.\n\nThis is a replication of the quadratic claim in the supplied research archive. The earlier scripts and reported result were inspected before the plan was written. It is not a new discovery or a blind test. A fresh enumerator and a separately implemented checker agree; human review remains pending.\n\nThis extends the [full-alphabet affine experiment](#/experiments/literal-prime-affine) by allowing an x² term. It does not rule out every arithmetic cipher. A changing key, a formula applied only to a page's observed runes, or an operation on rune **indices** rather than prime values asks a different question.\n\n## Why an infinite range can be checked\n\nTrying moduli up to a convenient maximum would leave every larger modulus unresolved. Instead, three chosen inputs restrict which moduli can work.\n\nCall the prime alphabet S. The images of 2, 3 and 5 must be three different members of S; write them as u, v and w. There are `29 × 28 × 27 = 21,924` ordered choices. These three images determine the following integer expression:\n\n```text\nQ(x) = 2u(x−3)(x−5) − 3v(x−2)(x−5) + w(x−2)(x−3)\n```\n\nFor any polynomial fitting those three images, `6f(x) ≡ Q(x) (mod m)`. The factor 6 matters: it cannot simply be cancelled when the modulus is divisible by 2 or 3.\n\nFor each choice of u, v and w, find the first alphabet value x for which Q(x) is not six times an alphabet value. If the final output is some y in S, then m must divide the **nonzero integer** `Q(x) − 6y`. A nonzero integer has only finitely many positive divisors. Taking the divisors for all 29 possible y therefore gives a complete finite list for this branch, including moduli larger than a guessed search cutoff.\n\nThe downloaded certificate records each branch's three images, the chosen witness x, its Q(x), and every candidate modulus. For each candidate the scripts recover all possible coefficients and check the entire output alphabet directly.\n\n## The branch without a finite witness\n\nExactly one choice escapes that divisor reduction: `(u,v,w) = (2,3,5)`. In this branch Q(x) is exactly 6x as an integer, so a different argument is needed. All its possible maps have the form\n\n```text\nf(x) = x + a(x−2)(x−3) (mod m), with 6a ≡ 0 (mod m).\n```\n\nFor every integer x, `(x−2)(x−3)` is either 0 or 2 modulo 6. The only possible changes from identity are therefore a shift by 2a; the input 7 already tests that shift. If it is nonzero, its circular distance from zero is m/3. But two members of this alphabet differ by at most `109−2 = 107`. A valid nonidentity map in this branch would consequently need `m ≤ 321`.\n\nThe checker directly scans the coefficient residues for all moduli 110 through 321. None gives a nonidentity permutation of the alphabet. The argument above handles every larger modulus; those larger moduli are not silently dropped.\n\n## Results\n\n| Finite branches | Candidate-modulus checks | Coefficient checks | Surviving maps |\n| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |\n| Modulus coprime to 6 | 261,346 | 261,346 | 0 |\n| Modulus divisible by 2 or 3 | 2,420,451 | 7,993,284 | 0 |\n\nThese counts are branch checks: a modulus can occur under several different choices of anchor images. They are not counts of distinct modulus values across the whole experiment.\n\nThe separate identity-anchor branch contains 318 coefficient expressions representing identity within the checked interval. **Different coefficients need not mean a different function.** For example, modulo 110,\n\n```text\n55x² + 56x = x + 55x(x+1) ≡ x.\n```\n\nThe product x(x+1) is always even, so the extra term is divisible by 110. Reporting that quadratic coefficient as a nonidentity solution would be a mistake.\n\n## Where the conclusion stops\n\nThe requirement to preserve the **whole** alphabet is essential. On only the three inputs `{2,3,5}`, the quadratic `22x² + 16x + 10 (mod 127)` swaps 2 and 3 and fixes 5. However, it sends 7 to 57, outside the prime alphabet. A smaller observed alphabet can therefore permit maps excluded by the full-alphabet test. See the [affine page-support variant](#/experiments/literal-prime-affine-pages) for a separate example of why page-level scope matters.\n\nInjectivity is essential too: the constant function f(x)=2 always stays inside S, but destroys the distinctions between runes. Working with rune indices instead of their literal primes changes the domain. Higher-degree formulas, word-dependent operations, varying coefficients, and polynomial key sequences combined with unknown plaintext are also outside this experiment.\n\nNo candidate plaintext was scored. There was no selection of words that happened to look meaningful, and no claim about the language of the unsolved pages follows from this result.\n\n## How to reproduce it\n\nUse Python 3 with its standard library. No network service or model is needed. From the repository root, choose output filenames that do not already exist:\n\n```sh\npython -m unittest discover -s scripts -p test_quadratic_palette.py\npython scripts/run_quadratic_palette.py --output quadratic-certificate.json\npython scripts/check_quadratic_palette.py quadratic-certificate.json --receipt quadratic-audit.json\n```\n\nThe first command compares both coefficient solvers against every coefficient triple for moduli 2 through 18, including cases where division by 6 is invalid. It also checks divisor generation and the scope counterexamples above.\n\nThe producer scans divisor pairs up to the square root and solves congruences using modular inverses after accounting for the greatest common divisor. The checker imports none of that code: it reconstructs divisors by prime factorization and obtains coefficient solutions by lifting a congruence to integer equations. It then checks every finite branch and the bounded identity branch against the saved certificate. The receipt identifies the certificate and checker by SHA-256.\n\nAgreement between these implementations supports the computation. The all-modulus conclusion additionally depends on the reduction explained above. It has not been presented as a proof-assistant result or as completed human review.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/literal-prime-quadratic/article.md",

  "article": "# What remains when the four LP1 message borders are removed?\n\nThe four signed messages hidden in **LP1-10–13** display the same seven-row ASCII number diagram with a changing outer digit. In page order, the border digits are **3, 3, 0, 1**. Remove the top and bottom rows and the first and last character from each remaining row: the interior is byte-identical in all four messages, without rotation or reflection.\n\n![Four ASCII diagrams with their changing perimeter marked in orange and common interior in blue](experiments/records/lp1-payload-outer-ring/four-borders-one-interior.svg)\n\nThis checks a reported observation connected to the solved text's phrase about *shedding the circumference*. The source note says removing the outer number of each repeated square leaves an identical number grid. It does **not** supply an LP2 decryption rule or an output. The match is a property of the four embedded messages, not evidence that stripping a perimeter solves an unsolved manuscript page.\n\n## The four source objects\n\nEach page image has an extracted OutGuess payload containing a PGP-signed instruction. The repository retains the exact body text and page metadata recording successful signature verification. This audit rechecks the body hashes and that recorded verification status; it does not independently re-run GPG. The bodies instruct the reader to create a Tor hidden service and submit three magic squares. Their diagrams have the same spacing and numeric interior. LP1-10 and LP1-11's whole body files are byte-identical; LP1-12 and LP1-13 change the diagram's border digit.\n\n| Embedded body | Border digit | Retained numeric rows |\n| --- | ---: | --- |\n| LP1-10 | 3 | `10 12 10` / `12 14 12` / `10 12 10` |\n| LP1-11 | 3 | Same |\n| LP1-12 | 0 | Same |\n| LP1-13 | 1 | Same |\n\nThe [fixed plan](experiments/records/lp1-payload-outer-ring/plan.json) defines the operation before comparison. It requires exactly one diagram bounded by two 16-character rows of equal digits; removes only that one-character perimeter; retains spacing in the five interior rows; and parses the three numbered rows. The [complete result](experiments/records/lp1-payload-outer-ring/results.json) preserves every original and retained line, the source hashes, and the derived matrix.\n\nThe common matrix is:\n\n```text\n10  12  10\n12  14  12\n10  12  10\n```\n\nIts row sums are **32, 38, 32**. It is therefore not a magic square under the ordinary equal-row-sum definition. The border sequence happens to read `3301` in page order; the audit does not infer a further instruction from that fact.\n\n## A distinct reading that fails\n\nThere are also two *visible* five-by-five LP1 squares: the mixed number-and-rune square on LP1-05, which needs Gematria Primus conversion, and the decimal square on LP1-16. If “remove the outer ring” is instead applied to those, their central three-by-three grids differ:\n\n```text\nLP1-05 converted       LP1-16 printed\n199 130 320            812 934 280\n245  91 245            620 809 620\n320 130 199            280 934 812\n```\n\nNone of the five-by-five core values occurs in the other core. Rotation or reflection cannot make them identical. These are not the repeated signed-message diagrams described in the source discussion. Keeping the objects separate matters: the same verbal instruction cannot be reported as verified on a different pair of squares.\n\n## Reproduce the comparison\n\nFrom the repository root, with Python 3 and no added packages:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/lp1-payload-outer-ring/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/lp1-payload-outer-ring/check.py\npython experiments/records/lp1-payload-outer-ring/plot.py --check\n```\n\nThe run script extracts the diagrams from four hashed message bodies and converts the separate LP1-05 and LP1-16 page transcriptions for the exclusion check. The independent checker parses the ASCII blocks with a different pattern and compares all four exact lines and all nine core values against an explicit oracle. The result is an input and source-identity audit. It does not test whether a perimeter-removal operation helps decrypt LP2.\n",
