    }
  ],
  "article": "# Does preserving each section change the column-balance result?\n\nThe fixed 464-word arrangement remains unusually flat under a null that shuffles word lengths only within their original four sections. All original section slots and the continuous sixteen-column layout are preserved. This is a sensitivity variant of `lp1-word-length-balance`, not an independent discovery.\n\n| Quantity | Unrestricted baseline | Within-section variant |\n| --- | ---: | ---: |\n| Observed integer score | 128256 | 128256 |\n| Observed column-mean variance | 501/13456 | 501/13456 |\n| Observed variance / model expectation | 0.25150357 | 0.25209625 |\n| Null trials | 49,999 | 49,999 |\n| Trials at or below observed, including ties | 54 | 88 |\n| Plus-one lower-tail estimate | 0.0011 | 0.00178 |\n\nThe constrained expectation is calculated separately. Its exact expected integer score is `612019253902976/1202967183`, and expected column-mean variance is `4781400421117/32374252828896`. The unchanged observed variance divided by that expectation is `1205373117366/4781400421117`.\n\nThe four sections contain 45, 124, 208 and 87 words. Their boundaries do not reset the column position. The report preserves every section's slot counts in all sixteen columns, exact expected column sums and variances, and all 49,999 null scores. A singleton-section boundary and unequal section sizes are covered by small exhaustive controls.\n\n## What changes between the two models?\n\nThe baseline permits any word length to move to any of the 464 slots. This variant permits a word length to move only to a slot in its original section. The lengths themselves, section order and observed arrangement remain unchanged. A section may occupy different numbers of slots in different columns, so keeping its slots matters as well as keeping its histogram.\n\nThe slot diagram shows those fixed memberships. Colors identify the four sections, not high or low word lengths. The same word may have several interchangeable positions within its color. A single section boundary can cut across a row; the next section continues at the next column.\n\nThe two histogram panels use identical integer-score bins, displayed on a common column-mean variance scale. The dashed line is the unchanged observed variance. Lower variance means more similar column means. Every one of the 49,999 null scores per model contributes to its panel; the complete bin counts are downloadable as CSV. The shared seed number does not pair individual trials because the procedures consume random choices differently.\n\n## Why the expectation changes\n\nUnder unrestricted shuffling, every slot samples the same pool of lengths. Under within-section shuffling, each slot samples only its section's pool. The four pools have different means and variances. Columns also contain different section slot counts. Consequently, their expected sums need not be identical, even though every column still contains 29 words.\n\nFor section size N, population variance v and c slots in one column, its sum contributes variance `c*(N-c)*v/(N-1)`. Contributions from independently shuffled sections add. The expected squared distance from the fixed overall mean also includes the difference between each column's expected sum and the overall mean. The script uses exact fractions; the checker obtains the same expectation through pairwise position moments. The ratio in the table therefore uses each model's own expectation.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nExtract the experiment ZIP with folders intact, or use the repository. Python 3 standard library is sufficient. Run `python experiments/records/lp1-section-balance/run.py --check` to reproduce all constrained scores, run the independent checker and verify the figures. Use `--output section-replay` to retain new files in a new directory.\n\nThe individual stages can also be run from the root with new output paths:\n\n```sh\npython scripts/test_lp1_section_balance.py\npython scripts/lp1_section_balance.py --output section-results.json\npython scripts/check_lp1_section_balance.py section-results.json --receipt section-audit.json\n```\n\nThe [protocol](experiments/plans/lp1-section-balance.md) was committed before constrained shuffles were generated. The producer uses the hashed word ledger and source dependencies. The checker independently scans the original archived text, verifies all 464 words, reconstructs every permutation with explicit index swaps, and calculates the expectation through position-pair second moments. It imports no producer code. Both implementations share Python's pseudorandom primitive.\n\n## Interpretation and publication status\n\nBoth estimates are below the predeclared 0.05 threshold. Preserving section-level length distributions does not remove the low-variance result in this fixed test. The two tests share the same selected arrangement; their p-values must not be combined as independent evidence. The original exploration is not included in either null. Neither model preserves sentence syntax, and neither tests a grille, carrier text, authorial intent or a decryption.\n\nHuman review remains pending. Saved results and the independent receipt are preserved here without overwriting the original baseline. The figures and histogram CSV are generated from those saved reports; the baseline distribution is reused from its published record, not simulated as part of this variant.\n\n## Related explanations\n\nSee [the unrestricted baseline](#/experiments/lp1-word-length-balance), [word-length conventions](#/wiki/word-lengths), and [null models and selection](#/wiki/null-models). The [section-order variant](#/experiments/lp1-section-order) now searches all 24 orders with matching selection in every control. Preserving sentences remains a separate, untested constraint.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/lp1-section-balance/article.md",

  "article": "# LP1 column balance after searching section orders\n\nThis variant belongs to the LP1 word-length and column-balance family. Human review remains pending.\n\n## What was tested\n\nThe original 464-word sequence fills a table of 29 rows and 16 columns. Its column totals are unusually similar under the previously declared shuffle controls. This variant asks whether that comparison changes when a solver may rearrange the four intact sections and keep whichever arrangement has the most similar column totals.\n\nThe sections are Warning (45 words), Welcome (124), first koan (208), and second koan (87). Word order within each observed section remains unchanged. Every arrangement fills the table continuously, without resetting at section boundaries. The score is `Q = sum((16 * column_total - 1796)^2)`; lower scores mean more balanced columns.\n\nThe [protocol](experiments/plans/lp1-section-order.md) was committed before calculating the order search. It disclosed the already-known fixed-order results. Each of 49,999 controls shuffles lengths within the original sections, searches the same 24 orders, and retains its minimum. It would be unfair to search the observed data but compare that selected result with controls given only one arrangement.\n\n## Results\n\nNo alternative order improves the original score, **128256**. Four orders tie for that minimum because they are cyclic rotations of the original arrangement.\n\n| Representative order | Score Q |\n| --- | ---: |\n| Warning → Welcome → first koan → second koan | 128256 |\n| Warning → Welcome → second koan → first koan | 295680 |\n| Warning → first koan → Welcome → second koan | 257280 |\n| Warning → first koan → second koan → Welcome | 407296 |\n| Warning → second koan → Welcome → first koan | 215808 |\n| Warning → second koan → first koan → Welcome | 337664 |\n\nEach row represents four cyclic rotations with exactly the same score. Rotating the 464-word sequence shifts its sixteen column totals without changing their balance, since 464 is divisible by 16. Thus the 24 arrangements form six classes; this does **not** make the six scores independent.\n\n**440 of 49,999 controls** have a selected minimum no greater than the observed minimum, ties included. The plus-one estimate is `(440 + 1) / 50000 = 0.00882`. The fixed-order within-section comparison was `0.00178`. The larger estimate reflects the extra opportunities given to every control, even though the observed minimum did not improve.\n\nThe result remains below the protocol's 0.05 threshold. It describes this precise word sequence, table width, score, shuffle model and section-order search. It does not estimate the probability of intentional design, provide a decryption, or correct for the wider exploration that originally selected the 464-word object and sixteen-column layout. The two estimates use the same shuffled sections and are not independent evidence.\n\n## Verification and reproduction\n\nThe independent checker reconstructs the source tokens, generates permutations through explicit index swaps, and computes all 24 scores in every control using section-column accumulation. It does not import the producer. It checks **1,199,976 null order scores**, all observed orders, every minimum and tie list, and the full tail count. Every baseline-order control score also matches the earlier section-preserving report. Both implementations share Python's pseudorandom primitive.\n\nThe toy tests exhaust small section permutations with unequal section sizes and repeated values. A non-divisible example demonstrates why the cyclic reduction requires complete rows.\n\nFrom the repository root, choose new output paths:\n\n```sh\npython scripts/test_lp1_section_order.py\npython scripts/lp1_section_order.py --output order-replay.json\npython scripts/check_lp1_section_order.py order-replay.json --receipt order-replay-audit.json\n```\n\nThe producer checks the frozen input hashes. Compare the replay report's SHA-256 with `report_sha256` in the independent audit receipt. The downloadable result retains the full order mapping, observed scores, all six class scores for every trial, and all minimizing orders; none of the searched arrangements is omitted from that representation.\n\n## Read the figures\n\nThe order diagram lists all 24 arrangements in six groups. Every arrangement in one group has the same Q; the bar represents that shared score. Letters label sections, not rune values. The histogram shows the minimum score retained from every complete 24-order search. Its vertical scale counts trials, and its dashed line is the observed minimum. All 49,999 trials are included; the bin counts are downloadable as CSV.\n\n## Run the complete reproduction\n\nExtract the experiment ZIP with folders intact. Run `python experiments/records/lp1-section-order/run.py --check` from its root. Python 3 standard library is sufficient; the run is offline. Use `--output order-replay` to retain results in a new directory. The wrapper repeats the simulation, independently checks every order score, and reproduces the figures and histogram.\n\nSee the [fixed-order section-preserving comparison](#/experiments/lp1-section-balance), [original baseline](#/experiments/lp1-word-length-balance), and [search-space explanation](#/wiki/search-space).\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/lp1-section-order/article.md",

  "article": "# LP1 seven-word GP-825 match\n\nOne proposed LP2 reading was compared with a seven-word stretch of the solved LP1 warning. This test checks the **LP1 side of that comparison**: how many seven-word stretches have exactly 21 runes and a Gematria Primus sum of 825?\n\n## Result\n\nAmong **652** seven-word windows kept within their solved LP1 sections, **one** meets both conditions. It starts at zero-based word 9 of the warning: `YOU CNOW TO BE TRUE TEST THE`. The decoded-rune trace gives it 21 runes, GP sum 825 and zero-based rune-index sum 232. The source discussion reported 716 windows; that denominator does not reproduce with these seven sections and word boundaries. Even joining all 694 words across section breaks gives only 688 possible starts.\n\n![One qualifying LP1 window among 652 section-internal windows](experiments/records/lp1-seven-word-825-census/windows.svg)\n\nThe result confirms an exact match in LP1 under the declared trace. It does **not** establish that the proposed LP2 phrase has the stated rune spelling or sum, that the two passages are linked, or that a decryption rule follows. The phrase and numeric criteria were selected during exploration, so `1/652` is a census of these LP1 windows, not a chance probability for the full search.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nRun `python experiments/records/lp1-seven-word-825-census/run.py --check` from the repository root. The [saved census](research/source-intake/lp1-seven-word-825-audit.json) includes all seven section counts and input hashes. Word separators come from the archived runes; decoded symbols come from the published reading traces. The [source note](research/source-intake/lp1-seven-word-825-audit.md) explains the one documented LP1-10 rune swap and the Latin-label spelling difference.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/lp1-seven-word-825-census/article.md",

  "article": "## Does searching other widths change the balance result?\n\nThe original comparison arranged 464 word lengths in sixteen columns. This variant asks a different question: if we may choose among six widths, how unusual is the smallest normalized column imbalance we can obtain? Every shuffled control receives exactly the same choice.\n\nThe fixed rule selects **width 2**, with normalized imbalance R about **0.01694**. Of 49,999 shuffled controls, 6,035 obtain a minimum no greater. The plus-one lower-tail estimate is **0.12072**, above the declared 0.05 threshold. This test does not support an unusually small minimum-R under its unrestricted-shuffle model.\n\nThat conclusion needs a precise qualification: **this is not an adjustment of the smallest fixed-width p-value**. Width 32 has the smallest unadjusted tail in the table below; width 2 has the smallest R. Choosing between those criteria after seeing the results would change the experiment.\n\n## What is fixed, and what changes?\n\nUse the same Warning, Welcome, first koan and second koan as the [464-word baseline](#/experiments/lp1-word-length-balance). Keep their order, headings, interruption runes, word boundaries and internal apostrophes. Count native runes per word. The source population contains 464 words and 1,796 runes.\n\nTry only widths **2, 4, 8, 16, 32 and 64**. Word i, counted from zero, goes in column i modulo the width. Do not rotate the start, reorder sections or pad the final row. Widths 32 and 64 leave unequal column sizes, so the statistic explicitly weights by the number of words in each column.\n\nThe width set follows the earlier power-of-two discussion, including 64. The original width-16 result and qualitative observations about other widths were known before this protocol. The protocol was committed before these new measurements; that does not erase the earlier exploration.\n\n## Why divide by an expectation?\n\nLet n be the number of words, T their total length, n_j the size of column j and S_j its length sum. Define weighted imbalance as Q = sum(S_j² / n_j) − T² / n. Lower Q means more similar column means. Let D = sum(x_i²) − T² / n, where x_i is each word length.\n\nUnder an unrestricted permutation of those fixed lengths, the expected Q for k columns is (k−1)D/(n−1). We use **R = Q / expected Q**. At width 16, this equals the baseline's normalized variance of column means. The derivation and exact arithmetic are preserved in the research README.\n\nDividing by the expectation makes the mean equal to one under each width's null distribution. It does **not** make those distributions have the same shape. An R of 0.02 at one width can be less unusual than an R of 0.3 at another. The declared selection rule nevertheless chooses the minimum R, and its control distribution must repeat precisely that rule.\n\n## Every tested width\n\nThe fixed-width tails below include ties and use the plus-one correction. They are diagnostic, unadjusted comparisons—not independent evidence or six corrected tests.\n\n| Width | Words per column | Observed R | Fixed-width tail / 49,999 | Unadjusted estimate |\n| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |\n| 2 | 232 | 0.01694 | 6,006 | 0.12014 |\n| 4 | 116 | 0.14684 | 3,429 | 0.06860 |\n| 8 | 58 | 0.34531 | 3,317 | 0.06636 |\n| 16 | 29 | 0.25150 | 54 | 0.00110 |\n| 32 | 14 or 15 | 0.31188 | 5 | 0.00012 |\n| 64 | 7 or 8 | 0.73060 | 2,044 | 0.04090 |\n\nThe width-16 exact R and 54-control tail reproduce the original baseline. The same random seed and fresh-copy shuffle sequence are used, so this agreement is a reproduction check, not an independent replication.\n\n## Matching the selection in every control\n\nGenerate 49,999 unrestricted permutations using Python's Random with seed 330146. For each one, calculate all six R values and retain the minimum, including every tying width. Compare those minima with the observed minimum using exact rational arithmetic. The result is (6,035 + 1)/(49,999 + 1) = **0.12072**.\n\nThe null figure includes all controls. Its bins are for display only; the tail count uses the exact values, not histogram bins. The saved report retains all 299,994 null width scores, their minima and ties.\n\nThis does not account for every width, every possible grouping of text, the original selection of the 464-word object, or choosing the statistic itself. It also does not preserve coherent sentences or each section's length distribution in the controls. The [within-section variant](#/experiments/lp1-section-balance) and [section-order variant](#/experiments/lp1-section-order) address different choices. No result here identifies a grille or the unsolved cipher.\n\n## Reproduce and inspect\n\nDownload this experiment's ZIP and extract its folders. Python 3's standard library is sufficient; the bundle includes the source transcriptions and baseline dependencies. No network access, API or model is used.\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/lp1-width-selection/run.py --check\n```\n\nTo retain a fresh replay instead of using a temporary directory:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/lp1-width-selection/run.py --output my-width-replay\n```\n\nThe producer reconstructs the baseline words and scores nested power-of-two columns with exact integer ratios. The independent checker imports neither the producer nor its word tokenizer: it scans the source characters, explicitly replays Fisher–Yates and calculates each Q from direct column slices with rational arithmetic. It checks all observed scores, all 299,994 null scores, minima, ties and tail counts. Both computations agree; human review remains pending.\n",

  "article": "## Question\n\nDo the original-order rune-word lengths from the Warning, Welcome, first koan and second koan give unusually similar means in sixteen columns, compared with unrestricted permutations of those same lengths?\n\nThis record reproduces a supplied numerical observation. The arrangement and approximate result were already known. It tests one stated comparison, not whether the authors intentionally designed the text this way.\n\n## Reconstruct the object before testing it\n\nUse the archived ciphertext, in manuscript order. Count runes, not Latin letters: a rune labeled TH still has length one. Include headings and the interrupting F runes. Remove slash and newline wrapping, concatenate successive pages within each section, and retain other word boundaries. An internal apostrophe belongs to the same word and contributes no rune.\n\n| Section | Pages | Words | Runes |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| Warning | LP1-01 | 45 | 184 |\n| Welcome | LP1-03–04 | 124 | 515 |\n| First koan | LP1-06–09 | 208 | 778 |\n| Second koan | LP1-14–15 | 87 | 319 |\n| Total | Nine pages | 464 | 1796 |\n\nAll 464 reconstructed lengths match the supplied vector exactly. Treating the apostrophe in DON'T as a word separator instead produces 465 tokens: two pieces of lengths three and one replace one four-rune word. That would shift all later column assignments.\n\nThe table is filled across each row from left to right, sixteen words at a time. There are 29 rows. Word 1 goes in row 1, column 1; word 16 in row 1, column 16; word 17 in row 2, column 1. Section boundaries do not reset the column counter.\n\nThe full [29-by-16 length table](experiments/records/lp1-word-length-balance/length-table.csv) is downloadable. The [word ledger](experiments/records/lp1-word-length-balance/words.json) gives each word's original ciphertext, rune length, section, contributing pages, row and column. A word crossing a page boundary records both pages. Neither file silently substitutes contextual English.\n\n## Statistic and exact expectation\n\nLet N = 464, k = 16 columns and m = 29 words per column. For column j, let S_j be its total rune count and M_j = S_j / m its mean word length. Let M be the overall mean word length, 1796/464.\n\nUse the population variance across the sixteen column means:\n\n```\nV = sum((M_j - M)^2) / k\nR = V / E[V under the declared shuffle model]\n```\n\nEach shuffle uniformly permutes the same list of 464 lengths. It keeps the overall distribution and total rune count but destroys word order, sentence structure and section membership. Duplicate lengths remain duplicate observations; there is no sampling of newly invented words.\n\nFor population variance sigma² of the fixed 464 lengths, the finite-population expectation is:\n\n```\nE[V] = sigma² × (k - 1) / (N - 1)\n```\n\nWhy? Each column is a sample of m positions without replacement. Its mean has variance sigma² × (N-m)/(m(N-1)). The grand mean is fixed, so averaging the squared deviations of the column means has this same expectation; N = km gives the expression above. Independence between columns is not assumed.\n\nThe script uses exact rational arithmetic for this expectation and the observed ratio. For shuffle comparisons it uses an integer multiple of V, avoiding floating-point decisions at the tail boundary.\n\n## Findings\n\nThe sixteen column totals are:\n\n```\n113, 105, 119, 111, 112, 118, 110, 111,\n112, 112, 109, 101, 109, 126, 111, 117\n```\n\nEach total is divided by 29 to get its mean. Their deviations from the mean column total, 112.25, have squared sum 501.\n\n| Quantity | Result |\n| --- | --- |\n| Observed variance of column means | 501/13456 |\n| Exact shuffle expectation | 922305/6230128 |\n| R | 77321/307435 = 0.25150356986029565 |\n| Shuffles | 49,999 |\n| Seed | 330146 |\n| Shuffles with variance no greater than observed | 54 |\n| Corrected lower-tail Monte Carlo estimate | (54 + 1)/(49,999 + 1) = 0.0011 |\n\nThe observed variance is about 25.15% of this model's expectation. It falls in the lower tail of the specified comparison, below the predeclared 0.05 threshold. The ratio and expectation are exact; the tail probability is estimated by simulation. Its Monte Carlo standard error is roughly 0.00015, not zero.\n\nThe [results file](experiments/records/lp1-word-length-balance/results.json) includes every simulated integer score, not only the tail count. The chart shows the observed column means. It does not plot the null distribution.\n\n## What this does and does not establish\n\nThe counts, ordering and stated ratio reproduce from the archived runes. Under unrestricted permutations of this fixed multiset, arrangements at least this flat were uncommon in our run.\n\nThis is not a test against ordinary English. Unrestricted shuffling discards linguistic and section structure; an unusual result under that model need not be unusual among coherent texts. It is also not the probability that the observation is a coincidence, that the text was deliberately constructed, or that this arrangement is useful for decryption.\n\nThe original observation resulted from exploration. We knew the selected four sections, width and approximate ratio before this run. The plan was committed before this simulation, but that does not make the original discovery prospective. The reported tail estimate does not account for all earlier choices of populations, widths, orders and statistics.\n\nThe supplied Alice, Gateless Gate and other-LP window counts have not been reproduced here. Exact corpora and conversion rules would be needed. Overlapping windows are dependent, so a fraction of matching windows is not automatically an independent-trial significance calculation.\n\nKeeping punctuation and word boundaries fixed while applying one-output-rune-per-input-rune substitutions preserves these lengths. Decoding does not provide independent confirmation of the same length pattern. Read [cipher invariants](#/wiki/cipher-invariants) and [search space and bounds](#/wiki/search-space) before extending the claim.\n\n## Reproduce and inspect\n\nExtract this experiment's ZIP with its directory structure intact. Python 3 is sufficient; there are no third-party dependencies or network calls.\n\n```\npython experiments/records/lp1-word-length-balance/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/lp1-word-length-balance/check.py\n```\n\nThe first command repeats all 49,999 shuffles and compares the complete results and word ledger. The independent checker uses a character scanner rather than the runner's regular expression, compares every token and length, calculates the observed variance directly from rational column means, and validates the null expectation by exhaustively enumerating two four-element teaching populations. It also independently calculates the first 32 null scores and audits the full saved tail count. A full rerun agreed.\n\nTo regenerate the CSV and chart from the saved outputs:\n\n```\npython experiments/records/lp1-word-length-balance/plot.py\n```\n\nComputational review is complete; human review is pending. The scripts and fixed input hashes define this result. The supplied vector is included only as a comparison target, not used to generate the measured lengths.\n\n## Related questions remain separate\n\nA within-section shuffle is a natural sensitivity test: preserve each section's length distribution while changing its internal order. Other variants can compare section orders, widths or removal rules, with a declared selection procedure.\n\nSection-contribution ledgers, sentence-removal scans, unchanged-rune grilles and the proposed 928-word carrier answer different questions. They are not findings of this record. In particular, 464 is a word count and 1,796 is a rune count; subtracting a count of unchanged runes from 464 would mix units.\n\n## Sources and selection history\n\nInputs are the nine archived LP1 transcription files, with SHA-256 hashes in the plan and record. The complete supplied numerical vector is preserved in submitted-lengths.json. No missing screenshots, spreadsheets or named attachments were treated as available data. The initial count and exact-R reconstruction preceded the frozen simulation plan; that exploratory step is disclosed rather than described as a blind test.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/lp1-word-length-balance/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "5e09fe97ea9b825c2ea4c844a8579df1c05fa9f9544b0db949647083578d367a",

  "reader_question": "Is the 35-rune repetition gap on the opening pages a real periodic clue?",
  "summary": "Lag 35 has 42/694 equal pairs and z=3.759, but 82 of 999 step-shuffled controls reach at least that high a maximum after the same 242-lag scan.",

Also record the predetermined-lag-35 tail and a planted period-35 positive check.",

      "label": "Published lag and parity test",
      "url": "https://github.com/Leo-Y-Zhang/LiberPrimusAnalysis/blob/a32bdc0e06ea58532fbaf4329acae4a0b1020513/lag_and_parity_tests.py"

      "label": "Published original lag results",
      "url": "https://github.com/Leo-Y-Zhang/LiberPrimusAnalysis/blob/a32bdc0e06ea58532fbaf4329acae4a0b1020513/results/lag_and_parity.txt"

  "related": [
    "doublet-lag-profile"

  "article": "## Finding\n\n**The lag-35 peak is real in the transcription, but it is not unusual once the search over 242 lags is counted.** On LP2-00–02, 42 of 694 rune pairs separated by 35 positions are equal, a standardized score of **3.759** against a uniform 29-rune reference. It is the largest score among lags 1–242. Yet **82 of 999** step-shuffled controls have a peak at least this large after undergoing the *same* 242-lag search (one-sided plus-one proportion **83/1,000**).\n\n![The lag-35 score is in the upper, but ordinary, part of the best-of-242 control distribution.](experiments/records/lp2-00-02-lag35-selection/selection.svg)\n\n## Why the search matters\n\n[A public analysis](https://github.com/Leo-Y-Zhang/LiberPrimusAnalysis/blob/a32bdc0e06ea58532fbaf4329acae4a0b1020513/lag_and_parity_tests.py) reported lag 35 as the highest coincidence score in the 729-rune opening section and observed no repeated peaks at 70, 105 or 140. That arithmetic reproduces here. If **35 had been specified before looking**, none of our 999 controls would reach its score at that fixed lag. But 35 was selected as the strongest among 242 candidates; the comparison must select the strongest lag in every control as well.\n\n| Lag | Equal pairs | Standardized score |\n| ---: | ---: | ---: |\n| 35 | 42 / 694 | 3.759 |\n| 70 | 22 / 659 | −0.155 |\n| 105 | 26 / 624 | 0.983 |\n| 140 | 22 / 589 | 0.382 |\n\nThe controls keep the exact inventory of all **728 modular differences between adjacent runes**—including four zero steps, the section's adjacent doublets. Each trial shuffles those differences, reconstructs a 729-rune stream from the original first rune, scans lags 1–242, and retains its largest score. The strongest control scores range from **2.007 to 5.318**; their median is **2.950**. This is a conditional reference for the observed step composition, not a simulation of the manuscript's encryption. The [results](experiments/records/lp2-00-02-lag35-selection/results.json) include all 242 observed lag counts and all 999 maxima.\n\n## What the test can say\n\nThere is no convincing **period-35 recurrence by this coincidence statistic**. A genuine repeating key could leave a peak at 35 or a harmonic, but a weak or interrupted one might not. The absence of harmonics here is descriptive; it does not rule out every interrupted, changing or compound key. The control scan only corrects for choosing among these 242 lags in this section. It does not adjust for choosing the section itself, alternative transcriptions, scoring rules, or many other ideas tried elsewhere.\n\nAs a basic power check, the script plants a 35-periodic 29-symbol sequence with 55% of positions independently replaced. Its strongest scanned lag is 35, with z **29.139**. This is deliberately easy to detect; it verifies the code can recognize a substantial planted recurrence and does not establish power for subtle ones.\n\nReproduce offline with `python experiments/records/lp2-00-02-lag35-selection/run.py --check`, then run `python experiments/records/lp2-00-02-lag35-selection/check.py`. The independent checker recounts the manuscript peak and rebuilds the first ten controls through a separate pair-count calculation. Both scripts use Python's standard library and the archived transcription.\n",

  "article": "# Möbius values of the LP2-15 number panel\n\nA [reported suggestion](#/wiki/reported-attempts?section=lp2-15-mobius-square-transform) applies the arithmetic Möbius function to the numbers at the top of [LP2-15](#/reader/lp2-15). This is a small but exact question: what comes out when we transform **all sixteen printed entries in place**? The source transcript refers to an output image that is not retained in the supplied text, so this is a reconstruction of the stated operation, **not an exact comparison with that historical image**.\n\nThe numbers in the upper part of each cell below are printed on the page; the `μ` values beneath them are calculated. The red `3299` stays in its original row and column. Neither a Fibonacci spiral nor subtraction from 3301 is applied here.\n\n![Four-by-four LP2-15 panel showing each printed decimal number above its calculated arithmetic Möbius value. Only the second row is nonzero.](experiments/records/lp2-15-mobius-panel/panel.svg)\n\n[Open the diagram](experiments/records/lp2-15-mobius-panel/panel.svg) · [View the original page](images/lp2-15.jpg)\n\nThe output matrix, in printed row order, is:\n\n| Row | Column 1 | Column 2 | Column 3 | Column 4 |\n| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |\n| 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |\n| 2 | −1 | −1 | −1 | +1 |\n| 3 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |\n| 4 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |\n\nFor a positive integer `n`, the arithmetic Möbius function is **zero if a prime square divides `n`**. Otherwise it is `−1` for an odd number of distinct prime factors and `+1` for an even number. That rule accounts for each cell; no visual judgement is required to obtain this matrix.\n\n| Printed cell | Factorization | μ |\n| --- | --- | ---: |\n| r1c1 · 3258 | 2 × 3² × 181 | 0 |\n| r1c2 · 3222 | 2 × 3² × 179 | 0 |\n| r1c3 · 3152 | 2⁴ × 197 | 0 |\n| r1c4 · 3038 | 2 × 7² × 31 | 0 |\n| r2c1 · 3278 | 2 × 11 × 149 | −1 |\n| r2c2 · **3299, printed red** | 3299 (prime) | −1 |\n| r2c3 · 3298 | 2 × 17 × 97 | −1 |\n| r2c4 · 2838 | 2 × 3 × 11 × 43 | +1 |\n| r3c1 · 3288 | 2³ × 3 × 137 | 0 |\n| r3c2 · 3294 | 2 × 3³ × 61 | 0 |\n| r3c3 · 3296 | 2⁵ × 103 | 0 |\n| r3c4 · 2472 | 2³ × 3 × 103 | 0 |\n| r4c1 · 4516 | 2² × 1129 | 0 |\n| r4c2 · 1206 | 2 × 3² × 67 | 0 |\n| r4c3 · 708 | 2² × 3 × 59 | 0 |\n| r4c4 · 1820 | 2² × 5 × 7 × 13 | 0 |\n\nTwelve entries vanish; the only nonzero row is `−1, −1, −1, +1`. All but the red entry are even, but **evenness alone does not imply μ = 0**: the three other numbers in row 2 are squarefree. The table shows which prime square makes every zero. The row alignment is an observation of this fixed transform, not a decryption or a significance estimate after possible functions and arrangements have been considered.\n\n## Reproduce it\n\nFrom a checkout or the experiment download, run:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/lp2-15-mobius-panel/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/lp2-15-mobius-panel/check.py\npython experiments/records/lp2-15-mobius-panel/plot.py --check\n```\n\nThe [plan](experiments/records/lp2-15-mobius-panel/plan.json) fixes the source page hash and all sixteen inputs. The producer uses integer factorization; the separate checker searches independently for prime-square divisors and counts distinct prime factors. The [results](experiments/records/lp2-15-mobius-panel/results.json) preserve every coordinate, number, factorization, calculated μ value and the matrix. The diagram is generated from that ledger. The source transcript is identified by hash in the [reported-attempt register](#/wiki/reported-attempts?section=lp2-15-mobius-square-transform), rather than reproduced without its missing image.\n\n**What this establishes:** the stated arithmetic operation is reproducible on the complete printed panel. It does not show that this was exactly the unseen image in the discussion, that a particular row or spiral is a key, or how a `−1/0/+1` stream would act on the runes. A solving test would first have to fix that operation, its order, boundaries and acceptance criterion, then compare continuous output with controls.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/lp2-15-mobius-panel/article.md",

  "article": "# A totient variant of the LP2-15 number panel\n\nThe printed [LP2-15](#/page/lp2-15) panel has sixteen integers. One is prime: the red **3299**. A supplied January 2026 discussion proposes taking Euler’s totient of the prime entries, subtracting the results from 3301, and reading Fibonacci gaps in the resulting prime positions. Its three 4×4 arrays make most of that proposal checkable. They do **not** specify a rule for turning the numbers into plaintext.\n\nThis audit keeps the reported arrays intact. The exact posted gap at row 4, column 1 is **317**, and the row 2, column 2 gap is marked uncertain; neither is silently corrected. The [source intake entry](#/wiki/reported-attempts?section=lp2-15-totient-before-prime-gap) identifies the supplied transcript and its SHA-256 hash.\n\n![Every printed panel cell beside the source's prime candidate, ordinal and proposed Fibonacci gap](experiments/records/lp2-15-totient-gap-audit/panel-audit.svg)\n\n## What the arithmetic actually does\n\nEuler’s totient φ(n) counts positive integers at most n that are coprime to n. For a prime p, φ(p) = p − 1. Only **3299** is prime among the sixteen printed cells, so this first step changes only that cell, to **3298**. The source’s post-totient array matches the computed array in all 16 positions. It now has two adjacent 3298s.\n\nFor each post-totient value x, we calculated **both** 3301 − x and 3301 + x. The source’s second array matches one of these two values at every cell, and all sixteen selected values are prime. Fourteen selected values use subtraction; the entries **4516** and **1206** in the bottom row use addition, producing **7817** and **4507**. Thus the posted label “3301 − X” does not describe the whole array. A single literal subtraction rule would miss those two cells.\n\nPrimality alone leaves a further choice at both 3298 cells: **3** and **6599** are prime. Their zero-based prime ordinals are **1** and **852** respectively. Requiring a *Fibonacci-valued ordinal* selects 3, since 1 is a Fibonacci value and 852 is not. This filter leaves one sign per cell, but the source does not state it as a forward sign-selection rule. The two 3298 cells both become prime **3**, so ordinal **1** is duplicated and ordinal **0** (prime 2) is absent.\n\n| Stage | Match with posted array | Qualification |\n| --- | ---: | --- |\n| Prime-only totient of printed panel | 16/16 | Changes only red 3299. |\n| Candidate from 3301 ± transformed cell | 16/16 | Two cells require `+`; primality alone leaves two cells with either sign. |\n| Selected candidate has Fibonacci zero-based prime index | 16/16 | This condition resolves the sign ambiguity after the candidate set is inspected. |\n| Posted Fibonacci predecessor gap | 14/15 specified | Row 4, column 1 reports 317, while index 987 follows 610 and gives 377; one other cell is marked `?`. |\n\nThe gap calculation is easiest to see in the first row. Prime **43** has zero-based ordinal **13**; the preceding distinct Fibonacci value is **8**, so its gap is **5**. Prime **79** has ordinal **21**, following 13, so its gap is **8**. At bottom left, prime **7817** has ordinal **987**, following **610**, so the corresponding gap is **377**, not the posted 317. The source’s comment `0 /* ? */` leaves the other exceptional cell unresolved. Because the canonical Fibonacci sequence starts **0, 1, 1**, the predecessor of an occurrence of ordinal 1 also depends on which repeated 1 that occurrence is assigned to. The post does not give that assignment.\n\n## What this settles—and what it does not\n\nThe arithmetic reproduces a coherent **derived pattern** from the printed square if the two plus signs and Fibonacci-index sign filter are allowed. It does not construct the original square from independent inputs: it begins with the printed numbers, changes the red one, and then selects signs that produce the reported primes. The established [Fibonacci-indexed prime construction](#/wiki/lp2-15-panel) starts independently with a declared index list, uses absolute distance from 3301, and matches all sixteen printed cells. These are different claims.\n\nNo rule is supplied for which of the source’s arrays should become a cipher key, how it advances through runes, what to do with the duplicate 3 or uncertain gap, or how to score a result. The discussion itself suggests only that a related manipulation *might* apply to the text. This record therefore audits the numbers; it is **inconclusive as a decoding method**.\n\n## Reproduce the audit\n\nFrom the repository root or this experiment’s extracted ZIP, use Python 3 with no external packages:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/lp2-15-totient-gap-audit/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/lp2-15-totient-gap-audit/check.py\npython experiments/records/lp2-15-totient-gap-audit/plot.py --check\n```\n\nThe [plan](experiments/records/lp2-15-totient-gap-audit/plan.json) fixes the source’s three arrays and source hash. The [results](experiments/records/lp2-15-totient-gap-audit/results.json) retain both signs, primality and prime ordinal for every cell. The independent checker uses a sieve and a coprimality count rather than the producer’s factoring and totient implementation. Neither script chooses a plaintext interpretation.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/lp2-15-totient-gap-audit/article.md",

  "article": "# LP2-31: periodic IoC for periods 2–20\n\n**Computationally checked; human review pending.** Codex reran the script and reviewed the separate position-pair oracle on 20 October 2026. This is a bounded statistical result, not a decipherment or a human-reviewed conclusion.\n\nPut every 13th rune of LP2-31 in the same column and ask whether equal runes meet within those columns more often than they would after shuffling the page. Period 13 gives the largest score among the tested periods 2–20, but **213 of 999 shuffled pages reached at least that high a best-period score**. The experiment does not support singling out period 13 at its declared 0.05 threshold. The question, counting rule and other limits follow below.\n\n## Question\n\nDoes LP2-31 have an unusually large within-column coincidence score at any period from 2 through 20, relative to random reorderings of the same rune multiset?\n\nThis is a test of one ordering statistic. It does not attempt decryption or determine whether the page uses Vigenère.\n\n## Scope fixed before the first run\n\nThe plan is in `plan.json`, committed as `e515465` before computing the first result. It selects LP2-31, periods 2–20 inclusive, offset zero, 999 shuffles, seed 330131 and a 0.05 threshold. These are declared choices for this run, not a claim that the question or page was selected independently of all prior research.\n\nThe input is the complete archived rune stream, including headings. Remove every character outside the 29-rune alphabet before assigning positions. No corrections, decryption, region selection or cross-page concatenation are applied. The resulting length is 269 runes. Input paths and SHA-256 hashes are in `record.json` and `results.json`.\n\n## Method\n\nFor period k, put positions with the same remainder modulo k in the same column. Count matching ordered pairs in each column and add them. Divide by the total number of ordered pairs available within all columns:\n\n```\npooled IoC(k) = sum over columns and symbols of n(c,s)*(n(c,s)-1)\n                / sum over columns of N(c)*(N(c)-1)\n```\n\nThis weights columns by their number of pairs; it is not the unweighted mean of column IoCs. No pairs between different columns count.\n\nTake the maximum over all 19 periods. Shuffle the original rune list afresh for each trial, preserving its exact symbol counts. Repeat the entire 19-period scan on every shuffled version and retain that trial's maximum. Compare maxima to maxima, rather than comparing the selected observed peak with an unselected single-period null distribution.\n\nThe random generator is Python's `random.Random(330131)`, using `shuffle`. Exact rational comparisons include ties. The Monte Carlo value is:\n\n```\n(1 + number of shuffled maxima >= observed maximum) / (999 + 1)\n```\n\nAll observed period scores are retained. Each shuffled trial stores all 19 numerators, aligned with the observed periods. Their denominators do not depend on rune order and are stored once in the observed rows. The trial maximum is also stored as an exact fraction.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nFrom the repository root, using Python 3.12.10 and its standard library:\n\n```\npython experiments/records/lp2-31-periodic-ioc/check.py\npython experiments/records/lp2-31-periodic-ioc/run.py --check\n```\n\nThe independent check enumerates pairs of positions directly, instead of counting frequencies in columns. It checks a constant string, an alternating string, and every tested period of the actual page. The alternating control has pooled IoC 1 at period 2.\n\nThe full rerun compares every stored field, including all shuffle scores and input hashes. It should report exact reproduction and:\n\n```\nn: 269\nbest_periods: [13]\nexceedances: 213\nmonte_carlo_p: 0.214\nbelow_threshold: false\n```\n\nTo save a separate report:\n\n```\npython experiments/records/lp2-31-periodic-ioc/run.py --output my-periodic-ioc.json\n```\n\nAn existing output file is never overwritten. No network service, model, API key or third-party package is used. A changed input hash or random-generator behavior can prevent byte-for-byte reproduction; investigate rather than replacing the expected output automatically.\n\n## Results\n\n![Observed pooled IoC by period. The highest bar is period 13; the maximum-adjusted shuffle comparison is p = 0.214.](experiments/records/lp2-31-periodic-ioc/period-scan.svg)\n\n\nPeriod 13 has the unique largest observed score: 216 / 5300 = 0.04075471698. Its columns contain 20 or 21 runes.\n\nOf 999 random reorderings, 213 have a maximum at least this large somewhere in the same period range. The corrected Monte Carlo value is 214 / 1000 = 0.214. It is not below the declared 0.05 threshold.\n\nFor scale, the approximate Monte Carlo standard error of the estimated tail frequency is 0.013, using sqrt(q*(1-q)/999) with q = 213/999. This describes simulation uncertainty, not uncertainty about a cipher or plaintext. The reported Monte Carlo value has increments of 0.001.\n\n## Interpretation and limitations\n\nThis run does not provide evidence, at the declared threshold, for singling out period 13 from this scan. It does not establish that LP2-31 lacks periodic structure. A cipher may produce structure that this statistic, input convention or period range does not detect.\n\nThe null model treats rune order as exchangeable conditional on its counts. It does not preserve word lengths, punctuation positions, local repeated patterns or possible region boundaries. Rejecting it would not prove any particular encryption method. Failing to reject it does not prove randomness.\n\nThe maximum comparison accounts for selecting among periods 2–20 in this run. It does not correct for choosing LP2-31, trying different text regions or previous unrelated tests. Periods outside the range, other pages, corrected streams, alternative statistics and actual key searches remain untested here.\n\nNo shift or Vigenère key is inferred. The period-13 peak is retained as a descriptive result, not promoted to a solution.\n\n## Sources and related work\n\n- [LP2-31 record and original-source links](https://jelliottdev.github.io/#/page/lp2-31)\n- [IoC definition, baseline and invariants](https://jelliottdev.github.io/#/wiki/index-of-coincidence)\n- [Reproducibility requirements](https://jelliottdev.github.io/#/wiki/reproducibility)\n\nThe whole-page baseline does not test ordering: shuffling preserves global IoC. This experiment adds an order-sensitive column statistic and a declared shuffle comparison. No earlier experiment is imported as a completed run.\n\n## Retest and changes after inspection\n\nOn 20 October 2026, the independent position-pair check passed, and all observed and simulated numerical fields reproduced exactly. The only difference from the first saved output was the SHA-256 of `data/index.json`, whose page metadata had since changed. The plan and rune input hashes were unchanged. No period range, threshold, seed, sample count, or scoring rule was changed.\n\nThe original report is preserved as [original output](experiments/records/lp2-31-periodic-ioc/results-original.json). The [current report](experiments/records/lp2-31-periodic-ioc/results.json) records the current input hash. The checked script reproduces the current report exactly, including all 999 trials. The [chart script](experiments/records/lp2-31-periodic-ioc/plot.py) reads that report without running another experiment.\n\nThis record is the baseline for the periodic-IoC shuffle family. Future variants must identify each changed scope field and give their own plan, output and interpretation. A [within-row shuffle variant](#/experiments/lp2-31-row-shuffle-ioc) now preserves each archived row’s length and rune counts while leaving the observed statistic unchanged. Human review is still pending; the computational review was performed by Codex, not by an independent human researcher.\n",

  "article": "# LP2-31 periodic IoC: preserving row composition\n\n## Why change the null model?\n\nThe baseline shuffles all 269 runes together. That preserves the page's total counts but can move any rune to any row. If rows differ in composition, that comparison removes those differences as well as the ordering under investigation.\n\nThis variant instead preserves each archived row's length and exact rune counts, shuffling only within that row. It asks a conditional question about order after holding row composition fixed. This is not automatically a better model; it makes a different assumption visible.\n\nLP2-31 has twelve ordinary text rows and no separately identified heading. No row was removed or renamed as a heading for this test. Archived transcription lines provide the boundaries.\n\n## Plan and relation to the baseline\n\nThe plan and runner were committed as `8dfc7c0` before executing the variant. The variant was motivated after the whole-page result was known; it is not independent confirmation and does not account for selecting among null models.\n\nOnly the shuffle procedure changes. The input remains the same 269 runes, periods remain 2–20 inclusive, the statistic remains pooled within-column matching pairs, and each trial's maximum is compared with the observed maximum. There are still 999 trials, seed 330131, greater-than-or-equal ties, plus-one Monte Carlo correction, and a 0.05 threshold.\n\nThe twelve row lengths are:\n\n```\n23, 22, 24, 24, 22, 22, 21, 22, 21, 24, 22, 22\n```\n\nRemove non-alphabet characters inside each row, shuffle that row's runes, then concatenate rows in their original order. Column positions run across the concatenated page; they do not restart at row boundaries. The same seed does not make the two models' individual shuffled pages equivalent or create a paired statistical test.\n\n## Results\n\n| Quantity | Whole-page baseline | Within-row variant |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| Input runes | 269 | 269 |\n| Observed peak period | 13 | 13 |\n| Observed peak fraction | 216/5300 | 216/5300 |\n| Null maxima at least observed | 213/999 | 245/999 |\n| Plus-one Monte Carlo p | 0.214 | 0.246 |\n| Below declared 0.05 threshold | No | No |\n\nThe observed scores agree exactly for every period, as they should: the observed input and scoring procedure did not change. The within-row comparison is 246/1000 = 0.246. Its approximate Monte Carlo standard error is 0.014, using sqrt(q*(1-q)/999) with q=245/999. This describes simulation uncertainty, not confidence in a cipher.\n\nThe two runs give the same threshold decision under their different assumptions. The difference between 0.214 and 0.246 is not evaluated as a separate statistical effect, and neither p-value is the probability that period 13 is the true key length.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nFrom a repository checkout with Python 3.12.10:\n\n```\npython experiments/records/lp2-31-row-shuffle-ioc/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/lp2-31-row-shuffle-ioc/check.py\n```\n\nThe runner compares every observed field and all 999 stored trial records. The separate checker verifies the twelve row lengths, exact agreement with the baseline's observed scores, and a position-pair oracle for all observed periods and the first three seeded null trials. That oracle directly enumerates position pairs rather than using column-frequency counts. The runner also asserts preservation of each row's multiset in every trial.\n\n[Download the complete variant output](experiments/records/lp2-31-row-shuffle-ioc/results.json). All 19 period numerators are stored for every shuffle; the denominators are in the observed rows. The comparison diagram is generated from the two saved reports. Neither the checker nor the plot interprets candidate plaintext or calls an AI service.\n\n## Retest and changes after inspection\n\nCodex reran the complete variant and performed the separate checks on 20 October 2026. Every stored field reproduced. No null rule, period range, input boundary, seed, threshold or statistic changed after the variant's first result. The checker and comparison graphic were added afterward for verification and presentation. Human review remains pending.\n\n## Interpretation and remaining limits\n\nThis row-conditioned null preserves more local composition than the whole-page null, but still discards within-row word boundaries and local patterns. It treats all rune permutations within a row as exchangeable. Neither model is a full model of a particular cipher or language.\n\nThis variant does not show that the page is random, that period 13 is impossible, or that Vigenère is absent. It also does not test different pages, period ranges, row selections, alternative statistics or key searches. Those changes must be documented separately rather than silently folded into this result.\n",

  "article": "# LP2-32 grid sums and the 2016 message\n\nThis recount reproduces three numerical equalities: **563, 569 and 1136**. They are the first-row sum, first-column sum and central 5×5 perimeter sum of a specified arrangement of LP2-32. The preserved 2016 image measures 563×569 pixels, and its extracted payload contains 1,136 bytes.\n\n“Supported” refers to these exact calculations. It does not establish that the correspondence was intended, statistically unusual or useful for decryption.\n\n## Construct the grid\n\nUse the archived LP2-32 text. Keep all 121 alphabet runes, remove separators, and place the stream left-to-right into eleven rows of eleven. Do not reverse, rotate, pad or omit runes. Replace each rune with its stored Gematria Primus prime value.\n\nThis is an analytical rearrangement. It is not a claim that the original manuscript has eleven printed lines. The JSON records every grid cell, its original rune ordinal and its source-text character offset so the rearrangement can be followed back to the page.\n\n## Exactly which cells are summed?\n\nThe first row is grid row 1, columns 1–11. The first column is column 1, rows 1–11. They share the top-left cell, so these measurements are not disjoint.\n\nThe central 5×5 block occupies rows 4–8 and columns 4–8, using one-based coordinates. Sum its outer border, counting each corner once. That is 16 cells: five across the top, five across the bottom, and three additional cells down each side. Do not include the central nine cells or count corners twice.\n\nIn the enlarged figure, the top border sums to 275 and the bottom border to 373. The three remaining left-edge cells sum to 231; the three remaining right-edge cells sum to 257. Thus `275 + 373 + 231 + 257 = 1136`. This decomposition counts each corner exactly once.\n\n| Quantity | Value |\n| --- | --- |\n| Rune count | 121 |\n| Sum of all 121 prime values | 6045 |\n| First row | 563 |\n| First column | 569 |\n| Central 5×5 perimeter | 1136 |\n| Original 2016 JPEG width × height | 563 × 569 |\n| Preserved OutGuess payload bytes | 1136 |\n\nThe output also lists all eleven row sums, all eleven column sums and all 49 placements of a contiguous 5×5 block within this grid. Only the central block has perimeter sum 1136 under these rules. That statement concerns those 49 placements; it is not a chance probability over other layouts, page choices or target numbers.\n\n## What was compared with the grid?\n\nThe image measurement comes from the original JPEG frame header, not a displayed preview. Payload length means raw bytes in the preserved extracted signed message, including its armor and formatting. It does not mean visible characters, plaintext letters, pixels or the JPEG file size.\n\nThe [later-message guide](#/wiki/later-messages) separately documents an exact OutGuess extraction and signature verification. This recount uses those preserved bytes and hashes them; it does not need to run OutGuess again. The [Wing and Tree guide](#/wiki/wing-and-tree) locates the manuscript drawing. A numerical match does not prove that the two tree images have the same source.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nExtract this experiment’s ZIP with its directory structure intact. It includes the payload, scripts and text inputs. Download the [original 2016 JPEG](images/message-2016.jpg) separately and save it as `images/message-2016.jpg` inside the extracted folder. The ZIP’s image-input manifest gives its checksum. Python’s standard library is sufficient.\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/lp2-32-message-grid/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/lp2-32-message-grid/check.py\n```\n\nThe producer reads the rune text and parses JPEG segment headers. The checker reads the separate archived page record, uses flat-index cell sets to recount the perimeters, and checks the image’s baseline frame header independently. Both use the same stored alphabet, so their agreement does not independently resolve transcription ambiguities.\n\n## Limits and follow-up\n\nThe original lead selected this page, arrangement and central border for inspection. No null model or accounting for other explored arrangements is supplied here. A follow-up can test a stated family of layouts or a fixed shuffle model, but should not describe this one successful comparison as an exhaustive search. See [search space and bounds](#/wiki/search-space) and [null models](#/wiki/null-models).\n\n## Recreate the diagram\n\nThe SVG is included in the experiment ZIP. The drawing reads the stored cell ledger directly; its numbers are not manually retyped. Install Matplotlib if you want to recreate it, then choose a new output filename:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/lp2-32-message-grid/plot.py --output my-grid.svg\n```\n\nThe drawing script refuses to overwrite an existing file. Plotting is optional; the producer and independent checker still use only Python’s standard library.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/lp2-32-message-grid/article.md",

  "article": "## What was tested?\n\nThe lower text block on [LP2-39](#/page/lp2-39) starts with three red runes, followed by punctuation. The first rune is enlarged across several rows. Read in manuscript order, the archived prefix is IA + C + S, with zero-based indices 27, 5 and 15. The Latin labels describe the ciphertext symbols; they are not an English reading.\n\nA **crib** is a proposed plaintext fragment. This experiment takes twenty suggested words and asks whether any single affine substitution maps the word to those three runes. It checks the entire declared key space, rather than adjusting a separate shift for each position.\n\nThe candidate list is fixed in plan.json. It is a selected list, not a dictionary or an unbiased sample of possible headings. WHY was already in the list before this calculation; no new words were added after inspecting the result.\n\n## Representation comes before the key search\n\nWords are uppercased and split in every possible way using the 29 Latin labels stored in the [GP alphabet and rune values](#/wiki/rune-values). There are no pronunciation rules or spelling substitutions. TH may be one label or T + H; NG may be one label or N + G.\n\nBEING does **not** have a three-rune representation under these rules. Its two segmentations are B + E + I + NG (four) and B + E + I + N + G (five). The suggested B + EI + NG would need an EI label that is absent from this alphabet. A proposed alias can be tested separately, but it must be declared rather than silently substituted.\n\nTHUS has three runes as TH + U + S, or four as T + H + U + S. Their prime sums are 61 and 138 respectively. These sums are recorded for transparency; primality is not used to select a candidate or key. See [word lengths](#/wiki/word-lengths) and [spelling and prime sums](#/wiki/prime-sums).\n\n## Search bounds and complete result\n\nThe encryption rule is C = (aP + b) mod 29, using rune indices rather than prime values. Test every a from 1 through 28 and every b from 0 through 28: **812 keys**. Multiplication by any allowed a is invertible modulo 29. This space includes ordinary shifts and shifted alphabet reversals.\n\nThe twenty words give 22 segmentations. Seventeen have the required three runes, so the complete search contains **17 × 812 = 13,804 candidate/key trials**. Wrong-length candidates are retained below instead of disappearing from the report.\n\n| Candidate | Rune lengths | Result |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| AND | 3 | No affine fit |\n| BUT | 3 | No affine fit |\n| WHY | 3 | a = 7, b = 7 |\n| HOW | 3 | No affine fit |\n| WHO | 3 | No affine fit |\n| YOU | 3 | No affine fit |\n| HER | 3 | No affine fit |\n| HIM | 3 | No affine fit |\n| HIS | 3 | No affine fit |\n| ONE | 3 | No affine fit |\n| TWO | 3 | No affine fit |\n| WAY | 3 | No affine fit |\n| MAP | 3 | No affine fit |\n| LAW | 3 | No affine fit |\n| GOD | 3 | No affine fit |\n| BEING | 5, 4 | Wrong length |\n| OLD | 3 | No affine fit |\n| THUS | 3, 4 | No affine fit |\n| FOLLY | 5 | Wrong length |\n| WISDOM | 6 | Wrong length |\n\nOnly WHY matches. Its rune indices are W = 7, H = 8 and Y = 26. The single key a = 7, b = 7 produces:\n\n| Position | Proposed index P | 7P + 7 | Reduced modulo 29 | Cipher label |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| 1 | 7 | 56 | 27 | IA |\n| 2 | 8 | 63 | 5 | C |\n| 3 | 26 | 189 | 15 | S |\n\n## Why this is not a solution\n\nThree symbols provide very little independent constraint. Because the first two proposed indices differ, they determine an affine key; the third position tests that key. Here the check was repeated across seventeen eligible candidates. Finding one fit does not establish that the authors intended WHY, or that this key applies to the following text.\n\nFor this three-symbol ciphertext, the 812 invertible affine keys produce 812 distinct three-symbol candidate plaintexts. A short word among those outputs needs further evidence. This is a search-space count, not a probability estimate for English words or for the authors' choices.\n\nThis experiment does not score the remaining text, use a language model, or select a key by how promising the continuation sounds. The recorded outcome is **inconclusive** about the reading. The exact header fit is reproducible; a decipherment is not established.\n\nA follow-up should freeze the surviving key and test text outside the three-rune crib against an explicit criterion. If it fails, inventing fresh per-position shifts would define a different method, not rescue this affine result. Keep such changes in separate variants within this family. See [search space and bounds](#/wiki/search-space) and [cipher invariants](#/wiki/cipher-invariants).\n\n## Reproduce and inspect\n\nDownload this experiment's ZIP and extract it with its folders intact. Both commands use Python's standard library and run offline:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/lp2-39-header-cribs/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/lp2-39-header-cribs/check.py\n```\n\nThe first script enumerates label prefixes and all affine keys. The independent checker enumerates every possible cut in each spelling, locates the header from the archived paragraph boundary, and derives a key algebraically from the first two positions before checking the third. It does not import the search implementation.\n\nresults.json retains every segmentation, its indices, rune count, prime sum and matching keys. plan.json fixes the candidate list, normalization, source position and key bounds. Changing any of these should produce a named variant, with the old result retained for comparison.\n",

  "visuals": [
    {
      "path": "experiments/records/lp2-54-55-autokey-reset/period-profile.svg",
      "caption": "Observed pooled IoC by period: no interruptions versus the best of all 64 F masks. Each point on the upper curve can use a different mask. The statistical test compares the maximum over the entire search, not each point separately."

  "article": "## What is being tested?\n\nA reported periodic-IoC peak on LP2-54–55 motivates this test. The index of coincidence (IoC) measures how often symbols match within groups of positions. We ask whether a specified ciphertext-feedback rule, with some F runes treated as interruptions, makes that score unusually high after searching every permitted interruption pattern and period.\n\nThe answer under the declared comparison is **no**: 543 of 999 shuffled inputs produced a maximum at least as high as the manuscript's. This is a new bounded implementation. The source discussion names scripts and plots, but their complete files were not supplied, so we cannot claim to reproduce their exact processing or graphs.\n\n## Ciphertext feedback, step by step\n\nRepresent each rune by its zero-based index in the 29-rune alphabet. F has index zero. Keep a state containing the preceding ciphertext value, initially zero. For an ordinary rune:\n\n```\noutput = (current ciphertext - previous ciphertext state) mod 29\nprevious ciphertext state = current ciphertext\n```\n\nThat is ciphertext feedback: the state receives the input rune, not the decoded output. Plaintext autokey is a different recurrence.\n\nFor a selected F interruption, emit F unchanged, set the previous ciphertext state to zero, and exclude that emitted F from the scored stream. Unselected F runes follow the ordinary rule. After removing selected Fs, number the remaining output consecutively from zero for the periodic calculation.\n\nThe sibling [skip variant](#/experiments/lp2-54-55-autokey-skip) changes only how the state behaves at a selected interruption. A useful distinction: in reset mode, ordinary adjacent ciphertext differencing already uses F=0 as the next state. Selecting an F therefore removes its own scored output without otherwise changing the following arithmetic. Skip mode instead changes the next non-interruption output by retaining the earlier ciphertext value.\n\n## A small control before the manuscript\n\nIn a teaching alphabet modulo ten, encrypt plaintext 1,2,0,3,4 with initial state zero and the third position selected as an interruption:\n\n| Rule | Ciphertext |\n| --- | --- |\n| Reset state at the selected zero | 1,3,0,3,7 |\n| Retain state across the selected zero | 1,3,0,6,0 |\n\nThe skip result is 13060, not 13064. Once the next ordinary symbol is processed, the state must update again; carrying an extra lag forward changes the cipher. The checker verifies encryption and decryption in both directions, including leading, adjacent and trailing interruptions.\n\n## Inputs and search bounds\n\nConcatenate archived LP2-54 and LP2-55, including the heading and removing punctuation. There are 232 + 76 = 308 runes. The state does not reset at the page break.\n\nThe six F positions in this combined stream are 41, 65, 195, 247, 257 and 273, counted from zero. A mask is a compact way to specify a subset: bit zero selects the first F, bit one the second, and so on. Mask 0 selects none; mask 63 selects all six. Every one of the 64 masks is tested.\n\nFor each output, test all periods 2 through 30 inclusive. Period k groups output positions by their remainder modulo k. Pool ordered equal-symbol pairs across those columns, then divide by all ordered within-column pairs:\n\n```\npooled IoC = sum over columns and runes of count * (count - 1)\n             / sum over columns of length * (length - 1)\n```\n\nThis weights columns by their available pairs. It is not an unweighted average of column IoCs. The search has 64 × 29 = 1,856 parameter configurations; that count does not claim independent evidence from every configuration. See [index of coincidence](#/wiki/index-of-coincidence) and [search bounds](#/wiki/search-space).\n\n## Comparison model\n\nEach of 999 trials retains all six F positions and shuffles the other 302 ciphertext values. It preserves the complete rune counts and length but discards the order of non-F symbols. Each trial starts from a fresh copy; the random seed is 330154.\n\nRepeat the entire 64-mask, 29-period search on every shuffled input and retain its maximum. Comparing the observed maximum with these maxima accounts for mask and period selection inside this declared search. It does not account for the earlier exploration that suggested the pages, cipher model or broader analysis choices.\n\nThe two modes use the same shuffled inputs. Their results are related comparisons, not independent replications. We report individual upper-tail estimates and Bonferroni-adjusted estimates for the two planned modes. This adjustment does not turn the original discovery into a prospective test.\n\n## Result\n\n| Quantity | Measured result |\n| --- | --- |\n| Unique winning mask | 0: no selected interruptions |\n| Winning period | 13 |\n| Largest pooled IoC | 332/6992 = 83/1748, approximately 0.04748284 |\n| Null maxima at least as large | 543 of 999 |\n| Corrected Monte Carlo estimate | (543 + 1)/1000 = 0.544 |\n| Adjusted for the two planned modes | 1.0 |\n\nNeither the individual estimate nor its two-mode adjustment is below the declared 0.05 threshold. A period-13 peak exists descriptively in this processing, but the test finds no evidence that the selected maximum exceeds this conditional shuffle reference. This is not a decryption and does not rule out period 13, ciphertext autokey or different interruption rules generally.\n\nThe [period profile CSV](experiments/records/lp2-54-55-autokey-reset/period-profile.csv) records the best mask at each period alongside the no-interruption score. Its chart joins those observed scores for readability; the upper line may switch masks between points. The [complete results](experiments/records/lp2-54-55-autokey-reset/results.json) retain all 1,856 observed ratios, every null maximum and its winning configurations, plus a source-position trace for each observed winning mask.\n\n## Reproduce and audit\n\nExtract this record's ZIP with its directories intact. The skip variant includes shared code under the reset record's directory; do not flatten the folders. No third-party packages, network calls or AI service are required.\n\n```\npython experiments/records/lp2-54-55-autokey-reset/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/lp2-54-55-autokey-reset/check.py\n```\n\nThe full rerun reproduces the observed scores, winning traces and all 999 null maxima. The independent checker uses direct ciphertext indexing instead of mutable feedback state, enumerates same-column pairs to audit every observed score, reconstructs the first two complete null searches with frequency counts, verifies winning traces by re-encryption, and audits the saved tail count. Both checks passed; human review remains pending.\n\nTo rebuild the chart and CSV:\n\n```\npython experiments/records/lp2-54-55-autokey-reset/plot.py experiments/records/lp2-54-55-autokey-reset\n```\n\n## Remaining questions\n\nThis model conditions on the observed F locations. It does not measure whether those locations themselves are unusual. It also says nothing about a prose-generating model, different interruption symbols, primers, heading omissions, page-local resets, other period ranges or language-scored candidates. Each changed question needs explicit scope and fresh controls. A high score from any such later search must be compared with a reference that repeats that search.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/lp2-54-55-autokey-reset/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "71af5f8e5e0b05e6294eda373276532bad6cadda9cc68955ab1ab3531fe76716",
  "record_type": {
    "id": "measurement",
    "label": "Manuscript measurement",
    "description": "Measures a stated feature or statistical comparison; it does not test a complete decoding rule."
  }
}

No third-party packages, network calls or AI service are required.\n\n```\npython experiments/records/lp2-54-55-autokey-skip/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/lp2-54-55-autokey-skip/check.py\n```\n\nThe full rerun reproduces the observed scores, winning traces and all 999 null maxima. The independent checker uses direct ciphertext indexing instead of mutable feedback state, enumerates same-column pairs to audit every observed score, reconstructs the first two complete null searches with frequency counts, verifies winning traces by re-encryption, and audits the saved tail count. Both checks passed; human review remains pending.\n\nTo rebuild the chart and CSV:\n\n```\npython experiments/records/lp2-54-55-autokey-reset/plot.py experiments/records/lp2-54-55-autokey-skip\n```\n\n## Remaining questions\n\nThis model conditions on the observed F locations. It does not measure whether those locations themselves are unusual. It also says nothing about a prose-generating model, different interruption symbols, primers, heading omissions, page-local resets, other period ranges or language-scored candidates. Each changed question needs explicit scope and fresh controls. A high score from any such later search must be compared with a reference that repeats that search.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/lp2-54-55-autokey-skip/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "61519888e03b79102eaa10e775dcb993c0109610ee90d8482aedba39b580e5d9",

  "related": [
    "sectionwise-rune-profile"
  ],
  "article": "# Can the last two pages form an 8×8 word grid?\n\n**Yes, under the proposed heading exclusion.** The archived text has **66 words** beginning on LP2-54–55. The red opening is a one-rune word followed by an eight-rune word. Removing those two leaves **64 words**: 48 begin on LP2-54 and 16 on LP2-55. In manuscript order, they fill exactly six rows and two rows of an 8×8 grid.\n\n![Eight-by-eight grid of word positions: six rows start on LP2-54 and two on LP2-55.](experiments/records/lp2-54-55-word-square/word-square.svg)\n\nThis is a clean **arrangement**, not a reading. One of the 64 words crosses the page boundary; the grid keeps it whole and assigns it to the page where it starts. An independent check reconstructs all 66 words directly from the two page transcriptions and agrees with the archived word-token export.\n\nThe proposed “labyrinth” continuation does not give a start corner or turning direction. Even the simplest inward orthogonal spiral has **eight** different corner/direction variants on this grid. All visit every cell once, and each begins with a different sequence. The [saved result](experiments/records/lp2-54-55-word-square/results.json) lists all eight routes; it does not select the one whose output looks best. A decipherment test still needs a fixed route, a rule for turning words into cipher material, and an output criterion set before reading it.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nRun `python experiments/records/lp2-54-55-word-square/run.py --check` and `python experiments/records/lp2-54-55-word-square/check.py` from the repository root. The [plan](experiments/records/lp2-54-55-word-square/plan.json) pins the page transcriptions, word export and page images. The source suggestion is recorded in the supplied September 2026 discussion; the [page record](#/page/lp2-54) shows the red opening.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/lp2-54-55-word-square/article.md",

  "article": "# LP2-54: do the simple header autokeys make an eight-rune word?\n\nThe red opening of [LP2-54](#/reader/lp2-54) has a single rune followed by eight: `ᚪ-ᛗᛝᛞᛡᚦᛉᛁᛗ`. A reported attempt proposed **A**, **I** or **O** for the first plaintext rune and considered autokey feedback for the next word. The [earlier fixed-rule record](#/experiments/lp2-54-header-feedback) calculates all nine output runes for both simple feedback rules. Here the narrower question is whether **any of those six eight-rune outputs is an English word in a fixed corpus**.\n\n![The six fixed outputs, all without a corpus match.](experiments/records/lp2-54-header-dictionary/header-cribs.svg)\n\n**Result: zero of six match.** The pinned corpus has **19,715 distinct eight-rune spellings** among 138,466 entries. The same six calculations on **all 13** visible one-rune/eight-rune word pairs across LP2-00–55 also produce no corpus matches. Both planted `A MOUNTAIN` controls decode correctly, one for each feedback rule. The all-page comparison is context, **not a p-value**: those 13 pairs were not random draws from English.\n\nThe rules are exact. Convert the nine cipher runes to zero-based Gematria Primus indices modulo 29. Choose A, I or O at position zero, which fixes the primer. With ciphertext feedback, each later plaintext index is the current cipher index minus the *previous cipher* index. With plaintext feedback, subtract the *previous plaintext* index instead. Keep the printed one-plus-eight break. We looked up only the resulting eight-rune sequence, after mapping the corpus's alternate J rune to the manuscript's J rune. No word was selected to influence a key or an alignment.\n\n| First rune | Feedback | Eight-rune output, by GP label | Corpus match |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| A | Ciphertext | A TH TH R R EO AE N | No |\n| A | Plaintext | A Y Y U U P Y OE | No |\n| I | Ciphertext | A TH TH R R EO AE N | No |\n| I | Plaintext | N EO J T S EA J H | No |\n| O | Ciphertext | A TH TH R R EO AE N | No |\n| O | Plaintext | T C/K E N OE NG E U | No |\n\nThe repeated ciphertext-feedback row is expected: after the first position, that rule depends only on adjacent ciphertext, so changing the first-rune crib cannot change the second word. The pinned corpus is a finite vocabulary, not every possible English spelling or phonetic rune transliteration. A word miss therefore excludes **these two literal one-step rules with these first-rune choices and this corpus**. It does not test the source discussion's unspecified C/K/D functions, extra cipher layers, changed word boundaries, interruption positions, or a complete LP2 reading. A more flexible search must state its transforms and total candidate count before judging a hit.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nUse the [experiment bundle](downloads/experiments/lp2-54-header-dictionary.zip) or a checkout, then run:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/lp2-54-header-dictionary/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/lp2-54-header-dictionary/check.py\npython experiments/records/lp2-54-header-dictionary/plot.py --check\n```\n\nThe [plan](experiments/records/lp2-54-header-dictionary/plan.json) specifies the rules and exclusions. The [full result](experiments/records/lp2-54-header-dictionary/results.json) lists every eligible page pair and all 78 outputs. The preserved word list is separately attributed to [Liber Primus Crib Assist at revision `9c10caf`](https://github.com/mortlach/Liber-Primus-Crib-Assist/tree/9c10cafce02e512840cc9e173127930594a56281/data/1_grams-full); it is not claimed to be the exact dictionary used by the original reporter.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/lp2-54-header-dictionary/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "19687e94e9ccbf64cbae40582ea974a6f8d181f5956d1e8612e13e1b76720497",

}
