  "visuals": [
    {
      "path": "experiments/records/lp2-trigram-repeats/null-distribution.svg",
      "caption": "Observed matching-trigram pair total (55) against 999 full-dataset shuffles preserving each page’s rune counts. Windows overlap; comparisons never cross pages. Upper-tail p=0.799."
    }
  ],
  "article": "# Are three-rune repeats unusually frequent?\n\nFinding a repeated group of runes is easy to notice. Deciding whether there are more repeats than the page's symbol frequencies would ordinarily produce is a different question. This experiment compares a fixed repeat count across LP2-00–55 with whole-page shuffles that preserve every page's rune frequencies.\n\nThe archived input contains **55 matching pairs of three-rune windows**. Of 999 shuffled datasets, 798 have at least 55. The corrected upper-tail p-value is **0.799**, above the predeclared 0.05 threshold. This test provides no evidence of excess trigram repetition under this particular model.\n\n## Count pairs, not just patterns\n\nA trigram is a window of three consecutive runes. Move the window one rune at a time, including overlaps. A stream of N runes supplies `max(0, N − 2)` windows.\n\nIf one trigram occurs c times on a page, it contributes `c × (c − 1) / 2` matching pairs. The statistic adds these contributions over patterns and then over pages. It never compares a window on one page with a window on another.\n\n| Invented stream | Three-rune windows | Matching pairs |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| ABC | ABC | 0 |\n| AAAA | AAA, AAA | 1 |\n| AAAAA | AAA, AAA, AAA | 3 |\n| ABABA | ABA, BAB, ABA | 1 |\n\nFor AAAAA, the three starting positions are 0, 1 and 2. The matching pairs are (0,1), (0,2) and (1,2). Counting “one repeated pattern” would measure something different. These letters are illustrative single symbols, not manuscript plaintext.\n\n## Input and boundaries\n\nThe input retains all recognized alphabet runes from the archived transcriptions, including headings. Punctuation, word separators, line markers and other non-rune characters are removed. Windows can therefore cross an archived word or line boundary. They do not wrap around the end of a page.\n\nLP2-50 has no recognized runes. It remains in the report with zero windows and zero matching pairs. Across the other 55 pages there are 12,846 windows. The input hashes and full alphabet source are recorded in the plan.\n\nThis test concerns the archived rune stream. It is not a fresh visual transcription, a count of repeated words, or a comparison of decoded English. See the [n-gram guide](#/wiki/rune-ngrams) for source-position conventions and examples of repeats that cross separators.\n\n## What the shuffles preserve\n\nEach simulated dataset independently rearranges the full rune stream of every page. It preserves each page's length and every single-rune count. Runes never move between pages. The procedure then calculates the same overlapping-window statistic on the shuffled pages and adds their scores.\n\nThis changes adjacency. It does not preserve row composition, word lengths as linguistic units, existing bigrams or repeated phrases. A different comparison model could answer a different question.\n\nThe calculation does not assume the overlapping windows are independent observations. It simulates whole streams and applies the full counting rule, including overlaps, to each simulated stream.\n\n## Recorded result\n\n![Distribution of matching trigram-pair totals across 999 shuffled LP2 datasets, compared with the observed total of 55.](experiments/records/lp2-trigram-repeats/null-distribution.svg)\n\n| Quantity | Result |\n| --- | --- |\n| Observed matching pairs | 55 |\n| Distinct repeated patterns, counted within page | 55 |\n| Shuffled datasets | 999 |\n| Shuffled total range | 33–89 |\n| Mean shuffled total | Approximately 61.39 |\n| Shuffled totals at least 55 | 798 |\n| Corrected upper-tail p-value | (798 + 1) / (999 + 1) = 0.799 |\n| Declared threshold | 0.05 |\n\nIn this observed dataset, each repeated pattern occurs exactly twice within its page, so the pattern count and pair count happen to agree. The controls above show why those counts need not agree generally.\n\nThe upper tail includes ties. The numerator and denominator each receive a one-count correction for the sampled permutation calculation, as described in the [SciPy permutation-test documentation](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy-1.16.0/reference/generated/scipy.stats.permutation_test.html). The runner uses its own standard-library shuffles and integer score, not SciPy's implementation.\n\nThe simulation is an estimate, not an enumeration of every possible arrangement. Its approximate Monte Carlo standard error is 0.013, using `sqrt(q × (1 − q) / 999)` with `q = 798 / 999`. That sampling uncertainty does not account for transcription uncertainty or a poorly chosen model.\n\nThe observed total is below the simulation mean, but the declared question concerns an **excess**. This record does not reinterpret the result as a significant deficit or switch to a lower-tail test after inspection.\n\n## Reproduce and inspect\n\nFrom the repository root, using Python 3.12.10 and its standard library:\n\n```sh\npython experiments/records/lp2-trigram-repeats/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/lp2-trigram-repeats/check.py\n```\n\nThe first command repeats all observed counts and 999 complete-dataset shuffles with seed 330134, comparing every field against the saved report. Random-number implementation details are part of reproducibility; use the recorded Python environment when comparing exact simulated sequences.\n\nThe separate checker compares window pairs directly instead of using the runner's frequency formula. It checks every observed page and the first three simulated datasets, then audits all 999 saved score vectors, totals, tie decisions and the corrected tail calculation. It also verifies the complete observed pattern list and every starting position. A full second run separately verifies the remaining simulated values.\n\n[Download per-page counts as CSV](experiments/records/lp2-trigram-repeats/observed-pages.csv), including the zero-rune page. [Download the full JSON report](experiments/records/lp2-trigram-repeats/results.json) for every repeated pattern, its rune indices and zero-based starting positions, plus all simulated page-score vectors. These vectors follow `null_page_order`; they are retained for auditing, not presented as separate page-level significance tests.\n\nTo save another run without replacing the reviewed result:\n\n```sh\npython experiments/records/lp2-trigram-repeats/run.py --output trigram-rerun.json\n```\n\nThe destination must not already exist. To regenerate the chart and CSV from the stored result:\n\n```sh\npython experiments/records/lp2-trigram-repeats/plot.py\n```\n\nThese commands read local files and do not use an AI service.\n\n## What was decided before running\n\nThe plan and runner were committed as `70b8095` before the full-dataset calculation. Window length three, all declared pages, the aggregate pair statistic, upper tail, shuffle model, seed, trial count and threshold were fixed in that plan. None changed after the result.\n\nThe existing descriptive guide already reported no repeated trigrams on LP2-31. Repetition was also a topic of interest before this experiment. The plan discloses that prior knowledge; this is not a blind investigation of previously unseen manuscript data.\n\nCodex performed the full rerun and independent checks on 20 October 2026. Human review remains pending.\n\n## Limits and related tests\n\nA large p-value does not demonstrate randomness or exclude encryption. This result concerns the aggregate excess of within-page exact trigrams under one model. It does not establish the status of a particular repeated phrase, a selected page, another window length, approximate matches or repeats between pages.\n\nChanging window length or preserving additional structure in the shuffles belongs in a planned family variant. If the next test selects the strongest result among several lengths or regions, that selection must also be repeated in its comparison procedure. The [null-model guide](#/wiki/null-models) explains why.\n\nThis measurement also cannot distinguish a fixed one-to-one alphabet substitution from its input: renaming symbols preserves equal-window relationships. Rearranging rune positions can change those relationships. See [cipher invariants](#/wiki/cipher-invariants) before using a repeat score to rank candidate transformations.\n",

  ],
  "article": "# Drawing a path from LP2’s rune numbers\n\nCan the manuscript’s numbers be read as drawing instructions? A [published test](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round22/B-turtle-spatial-render/PREREG.md) turns each rune into a number, then uses that number to turn and advance an imaginary pen. We independently rebuilt its **72 fixed drawing rules** and checked the resulting paths against its [archived measurements](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round22/B-turtle-spatial-render/ledger.json). The test asks whether any path forms an unusually orderly figure. It does not turn a path back into decoded words.\n\n![A deliberately planted square, the LP2 prime-value path, and its shuffled control drawn by the same rule](experiments/records/lp2-turtle-spatial-replay/paths.svg)\n\nThe left path is a known square placed to check that the renderer can show an obvious shape. The other two use **relative turns and unit steps modulo 4**. One uses the manuscript’s rune order; the other shuffles those same numbers. The manuscript and shuffle panels share a coordinate scale. Their resemblance is a visual comparison for this one rule, not a test of all 72 by itself.\n\n| Question | What this replay found |\n| --- | --- |\n| Does the published construction reproduce? | **Yes.** The local rune files give the same 12,956-symbol input as the pinned public transcription, and all 72 path settings were rebuilt. |\n| Can the drawing method show a deliberate shape? | **Yes.** A planted square closes, and a planted block-comb has perfect measured symmetry. The controls separate from their 200 shuffled versions on multiple recorded measures. |\n| Was a decoding rule found? | **No.** A geometric path is not plaintext. The source’s full comparison flagged no path as a glyph or pointer under its declared rule. Our replay reports its precise coverage and statistical limits below. |\n\n## The drawing rule\n\nEvery rune has a Gematria Primus prime value. The source tried three number streams: the **prime itself**, its **one-based prime index**, or its **totient** (one less than the prime). For each number it chose a turn on one of six angular grids (4, 6, 8, 12, 29 or 360 directions). The heading either becomes that angle or rotates by that angle. The pen then advances one unit or a distance proportional to the number. These choices make **3 × 6 × 2 × 2 = 72** paths, with no hand-selected route between runes.\n\nThe source’s phrase “LP2 pages 0–54” means its first **55 nonempty transcription segments**. Its file omits the blank LP2-50, so its final segment corresponds to **Liberpedia LP2-55**. We verified the source stream against local LP2-00–49 and LP2-51–55 text, rune for rune; the UTF-8 rune-stream SHA-256 is `79b14e630946b64cdca838f328e73904f506df576d15e21fcb46271d4b4c8040`. This matters: stopping at Liberpedia LP2-54 would draw a different 12,880-rune path.\n\n## What the comparison can say\n\nThe [source report](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round22/B-turtle-spatial-render/RESULTS.md) compared each path with 200 histogram-preserving shuffles. It measured path closure, sampled self-crossings, occupied raster cells, displacement relative to total travel, symmetry and connected components. We reran **all 14,400 shuffled paths** and reproduced the same **six path/measure pairs** passing the initial, uncorrected screen. None passed the source’s later rule for flagging a candidate figure. That is a **bounded result for these 72 drawing rules and this shape detector**, not a proof that all number-based or geometric readings fail.\n\nThe independent path measurements agree with the source to numerical precision except for one sampled crossing in one case; the screen-level conclusion is unchanged. Some reported tail values differ where a real measurement and shuffled values are equal to machine precision. The source’s two-sided counting formula can even return a value above 1 for ties, so those numbers are best read as screening ranks rather than precise probabilities.\n\nTwo of the six measurements, **closure** and **caging**, are the same net-displacement divided by path-length formula. They should not be read as separate confirmation. The source also used a normal-tail approximation to refine rare events beyond what 2,000 shuffled samples can measure directly; that tail estimate depends on the approximation, especially for discrete counts such as connected components. The source therefore reports a useful controlled screen, while a strong claim about a specific picture would still need an independently frozen recognizer and a larger suitable null.\n\nThis record keeps geometry separate from language. A meaningful text read along a path could leave no distinctive drawn figure. Conversely, a visually suggestive walk would need an explicit rule for selecting and reading symbols before it could count as a decryption.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nFrom the repository root:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/lp2-turtle-spatial-replay/run.py --check\n```\n\nThis checks the pinned rune stream, all 72 constructed paths, the planted controls and the saved result. `--full-null --check` additionally repeats the 200 shuffles for every path. The script needs Python 3, NumPy and SciPy; the visual is regenerated with `python experiments/records/lp2-turtle-spatial-replay/plot.py`. The [saved results](experiments/records/lp2-turtle-spatial-replay/results.json) contain every path’s measurements and comparison differences; [source measurements](experiments/records/lp2-turtle-spatial-replay/source-ledger.json) are preserved verbatim from the pinned revision for offline checking.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/lp2-turtle-spatial-replay/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "03f9427c9df4e2dcff12ef1067b8f38c81245a3bb0500ac85471abd66699237d",
  "record_type": {
    "id": "replay",
    "label": "Method replay",
    "description": "Reconstructs a supplied proposed method and its choices; reproduction is not independent confirmation of a reading."
  }
}

  "article": "# Reversing the order of word-like segments\n\n“Read the words backwards” can mean two different operations. You might reverse the runes inside each word, or read the last word first while leaving its runes alone. This experiment tests the second interpretation across each complete page.\n\nThe archive gives us rune runs separated by punctuation and line markers. Calling these runs “segments” avoids assuming that they are established plaintext words. The input is LP2-00–55, including headings. LP2-50 has no recognized runes and contributes no candidates.\n\n## What changes?\n\nThe [within-segment reversal experiment](#/experiments/lp2-word-reversal) keeps segment order and reverses their contents. Here the contents stay in their original order and the segment order reverses.\n\nUsing invented letters as single symbols:\n\n```text\nSegments:                 AB | C | D | EF\nReverse inside segments:  BA | C | D | FE  -> BACDFE\nReverse segment order:    EF | D | C | AB  -> EFDCAB\nReverse the whole stream: FE | D | C | BA  -> FEDCBA\n```\n\nThese are three distinct transformations. Applying both segment-order reversal and within-segment reversal gives whole-stream reversal. That identity helps detect duplicated search coverage; the combined operation does not need to be advertised as a new method.\n\n## Declare the boundaries\n\n| Convention | Rule | Toy input `AB/C-D` followed by a newline and `EF.` |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| Split lines | Every non-rune ends the current segment. | Segments AB, C, D, EF produce EFDCAB. |\n| Join lines | Ignore slash, carriage return and newline before locating segments; every other non-rune remains a boundary. | Segments ABC, DEF produce DEFABC. |\n\nHyphens, periods and spaces remain boundaries in both conventions. There is no reversal limited to an individual row: the segment sequence spans the complete page. Headings are not removed, and their segments move with the rest. No additional alphabet substitution is applied.\n\nThis record belongs to the reading-route family. Its formal comparison is against the [row/column baseline](#/experiments/lp2-row-column-routes), so multiple scope fields change. For the closer comparison with its within-segment sibling, the pages, boundary rules and nine expected beginnings stay the same; the reversal operation changes.\n\n## Inspect the source trace\n\n![First six LP2-31 output positions under segment-order reversal, showing the last segment read forwards before the preceding segment.](experiments/records/lp2-word-order-reversal/source-trace.svg)\n\nLP2-31 contains 269 runes. Under both conventions its final three-rune segment occupies original rune positions 266, 267 and 268, counted from zero. Those positions appear first and keep their internal order. The next output position jumps back to source rune 258. This is not the sequence 268, 267, 266 that whole-page reversal would produce.\n\nBoth conventions agree on these six positions but produce different full outputs. The report retains every source rune ordinal, source character offset and output index. Character offsets refer to Unicode characters in the decoded input, not UTF-8 bytes.\n\n## Findings and limits\n\n| Quantity | Result |\n| --- | --- |\n| Declared pages | 56 |\n| Pages containing recognized runes | 55 |\n| Boundary conventions per nonempty page | 2 |\n| Completed cases | 110 |\n| Distinct full outputs, counted within page | 110 |\n| Exact opening comparisons | 990 |\n| Matching cases | 0 |\n\nEach case compares its first twelve output rune indices with nine fixed known beginnings: Warning, Welcome, Some Wisdom, the first koan, Loss of Divinity, the second koan, Instruction, LP2-56 and LP2-57. The plan records the exact vectors and hashed source traces.\n\nNo case begins with those specified sequences. This does not establish that reversing segment order cannot work: other beginnings, regions and combined ciphers remain untested. There is no general language score or significance test. The [candidate-reading guide](#/wiki/candidate-readings) explains this distinction.\n\nThe [page summary CSV](experiments/records/lp2-word-order-reversal/page-summary.csv) includes LP2-50 with zero cases. Counts of distinct outputs do not imply statistically independent evidence.\n\n## Plan and verification\n\nThe plan, runner and checker were committed as `0429f5a` before generating the full result. The earlier within-segment and row/column results were already known; this is a declared exploratory follow-up. No boundary or acceptance rule changed after the run.\n\nThe runner scans characters to form segments and reverses the list of segments. The checker instead finds regex spans, assigns segment numbers, and sorts positions by descending segment number and ascending position within the segment. It checks all 110 source permutations, full outputs and match decisions, plus source hashes and the reference beginnings. Hand-calculated examples cover both boundary conventions.\n\nFor every page and convention, a second check confirms that the new output is the whole-stream reversal of the saved within-segment output. This is an algebraic consistency check, not independent support for a decoding. A complete rerun reproduces the saved report. Review is computational by Codex; human review remains pending.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nExtract the reference-data bundle with its folders intact, or use the repository checkout. From its root, with Python 3:\n\n```sh\npython experiments/records/lp2-word-order-reversal/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/lp2-word-order-reversal/check.py\n```\n\nThe summary should report 110 cases, 110 distinct page outputs, 990 comparisons and zero matching cases. All scripts use the standard library and local files.\n\nTo save a fresh result without overwriting the reviewed one:\n\n```sh\npython experiments/records/lp2-word-order-reversal/run.py --output word-order-rerun.json\n```\n\nThe destination must not already exist. In each page's `cases`, `segment_lengths` describes the original segment order. `source_ordinals` and `source_character_offsets` give the actual output traversal. `output_indices` contains the full result, not only its opening.\n\nRegenerate the chart and summary CSV from the saved report:\n\n```sh\npython experiments/records/lp2-word-order-reversal/plot.py\n```\n\n## What would be a new test?\n\nReversing segment order within each row, excluding headings, choosing other boundaries, or combining reversal with substitution changes the scope. Declare those choices and an acceptance criterion before inspecting outputs. An alternate reading rule should not be judged by whole-stream IoC: every pure permutation preserves it. See [cipher invariants](#/wiki/cipher-invariants) and [planning a follow-up](#/wiki/reproducibility?section=follow-up).\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/lp2-word-order-reversal/article.md",

  }
}

      "path": "experiments/records/lp2-word-reversal/boundary-trace.svg",
      "caption": "The first six boundary-dependent LP2-31 output positions, traced to original rune ordinals. Both conventions preserve all runes; the numbers identify positions, not plaintext."
    }
  ],
  "article": "# Reversing runes within word-like segments\n\nA natural first idea is to read each word backwards while keeping the words in their original order. On an unsolved page, however, the archive gives us separators and line markers—not independently established plaintext words. This experiment makes that distinction explicit.\n\nIt tests two precise interpretations of the archived boundaries on LP2-00–55. All 110 cases completed and produced 110 distinct full page outputs. None matched any of the nine declared 12-rune openings. LP2-50 contains no recognized runes and contributes no candidates.\n\n## What counts as a segment?\n\nBoth conventions include headings, preserve segment order, and reverse rune positions inside each segment. Neither changes the rune alphabet.\n\n| Convention | Rule | Consequence |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| Split lines | Every non-rune ends the current segment. | A slash or newline ends a segment even without a word separator. |\n| Join lines | Remove slash, carriage return and newline before finding maximal rune segments. Every other non-rune still ends a segment. | Runes across a line boundary join unless another delimiter intervenes. |\n\nHyphens and periods remain boundaries under both conventions. Spaces and other non-rune characters also remain boundaries. No inference about the author's intended word division is made.\n\nIn this invented example, letters stand for single rune symbols:\n\n```text\nInput: AB/C-D\n       EF.\n\nSplit lines: BA | C | D | FE  -> BACDFE\nJoin lines:  CBA | FED       -> CBAFED\n```\n\nThe slash and newline are archive boundaries. The vertical bars in the output explanation show the segments; they are not additional input characters. A hyphen before a line break would still prevent joining.\n\n## Difference from the row and column experiment\n\nThe [row and column baseline](#/experiments/lp2-row-column-routes) traverses rows or ordinal columns as whole groups. Here the groups are maximal rune segments under one of the two boundary rules. This is a separate experiment in the same reading-route family.\n\nMore than one scope field changes: the grouping representation, traversal procedure, number of configurations and exclusions. The comparison is not an attempt to isolate one numerical parameter. The family comparison lists these differences explicitly.\n\nWhole-page reversal, reversing the order of words, alphabet substitution after reversal, and arbitrarily regrouping runes are not tested here.\n\n## Inspect a real source trace\n\n![The first six LP2-31 output positions where splitting and joining lines produce different source-position traces.](experiments/records/lp2-word-reversal/boundary-trace.svg)\n\nThe diagram reads positions from the saved result. Each number identifies a rune in the original page stream, counted from zero. The full report also retains zero-based Unicode character offsets into the exact UTF-8-decoded source file. Character offsets are not byte offsets: a rune occupies more than one UTF-8 byte.\n\nBoth permutations use every source rune exactly once. Consequently, they preserve rune counts, whole-stream IoC and single-rune entropy. Those measurements cannot choose between these two outputs; see [cipher invariants](#/wiki/cipher-invariants).\n\n## What the result establishes\n\n| Quantity | Recorded result |\n| --- | --- |\n| Declared pages | 56, including the zero-rune LP2-50 |\n| Nonempty pages | 55 |\n| Boundary conventions per nonempty page | 2 |\n| Candidate configurations | 110 |\n| Distinct full page outputs, counted within page | 110 |\n| Exact opening comparisons | 990 |\n| Matching cases | 0 |\n\nThe nine reference beginnings are Warning, Welcome, Some Wisdom, the first koan, Loss of Divinity, the second koan, Instruction, LP2-56 and LP2-57. The plan stores the exact first twelve decoded rune indices and the hashes of their source traces.\n\nThis result excludes only those beginnings under the stated rules. A genuine reading beginning differently would fail this test. No general English score, later-position search or statistical significance calculation was used. The [candidate-reading guide](#/wiki/candidate-readings) explains why a failed opening test is not a general rejection of a cipher idea.\n\n## Controls and retest\n\nThe plan and runner were committed as `9b081f6` before the full page search. Neither the boundary conventions nor the acceptance rule changed after inspecting outputs.\n\nThe runner groups positions with a character-by-character scan. The checker independently locates segments with regular expressions after the declared normalization, then calculates reflected source positions for every segment. It compares every saved permutation, output and match decision, checks source hashes and opening vectors, and verifies the complete case set. The small example above also checks the production segmenter directly.\n\nA complete second execution reproduces the saved result. This is computational review by Codex; human review remains pending.\n\n## Reproduce and inspect\n\nFrom the repository root with Python 3:\n\n```sh\npython experiments/records/lp2-word-reversal/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/lp2-word-reversal/check.py\n```\n\nSave a fresh full result without overwriting the reviewed file:\n\n```sh\npython experiments/records/lp2-word-reversal/run.py --output word-reversal-rerun.json\n```\n\nThe destination must not already exist. All commands use the standard library and local files. Each page has a `cases` array containing the boundary convention, segment lengths, source ordinals, character offsets, complete output indices and any matching opening IDs.\n\nTo regenerate the diagram:\n\n```sh\npython experiments/records/lp2-word-reversal/plot.py\n```\n\n## Useful follow-ups\n\nA proposal to reverse word order, omit headings or add a substitution is a new scope. Specify its boundaries and acceptance rule before inspecting results, and retain the full traces. A broader language-ranking test needs a declared corpus, scoring rule and evaluation procedure; it should not silently replace this record's fixed-opening criterion.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/lp2-word-reversal/article.md",

  "article": "# How much freedom remains in a magic square?\n\n## Question\nDoes a fixed line sum, half-turn symmetry and one fixed entry determine the rest of a five-by-five magic square?\n\nNo. Under precisely these conditions, five rational degrees of freedom remain. We also construct positive-integer alternatives to both LP1 examples, keeping any one chosen cell unchanged. This tests uniqueness of numerical grids, not a cipher or the authors’ intentions.\n\n## Why this matters\nIt is tempting to count twelve line-sum equations, subtract twelve from the number of cells, and conclude that almost everything is forced. That subtraction only works for independent equations. For example, the sum of all row totals already equals the sum of all column totals. Symmetry creates further dependencies.\n\nA **degree of freedom** is an independent parameter that can vary while all the equations remain satisfied. It is not a count of solutions and does not mean that every integer assigned to those parameters produces an allowed square.\n\n## Scope and plan\nThe [recorded plan](experiments/records/magic-square-freedom/plan.json) specifies orders 3, 5 and 7, with four symmetry conditions each. Every row, column and both main diagonals have the same fixed sum. We distinguish:\n\n- No additional symmetry.\n- Half-turn symmetry: the cell at row r, column c equals its opposite after a 180-degree rotation.\n- Transpose symmetry: swapping row and column leaves the entry unchanged.\n- Both symmetries together.\n\nThe actual LP1-05 converted square and LP1-16 printed square have half-turn symmetry. Neither is transpose-symmetric: compare their cells at row 1, column 2 and row 2, column 1. Imposing transpose symmetry would therefore change the model and exclude both observed grids.\n\nThe supplied discussion had already proposed uniqueness, retracted that claim, and suggested possible dimensions. Those claims were known before calculation. This is a deterministic audit, not a blind prediction or significance test. The plan was written before running but was not externally timestamped or preregistered.\n\n## Method\nLet A be an existing square and D a change to it. The square A+D retains the same line sums exactly when every row, column and diagonal of D sums to zero. The same symmetry equations apply to D. Keeping one cell unchanged adds the equation that its change is zero.\n\nThe script forms these linear equations and reduces them with exact rational arithmetic. Rank counts the independent equations; dimension equals the number of cells minus rank. The saved nullspace basis describes all rational changes satisfying the equations. A uniform rational grid with entry equal to the line sum divided by the order supplies a solution for every prescribed rational sum, so the reported affine dimensions are not dimensions of an empty set.\n\nFor each of the 25 cell positions in each actual five-by-five square, the script selects the first basis vector that preserves that cell, clears denominators, and divides out the common integer factor. It tries adding that primitive change, then subtracting it. It stops after those two possibilities; this is not an exhaustive positive-integer enumeration.\n\n## Results\nAll twelve comparison models completed. These dimensions assume a fixed common line sum:\n\n| Order | No symmetry | Half-turn | Transpose | Both |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| 3 | 2 | 0 | 1 | 0 |\n| 5 | 14 | 6 | 8 | 4 |\n| 7 | 34 | 16 | 19 | 10 |\n\nFor order five, fixing any one cell reduces the half-turn dimension from six to five. For order seven it reduces sixteen to fifteen. This is not a statement about an audited historical seven-by-seven square; order seven here is a mathematical comparison. For order three, the half-turn model already has dimension zero: with a fixed sum, it forces the uniform rational square.\n\nEvery one of the **50 fixed-cell tests** produced a different positive-integer square. Each preserves its original line sum and half-turn symmetry, and keeps the chosen entry unchanged. The complete [results and witnesses](experiments/records/magic-square-freedom/results.json) include all cases, bases, positions and input hashes.\n\n### An example you can check by hand\nKeep the center 809 in LP1-16. Add 1 to row 2, column 1 and row 4, column 5; subtract 1 from row 2, column 5 and row 4, column 1. Leave every other cell alone.\n\n```text\n 434 1311 312  278  966\n 205  812 934  280 1070\n 626  620 809  620  626\n1070  280 934  812  205\n 966  278 312 1311  434\n```\n\nEach affected row and column gains one and loses one. Neither diagonal changes. Opposite entries still agree, all entries remain positive, and every line still sums to 3301. Thus the center value 809 cannot uniquely determine the original grid under these rules. These numbers are a constructed counterexample, not a transcription correction.\n\n## Reproduce\nPython 3.12 standard library; no network, packages or AI calls. From the repository root, run:\n\n```sh\npython experiments/records/magic-square-freedom/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/magic-square-freedom/check.py\n```\n\nThe first command recomputes every case and compares the complete report. The second independently constructs the equations and checks rank modulo two large primes. It directly verifies every rational null vector and its independence. A matching modular rank gives a lower bound; the independent null vectors give the matching upper bound, certifying the rational rank. It also checks every positive-integer counterexample by summing its actual rows, columns and diagonals and comparing opposite cells.\n\nUse `--write` instead of `--check` to regenerate results. Preserve the old output if changing the plan or input transcriptions.\n\n## Retest and changes\nOn 20 October 2026, Codex recomputed the saved result and ran the separate checker. All twelve ranks, fixed-cell dimensions and fifty witnesses passed. This is computational review by the same agent; independent human review is pending. No model, bounds or criterion changed after inspecting the results.\n\n## What remains open\nThis disproves uniqueness under the stated constraints. It does not count all positive-integer solutions, impose prime patterns or distinct entries, reconstruct a historical server validator, or show which values the authors deliberately selected. A rational basis is not automatically a basis for all integer solutions: clearing each vector’s denominators is enough to construct these witnesses, but is not an integer-lattice enumeration method.\n\nAn extra requirement can shrink the space. To test one, state it as a separate variant and show exactly which constraints changed. A theory that fixes many cells, restricts values to a list, or imposes a primality pattern is not ruled out by this result.\n\nSee [the magic-square guide](#/wiki/magic-squares) for the original images and rune-value conversion, and [search space and bounds](#/wiki/search-space) for why a claim must name the space it covers.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/magic-square-freedom/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "83d3474caaf0cc50019244bd8010088b04c93201c1e4bbd705a5126f78aa93ce",

  }

  "article": "# Candidate words for the LP1-05 mixed square\n\nThis experiment checks sixteen supplied word-and-total pairs. It asks whether each spelling can be segmented into Gematria Primus rune labels to produce the proposed number. It does not try the words as keys or replace text on unsolved pages.\n\n## Scope and normalization\n\nThe list was fixed before enumeration. Uppercase each word and replace V with U; make no other spelling substitutions. Enumerate every exact segmentation into the 29 Latin rune labels in the archived alphabet. For example, TH can be one rune label or the two labels T and H. These are spelling segmentations, not a phonetic transcription algorithm.\n\nThere are 16 candidates and 24 total segmentations. Every candidate has exactly one segmentation matching its supplied total. Fourteen candidates have only one possible segmentation under these rules; THAN has two and AETHEREAL has eight. The candidate list was supplied because its sums were of interest, so the 16 matches are not an unbiased success rate or a chance probability.\n\n## Matching segmentations\n\nEach row below records the exact rune labels needed. VOID is retained as the submitted word, with V explicitly normalized to U.\n\n| Candidate | Rune labels | Sum |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| OR | O · R | 18 |\n| FORM | F · O · R · M | 91 |\n| VOID | U · O · I · D | 130 |\n| THAN | TH · A · N | 131 |\n| WHEN | W · H · E · N | 138 |\n| FIND | F · I · N · D | 151 |\n| BUFFERS | B · U · F · F · E · R · S | 199 |\n| MOURNFUL | M · O · U · R · N · F · U · L | 199 |\n| MOBIUS | M · O · B · I · U · S | 226 |\n| OBSCURA | O · B · S · C · U · R · A | 245 |\n| IMPOSE | I · M · P · O · S · E | 272 |\n| CARNAL | C · A · R · N · A · L | 320 |\n| ANALOG | A · N · A · L · O · G | 320 |\n| SHADOWS | S · H · A · D · O · W · S | 341 |\n| CABAL | C · A · B · A · L | 341 |\n| AETHEREAL | AE · TH · E · R · EA · L | 366 |\n\n## What the Latin spellings leave undecided\n\nTHAN gives **131** with TH–A–N, but **208** with T–H–A–N. AETHEREAL has the following eight exact-label segmentations:\n\n| Rune labels | Sum |\n| --- | --- |\n| A · E · TH · E · R · E · A · L | 484 |\n| A · E · TH · E · R · EA · L | 429 |\n| A · E · T · H · E · R · E · A · L | 561 |\n| A · E · T · H · E · R · EA · L | 506 |\n| AE · TH · E · R · E · A · L | 421 |\n| AE · TH · E · R · EA · L | 366 |\n| AE · T · H · E · R · E · A · L | 498 |\n| AE · T · H · E · R · EA · L | 443 |\n\nWhen the original manuscript supplies rune symbols, use those symbols directly. The ambiguity here arises when converting a Latin candidate back into runes. Choosing the segmentation because it hits a target is a search choice and must be recorded; the Latin word alone does not fix the sum.\n\n## Why equal totals do not recover words\n\nThe [mixed-square guide](#/wiki/magic-squares?section=sum-collisions) already shows distinct printed words sharing values: BUFFERS and MOURNFUL both give 199, CARNAL and ANALOG both give 320, and SHADOWS and CABAL both give 341. A sum discards order and other information. A number-to-word replacement can therefore have multiple candidates even in this small supplied list.\n\nIf every cell of a magic square is replaced by a word with exactly the same numerical total, all its line sums remain unchanged by construction. Preserving 1033 would check the replacements' arithmetic; it would not independently select the words or establish a hidden sentence. The [known conversion](#/wiki/magic-squares?section=rune-cells) goes from visible runes to numbers; reversing that process is a different problem.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nRun the producer and independent checker from the extracted experiment bundle or repository:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/mixed-square-word-sums/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/mixed-square-word-sums/check.py\n```\n\nWithout `--check`, the producer prints all results as JSON. The producer recursively matches alphabet labels at the start of each remaining suffix. The independent checker instead tries every cut/no-cut pattern between Latin letters, keeps only pieces in the alphabet, and compares the complete set of segmentations and sums. Both use the same declared alphabet; agreement is not an independent verification of that alphabet against the manuscript.\n\nThe plan fixes the words and target totals. The JSON retains every segmentation, including nonmatching ones. No dictionary, language model, network access or paid service is needed.\n\n## Limits and related experiments\n\nThis is an arithmetic audit of a selected list, not an exhaustive dictionary search, plaintext result or test of authorial intent. It does not establish that an unsolved rune word with one of these totals should be decrypted using the corresponding candidate. That would require a defined transform, alignment, key-advance rule and scoring criterion.\n\nA future variant can change the vocabulary or transliteration rules while preserving this baseline. A dictionary search must pin the dictionary and report all matching entries, not just appealing words. A cipher search must state its [search space and bounds](#/wiki/search-space) separately. The [magic-square freedom experiment](#/experiments/magic-square-freedom) concerns numerical constraints; it answers a different question.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/mixed-square-word-sums/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "fa37d2e9e709b8f1e1685666ad2a2d067aaeacd6de523abd176c745921a833cc",

    "description": "Measures a stated feature or statistical comparison; it does not test a complete decoding rule."
  }
}

  "article": "# Does a Möbius-of-totient zero survive a known LP2 decoding?\n\nA reported LP2-00 reading proposes a necessary rule: if the ciphertext rune has Möbius value zero after applying Euler's totient to its Gematria Primus prime, the plaintext rune at that position must also have zero. That is a checkable statement, separate from the proposed sentence. This control applies the same rule to **LP2-56**, whose [published reading](#/page/lp2-56) uses a uniform one-step subtraction in the 29-rune alphabet. It does not test the author's selected LP2-00 words or claim that LP2-00 uses the same cipher.\n\nFor a GP prime value *p*, Euler's totient is φ(*p*) = *p* − 1. The Möbius value μ(*p* − 1) is zero exactly when *p* − 1 contains a squared prime factor. A ciphertext zero therefore has a simple, independently checkable definition. For example, J has GP prime 37; φ(37) = 36 and μ(36) = 0. LP2-56's known shift maps its rune index 11 (J) to index 10 (I), whose prime is 31; μ(30) = −1. That is a counterexample to the stated one-way zero rule at rune position 1 (counting from zero).\n\n![Möbius zero-mask mismatch counts under all 29 fixed shifts on LP2-56. The published one-step shift is highlighted.](experiments/records/mobius-zero-mask-known-page/mismatches.svg)\n\n## Fixed input and result\n\nThe script reads the [archived LP2-56 transcription](#/reader/lp2-56) and the stored GP alphabet. It keeps all 85 rune symbols in manuscript order, discards non-rune punctuation and the printed hexadecimal hash, and computes μ(*p* − 1) for each symbol. The decoded index is `(cipher index − 1) mod 29`. We count zero-to-nonzero failures separately from nonzero-to-zero changes; only the first direction is required to refute the reported one-way condition.\n\n| Check on the published shift | Positions |\n| --- | ---: |\n| Ciphertext zero → plaintext nonzero | **28 / 85** |\n| Ciphertext nonzero → plaintext zero | 22 / 85 |\n| Either zero-state changes | 50 / 85 |\n\nThe first one-way failures, at zero-based positions 1, 3 and 7, are J→I, S→X and L→M. The saved result lists every position and the 29-rune Möbius table. As a comparison, the script applies every fixed shift 0–28 to the same input. The identity shift has zero mismatches by construction; that is a positive calculation check, not evidence for a cipher. The published shift is highlighted in the figure.\n\n## What this closes\n\nThe zero-preservation rule is **not an invariant of known Liber Primus decoding**. It fails on a solved page even in the one-way form stated in the report. That does not logically disprove a special rule for LP2-00, and a chosen candidate phrase can still satisfy a zero mask accidentally. To assess LP2-00, a future test needs the exact proposed rune-by-rune plaintext, a fixed spelling/segmentation policy, the full count of admissible alternatives, and an untouched continuation or independent control. The source report's semantic filtering and unattached code files do not establish those bounds.\n\nRun `python experiments/records/mobius-zero-mask-known-page/run.py --check` to reproduce every shift and mismatch position. `check.py` independently identifies zero values by searching for squared divisors; it confirms 28 one-way failures. The [plan](experiments/records/mobius-zero-mask-known-page/plan.json) pins both inputs by SHA-256, and [results.json](experiments/records/mobius-zero-mask-known-page/results.json) provides the complete comparison. The report being evaluated is catalogued under [reported attempts](#/wiki/reported-attempts), with its source-text hash and replay limits.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/mobius-zero-mask-known-page/article.md",

    "id": "control",
    "label": "Control",
    "description": "Checks a search, decoder or scorer using synthetic inputs or reference text; it does not identify the cipher of an unsolved page."
  }

      "caption": "The zero-index rune and impossible zero-to-nonzero edges under literal multiplication."
    }

  "article": "## Finding\n\nThe literal multiplicative ciphertext-autokey rule **cannot produce the archived LP2-00–55 stream**. With rune indices modulo 29, it says `c[i] = p[i] × c[i−1]`. Rune index **0 is F**. Once ciphertext reaches zero, multiplication keeps it zero whatever plaintext follows. Yet the transcription has **450 edges from F to a non-F rune**, spread across **all 55 nonempty pages**. One such edge is enough to contradict the uninterrupted rule.\n\n![The archived stream has 458 index-zero runes and 450 zero-to-nonzero edges.](experiments/records/multiplicative-ciphertext-autokey/zero-state.svg)\n\nThis tests the proposed recurrence exactly as written, with a fresh page start but no exception inside a page. A rule that *skips* zero, resets the state, inserts a marker, changes the alphabet, or adds another term is a different proposal. It may avoid the contradiction, but needs an explicit encoder and decoder before it can be checked.\n\n## Why doublets alone are insufficient\n\nWhen the preceding ciphertext rune is nonzero, a repeated ciphertext rune under this recurrence means the plaintext rune at that step equals index **1**. That algebra can suggest a low doublet rate if index 1 is rare in the plaintext. It does not solve the zero-state problem. The saved result contains **82 nonzero doublets** and lists every zero-to-nonzero position, so the two observations can be checked separately.\n\nThe [additive-key doublet control](#/experiments/uniform-additive-doublets) and [single-rune deletion census](#/experiments/single-rune-null-doublets) examine different mechanisms; their findings should not be transferred to multiplication.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nFrom the repository root, using Python 3.12 and the standard library:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/multiplicative-ciphertext-autokey/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/multiplicative-ciphertext-autokey/check.py\n```\n\nThe independent checker reads each transcription again and verifies the [saved position ledger](experiments/records/multiplicative-ciphertext-autokey/results.json). The producer also confirms the absorbing-zero rule on a short synthetic plaintext.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/multiplicative-ciphertext-autokey/article.md",

  "article": "# N-rune gaps on LP2-00–02\n\nThis experiment reconstructs a proposed extraction from distances between successive N runes. It compares four configurations: position distance or intervening-rune count, each with page resets or cross-page continuation. It does not test whether the signpost artwork instructs this operation.\n\n## Inputs and scope\n\nUse the archived rune-only streams from LP2-00, LP2-01 and LP2-02, including headings. Preserve rune order; discard punctuation and whitespace for the distance calculation. There are 262, 266 and 201 runes respectively, with 12, 8 and 8 occurrences of N.\n\nThe proposal and initial output were known before the plan was written. This is an exploratory reproduction, not a preregistered confirmation. No other target rune or parameter search is included.\n\n## Two definitions of distance\n\nIf N occurs at rune positions 22 and 24, the position distance is 2, but only one rune lies between the two Ns. The first definition maps 2 to F through its Gematria Primus prime value. The second produces 1, which has no GP prime-value mapping.\n\nFor each adjacent pair of Ns, retain the exact distance and both source locations. Map a distance only when it equals one of the 29 GP prime values. Keep all other distances as a dot token. These dots mark unmatched observations; they are not manuscript punctuation. No gap is deleted or rearranged.\n\nPage resets produce 11, 7 and 7 gaps. Joining all three streams produces 27 gaps, including the two cross-page gaps. The four configurations yield eight reported streams because reset configurations return one stream per page.\n\n## Complete outputs\n\nEach space separates one gap observation. Do not read spacing as recovered word boundaries.\n\n### reset-at-page / position-distance / lp2-00\n\n```text\nF R O . M . . . . . I\n```\n\n### reset-at-page / position-distance / lp2-01\n\n```text\n. O . . . . .\n```\n\n### reset-at-page / position-distance / lp2-02\n\n```text\n. . . . . . .\n```\n\n### reset-at-page / intervening-runes / lp2-00\n\n```text\n. . . U . R . U P U .\n```\n\n### reset-at-page / intervening-runes / lp2-01\n\n```text\n. . . . X N R\n```\n\n### reset-at-page / intervening-runes / lp2-02\n\n```text\n. . I G . I .\n```\n\n### join-pages / position-distance / lp2-00, lp2-01, lp2-02\n\n```text\nF R O . M . . . . . I . . O . . . . . S . . . . . . .\n```\n\n### join-pages / intervening-runes / lp2-00, lp2-01, lp2-02\n\n```text\n. . . U . R . U P U . . . . . . X N R . . . I G . I .\n```\n\n## What the apparent fragment depends on\n\nLP2-00 starts with position distances 2, 11, 7, 4 and 71. Their output is F, R, O, dot, M. A contiguous FROM requires discarding the unmatched distance 4. That is a different extraction rule from retaining every observation.\n\nThe joined position-distance stream adds a distance of 40 across LP2-00 to LP2-01, which stays a dot, and 53 across LP2-01 to LP2-02, which maps to S. The S therefore does not arise within LP2-02 under the page-reset rule. Every endpoint is in results.json, with one-based page-local rune ordinals and zero-based source-character offsets.\n\nThe outputs reproduce a fragment that can invite an English reading after selection. They do not provide a full reading or establish an intended cipher. No p-value is calculated: accounting for choices among target runes, distance conventions, page boundaries and output selection would require a separate search and control model.\n\n## Reproduce and inspect\n\nRun from the repository or the extracted experiment ZIP, retaining its folder layout:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/n-rune-gaps/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/n-rune-gaps/check.py\n```\n\nPython 3 is sufficient. The first command regenerates all outputs and compares them with the saved report. The second independently splits the rune streams at N and checks gap lengths, mappings, source locations and cross-page flags. No network or model calls are made.\n\nThe result is inconclusive about a cipher, while the extraction itself is reproducible. Human review is pending. Further tests must state any changed target, omitted heading, character representation or filtering rule; record such changes within the same experiment family rather than presenting them as confirmations of this scope.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/n-rune-gaps/article.md",

      "caption": "Night IV–IX positions of the source's six reported passages in one pinned 1853 comparison edition."
    }
  ],
  "sources": [
    {
      "label": "Reported Night Thoughts pointer and supplied discussion identity",
      "url": "https://jelliottdev.github.io/#/wiki/reported-attempts?section=night-thoughts-729-book-pointer"
    },
    {
      "label": "Project Gutenberg ebook 33156, identified 1853 comparison text",
      "url": "https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/33156"
    },
    {
      "label": "Google Books volume linked in the reported discussion; edition not verified here",
      "url": "https://books.google.com/books?id=GsVHv1gACYAC"
    }
  ],
  "related": [
    "emerson-book-cipher-control",
    "cross-section-index-inversion"
  ],
  "article": "# Do the six proposed *Night Thoughts* lines point to 729?\n\nA [reported book-pointer idea](#/wiki/reported-attempts?section=night-thoughts-729-book-pointer) starts with the **729 runes** on LP2-00–02, then gathers what it calls line 729 from Nights IV–IX of Edward Young’s *Night Thoughts*. The discussion supplies six short quotations and a [Google Books volume](https://books.google.com/books?id=GsVHv1gACYAC), but does not verify the scan’s edition or give a cipher rule for using the collected lines.\n\nHere we checked the **six quoted locations**, using one pinned comparison text: the [1853 edition edited by George Gilfillan](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/33156), transcribed as Project Gutenberg ebook 33156. It is a later text, **not a claimed replay of the linked Google scan** or Blake’s 1797 illustrated volume. We retained its full UTF-8 text and license in the downloadable experiment, normalizing only CRLF line endings to LF, so its printed line-number markers can be checked offline.\n\n![Night IV through IX compared with the reported line 729; five entries show 729, while Night IX shows 731 in the pinned 1853 edition.](experiments/records/night-thoughts-729-line-audit/line-729.svg)\n\n## What the lookup shows\n\nThe archived page transcriptions contain **262 + 266 + 201 = 729** alphabet runes across [LP2-00](#/page/lp2-00), [LP2-01](#/page/lp2-01) and [LP2-02](#/page/lp2-02), counting headings and excluding every non-rune. That establishes the proposed *pointer value*, not a link to any book.\n\nThe six quoted passages are all identifiable in the pinned edition. Its right-margin verse numbers, checked against adjacent numbered lines, place **five** of them at line 729. The Night IX phrase, “And deep reception, in th’ intender’d heart,” is at **line 731**: the edition numbers “With gain, and joy, she bribes thee to be wise” as 728, followed by two intervening lines before the quoted phrase. The source’s wording also differs slightly from this edition in places, such as “series end” versus “series ends.”\n\n| Night | Short identifying words | Line in the pinned 1853 text |\n| --- | --- | ---: |\n| IV | “Hold her sacred still” | 729 |\n| V | “thunder scarce obtains your ear” | 729 |\n| VI | “in man the series ends” | 729 |\n| VII | “blind Passion! drive us on” | 729 |\n| VIII | “the Muse, to win thine ear” | 729 |\n| IX | “deep reception … intender’d heart” | **731** |\n\nThis **5-of-6 result is edition-specific**. The Google Books scan linked in the discussion might use different text or numbering; we could not verify its title page and all six page locations from a pinned copy. The source also lists printed pages 82, 110, 150, 182, 230 and 276 for the six selections. Their sum is 1030, but this audit does not certify those page labels in that scan. No probability of a literary connection follows from five positional matches in a book whose six passages were selected after inspection.\n\n## What a cipher test would still require\n\nCombining six lines in chapter order is a text selection, not a decryption. A test needs one identified edition; the exact extracted six lines, including the Night IX discrepancy; a normalization and rune conversion; a rule for applying the text to a stated manuscript span; and a success criterion assessed on an untouched continuation. Any search across alternative Nights, editions, page counts, RSA parameters or word arrangements must include those choices in its control search.\n\nThe [plan](experiments/records/night-thoughts-729-line-audit/plan.json) fixes the six source quotations, comparison edition and location procedure. The [result](experiments/records/night-thoughts-729-line-audit/results.json) preserves each exact line, file coordinate and neighboring numbered markers. From a checkout or extracted bundle, run:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/night-thoughts-729-line-audit/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/night-thoughts-729-line-audit/check.py\n```\n\nBoth use only Python’s standard library. The independent checker uses separately read line and marker coordinates and confirms the three page-rune counts; it does not import the producer.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/night-thoughts-729-line-audit/article.md",

    "description": "Checks image provenance, extraction or input coverage against a declared reference; it does not establish a decryption."
  }

    }
  ],
  "article": "# How much does an OBSCURA word-sum match narrow the search?\n\n**A GP-sum match is common in the LP2 text.** The sixteen fixed candidate words from the [OBSCURA table audit](#/experiments/mixed-square-word-sums) have thirteen distinct prime totals. Those totals match **104 of 2,928** visible words on LP2-00–55. A sum match can nominate a word for inspection, but it does not pick a unique key or operation.\n\n![The observed 104 matches lie inside the 77–114 central range of page-preserving shuffled controls.](experiments/records/obscura-sum-collision-control/sum-collisions.svg)\n\nTo test whether 104 is unusual, the script shuffles rune prime values **within each page** while leaving its rune inventory and every visible word length fixed. Across 2,000 seeded shuffles, the mean is **95.2 matches** and the central 95% of counts is **77–114**. In **375** trials, the count was at least 104. The observed count is therefore not an unusually selective signal under this control.\n\nFor example, the supplied candidates `BUFFERS` and `MOURNFUL` both have target total 199. A ciphertext word totalling 199 cannot distinguish those proposed words on the basis of the sum. The count also ignores whether either candidate has the same length, punctuation, or rune pattern as the ciphertext word. Those checks would need to be fixed before a word-level decoding attempt.\n\n## What this does and does not test\n\nThis measures the **first selection step** of a reported idea: pick encrypted words whose GP sums equal one of the table-word totals. It does not reproduce a word-specific cipher, because the discussion did not save one exact transformation or its complete output. The control preserves page rune frequencies and word lengths; it is a reference for match abundance, not a model of the manuscript's encryption.\n\nThe observation does not rule out a fully specified key scheme. Such a scheme would need a deterministic rule for choosing among equal-sum words, an exact transformation, and held-out words or pages it predicts without adjustment.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nDownload this experiment's ZIP or run from the repository root:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/obscura-sum-collision-control/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/obscura-sum-collision-control/check.py\n```\n\nThe [results](experiments/records/obscura-sum-collision-control/results.json) retain every target total's observed count and all 2,000 control counts. The second script independently recounts the original matches from page records.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/obscura-sum-collision-control/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "df33bbd47de6f984ce3326607b04156ca578425bb2017537938feb1a02759ada",

  "id": "outguess-default-key",
  "title": "Original JPEGs: default-key OutGuess sweep",
  "status": "published",
  "question": "What does default-key OutGuess retrieval return from all 75 manuscript JPEGs and the two historical cover/opening images?",
  "summary": "Ten known payloads reproduced; 21 other images yielded unverified bytes, five retrievals were rejected, and 41 ended abnormally in this Windows build. No image-wide absence claim is justified.",
  "tags": [
    "OutGuess",
    "steganography",
    "hidden message",
    "JPEG",

    "representation": "Original archived JPEG bytes with fixed SHA-256 hashes: 75 manuscript images plus opening-2014 and 1033. No recompression or image transformations.",
    "procedure": "One OutGuess retrieval per image with literal key Default key. Retain all output bytes and stderr/return codes; compare ten expected payload hashes. Repeat complete run for reproducibility.",
    "parameters": "77 images; one key; 20 seconds per invocation; pinned upstream commit 24810e14327c2bbeedeaadd3e24491f2a4425c02, Windows port binary SHA-256 b342b8b85d678d3b2ed26efab70fba2b3956725670be7149b89646868f0ebade.",
    "exclusions": "Other keys, other builds/platforms, other steganographic methods, recompressed files, signature verification, and interpretation of candidate bytes."
  },
  "outcome": "inconclusive",
  "finding": "All ten known payload hashes match. Other outcomes: 21 unverified nonempty outputs with exit 0; five exit-1 rejections; 41 abnormal exits with code 3221225620. Every status, diagnostic and output byte reproduced on rerun.",
  "limitations": "A successful process exit does not authenticate bytes. Failed retrieval does not prove no hidden data. The 41 abnormal exits are unresolved build/tool failures. Only one key and build were tested. Computational review only; human review pending.",
  "next_steps": "See the guarded-build variant for a completed comparison on the same 77 images. Further work includes independent-platform checks and separate validation of candidate bytes; preserve the original baseline failures.",
  "family": {
    "id": "outguess-original-jpegs",
    "title": "OutGuess retrieval from original JPEGs",
    "question": "Which payloads can a specified OutGuess build and key retrieve from the original image bytes?",
    "baseline": "outguess-default-key"
  },
  "variant": {
    "label": "Baseline: Default key, pinned Windows build",
    "changes": []
  },

  "visuals": [
    {
      "path": "experiments/records/outguess-default-key/coverage.svg",

  "article": "# Original JPEGs: default-key OutGuess retrieval\n\n## Why run this?\n\nSome known Liber Primus images contain messages recovered with OutGuess. A newcomer may reasonably try the same operation on the other images. This experiment records what that particular retrieval does, including failures and unverified output, instead of assuming that every byte stream is a message or every failure means an empty image.\n\n## Plan fixed before execution\n\nThe runner and plan were committed as `8bca8ba` before the first run. The scope is all 75 archived manuscript JPEGs, plus the 2014 opening image and the compasses cover. Every original-image SHA-256 is fixed in the plan. Thumbnails, screenshots and recompressed images are excluded.\n\nEach image receives exactly one invocation of OutGuess with retrieval mode and the literal key `Default key`. The timeout is 20 seconds per invocation. Ten expected payload hashes serve as positive controls. All output files, exit codes and stderr diagnostics are retained, including empty output files and abnormal exits. A second complete run checks reproducibility; it is not counted as 77 additional independent discoveries.\n\n## Result\n\nA subsequent [guarded-build comparison](#/experiments/outguess-guard-sweep) retains these original inputs and key. It reproduces all output bytes while replacing the 41 abnormal exits with explicit iterator-guard diagnostics. The table below remains the result of the original baseline build.\n\n| Observed category | Images | What it establishes |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| Known payload hash reproduced | 10 | Exact agreement with the archived extraction control |\n| Nonempty output, exit code 0, no control | 21 | Unverified candidate bytes only |\n| Retrieval rejected, exit code 1 | 5 | This retrieval did not succeed |\n| Abnormal exit code 3221225620 | 41 | An unresolved failure of this tool/build on these inputs |\n| Timeout | 0 | No invocation exceeded the declared time limit |\n\nAll 77 invocations were attempted. Ten controls matched. **The other 67 images are not established as free of hidden data.** The 21 candidate outputs are not authenticated messages, and the 41 abnormal exits prevent treating this as a clean image-wide negative result.\n\nThe repeated output length 58,152 occurs in 19 candidate records. It is a reported extraction length, not a discovered structure in the manuscript. The 21 candidate byte streams have distinct hashes. None contains the ASCII marker `-----BEGIN PGP SIGNED MESSAGE-----`; that limited observation neither validates nor rules out a different encoding or payload type. No signature verification or interpretation of candidate contents was performed in this experiment.\n\n## What the failure diagnostics tell us\n\nThe decimal process code `3221225620` is `0xC0000094`. Microsoft's [NTSTATUS reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/openspecs/windows_protocols/ms-erref/596a1078-e883-4972-9bbc-49e60bebca55) assigns that value to `STATUS_INTEGER_DIVIDE_BY_ZERO`. This identifies the Windows status associated with the saved exits. It does not locate an instruction, identify a faulty source line, or prove whether the cause lies in upstream code, port changes, or another part of the build. No crash dump or debugger stack trace is available in this record.\n\nA separate audit of the saved diagnostics finds the reported header `seed: 41408, len: 58152` on 65 images:\n\n| Recorded outcome for that same header | Images | Output recorded |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| Exit 0, unverified candidate bytes | 19 | 58,152 bytes each |\n| Exit 1, retrieval rejected | 5 | Zero bytes |\n| Exit 0xC0000094, abnormal termination | 41 | Zero bytes |\n\nThus the repeated header occurs with three different outcomes. The `len` diagnostic is the length reported by the tool, not confirmation that a valid payload of that size exists. Nor do the shared values establish intentional repeated content in the JPEGs. The logs alone do not explain their cause. Two other candidate outputs have different headers; the ten positive controls also use different headers.\n\nThe [diagnostic audit JSON](experiments/records/outguess-default-key/results/diagnostic-audit.json) preserves each image's reported seed, length, exit code and output size, tied to the original report's checksum. Reproduce this comparison from the experiment bundle without installing OutGuess or downloading the images:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/outguess-default-key/audit_diagnostics.py\n```\n\nThis command checks existing evidence; it is not another extraction trial. A useful debugging comparison would retain a positive control, a byte-producing case with the shared header, a rejected case, and an abnormal case. Keep the original files and key fixed, record the replacement executable and build settings, and collect a stack trace if it also terminates abnormally. A successful run with another build would still require checking the extracted bytes; it would not automatically validate them as a message.\n\n## How to reproduce\n\nUse Python 3.12.10 and a locally available OutGuess executable. See the [OutGuess guide](#/wiki/outguess) for original-file selection and the known-payload controls.\n\n```\npython experiments/records/outguess-default-key/run.py --outguess outguess --output my-outguess-run\npython experiments/records/outguess-default-key/check.py\n```\n\nThe first command creates a new directory, refuses to reuse an existing one, and records your executable's SHA-256. Replace `outguess` with its full executable path if necessary. The second command audits the saved experiment: every image hash, output hash, expected control and record count. It does not run OutGuess.\n\nTo repeat the exact saved run with the same executable:\n\n```\npython experiments/records/outguess-default-key/run.py --outguess outguess --check\n```\n\nThis checks the tool hash, all statuses, diagnostics and every saved payload byte. Paths to temporary files are normalized in diagnostics; diagnostic content is otherwise retained. A different binary or platform may legitimately produce different diagnostics or error behavior. Run it into a new directory and compare it as a build variant rather than replacing this baseline.\n\n## Tool and build limitation\n\nThe recorded binary was a local Windows port of upstream commit `24810e14327c2bbeedeaadd3e24491f2a4425c02`, built using MinGW-W64 GCC 16.1.0. Its SHA-256 is `b342b8b85d678d3b2ed26efab70fba2b3956725670be7149b89646868f0ebade`.\n\nThe existing build record describes use of the upstream allocation/read fallback instead of mmap, a compatibility byte-order helper, and binary-mode input on Windows. Matching the ten controls checks those particular extraction paths; it does not establish correct behavior on all other images. The 41 abnormal exits remain a substantial limitation. The executable is not included in the wiki downloads. A reader with a different build should preserve their new report as a comparison, not expect its executable hash to match.\n\n## Retest and review\n\nCodex ran the entire 77-image sweep twice on 20 October 2026. All return codes, normalized diagnostics and output bytes matched exactly. A separate saved-file audit checked all image and output hashes and the ten control comparisons. The original plan, key, timeout and image list did not change after the first run. The visual map was generated from the saved report; it does not run another extraction. Human review remains pending.\n\n## What to test next\n\nThe most informative next variant is another documented OutGuess build on exactly the same files and key, focusing on whether the 41 abnormal exits persist. A new key is a different variable and should not be changed simultaneously if the purpose is to isolate build behavior. Other steganographic methods require their own clearly scoped experiment.\n\n## Per-image results\n\nThe table below lists every invocation. Full diagnostics and exact hashes are in [the machine-readable report](experiments/records/outguess-default-key/results/report.json). Raw output downloads are listed under the record's output checksums; unverified bytes must not be described as decoded messages.\n\n| Image | Category | Exit code | Output bytes |\n| --- | --- | --- |   "outcome": "inconclusive",
  "finding": "All 77 payload byte streams match the baseline exactly. Thirty-one successful exits and five existing rejections retain their diagnostics. All 41 formerly abnormal cases now exit 1 with an explicit iterator skipmod-zero diagnostic. Ten known controls pass.",
  "limitations": "This compares two Windows builds from the same upstream source, not independent implementations or platforms. The patched diagnostic is not a stack trace from the original build.   "visuals": [
    {
      "path": "experiments/records/outguess-guard-sweep/results/comparison.svg",
      "caption": "Exit categories for 77 original JPEGs. Bar lengths count images, not verified hidden messages."
    }
  ],
  "article": "# Original JPEGs: guarded OutGuess build comparison\n\n## What this test asks\n\nThe original default-key sweep had 41 abnormal exits. Those failures leave an important question: did the retrieval reach an identifiable error condition, and would a more explicit check change the extracted bytes?\n\nThis variant uses a clean build with three diagnostic guards. A guard checks a condition before an operation that would otherwise be invalid and stops with an explanatory message. Here the checks concern the retrieval bit position, iterator capacity, and a zero iterator value used by a remainder operation. They are diagnostic changes, not a new decryption method.\n\nThe [original baseline](#/experiments/outguess-default-key) remains available with its unchanged results. Both records belong to the same experiment family.\n\n## What stayed fixed\n\nThe inputs are all 75 manuscript JPEGs plus the 2014 opening image and compasses cover, in their original bytes. Image hashes, the literal key `Default key`, and the 20-second timeout match the baseline. No image was recompressed or edited. The ten known payload controls run first; a control failure would stop the sweep.\n\nThe scope and runner were committed as `40890c5` before execution. The earlier 13-case pilot helped establish the build procedure; those cases are included here and are not presented as unseen validation. This is one complete 77-image comparison, not a search over keys or build settings.\n\n## What changed\n\nThe recorded executable was compiled afresh from upstream commit `24810e14327c2bbeedeaadd3e24491f2a4425c02`, with the documented Windows portability changes and explicit guard patches. All 54 C files were compiled; object files from the original build were not reused. The build specification records compiler identity, source hashes and commands.\n\nThe clean guarded Windows executable has SHA-256 `bdc1810e59cb1152e7c3da88b38eaedfe49eba1656b4a4ab6f8c2b3f40126273`.\n\nThe clean executable differs in hash from the archived pilot executable, although it reproduced all 13 pilot results exactly. The full comparison below uses the clean executable. This does not establish bit-for-bit reproducible compilation across toolchains.\n\n## Results\n\n| Baseline outcome | Guarded outcome | Images |\n| --- | --- | ---: |\n| Successful exit | Same successful exit, diagnostic and bytes | 31 |\n| Existing rejection | Same rejection, diagnostic and bytes | 5 |\n| Abnormal exit | Explicit zero-iterator guard; unchanged empty output | 41 |\n\nAll ten positive controls match. The 31 successful exits consist of those ten controls and 21 unverified outputs. Every one of the 77 payload byte streams matches the baseline exactly; no new candidate output appeared.\n\nAll 41 changed cases report `Guard: iterator skipmod zero`, with their individual bit counts and offsets retained in the saved report. For example, LP1-14 reports `Guard: iterator skipmod zero at off=645437 bits=645682`. The guarded build checks this zero value before the iterator's remainder operation.\n\nThe [comparison graphic](experiments/records/outguess-guard-sweep/results/comparison.svg) summarizes the counts. The [per-image comparison](experiments/records/outguess-guard-sweep/results/comparison.json) and [complete diagnostics](experiments/records/outguess-guard-sweep/results/report.json) retain the underlying evidence.\n\n## What the result means\n\nThe new build gives a specific diagnostic for all 41 previously abnormal cases. This is useful for investigating the implementation and for preventing those failures from being mistaken for clean negative results.\n\nIt does not authenticate the 21 candidate outputs. It does not prove any image lacks hidden data. Both executables share the same upstream source and Windows port, so this is not validation by an independent implementation or another platform. The guarded run is also not a captured stack trace from the original executable.\n\n## Reproduce the saved comparison\n\nDownload this experiment's bundle and the original-images archive, then extract both into the same folder, preserving their paths. Follow the bundle's START-HERE file to verify the archive and required image hashes. From that folder run:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/outguess-guard-sweep/compare.py --check\n```\n\nThis needs Python and the supplied data, but does not execute OutGuess. It verifies the plan dependencies and image hashes, checks both sets of saved outputs, and compares bytes and diagnostics directly. It recomputes the saved comparison instead of trusting its reported equality flags.\n\nTo regenerate the chart after that audit:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/outguess-guard-sweep/figure.py\n```\n\n## Repeat retrieval from a source build\n\nSupply a clean checkout of the pinned upstream source and a compatible MinGW-W64 GCC toolchain. The included build script does not fetch or install these dependencies. Choose an output directory that does not yet exist:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/outguess-guard-pilot/build.py --source /path/to/outguess-source --output /path/to/new-build\npython experiments/records/outguess-guard-sweep/run.py --outguess /path/to/new-build/outguess.exe --output /path/to/new-results\n```\n\nThe runner requires the recorded executable hash. If compilation produces a different hash, preserve its build report and define a separate comparison; do not overwrite the expected hash to make the check pass. The new-results directory must not already exist. The saved-evidence audit above checks the committed results, not this new directory. To rerun retrieval and compare directly with the committed results, use `run.py --outguess /path/to/new-build/outguess.exe --check`.\n\n## Remaining work\n\nHuman review is pending. An independently documented platform or implementation would address a different uncertainty from the guard comparison. Candidate-payload analysis should be a separate bounded experiment, retaining all outputs and avoiding the assumption that process success implies a message.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/outguess-guard-sweep/article.md",

  "id": "page-join-sensitivity",
  "title": "LP2 page joins: sensitivity of word-length counts",
  "status": "published",
  "question": "How much do word-based LP2 statistics change when each unresolved rune-to-rune page edge is treated as a separator?",
  "summary": "Separating all 32 candidate edges changes the token count from 2,896 to 2,928 and the count of tokens at least ten runes long from 109 to 104; the ordered rune stream is unchanged.",
  "tags": [
    "page boundaries",
    "word lengths",
    "transcription",
    "tokenization",
    "sensitivity",
    "search space",
    "LP2"
  ],
  "scope": {
    "pages": [],
    "artifacts": [
      "text/lp2-00.txt"

    "representation": "Archived LP2-00–55 UTF-8 transcription text and the 29-rune site alphabet; all 32 rune-to-rune page edges are candidate separators, not verified word splits.",
    "procedure": "Remove slash and CR/LF row wraps; preserve other delimiters. Compare fully joined, all 32 candidate edges separated, and every single candidate edge separately split using the same rune-token rule. Report token lengths and selected word-based counts.",
    "parameters": "Fixed 56-page corpus, 32 identified candidate edges, no random search, 29-rune alphabet, headings retained, apostrophes internal to tokens but zero rune length.",
    "exclusions": "No image review, inferred English words, plaintext scoring, cipher trial, alternate transcription, LP2-56–57, or claim that either endpoint is the intended manuscript segmentation."
  },
  "outcome": "supported",
  "finding": "Under the specified tokenizer, each of the 32 candidate edge splits adds one token. The 11–11–10 length window count remains one.",
  "limitations": "The candidate edges are based on archived characters, not verified manuscript word boundaries. The all-split case is an endpoint sensitivity comparison, not a corrected transcription. This result measures segmentation sensitivity rather than evidence for a particular cipher.",
