  "visuals": [
    {
      "path": "experiments/records/page-join-sensitivity/token-lengths.svg",
      "caption": "Rune-token length counts under all-joined and all-candidate-edges-separated policies, using the same rune stream."
    }
  ],
  "article": "# How much do unresolved LP2 page joins change word-length counts?\n\nThe published LP2 word-length census joins adjacent pages when their archived text meets rune to rune. That rule yields **2,896 rune tokens**. If a separator is inserted at each of the **32 rune-to-rune page edges**, the same 12,956 runes yield **2,928 tokens**. This experiment measures how much the statistics depend on that parsing choice. It does not decide which edges actually split words in the manuscript.\n\n![Side-by-side rune-token length counts for joined and separated page edges](experiments/records/page-join-sensitivity/token-lengths.svg)\n\n## Fixed comparison\n\nUse the archived text for LP2-00–55 and the site's 29-rune alphabet. Remove slash and CR/LF row wraps, retain headings and other punctuation, and count rune runs with optional internal apostrophes. There are three prespecified readings: concatenate every page; insert a space at all 32 edges whose archived end and start are both runes; and insert a space at each such edge one at a time. No rune is changed or omitted. The [boundary inventory](#/wiki/transcription-checking?section=page-joins) supplies the distinction between a rune-to-rune candidate and a verified word join.\n\n| Measure | All edges joined | All 32 candidates separated |\n| --- | ---: | ---: |\n| Rune tokens | 2,896 | 2,928 |\n| One-rune tokens | 83 | 99 |\n| Two-rune tokens | 448 | 465 |\n| Three-rune tokens | 720 | 726 |\n| Tokens at least 10 runes long | 109 | 104 |\n| Maximum token length | 14 | 14 |\n| 11–11–10 length windows | 1 | 1 |\n\nAll 32 individual splits add exactly one token under this tokenizer. Five individual edges—LP2-21/22, 24/25, 42/43, 46/47 and 52/53—each reduce the number of tokens at least 10 runes long by one. The [machine-readable result](experiments/records/page-join-sensitivity/results.json) lists every edge separately. The LP2-21 11–11–10 observation survives both endpoint policies, but this says nothing about its chance frequency or interpretation.\n\nThese endpoints are sensitivity cases, not manuscript corrections. A real reading could join some edges and split others. The source text can also omit a mark, and rune-to-rune edges can cross section boundaries. Word counts, repeated-token counts and word-reset cipher inputs depend on the boundary rule; rune frequencies and whole-stream IoC do not, because both versions contain the identical ordered runes. The reported 2,896 tokens are a transparent parsing convention, not 2,896 established words.\n\n## Reproduce and extend\n\nWith Python 3 and no packages, run `python experiments/records/page-join-sensitivity/run.py --check` and `python experiments/records/page-join-sensitivity/check.py` from the repository root or the [experiment bundle](downloads/experiments/page-join-sensitivity.zip). The first command checks the source hashes, complete report and figure. The second uses an independent character scanner to verify the 32 candidate edges, the two histograms, every one-edge token count, and the invariant 12,956-rune total. The plan fixes the inputs and three comparisons before interpreting them.\n\nThe next useful refinement is to record image-reviewed separators at particular edges and rerun the same script with those decisions frozen. Until then, a word-based cipher claim should specify its page-edge policy and show whether its result survives plausible changes at the relevant edges. See the [word-length guide](#/wiki/word-lengths) for the counting rules and complete token ledger.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/page-join-sensitivity/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "42348625496957f855de1ad41411e8fea4b523a179437e8ac5c798e5b0cff771",

  }
}

      "url": "https://jelliottdev.github.io/#/wiki/reported-attempts?section=shed-circumference-page-margin-join"

  "visuals": [
    {
      "path": "experiments/records/page-margin-row-alignment/row-alignment.svg",
      "caption": "All 36 fixed-crop row-mask similarities. Adjacent pairs are outlined; several nonadjacent controls are equally perfect."
    }
  ],
  "article": "# Does trimming page margins reveal a special line alignment?\n\nA source discussion suggested reading “shed the circumference” as an instruction to remove manuscript margins and place pages side by side. It described this as something to try, not as a finished decryption. A side-by-side picture is easy to make but easy to overread: text lines can align because pages share a layout. This experiment asks the narrower, measurable question: **do adjacent LP2 pages line up more distinctively than other pages of the same design?**\n\n![All 36 fixed-crop row-alignment scores among LP2-40–48; outlined cells are adjacent pairs](experiments/records/page-margin-row-alignment/row-alignment.svg)\n\n## What was fixed\n\nThe nine original JPEGs LP2-40–48 are all 2400 × 3600 pixels. This is a continuous run of text-heavy pages with the same plant-border design; the source proposal did **not** designate these pages. From every image, take the same rectangle, x = 650–1749 and y = 620–2899. This sheds both illustrated sides and keeps the central writing. Preserve the original y coordinates: no page is shifted to fit another.\n\nFor each y row, sample every third x pixel. Call the row occupied when more than 12 samples have grayscale value below 90. The similarity of two row masks is their occupied-row intersection divided by their union (Jaccard score). Compare all **eight consecutive pairs** with **all 28 nonconsecutive pairs** from the same run. The [plan](experiments/records/page-margin-row-alignment/plan.json) fixes the crop, threshold, score and controls; [results.json](experiments/records/page-margin-row-alignment/results.json) gives every pair and each page’s row bands.\n\n## What the pages show\n\nThe mean score is 0.764 for consecutive pages and 0.672 for controls. That difference by itself is not evidence of a special join: four adjacent pairs score exactly 1.000, **but six nonadjacent controls also score 1.000**. In particular, every pair within LP2-44–48 has the same row mask under this rule. The text grid is reused across multiple pages, so an apparently perfect horizontal alignment cannot identify the correct next page. LP2-40’s enlarged red initial and the larger gaps on some earlier pages also change the measured bands. Every pair, including poor fits, appears in the figure and result file.\n\nThis tests only vertical placement of dark text rows after one fixed crop. It cannot tell whether the final rune of one line continues at the beginning of another, whether a word crosses a page boundary, or whether “shed the circumference” refers to physical page margins at all. The source left crop, page order, registration and success condition open. Selecting those *after* seeing an attractive join would create a large search space. The observed score difference has no significance test because pair comparisons share pages and the groups were not random independent samples.\n\n## Reproduce or extend\n\nRun `python experiments/records/page-margin-row-alignment/run.py --check` and `python experiments/records/page-margin-row-alignment/check.py` from the repository root or extracted bundle. They require Python 3 and Pillow. `run.py` checks each JPEG’s SHA-256 and the complete saved result; `check.py` scans the image buffers independently and recomputes all 36 scores. `plot.py` regenerates the SVG.\n\nA stronger visual continuation test would need a page sequence and a predeclared rune-level seam rule, plus nonadjacent pages matched for template and line count. The [page-join sensitivity record](#/experiments/page-join-sensitivity) separately measures what happens to word statistics when text transcripts are joined or split at page edges. Neither result supplies an LP2 plaintext.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/page-margin-row-alignment/article.md",

  "article": "# What does the LP2-40 “FOR EVERY” calculation actually establish?\n\nA [reported attempt](#/wiki/reported-attempts?section=page40-for-every-mobius) reads the first two rune groups on [LP2-40](#/reader/lp2-40) as **FOR EVERY**. It interprets mirrored border work as a reason to use Atbash, floral details as the numbers 13 and 31, and their difference, 18, as a shift. It then adds a prime-minus-one stream, treats the initial F as a skipped zero, and suggests a Möbius-directed running key for the difference still needed. Those links from artwork to operations are the solver's proposed interpretation; this audit does not establish them as intended clues.\n\nThe source discussion itself describes the example as a working theory built partly backwards from a desired reading. Its linked spreadsheet was described as changing over time. We identify the preserved discussion by SHA-256 `2338de900f4ec231d42791c988640317241880675b35ff68af42ee162cb6573a`; the file is not redistributed here. The replay uses the numerical rows printed in that discussion, the [archived LP2-40 transcription](#/page/lp2-40), and the stored Gematria Primus table.\n\n## Eight positions, one fixed calculation\n\nThe first two archived groups contain three and five runes. Their indices are `0, 9, 19 / 26, 6, 23, 25, 8`, matching the source's quoted ciphertext row. The proposed **FOR EVERY** indices are `0, 3, 4 / 18, 1, 18, 4, 26`. On the seven positions after F, shifting each proposed plaintext index by 18 and reflecting with Atbash gives `7, 6, 21, 9, 21, 6, 13`. Adding the source's prime-minus-one stream modulo 29 gives the intermediate row `0, 8, 8 / 25, 15, 2, 18, 0`.\n\n![The fixed rule is compared with eight archived indices. Seven non-F outputs differ; the final row is a residual derived from the observed ciphertext.](experiments/records/page40-for-every-arithmetic/first-eight-trace.svg)\n\nThe fixed layers match **zero of seven non-F positions**. The initial F matches because the source holds it at zero rather than transforming it. Subtracting the intermediate row from the observed ciphertext yields residuals `0, 1, 11, 1, 20, 21, 7, 8` modulo 29. The source writes `−8` instead of `21` at the sixth position; these are the same modulo 29. These residuals are calculated *after looking at the ciphertext*. Adding them back necessarily reconstructs the target and is not yet evidence for a running-key rule.\n\nThe proposed phrase's GP sums are **FOR = 20** (composite), **EVERY = 251** (prime), and **FOR EVERY = 271** (prime). Thus the whole phrase satisfies a prime-sum filter, while both words individually do not. A prime sum is a property of this candidate, not an independent reading of the runes.\n\n## Where the replay stops\n\nThe discussion does not fix the Möbius argument or starting point, how neighboring values form the proposed trigram state, which of the eight possible key formulas belongs to each state, how signs and zero are treated, or exactly when the stream advances over F and separators. Its later notes explore modified Slidefair, Quagmire-like matrices and a Fibonacci autokey as different follow-ups; those are **not** tested here. The incomplete spreadsheet and absent fixed state table prevent an honest end-to-end replay of the proposed running key. The source itself says the state flexibility could make the arithmetic fit.\n\nTo turn the running-key idea into a test, choose a complete state table and seed **before** inspecting additional text; specify plaintext-versus-ciphertext feedback, order of operations, F handling and word boundaries; then compare a continuous output on held-out page text with matched controls. A crib fit on these eight positions alone cannot do that work.\n\n## Reproduce this audit\n\nFrom the repository root or [downloadable experiment bundle](downloads/experiments/page40-for-every-arithmetic.zip), run:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/page40-for-every-arithmetic/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/page40-for-every-arithmetic/check.py\npython experiments/records/page40-for-every-arithmetic/plot.py --check\n```\n\nThe [plan](experiments/records/page40-for-every-arithmetic/plan.json) pins the source's printed rows, input hashes, fixed formula, success criterion and stopping rule. The [complete result](experiments/records/page40-for-every-arithmetic/results.json) lists every intermediate and fitted difference. The checker independently reads the rune text, recomputes the seven transformed indices and verifies each congruence and prime sum. This is an **arithmetic audit of one proposed opening**, not a disproof of every artwork-based or running-key method.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/page40-for-every-arithmetic/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "98b9828471565b1017714879af2c1bad56e75cf50e4f126c5ca24385822d4b02",

  "article": "## What changed from the baseline\n\nThe [full-corpus comparison](#/experiments/parallel-languages) used 1,012 evaluation sentences per language. Here we divide that evaluation split into **eight consecutive, disjoint blocks** and compare shorter passages. Each block contains the same sentence IDs in all eight languages. No sentences were chosen because their statistics looked promising.\n\nThe first four blocks contain 127 sentences each, and the last four contain 126. Exact one-based sentence ranges are recorded in the results. The tokenization and distance definitions are unchanged.\n\n## Results\n\n**English is the closest of the eight language profiles to the pooled manuscript in all eight blocks, in each of the three representations.** This supports the stability of that relative ranking across these shorter passages. It does not identify the plaintext language.\n\nUsing letter units, the block sizes and manuscript distances are:\n\n| Language | Tokens per block, range | Word-length distance, range |\n| --- | ---: | ---: |\n| English | 2,613–3,002 | 0.0710–0.1035 |\n| Finnish | 1,927–2,105 | 0.3726–0.4316 |\n| French | 3,047–3,318 | 0.1731–0.2079 |\n| German | 2,623–2,927 | 0.1696–0.1961 |\n| Italian | 2,880–3,181 | 0.2274–0.2467 |\n| Portuguese | 2,818–3,147 | 0.2007–0.2300 |\n| Spanish | 3,106–3,467 | 0.2091–0.2402 |\n| Welsh | 2,884–3,206 | 0.1416–0.1940 |\n\nThe target has 2,896 rune tokens. These are smaller aligned passages, not exactly size-matched samples: their token counts range from **1,927 to 3,467**. Translating the same content changes word counts. Keeping the same sentence ranges preserves the content control; truncating every language at exactly 2,896 words would no longer compare exactly the same passages. This design documents that tradeoff rather than hiding it.\n\n## Does the statistic recognize known languages at this scale?\n\nFor each block, we compare its word-length histogram against all eight full development-language histograms. The closest development profile is the corresponding language in **64 of 64 decisions**, separately for letter units, accent-folded letters, and GP grouping. The raw report includes every distance and the full confusion matrices, including zeros.\n\nThat is a control on these eight translated languages within FLORES. It is not a success rate for cipher language identification. The corpus shares translation practices and source genre; the manuscript does not. The three representations also reuse the same text and are not independent replications.\n\n## Bounds and limitations\n\n- All 1,012 evaluation sentences are used once per language, with no overlap between blocks. Development text is used only for the reference profiles.\n- A source article can cross a block boundary. Blocks are therefore not independent draws, and the 64 decisions are not treated as independent trials. No binomial accuracy interval or language posterior is calculated.\n- The manuscript remains pooled LP2-00–55, with headings and the baseline boundary convention. This does not test each section separately.\n- Word-length comparison requires preserved boundaries and one ciphertext rune per counted plaintext unit. GP grouping remains an orthographic sensitivity, not a validated phonetic transcription.\n- No genre-matched corpus or known decoded LP control is included in this variant. The separate [known-reading control](#/experiments/known-reading-languages) now covers the nine documented LP sections. A genre-matched corpus remains open.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nThe experiment download includes the aligned corpus, token ledger, baseline helper, independent tokenizer, frozen plan and result ledger. Python 3 standard library only; no network, API or model is used.\n\n```sh\npython experiments/records/parallel-language-blocks/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/parallel-language-blocks/check.py\n```\n\nThe plan was committed before block scoring; its dependency hash was refreshed for a chart-only baseline change before scoring began. The first command verifies input hashes and recomputes the full report. The second independently reconstructs all 192 block profiles with a regex tokenizer and exact rational total-variation distances, checks all nearest-reference decisions, and verifies that the block ranges cover the evaluation sentences exactly once.\n\n[Results and confusion matrices](experiments/records/parallel-language-blocks/results.json) · [Frozen plan](experiments/records/parallel-language-blocks/plan.json) · [Baseline distributions and source attribution](#/experiments/parallel-languages)\n\nFLORES source text and this derived account are offered under CC BY-SA 4.0. See the source attribution included with the baseline files.\n",

  "article": "## What this comparison tells us\n\n**English has the closest word-length distribution among the eight reference languages tested.** This comparison is useful only if the manuscript's separators correspond to plaintext word boundaries and the encryption preserves one counted unit per rune. Those conditions are unverified for unsolved LP2. The ordering of other close candidates changes when a fixed GP-style grouping is applied to all eight. A nearest distribution is not a plaintext identification or a decoded word.\n\nThe experiment uses translations of the **same 997 development sentences and 1,012 evaluation sentences** from FLORES-200. The languages were fixed before scoring: English, Welsh, German, French, Spanish, Italian, Portuguese and Finnish. They give a manageable Latin-script comparison without adding a transliteration model for other scripts. They are not a shortlist inferred from the manuscript, and the ranking is not a search across all languages.\n\nThe plan and source files were committed in `738a812` before any scores were calculated. It is a predeclared comparison within this project, not an external preregistration. Human review is pending.\n\n## Word-length results\n\nThe distance is **total variation** between word-length distributions: half the sum of their absolute frequency differences. Zero means identical distributions; one means no overlap. We count lengths 1 through 15 separately and put longer words in a final 16+ bin. A value of 0.084 is a distance, not an 8.4% chance of anything.\n\n| Language | Letters | GP grouping sensitivity |\n| --- | ---: | ---: |\n| English | 0.0840 | 0.1148 |\n| Welsh | 0.1721 | 0.1731 |\n| German | 0.1757 | 0.1708 |\n| French | 0.1827 | 0.1759 |\n| Portuguese | 0.2131 | 0.2058 |\n| Spanish | 0.2240 | 0.2127 |\n| Italian | 0.2359 | 0.2311 |\n| Finnish | 0.4022 | 0.3927 |\n\n[Open the comparison chart](experiments/records/parallel-languages/comparison.svg). The chart shows the same results with article-resampling ranges. The JSON also contains the accent-folded letter comparison, which keeps the same language order.\n\nThe ordering depends on the counting convention. A language ranking is conditional on both the corpus and the assumed relationship between plaintext units and ciphertext runes. The full table keeps every tested candidate visible.\n\n## Why the rankings differ\n\nThe manuscript has a pronounced peak at length three: **24.86% of its tokens contain three runes**. The language profiles differ in how much mass they place at each length. The distribution chart shows the manuscript first, followed by all eight languages alphabetically, using identical scales and the same styling for every language.\n\nThe first-place result still has a visible mismatch: English has 19.07% three-letter words, below the manuscript's three-rune share. A ranking measures relative closeness among the tested profiles; it does not establish that the nearest profile is a good explanation of the ciphertext.\n\n[Open all nine distribution panels](experiments/records/parallel-languages/distributions.svg). Lengths 9 and above are combined only for display; scoring retains the original 16 bins. Every full distribution is also available in the results JSON.\n\n## The assumptions that make lengths useful\n\nThis comparison requires manuscript word boundaries to preserve plaintext word boundaries, and one counted plaintext unit to correspond to one ciphertext rune. A position-dependent substitution can preserve lengths even when letter frequencies change. Inserted nulls, deleted symbols, word splitting, different spacing, or units representing syllables can break the comparison.\n\nThe manuscript target is the existing [rune-token ledger](exports/unsolved-word-tokens.json): **2,896 tokens and 12,956 runes from LP2-00–55**, including headings. Line wraps and slash wraps are removed; tokens can continue across page boundaries. Internal apostrophes count zero, and decimal labels are excluded. See [word lengths](#/wiki/word-lengths) for the exact boundary convention and its historical alternatives. Pooling the pages assumes their aggregate is meaningful; it does not establish that every section has one language or cipher.\n\nFor FLORES, letters are lowercased and normalized to NFC. Alphabetic runs are words; internal straight or curly apostrophes are removed without splitting the word. Hyphens and other nonletters separate words. Numbers contribute no letters. Each sentence is tokenized independently. This is an explicit mechanical convention, not a linguist's definition of a word. The comparison retains every aligned sentence; it does not truncate each language to a different passage to equalize word totals.\n\nThe GP sensitivity folds combining accents and greedily groups ING, TH, EO, NG, OE, AE, IA, IO and EA, longest first. ING/NG, IO/IA, K/C and Z/S share symbols. Other letters remain. **This is not a validated translation into Gematria Primus.** Pronunciation, ambiguous segmentation and unsupported letters remain unresolved. A supplementary mechanical Welsh-digraph calculation is retained in the raw data as a representation check, not as a separate candidate category or a preferred model. It groups CH, DD, FF, NG, LL, PH, RH and TH and gives a length distance of 0.1466; it does not resolve morphological parsing. The raw-letter and GP profiles can contain more than 29 distinct symbols, so they cannot be literal bijective mappings into a 29-rune alphabet as written. This inventory mismatch is reported in the downloadable results rather than silently repaired by deleting rare letters.\n\n## Repetition gives a different test\n\nIoC is the probability that two different sampled positions contain the same symbol. Adjacent repetition here counts equal neighbors **within words only**. Both require stronger assumptions than lengths: equality must survive a fixed one-to-one substitution. They are not preserved by a general polyalphabetic cipher.\n\n| Text, using letter units | IoC | Equal adjacent pairs |\n| --- | ---: | ---: |\n| Unsolved rune target | 0.03448 | 0.63% |\n| English | 0.06597 | 2.42% |\n| Welsh | 0.06387 | 5.74% |\n| German | 0.07344 | 2.33% |\n| French | 0.06912 | 2.42% |\n| Portuguese | 0.07072 | 1.00% |\n| Spanish | 0.07111 | 0.77% |\n| Italian | 0.07305 | 4.57% |\n| Finnish | 0.07282 | 9.31% |\n\nThe language profiles have letter IoCs between **0.06387 and 0.07344**, far from the target's **0.03448**. None of these profiles supplies a close single-substitution explanation of the pooled manuscript. The GP sensitivity does not remove that discrepancy. Spanish is closest on the adjacent-repeat measure, yet has a much poorer word-length match. These conflicting rankings are why we do not blend the measures into an unexplained “language likelihood.”\n\nThis does not eliminate Welsh, English or any other language under a different cipher. It weakens the proposed fixed-substitution comparison under these text and unit conventions. See [cipher invariants](#/wiki/cipher-invariants) for what different transformations preserve.\n\n## Controls and sampling sensitivity\n\nEach development-language word-length profile was compared with each evaluation-language profile. The nearest development profile identified the corresponding evaluation language **8 out of 8 times in each of the three representations**. That is a useful check that this dataset and statistic can distinguish the chosen languages at this sample size. It is not 100% accuracy on unknown manuscripts: there are only eight whole-document controls, drawn from the same benchmark, and they are much longer than the target.\n\nFor the error bars we resample the **281 source-article URL groups** in the evaluation split, with replacement, 200 times using seed 3301. All sentences from a sampled article are kept. The same article draw is used for all eight languages, preserving the matched-content comparison and avoiding treating every sentence as independent. English has the smallest length distance in all 200 draws in all three representations. This is stability to this corpus resampling—not a 100% probability that the manuscript is English. The target transcription is held fixed; these intervals omit uncertainty about its boundaries, genre and cipher.\n\nFLORES contains translated web material. It controls subject matter across languages, but not the difference between that material and Liber Primus's philosophical style, historical spelling or possible nonstandard prose. Translation practices can also affect lengths. A separately fixed, genre-matched parallel corpus remains a follow-up. The [exact-token control](#/experiments/target-sized-languages) now checks complete 2,896-token samples: all reference samples identify their own language profile, but every manuscript-to-profile distance exceeds the corresponding observed control range. Those ranges are descriptive, not confidence limits or rejection thresholds. The [known-LP reading control](#/experiments/known-reading-languages) is now complete as a computational comparison, with human review pending. A separate [shorter aligned-block variant](#/experiments/parallel-language-blocks) now checks eight disjoint evaluation blocks per language; it preserves matching sentences rather than enforcing exactly equal word counts.\n\n## Reproduce it\n\nDownload this experiment's bundle. It includes the source translations, source-article metadata, plan, token ledger, scripts, result JSON and chart. No API, account, model download or network request is needed to rerun the analysis; Python 3's standard library is enough.\n\n```sh\npython experiments/records/parallel-languages/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/parallel-languages/check.py\npython experiments/records/parallel-languages/distribution_figure.py --check\n```\n\nThe first command verifies input hashes, recomputes the comparisons and the 200 resamples, and checks the saved report and chart. Without `--check`, it writes those two outputs. The second uses a separate regex tokenizer and integer-count formulas to verify the 24 language profiles, additional digraph sensitivity, manuscript profile, IoC, repeated neighbors, distances and ordering. It does not independently reimplement the bootstrap. The final command checks that the distribution chart matches the saved counts; it does not perform another experiment. The ledger itself has a separate [transcription/word-length reproduction](#/wiki/word-lengths).\n\n[Raw results](experiments/records/parallel-languages/results.json) · [Frozen plan](experiments/records/parallel-languages/plan.json) · [Source attribution](experiments/records/parallel-languages/SOURCE.txt)\n\n## Sources and reuse\n\n- [FLORES-200 documentation](https://github.com/facebookresearch/flores/blob/main/flores200/README.md): aligned translation benchmark and language list.\n- [Original archive](https://dl.fbaipublicfiles.com/nllb/flores200_dataset.tar.gz): exact extracted translation and metadata files; archive and extracted-file hashes are recorded in the plan.\n- [Dataset card and license](https://huggingface.co/datasets/facebook/flores): Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International. Source translations are redistributed unchanged. This derived analysis and its article are also offered under CC BY-SA 4.0.\n\n## Check against known LP readings\n\nThe [known-reading control](#/experiments/known-reading-languages) now tests all nine established reading sections and their pool. The pool ranks closest to English, while some individual sections do not. It also documents how LP2-56's embedded hash distorts an unfiltered letter-token count. This supplies a manuscript-specific caution beyond the within-FLORES controls.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/parallel-languages/article.md",

  "reader_limit": "Only fixed byte-zero readings and two event-gap definitions are tested.",
  "scope_summary": "LP2-49–51 grid · LP2-00–55 doublets · 14 fixed comparisons.",
  "article": "# Do the byte-grid values encode doublet spacing?\n\n**No direct rank alignment was found under seven specified byte readings.** The strongest absolute correlation is **0.119**, below the published 0.5 gate. This checks one way the [LP2-49–51 numerical grid](#/wiki/alphanumeric-grids) might encode positions of repeated adjacent runes elsewhere in LP2; it does not assess every possible use of the grid.\n\n![Seven payload readings compared with the gap sequence. All bars fall below the declared 0.5 gate.](experiments/records/payload-doublet-gaps/gap-correlation.svg)\n\nAn equal-rune pair is called a *doublet*. There are 86 such pairs within the archived LP2-00–55 page texts. Put their starting rune positions in page order, then subtract each from the next: that makes **85 gaps**. The first few are `85, 249, 197, 129`. We compared this sequence with numbers read from the published 256-byte grid file, beginning at byte zero each time.\n\n| Byte reading | Values used | Correlation with 85 gaps |\n| --- | ---: | ---: |\n| One unsigned byte per number | 85 | +0.043 |\n| Two-byte integers, little endian | 85 | −0.018 |\n| Two-byte integers, big endian | 85 | −0.026 |\n| LEB128, forward / reversed bytes | 85 each | −0.027 / +0.004 |\n| MSB-first base-128, forward / reversed bytes | 85 each | −0.040 / −0.004 |\n\nThe source's later varint test also prepended the one-based location of the first doublet, **122**, making an 86-value target. The largest absolute correlation across both targets is **0.119**: forward LEB128 against that 86-value sequence. [The full result table](experiments/records/payload-doublet-gaps/results.json) retains all 14 comparisons and the number of values each decoding produced.\n\n## How the comparison was checked\n\nThe statistic is Spearman's rank correlation: it asks whether large payload numbers tend to line up with large doublet gaps, without requiring their magnitudes to match. The test fixes the reading direction and starts at the first byte and first gap. It does **not** shift the payload until a favorable match appears. As an alignment check, we circularly shifted the 85-gap target through its other 84 positions, repeating the largest-of-seven comparison each time. **83 of 84** shifted alignments matched or exceeded the unshifted maximum. Those shifts are dependent descriptive controls, not a calibrated cipher null or a p-value.\n\nEncoding all 85 actual gaps into either varint format and decoding them again recovers every gap exactly. A separate checker recomputes all 14 correlations with a different midrank algorithm. This establishes that the tested encoders and rank calculations work; it does not prove the grid cannot hide a transformed gap list.\n\nThe [earlier published fixed-width check](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round16/zeroFP/zerofp_tests.py) used unsigned 8- and 16-bit values. A [later extension](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round28/L5/l5_payload_micro.py) tested the two variable-length readings and both byte directions. This replay uses the pinned source byte file and Liberpedia's separately archived [doublet coordinates](#/experiments/doublet-placement). No inference is made about alternate grid transcriptions, arbitrary offsets, other encodings or a decoder that first transforms the bytes.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nExtract this experiment and the reference-data bundle together, then run:\n\n```sh\npython experiments/records/payload-doublet-gaps/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/payload-doublet-gaps/check.py\n```\n\nBoth scripts use only the Python standard library.\n",

  "visuals": [
    {
      "path": "exports/figures/position-divisor-bound.svg",
      "caption": "LP2-00: the same F rune occurs at positions 7, 17 and 58. Subtraction removes the unknown origin. The stride assumption determines the conclusion."
    }
  ],
  "article": "# Can each rune label a divisor of its position?\n\n**Not with consecutive positions, under the rule tested here.** Every nonempty rune page in LP2-00–55 contains repeated occurrences whose spacing makes a fixed divisor greater than one impossible, regardless of where counting starts. This is a fresh reproduction of the supplied closure archive's C11 claim, not an original discovery.\n\n## Define the rule before testing it\n\nLet i be a zero-based rune position within a page. Choose an integer origin N and a fixed stride s. Assign each rune r an integer divisor q[r] greater than one, then require:\n\n```text\nq[r] divides N + s*i whenever position i contains r\n```\n\nThe same rune must keep the same divisor throughout that page. Divisors need not be prime, distinct, or equal to Gematria Primus values. Allowing all integers greater than one makes this test more permissive than an assignment restricted to primes. Each page may use its own origin, stride and assignment.\n\nThis is a necessary condition for a direct smallest-factor or largest-factor labeling proposal. It does not test prime-derived keys combined with plaintext or an arbitrary operation that merely uses prime numbers.\n\n## Why the origin cancels\n\nIf q divides both N+s*i and N+s*j, it divides their difference s*(j−i). The unknown N disappears. For several occurrences, q must therefore divide the stride multiplied by the gcd of the position gaps.\n\nFor unit stride, a gap gcd of 1 would require q to divide 1. That contradicts q > 1. Running the page backwards changes the origin and stride sign, not this obstruction.\n\nA rune appearing only once has no gap constraint. Two occurrences with gap 1 already suffice; otherwise several gaps may be needed. The report records every occurrence and, where available, a three-occurrence gcd-one witness. It uses gcd 0 for an empty set of gaps; that means no restriction from this particular test, not impossibility.\n\n## A witness on LP2-00\n\nF occurs at zero-based rune positions **7, 17 and 58**. Thus a fixed divisor must divide both 10 and 51 under unit stride. Their gcd is 1. This single repeated rune already rules out the model on that page; the report records the other rune labels as well.\n\nThese are positions in the filtered rune stream, including the heading. They are not image coordinates, Latin-letter offsets or positions that count punctuation.\n\n## What the full retest covers\n\nThe program reads all 56 archived text files LP2-00–55, retains alphabet runes and headings, and starts each page independently. All **55 nonempty streams** have at least one gcd-one rune. LP2-50 has no alphabet runes in this transcription and is skipped; its alphanumeric grid is not converted into runes.\n\nEvery page therefore excludes both forward and reverse unit-stride constructions, even when the origin and arbitrary integer divisor labels are chosen independently for that page. This is an exact contradiction under the stated model, not a low probability or a finite search over origins.\n\n## Why arbitrary strides remain different\n\nWith a gcd-one witness, the general condition is **q divides s**. It excludes a stride coprime to that rune's divisor. It does not exclude every nonunit stride.\n\nFor a concrete counterexample, set N=2, s=2 and q[r]=2 for every rune. Every position N+s*i is even, so every recorded rune passes the divisibility condition on every page. This construction assigns the same divisor to different runes, which the tested necessary condition permits. It supplies no decoding rule and does not identify which rune to emit at a position.\n\nIf a proposal requires distinct labels, literal GP primes, or a deterministic factor-selection rule, those extra requirements need separate analysis. The counterexample refutes the broader claim that this divisibility condition alone excludes all strides; it is not a successful cipher.\n\n## Reproduce and independently check\n\nDownload the experiment ZIP and keep its folders intact. Python 3's standard library is sufficient; no network, AI calls or additional packages are needed.\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/position-divisor-labels/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/position-divisor-labels/check.py\n```\n\nThe first program uses distances from each rune's first occurrence. The independent checker reads page JSON and computes the gcd of all pairwise occurrence distances. It also verifies every displayed triple, the stride-two counterexample on all 55 pages, a valid unit-stride control, and 450 small synthetic origin/stride cases.\n\nBoth text sources share archival ancestry: agreement is a computation check, not an independent manuscript transcription review. The earlier archive cites a Lean proof; this package provides elementary reasoning and fresh integer checks, without claiming that the Lean development was rerun.\n\n## Limits and reopening conditions\n\nChanging which characters advance the clock, resetting within a page, changing a rune's divisor over time, selecting an irregular sequence of integers, or transforming the factor labels changes the model. Such proposals are not ruled out here. A transcription correction also requires a new run. This result belongs alongside other bounded exclusions, not under a heading claiming that prime-based ciphers are impossible.\n",

  "article": "# Why the reported 53-digit reverse-add result is a palindrome\n\n## The precise claim\n\nA [prior LP2-15 discussion](#/wiki/reported-attempts?section=lp2-15-prime-distance-palindromes) reports distances from word-level GP sums to nearby primes. After concatenating a selected sequence of those distances, the author added the 53-character decimal string to its reversal and obtained a 53-digit palindrome. The thread corrected an earlier 46-digit claim to 53 digits.\n\nThis experiment checks **that arithmetic and one conditional baseline**. The companion [word-by-word source audit](#/experiments/prime-distance-word-derivation) now reconstructs the same section from the archived LP2-15–16 rune text; its complete 57-word sequence differs from the 53 reported digits. This record retains the exact reported string as its input so the historical arithmetic claim remains independently inspectable. The source excerpt is identified in the [structured intake](data/reported-attempts.json) by SHA-256.\n\n## Input and result\n\n```text\n  02311171210211215142515300303126131002122052400021111\n+ 11112000425022120013162130300351524151211201217111320\n= 13423171635233335155677430603477655153333253617132431\n```\n\nThe addition is correct and the result reads identically in either direction. The first operand's leading zero is retained when constructing the reversal; as an integer it has no value, but dropping it before reversing would define a different operation.\n\nThe more informative fact is that **every paired digit sum is at most 7**. No column carries. If a decimal string has digits `d[0] ... d[n−1]`, adding it to its reversal pairs `d[i]` with `d[n−1−i]`. These pair sums are necessarily mirror-symmetric. Whenever all are below ten, and the outer pair is nonzero, the decimal result must be a palindrome. The reported example meets both conditions. Its palindromicity follows from this elementary rule; it does not require a cipher mechanism.\n\n![Fifty-three paired sums from the reported digits mirror around the center and all remain below the decimal carry line of ten.](experiments/records/prime-distance-reverse-add/paired-sums.svg)\n\n## A matched-digit control\n\nThe plan fixes 100,000 pseudorandom shuffles of the **same 53 characters**, with Python's `random.Random(3301)` and no restrictions on a leading zero in the shuffled string. Each shuffled string is reversed and added as an integer exactly as above. **50,442 of 100,000** shuffles yield palindromes. In this run, exactly the same 50,442 satisfy the no-carry condition with a nonzero outer pair.\n\nThis is a conditional, descriptive control: it preserves the selected digit multiset but not any GP word order. It is not a p-value for the full search that produced the string. That search could choose pages, word boundaries, nearest-prime ties, zero separators, and which examples to present. A null model for the whole idea must include those choices. Randomly shuffling uniform decimal digits would be a different and less relevant comparison, because the reported distances concentrate at small digits (11 zeroes, 18 ones, 11 twos).\n\n## Reproduce\n\nExtract the [experiment bundle](downloads/experiments/prime-distance-reverse-add.zip) with folders intact, then run from its root:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/prime-distance-reverse-add/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/prime-distance-reverse-add/check.py\npython experiments/records/prime-distance-reverse-add/plot.py\n```\n\nThe first command recomputes the arithmetic and all 100,000 fixed shuffles. The independent checker verifies the 53 column sums, their symmetry, the no-carry proof condition, and the saved control's internal consistency. The plotter regenerates the SVG from `results.json`. All use the Python standard library. `plan.json` specifies the original digits, seed, trial count and post-selection scope; `results.json` preserves the full paired-sum list and control counts.\n\n## What remains open\n\nThe [companion audit](#/experiments/prime-distance-word-derivation) pins one source-to-digits derivation. Its archived first-section reading has 57 words, compared with 53 reported digits, and also yields a carry-free palindrome. The author's exact transcription or segmentation choices are not preserved in the supplied report. A full cipher test would still need a fixed operation on unsolved text and a comparison that repeats the complete choice of section, grouping and method.\n\nThis computational audit was run and checked by Codex on 2026-10-22. Human review of the source grouping and the mathematical interpretation is pending.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/prime-distance-reverse-add/article.md",

  "article": "# Can the reported prime-distance digits be derived from LP2-15–16?\n\nThe earlier [reverse-add record](#/experiments/prime-distance-reverse-add) checks the arithmetic of a reported 53-digit string. It does not show how each digit came from the manuscript. This source audit makes that missing step explicit: read every word in the same first section, sum its Gematria Primus rune values, and record its distance to the nearest prime.\n\nThe archived transcription yields **57 word distances**, while the supplied report lists **53**. The two strings have a minimum digit-edit distance of seven under ordinary insertion, deletion and substitution. That discrepancy matters for reproducing the reported derivation. It does **not** make the reverse-add observation disappear: the complete 57-digit sequence also produces a palindrome on the first addition.\n\n## Frozen reading rule\n\nThe input is the archived [LP2-15](#/reader/lp2-15) and [LP2-16](#/reader/lp2-16) rune transcription. We use the two-word heading on LP2-15, then every rune word after its `$` section marker through the word before the next section's `ᛈᚹᚷᚷ` on LP2-16. The first five values agree with the report's “red header” sequence; the first three body words are red on the page image. Printed square numbers are not words in this calculation.\n\nA hyphen or period separates words. A `/` followed by a line break is typographic wrapping, so runes on either side remain one word unless a hyphen intervenes. The page boundary also does not split its continuing word. For each word, sum the first 29 primes in Gematria Primus order and use the *absolute* distance to the closest integer prime. A tie between equidistant primes does not change the distance. The [plan](experiments/records/prime-distance-word-derivation/plan.json) pins both text hashes, the rune-to-prime table, the section end marker and the report's 53 digits.\n\nFor example, the heading words give `ᚠᚢᛚᛗ → 149 → 0` and `ᚪᛠᚣᛟᚪ → 489 → 2`. The [full token trace](experiments/records/prime-distance-word-derivation/results.json) lists all 57 words, their prime sums and nearest-prime distances, so any disputed separator or rune has an exact place to challenge.\n\n## Where the sequences differ\n\n```text\nReported: 02311171210211215142515300303126131002122052400021111   (53 digits)\nArchive:  023111712102410211215142515300303126141002122142400021111 (57 digits)\n```\n\n![The reported 53 digits aligned with 57 distances independently derived from archived LP2-15–16 words. Ochre columns mark gaps or differing digits.](experiments/records/prime-distance-word-derivation/word-distance-alignment.svg)\n\n[Open the alignment at full size](experiments/records/prime-distance-word-derivation/word-distance-alignment.svg).\n\nThe figure shows **one** minimum alignment: four archive word positions have no partner in the report and three paired digits differ. The minimum edit count is independently checked by dynamic programming. Repeated digits make the precise alignment non-unique, so these positions should not be read as proof of which words the original author skipped or transcribed differently. The reported list and archived source cannot be made identical under the stated rule without additional choices or corrections.\n\n## What happens to the palindrome?\n\nAdding the archive-derived string to its reversal gives:\n\n```text\n  023111712102410211215142515300303126141002122142400021111\n+ 111120004241221200141621303003515241512112014201217111320\n= 134231716343631411356763818303818367653114136343617132431\n```\n\nThe [independent checker](experiments/records/prime-distance-word-derivation/check.py) verifies the integer sum and each mirrored digit pair. The largest paired sum is eight, so no decimal carry occurs. That is why the 57-digit sum remains a palindrome.\n\nAs a conditional baseline, we shuffled the same **57 distance digits** 100,000 times with a fixed seed, reversed and added each shuffle, and obtained **53,845 palindromes**. This preserves the short-digit distribution that makes carry-free addition frequent. It does not reproduce the full historical search over pages, section boundaries and prime-related transformations. The sibling record's 53-digit control gives 50,442 palindromes in 100,000 shuffles of *its* fixed digit multiset. Neither rate is a probability of intentional construction.\n\n## Reproduce and limits\n\nFrom a full checkout or the [experiment ZIP](downloads/experiments/prime-distance-word-derivation.zip), run:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/prime-distance-word-derivation/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/prime-distance-word-derivation/check.py\npython experiments/records/prime-distance-word-derivation/plot.py --check\n```\n\nThe first command recomputes every word and all 100,000 shuffles. The checker uses a separate word scanner, a different nearest-prime search, direct column arithmetic, a minimum-edit calculation and a second control replay. The supplied discussion is identified by SHA-256 in the [reported-attempt intake](#/wiki/reported-attempts?section=lp2-15-prime-distance-palindromes); its full pasted transcript is not redistributed. The report may have used a different transcription or unpublished segmentation choices. Image-level verification of every word break and human review are still pending.\n\nThis is an **input-derivation audit**, not a decryption of LP2-15–22. A future cipher test would need a fixed way to use these distances on an unsolved passage and evaluate the complete output on text that did not determine the rule.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/prime-distance-word-derivation/article.md",

  "article": "# The circumference substitutions\n\nA [public failed-attempt record](https://github.com/LiberPrimus/Failed-Attempts/blob/d219a8099f8d24e52496e9ee3456ed9980893884/bruteforce/2%CF%80R/README.md) applies a circumference-inspired rule to each GP rune: use either its alphabet position or its associated prime as the radius, multiply by `2π`, then reduce modulo 29. The README says **round**, but the repository's [index-radius output](https://github.com/LiberPrimus/Failed-Attempts/blob/d219a8099f8d24e52496e9ee3456ed9980893884/bruteforce/2%CF%80R/pages_2piR.txt) and [prime-radius output](https://github.com/LiberPrimus/Failed-Attempts/blob/d219a8099f8d24e52496e9ee3456ed9980893884/bruteforce/2%CF%80R/pages_2piR_primes.txt) use **integer truncation** instead. We replay both interpretations so the source discrepancy is visible.\n\n## Finding\n\n![Distinct output runes under index and prime radii with nearest rounding or truncation.](experiments/records/public-circumference-substitutions/mapping-coverage.svg)\n\nOn LP2-00–55, the truncated index and prime maps reproduce the first nine runes on all **55 rune-bearing pages** in the pinned public outputs. LP2-50 has no runic line to compare. The README's nearest-rounding rule does not reproduce those outputs. It produces a different symbol map: the index version reaches 25 of 29 possible output runes instead of 26 under truncation. With GP prime values as radii, both rounding choices reach only **18 of 29** output runes, although the actual mappings differ.\n\nEach rule is a fixed one-rune substitution. In the prime-radius version, 11 output symbols are unreachable. This compression makes the rule non-invertible without additional information; it does not by itself establish that the manuscript was encoded by the inverse rule. The source reports no interesting reading, but supplies no scoring threshold or test that would justify a blanket negative conclusion. Our reproducible result is the exact map and the output agreement.\n\n## Method and limits\n\nThe [plan](experiments/records/public-circumference-substitutions/plan.json) pins the public revision, source-output hashes, two radius choices and two rounding choices. The [results](experiments/records/public-circumference-substitutions/results.json) contain all four 29-entry maps and hashes of the transformed text for LP2-00–55. The [independent check](experiments/records/public-circumference-substitutions/check.py) uses a separate floor-based calculation, checks every saved output hash, and can compare both source text files when supplied locally. Punctuation, line marks and decimal numbers remain unchanged; only runes are substituted.\n\nThis test neither scores candidate English nor searches secondary keys, alternative page groupings, or a reversible decoding scheme. In particular, a numerical motif is not evidence for a cipher merely because it can be applied to every symbol.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nRun `python experiments/records/public-circumference-substitutions/run.py --check` and `python experiments/records/public-circumference-substitutions/check.py`. For the source-output comparison, put the two text files named in the [plan](experiments/records/public-circumference-substitutions/plan.json) in one directory and run `check.py --source-directory PATH`. Their SHA-256 values are verified before comparison.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/public-circumference-substitutions/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "3c9a0f98e7349d82813465ab721476f9aa1ca0c6549a5e8b360ba6ab14d4b1d6",

  "article": "# Could LP2 be the key to another Cicada text?\n\nThe usual question is how to decode Liber Primus. This public test reverses the roles: it treats the **12,956 unsolved LP2 runes as a running key** and asks whether that key reveals a shorter Cicada object. It tests specific objects and rules; it does not directly decrypt LP2.\n\n## Finding\n\n**No tested pairing produced a readable English result.** The best of 40 runs scored **−7.032** on the source's English quadgram scale, below its predeclared **−5.5** advancement bar. The five highest-scoring configurations were also compared with 200 shuffled versions of their target each; none exceeded its corresponding highest shuffle score. A planted message encrypted under the same LP2 key *was* recovered, showing that this decoder can succeed on a constructed example of its assumed mechanism.\n\n![Five target groups and their best English scores, all below the advancement bar.](experiments/records/public-lp2-as-pad/scores.svg)\n\nThe graphic shows each target's best run. Higher scores are stronger *for this English model*; the plotted values do not measure an unconditional probability that a puzzle idea is true.\n\n## What entered the test\n\nThe source's key stream was the 55 nonempty unsolved LP2 transcription segments concatenated in page order. It tested four versions of that stream: forward, reversed, rune-index Atbash (`28 − index`), and negation modulo 29. Each was used with addition and subtraction in `plaintext = (target + sign × key) mod 29`. The decoder can skip up to three key positions at a time when searching for synchronization.\n\nFive targets entered the completed run:\n\n| Target | Input to decoder | Length actually scored |\n| --- | --- | ---: |\n| 2012–13 puzzle texts | English text converted to rune indices | first 500 |\n| Five solved LP1 pages | their recorded plaintext transliterations converted to rune indices | first 500 |\n| PGP message text | English text converted to rune indices | first 500 |\n| “AN END” byte sequence | hard-coded bytes reduced modulo 29 | 63 |\n| LP2 opening | first 200 runes of LP2 tested against the LP2 key | 200 |\n\nThe source proposed a sixth target, the pages 49–51 payload, but did **not** have the payload bytes needed to run it. It therefore ran five targets × four key variants × two signs = **40 decodes**. Negating the key and changing the sign gives the same arithmetic as an unnegated key with the original sign, so some decodes are equivalent; 40 is the run count, not 40 independent hypotheses. Every run starts at key offset zero.\n\nThe “AN END” input is the **63-byte hard-coded sequence in the source script**, which labels it a SHA-512 hash. This record preserves that exact input without asserting that the bytes independently authenticate an external artifact. The text-to-rune conversion is likewise the source's conversion, not a lossless representation of the original messages.\n\n## What the control and scores mean\n\nThe source first encrypted a known English sentence with the LP2 stream, including deliberate key skips. Its beam decoder recovered the planted transliteration exactly, scoring **−4.413**. A rigid decoder using the right key but no skip search scored **−7.334**. That is a useful positive control for this implementation; it cannot prove that an unknown real message, if present, would be found under every different skip pattern or encoding.\n\nThe strongest real-target result was the 2012–13 text under the forward LP2 stream with addition: **−7.032**. For that *selected* run, 200 target-order shuffles reached a highest score of **−6.972**, slightly stronger than the observed result. The null comparison was computed for only the top five selected configurations, and the shuffled controls do not repeat the whole selection process across all target and rule choices. We therefore report the observed absence of a hit under the source's gate, rather than a universal statistical exclusion.\n\nThis replay uses the [pinned F-01 executable](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round16/F-01/sweep.py) and [its declared plan](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round16/F-01/PREREG.md). The source's result prose speaks more broadly than its executed grid in places; the figures above come from the machine-readable run and the independent accounting check.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nDownload this experiment's ZIP from the record's download control to inspect the pinned code, input texts, result, and checker. From a Liberpedia repository checkout, run:\n\n```bash\npython experiments/records/public-lp2-as-pad/check.py\npython experiments/records/public-lp2-as-pad/run.py\n```\n\nThe checker is quick. The complete source replay takes several minutes and runs in a temporary copy, so it leaves the archived result bytes intact. It verifies the complete 40-configuration grid, the positive-control gate, the LP2 rune-stream checksum, the five selected null comparisons, and substantive equality with the pinned source output (excluding elapsed wall time).\n\nThe bundled [source results](experiments/records/public-lp2-as-pad/source/liber-primus/analysis/round16/F-01/results.json), [checker](experiments/records/public-lp2-as-pad/check.py), and [figure script](experiments/records/public-lp2-as-pad/plot.py) expose the exact values. The [source README and method notes](experiments/records/public-lp2-as-pad/source/liber-primus/analysis/round16/F-01/PREREG.md) are preserved as evidence of what was proposed, not as broader findings of this replay.\n\n**Remaining scope:** target material other than these five objects, a verified pages 49–51 payload, other key offsets, alternative page boundaries, or using the other objects as key material would require separate tests.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/public-lp2-as-pad/article.md",

  "article": "# Multi-rune feedback and autokey\n\nA feedback cipher can derive each new key symbol from earlier symbols. [This published screen](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round12/C1/RESULTS.md) tested whether LP2 behaves that way when the key depends on the previous two to six runes.\n\n## Finding\n\n**None of the 23,520 source configurations produced a convincing English reading.** The strongest result scored **−6.299**, below the source's required **−5.500**. It came from a **66-rune segment**, not the continuous manuscript: a five-rune plaintext-history XOR rule on the reversed segment, with an all-six seed. The source program successfully recovered all **21 planted cases** at history length three and gave wrong-rule decodes much lower scores.\n\n![The planted control clears the score threshold; the highest-scoring LP2 candidate remains below it.](experiments/records/public-multihistory-feedback/scores.svg)\n\nThese are English quadgram scores; higher means the transliterated output resembles the training text more closely. The strongest short fragment is still well below the planted English sample. A score by itself would never establish a solution without a coherent continuation.\n\n## How the tested rules work\n\nAt each position, the program reads the previous *k* symbols, passes them through one of seven fixed functions, then adds or subtracts the resulting value modulo 29. The seven functions are an index sum, prime-value sum, XOR, prime-of-index-sum, prime-of-prime-sum, last-symbol difference and alternating sum. It tries three kinds of history: the visible ciphertext, the plaintext decoded so far, or the modulo-29 sum of the two. The source also tries both directions of the rune stream and both arithmetic signs.\n\n![A five-rune history is mapped to a key value, then combined with the next ciphertext rune to produce a proposed plaintext rune.](experiments/records/public-multihistory-feedback/feedback.svg)\n\nThe screen covers the **12,956-rune continuous unsolved stream** plus its **55 nonempty source segments**. For ciphertext history, symbols after the first *k* positions do not depend on the initial seed. For plaintext and mixed history, the source tries only the **29 all-equal seeds** `0…0` through `28…28` at each *k*, then keeps the best score. That is a thin slice of the possible **29^k** initial states. In particular, a wrong initial plaintext state need not “lock on” to the correct state later; the source's broader claim that a genuine autokey would necessarily reveal itself under these seeds is not established by this test.\n\nThe source's 200 shuffled controls score the raw full stream, while its reported best is selected from thousands of configurations, many on short segments. That shuffle maximum is not a full best-of-grid null. The result is therefore **no supported English reading in the executed grid**, not a statistical exclusion of every feedback cipher.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nDownload the experiment ZIP and run from its extracted folder:\n\n```sh\npython experiments/records/public-multihistory-feedback/run.py\n```\n\nIt runs the 21 planted controls before the full sweep, then checks the saved result against the separately archived source output. The independent checker reconstructs the 12,956 source rune indices and **recomputes the winning XOR/plaintext-history decode and score** without calling the source's feedback decoder. For a quick check of the packaged outputs, run `python experiments/records/public-multihistory-feedback/check.py`. The full sweep takes several minutes.\n\nThe code, transcription and scoring table are included from [Dukotah/cicada3301 revision f08b20b](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/tree/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round12/C1), with the repository's license. This record matches that program's executed parameters; it does not claim to rule out other functions, alphabets, seed states or non-English plaintext.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/public-multihistory-feedback/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "c23294775a089aab88044cdee3a6f3a17934eaeade553cbc5383afe94fd2c461",
  "record_type": {
    "id": "replay",
    "label": "Method replay",
    "description": "Reconstructs a supplied proposed method and its choices; reproduction is not independent confirmation of a reading."
  }
}

  "article": "# Seven public PRNG constructions against LP2\n\nCould a seeded software random-number generator supply LP2's 29-symbol key stream? This reruns a [published seven-generator screen](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round16/prng/RESULTS.md) against the first 120 runes of the unsolved text.\n\n## Finding\n\n**No candidate in the executed grid reached the source's required English score.** The replay screened **52,556 decodes**: seven generator implementations, 1,877 fixed seeds, two addition signs and two key directions. The best candidate scored **−6.347**; a candidate needed at least **−5.500** to advance. A planted English message encoded with the source's PHP-style generator scored **−4.155** and was recovered exactly. The same program can therefore find one of its own planted signals under this setup.\n\nThese are English quadgram scores: they measure how much a four-letter pattern resembles the training text. **Higher is better**, but even a high score would still require a readable continuation and independent checks before it could count as a solution.\n\n![Three scores on the same scale: planted control clears the bar; the manuscript's best candidate does not.](experiments/records/public-prng-seed-sweep/score.svg)\n\nThe winning seed, generator, sign and direction match the archived run. This is evidence about the **specific seeded generators and seed slice below**, not evidence that LP2 uses no PRNG or no stream cipher.\n\n## What was tested\n\nThe seven source implementations are PHP-5-style `mt_rand`, .NET-4-style `System.Random`, a simplified single-integer-seeded ISAAC, Blum–Blum–Shub at two fixed moduli, a 32-bit LFSR and a Geffe combination of three LFSRs. Every stream is reduced modulo 29. The key-skip beam searches up to three rejected key symbols at each rune, using the source's English quadgram scorer. Its first-stage ciphertext is exactly the source's 120-rune LP2 prefix, regenerated from the pinned runic transcription.\n\nThe 1,877 seeds are **1,828 daily-spaced Unix seconds from 2011–2015 plus 49 fixed number/string-derived seeds**. The source's earlier plan described hourly sampling and an additional rejection reduction; the actual executable and result cover daily sampling and `mod29` only. That difference matters. The test also fixes key offset at zero and does not check other starting positions.\n\nThe source calls all seven generators “validated,” but most reference vectors in this script are computed by the same implementation being tested. Self-consistency and a planted decode show that the local program works consistently; they do **not** independently verify exact PHP, .NET or standard ISAAC runtime compatibility. The ISAAC variant expressly uses a simplified seed procedure. We therefore name them as the **source implementations**, not all production runtimes bearing those names.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nDownload this experiment's ZIP and run from its extracted folder:\n\n```sh\npython experiments/records/public-prng-seed-sweep/run.py\n```\n\nThe command executes the archived test program, then independently checks the reconstructed ciphertext, case count, control, winning configuration and score against the separately archived original result. It takes several minutes. For a quick integrity check of saved results, run `python experiments/records/public-prng-seed-sweep/check.py`.\n\nThe packaged source files are pinned to [Dukotah/cicada3301 revision f08b20b](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/tree/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round16/prng). The original generator code, documented plan and result are retained with this record. The only regenerated source input is `ct.bin`, constructed byte-for-byte from that revision's `krisyotam_runes.txt`; the checker confirms its 12,956 rune indices and SHA-256.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/public-prng-seed-sweep/article.md",

  "article": "# A public 43-key Vigenère sweep\n\nAn archived attempt tried Liber Primus-related words as repeating Vigenère keys. Its [README](https://github.com/LiberPrimus/Failed-Attempts/blob/d219a8099f8d24e52496e9ee3456ed9980893884/bruteforce/vigenere/README.md) describes a wordlist; its [output archive](https://github.com/LiberPrimus/Failed-Attempts/blob/d219a8099f8d24e52496e9ee3456ed9980893884/bruteforce/vigenere/vigenere-bruteforce-results.zip) contains **43** rune keys across 58 page files. The archive includes an additional DIVINITY key after the listed words. We take the keys from the archived output, rather than silently reducing the set to the README list.\n\n## Finding\n\n![A fixed-key sweep: 43 keys across 55 rune-bearing unsolved pages, with no 12-rune known-opening match.](experiments/records/public-wordlist-vigenere/key-sweep.svg)\n\nAll **2,365** rune-bearing key–page prefixes in our LP2-00–55 replay match the beginning of the pinned public output archive. LP2-50 contains only the alphanumeric grid, so its 43 nominal cases have no rune output. None of the 2,365 decoded starts equals any of nine predeclared, 12-rune known-reading openings: **0 of 21,285 comparisons**. A planted MOUNTAIN plaintext encrypts and decrypts correctly with the first source key.\n\nThis verifies the public arithmetic for the beginning of each output and rules out **these keys, at page-start phase zero, for these nine exact openings** on our transcription. It does not mean that every wordlist Vigenère attempt has failed. A different key, phase, word-boundary reset, alphabet, page segment, or plaintext beginning is outside this check. The source's “no good result” is an editorial observation, not a numerical language score, so we do not present it as a measured threshold.\n\n## What was done\n\nFor every rune position *j* on each page, we computed plaintext index `P[j] = C[j] − K[j mod length(K)] (mod 29)`. Non-rune marks and the number square remain visible but do not advance the key. We kept the GP rune order and the printed page boundaries fixed. The [plan](experiments/records/public-wordlist-vigenere/plan.json) pins all 43 rune keys and the public repository revision. The saved [results](experiments/records/public-wordlist-vigenere/results.json) give every page/key prefix and its input hash. The independent [check](experiments/records/public-wordlist-vigenere/check.py) recomputes those prefixes; when passed the original ZIP, it also checks all 2,365 nine-rune prefixes against the archived headings. The archive uses both `IA` and `IO` for one GP rune, which the checker treats as alternative labels for the *same* symbol.\n\nThis is related to the [two known Vigenère keys and nine openings](#/experiments/lp2-known-vigenere-keys), but it is a different fixed source key list and a narrower phase rule. The nine openings are a diagnostic: their absence does not prove that no decoded output contains meaningful text elsewhere.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nFrom the repository root, run `python experiments/records/public-wordlist-vigenere/run.py --check` and `python experiments/records/public-wordlist-vigenere/check.py`. To verify against the source's archived output, download the ZIP from the pinned GitHub revision, verify its SHA-256 against the [plan](experiments/records/public-wordlist-vigenere/plan.json), then pass it with `--source-archive PATH` to the checker.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/public-wordlist-vigenere/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "8dc8211ac0553c319922f176acef9110256e6c57f4d29c81247f0d6656d72cd3",

    "id": "replay",
    "label": "Method replay",
    "description": "Reconstructs a supplied proposed method and its choices; reproduction is not independent confirmation of a reading."
  }
}

      "path": "experiments/records/quagmirror-six-rune-replay/six-rune-trace.svg",
      "caption": "The source script processes six positions; this diagram shows its cipher, autokey, table and output values."
    }
  ],
  "article": "# How far does the QuagMirror draft run?\n\n**Result.** The pinned public script processes the first **six runes of LP2-00**, then deliberately stops. An independent replay obtains the same index streams and the transliteration **DCBWJO**. That is a match to the draft program's output, not a reading of the page. The code does not run its proposed method across a complete word or page.\n\nThe idea combines an autokey calculation with one of nine handwritten 29-symbol substitution tables. At each position, Möbius values associated with the position and a prime-derived totient choose the table. Previous cipher and output symbols feed the next autokey calculation. The first two positions contain explicit overrides in the source. Those choices are retained here; silently removing them would replay a different method.\n\n![A five-row diagram traces the six cipher indices through the autokey indices, selected mirror tables, output indices and Latin fragments.](experiments/records/quagmirror-six-rune-replay/six-rune-trace.svg)\n\n| Stage | Six values |\n| --- | --- |\n| Archived LP2-00 rune indices | 15, 8, 18, 3, 6, 19 |\n| Autokey indices | 15, 28, 2, 10, 3, 14 |\n| Output indices | 23, 5, 17, 7, 11, 3 |\n| Latin fragments | D C B W J O |\n\nThe replay checks the source's first six input indices against this site's LP2-00 transcription. It stores all nine permutation tables and every fixed choice in the [plan](experiments/records/quagmirror-six-rune-replay/plan.json), then calculates each row in the [result](experiments/records/quagmirror-six-rune-replay/results.json). The tables are permutations, but that property alone does not make the output intelligible or prove an encryption mechanism.\n\nThis is a **WIP source-version replay**. The repository contains several changing scripts; it would be misleading to combine their rules into one historical \"QuagMirror\" result. The particular file [Mobius_AT_QuagMirror.py at pinned commit 88ef1e60](https://github.com/sgroveman/cicada3301_lp/blob/88ef1e60b0738b8b28db96bc9dc44dc4da8dd307/Solving%20Attempts/Mobius_AT_QuagMirror.py) has SHA-256 `e317878190994910afbbdc5707a66af73a684b29abdd9d7e443563aba9d15a66`. Its `break` after six processed positions is part of the code, so this record cannot test its remaining page output, any later revisions or proposed thematic keywords. A complete candidate needs one frozen version, a declared rule for every position, full output and an untouched-text check.\n\nRun `python experiments/records/quagmirror-six-rune-replay/run.py --check` from the repository root. Python's standard library suffices. The saved plan and results make this exact six-position variant available offline without shipping the source discussion or changing its unfinished state.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/quagmirror-six-rune-replay/article.md",

  "related": [],
  "article": "## Finding\n\n**A straightforward rail-fence reading does not stand out in this bounded test.** Across LP2-00–55, the best of nine rail counts matched **70** words in a fixed English list. The same nine-way search on page-rotated controls had a median of **78** matches; **195 of 199** controls matched at least 70. The unchanged rune order matched 57. These are dictionary matches, not a translation.\n\n![The best rail-fence word count is below the median of the alignment controls.](experiments/records/rail-fence-visible-words/comparison.svg)\n\n## The proposal and the actual test\n\n[TheronEagle's public rail-fence script](https://github.com/TheronEagle/liber-primus-research/blob/a6c5d13f7591030367daace993c887af20a5e0ab/experiments/2026-09-24/rail_fence_test.py) decrypts each page using two through ten rails and scores the resulting letters as words in a dictionary. Its saved result names two rails as the highest scorer. The repository points to an absolute local path for its word list and another for its transcription; neither file is part of that repository. Its numeric result therefore cannot be exactly replayed from its published checkout.\n\nHere the input is Liberpedia's pinned LP2-00–55 rune text: **12,956 runes** arranged into **2,776 visible word slots**. As in the source code, a hyphen ends a slot; line-break marks and punctuation do not. The [fixed 369,652-word list](experiments/records/rail-fence-visible-words/lexicon.txt) is derived from the [Unlicense English-words repository](https://github.com/dwyl/english-words/blob/20f5cc9b3f0ccc8ce45d814c532b7c2031bba31c/words_alpha.txt), with the exact transform and source hash in [SOURCE.txt](experiments/records/rail-fence-visible-words/SOURCE.txt). A decoded slot counts only when its exact GP Latin transliteration is in that list. The denominator includes short slots that cannot score, so the counts should be compared only under this same scoring rule.\n\n| Reading | Matched slots |\n| --- | ---: |\n| Printed order, no rail transform | 57 |\n| Two, four, or nine rails | 70 each |\n| Median of 199 control maxima | 78 |\n\nEach control rotates the rune stream of *each page* by a seeded, nonzero offset, keeps its visible word lengths, tests all nine rail counts, and retains the best score. The page's rune inventory and contiguous ciphertext order remain intact; the rotation changes the alignment with word slots. This comparison asks whether the printed alignment of the proposed rail reading is better than the same method applied at other alignments. It is not a model of how Cicada composed the manuscript. The saved control maximum scores range from **67 to 90**. The complete nine-rail counts and all 199 control maxima are in [results.json](experiments/records/rail-fence-visible-words/results.json).\n\n## What this does and does not exclude\n\nThe decoder was checked two ways: the main script encrypts an actual solved-page rune sequence and recovers it at each rail count, while the separate checker recomputes all manuscript outputs through a different index permutation. This rules out a broken rail inverse as the explanation for the ordinary score.\n\nThe test covers **only** conventional page-by-page rail-fence decryption with two through ten rails, this word segmentation, this GP transliteration and this fixed dictionary. It says nothing about keyed columns, a rail count outside the range, combining pages, moving word boundaries, a preceding substitution layer, or a non-English plaintext. In particular, the source repository's wider statement that all transpositions are ruled out does not follow from these nine cases.\n\nTo reproduce offline, use the experiment ZIP and run `python experiments/records/rail-fence-visible-words/run.py --check`, followed by `python experiments/records/rail-fence-visible-words/check.py`. Both need Python 3 and the archived source files; no network call is made during the run.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/rail-fence-visible-words/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "5f7bed7c3ffacb3c5e616cc8b9c90ccb9b5b26805f6b10f0062a5a8ecfd15263",

    "label": "Method replay",
    "description": "Reconstructs a supplied proposed method and its choices; reproduction is not independent confirmation of a reading."
  }
}
