  "reader_note": "The corrected large-initial pages have ordinary spacing under the tested uniform-page reference. This does not test the rune identities or rule out other ways the artwork might carry information.",
  "reader_limit": "Two pages in the earlier 15-page list contain only small red text. The page-order test has narrow bounds, and its compression measure has little power on a 58-bit string.",
  "scope_summary": "LP2-00–57 · 13 pages with large red initials · five page-order tails · 100000 sampled controls and exact span/run counts.",
  "article": "## Result\n\n**The thirteen pages with large red initials do not have unusual spacing under this uniform-page comparison.** Their largest consecutive run is two pages; a random set of thirteen pages has a run of at least two **96.8%** of the time. Their first and last marked pages are LP2-00 and LP2-57, so their span is the full release; that cannot be unusually short. The variance of the twelve internal gaps is **12.85**; **32.8%** of 100,000 random sets have at least that much variance. This tests page placement, not whether the artwork carries a message.\n\n![The published total-red selection, corrected large-initial pages, and two planted spacing controls on the same 58-page axis.](experiments/records/red-initial-presence-order/page-order.svg)\n\nThe top row reproduces the [published total-red page list](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round22/D-illustration-dropcap/RESULTS.md). Its highlighted LP2-07 and LP2-53 are [small red text, not large initials](#/wiki/red-initials). The corrected row has thirteen pages. LP2-03 and LP2-33 each have two large initials; this test deliberately reduces each page to a single yes/no mark.\n\n## What was compared\n\nThe [image audit](research/red-initials-audit.csv) freezes which of the 58 LP2 pages contain a large red connected shape. The comparison draws **100,000** uniform 13-page subsets without replacement. It asks whether the actual pages have unusually variable internal gaps, a short overall span, a long run of adjacent pages, or an unusually compressible 58-bit presence string. Span and run probabilities are also counted exactly over all **3,155,581,562,280** possible 13-page subsets. Five declared tail directions are considered together; none approaches the adjusted threshold.\n\n| Measure | Observed | Comparison result |\n| --- | ---: | --- |\n| Variance of the 12 gaps | 12.85 | 32.8% of random sets are at least as variable; 67.4% are no more variable. |\n| Span, last minus first | 57 pages | All 13-page sets have a span of 57 or less. |\n| Longest consecutive run | 2 pages | 96.8% of random sets have a run of at least two. |\n| zlib size of the packed page bits | 16 bytes | 99,977 of 100,000 random sets also occupy 16 bytes; this score has almost no resolving power here. |\n\nThe comparison deliberately assumes every 13-page placement is equally likely. It is a baseline for visible spacing, **not** a model of how the manuscript was composed. A rule based on section boundaries, the identities of the initials, or two initials on one page is outside it.\n\n## Can these checks detect a planted pattern?\n\nThe lower two rows of the figure are fixed controls with the same thirteen marks. Approximately even spacing gives a very small gap-variance tail in the sampled comparison, while thirteen consecutive marks give an exact short-span and long-run probability of **46 / 3,155,581,562,280**. But both controls have low gap variance: that one statistic cannot tell even spacing from a single compact block. The evenly spaced control still compresses to 16 bytes, so the compression check would miss that visible regularity. These limitations matter when interpreting the ordinary manuscript result.\n\nThe earlier study also tested red-pixel centroids and an initial-rune string. Those are **not** reproduced here: its total-red mask includes two pages without initials, its centroids include all red marks rather than only the large shapes, and several pages have a second or later initial. A corrected identity or position test needs explicit annotation of each large initial before scoring.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nDownload the [original JPEGs](downloads/original-images.zip) if you want to repeat the image classification itself. With Python 3 and Pillow, NumPy and OpenCV installed, run `python scripts/audit_red_initials.py > research/red-initials-audit.csv`. The page-order test then needs only Python's standard library:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/red-initial-presence-order/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/red-initial-presence-order/check.py\npython experiments/records/red-initial-presence-order/plot.py\n```\n\nThe [plan](experiments/records/red-initial-presence-order/plan.json) pins the image-audit table and analysis rules. [Results](experiments/records/red-initial-presence-order/results.json) retain every observed statistic, tail count and planted control; the [separate check](experiments/records/red-initial-presence-order/check.json) verifies the exact arithmetic and repeats the gap comparison with another random stream. This is an exploratory correction after the source classification error was seen, not a preregistered test of all ways the manuscript could encode information.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/red-initial-presence-order/article.md",

    "lp2-00-02-lag35-selection",

  "article": "## Finding\n\n**The long repeats are real, but their number is not unusual under a control that preserves each section’s adjacent rune steps.** The 12,956-rune LP2-00–55 transcription contains **six distinct repeated five-rune sequences**, **one repeated six-rune sequence**, and **no repeated seven-rune sequence**. These match the [published inventory](https://github.com/Leo-Y-Zhang/LiberPrimusAnalysis/blob/a32bdc0e06ea58532fbaf4329acae4a0b1020513/results/characterize.txt), including the six-rune `DJUBEI` at zero-based corpus positions **6,555** and **12,950**.\n\n![How often the matched controls produce at least as many long repeated sequences.](experiments/records/repeated-long-ngrams/repeats.svg)\n\nThe two overlapping five-rune sequences `DJUBE` and `JUBEI` come from that same `DJUBEI` repeat. They are **not three separate pieces of evidence**. Of 999 controls, 300 reached at least six five-rune repeats, 150 reached at least one six-rune repeat, and 361 reached either threshold. The last comparison counts the decision to notice whichever of the two lengths looks more interesting. The corresponding plus-one proportions are 301/1,000, 151/1,000 and **362/1,000**.\n\n## What was compared\n\nEach control keeps the nine manuscript section lengths, each section’s first rune, and the **exact inventory of its adjacent modular differences**, including rare zero steps. It shuffles the order of those steps within each section, rebuilds the rune stream, joins the sections in manuscript order, and counts distinct repeated sequences of lengths five, six and seven. Windows may overlap and cross joined section boundaries in both the manuscript and controls, matching the source’s corpus-wide counting rule. A planted six-rune copy makes the checker’s repeat count rise from zero to one.\n\nThis control asks whether *these counts* distinguish the manuscript from streams with the same step composition. It does not model every possible cipher or decide whether a particular repeat is meaningful. A future claim about `DJUBEI` should specify its predicted location, transformation and successful decoding criterion before inspecting another position. The [complete results](experiments/records/repeated-long-ngrams/results.json) contain every repeated tuple and all 999 control counts.\n\nRun `python experiments/records/repeated-long-ngrams/run.py --check` and `python experiments/records/repeated-long-ngrams/check.py` from the repository root. The second script independently extracts the rune stream, recounts the observed tuples, and reconstructs the first twelve shuffled controls.\n",

  "article": "## Finding\n\n**No 54-byte window passed the specified strict RSA-structure checks.** The source proposed that the 256-byte payload spread over LP2 pages 49–51 might contain a 432-bit RSA signature or encrypted block inside it, rather than as the whole payload. A 432-bit block is 54 bytes, so there are exactly **203 contiguous positions** to inspect.\n\n![A sliding 54-byte window across each 256-byte payload reading, with the fixed directions and exponents.](experiments/records/rsa-window-54-source-replay/windows.svg)\n\nWe independently ran the pinned test on **three source payload readings**. For each window, it checks both byte orders as an encoded block and, when the numeric value is below the published 2013 modulus, raises it to exponents **65,537, 3 and 17**. That made **1,218 direct-block inspections** and **2,493 modular exponentiations** across the three readings. All three returned **zero strict PKCS#1 v1.5 or PSS structural matches**, exactly as the source reported.\n\nThere is one weaker PSS-shaped row per reading: window **62**, forward byte order, exponent **17**. It lacks the required eight zero-padding bytes, so the predeclared recognizer labels it *loose*, not a hit. The three payload readings differ at a few bytes, but none of those differences lies inside this particular window.\n\n## What makes the negative meaningful\n\nThe runner first planted **ten PKCS#1 v1.5–SHA-1 and five PSS–SHA-1 signatures** under a fresh 432-bit test key. It recovered all **15** at their planted windows. It then found **zero strict matches** in 200 random 256-byte buffers. Our separate checker verifies the pinned input bytes against their Git blob identities, recalculates every real-data window and match tier without importing the runner, and compares the totals to the source's saved result.\n\nThis is a bounded structural screen, **not** verification of a signature over a known message. In particular, the source's recognizer checks a known DigestInfo prefix or PSS block shape; it cannot check a message digest when no signed message is specified. The result applies to these three 256-byte readings, the published **2013 432-bit modulus**, 54-byte contiguous windows, both byte orders and those three exponents. It says nothing about other moduli, noncontiguous or bit-shifted selections, different block sizes or non-PKCS constructions.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nRun from the Liberpedia repository root with Python 3:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/rsa-window-54-source-replay/run.py\npython experiments/records/rsa-window-54-source-replay/check.py\n```\n\nThe [machine-readable result](experiments/records/rsa-window-54-source-replay/results.json), [pinned source file list](experiments/records/rsa-window-54-source-replay/source-manifest.json) and original MIT-licensed inputs are included. The local `source/results.json` is the published source result; the top-level `results.json` is our independent replay.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/rsa-window-54-source-replay/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "747243cadaccee2bc2add74c3f4e79408aa1f808e1cae85b73d09e574e772659",

      "path": "experiments/records/rune-direct-byte-packing/packing-screens.svg",
      "caption": "Counts from three fixed direct encodings over 56 targets. UTF-8 validity of prime bytes is syntactic, not readable text."
    }
  ],
  "article": "# Do the runes directly form file bytes?\n\n**No recognizable file beginning or complete printable text emerged** from three fixed encodings of the LP2 rune stream. This is a baseline for the suggestion to pack rune values as bytes, not a test of every possible encoding.\n\nThe input is each nonempty page of [LP2](#/pages) from 00 through 55, plus the pages joined in their printed order. The script tries three direct conversions: five bits per rune index in ordinary bit order, five bits with each token reversed, and one byte per Gematria Primus prime value. These are deliberately simple rules that can be replayed without guessing a format after viewing the output.\n\n![Results for three direct rune encodings; no full printable text or chosen file prefix.](experiments/records/rune-direct-byte-packing/packing-screens.svg)\n\nThere are **56 targets** (55 nonempty pages and one joined stream), making **168 encoded streams**. None is entirely printable ASCII (allowing tab and line breaks). None begins with a PNG, gzip, ZIP, PDF, ELF or Windows MZ signature. The two five-bit encodings also fail strict whole-stream UTF-8 on every target.\n\nThe prime-byte encoding passes the UTF-8 *syntax* screen on all 56 targets for a trivial reason: every GP prime is at most 109, so each is an individually valid one-byte ASCII code. The encoded streams contain control bytes and fail the printable-text screen. Calling that a text decoding would be misleading.\n\n## What this settles\n\nUnder these exact page boundaries and direct conversions, the runes do not already look like complete ordinary text or one of the six specified file starts. A header match, had one occurred, would still need a full format parser before it could count as a file. No bytes were executed.\n\nThis experiment does **not** test word-level prime sums, another bit width or byte order, transformed or compressed data, a header later in the stream, or selecting a different reading order. Those choices change the search space and need their own declared rule and control.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nDownload this experiment's ZIP or run from the repository root:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/rune-direct-byte-packing/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/rune-direct-byte-packing/check.py\n```\n\nThe [result file](experiments/records/rune-direct-byte-packing/results.json) lists each target, conversion, byte count, first eight bytes and stream hash. The second script independently rebuilds the streams from the page records. Both use Python's standard library only.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/rune-direct-byte-packing/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "ada97ab6e5e2da9399c8e5dfed7a5298dc14a13d6311986dfdada77ddf4f393b",
  "record_type": {
    "id": "replay",
    "label": "Method replay",
    "description": "Reconstructs a supplied proposed method and its choices; reproduction is not independent confirmation of a reading."
  }
}

  "article": "## Finding\n\n**The revised scorer raises all five known-reading scores, but its wrong-key scores do not become less variable in this test.** We replayed the pinned comparison using the same five solved pages and 200 seeded random-key decodes of *A Koan*. The revised model's weakest solved-page score rose from **−4.979 to −4.774**; both clear the source's **−5.5** recognition bar. The wrong-key score standard deviation changed from **0.0880 to 0.0895**, so the source's predeclared “less variable noise” gate fails.\n\n![Five known readings score higher under the revised model, while the observed wrong-key score spread widens slightly.](experiments/records/rune-matched-scorer-calibration/scorer-comparison.svg)\n\nThe separation between the weakest known reading and the wrong-key mean changes from **28.69 to 29.71 standard deviations**, about **3.6%**. That is a real improvement *in this particular comparison*, but much smaller than the earlier proposed **18%**. The source's saved JSON contains one narrative note saying “+2.9%”; its own tabulated values calculate to **3.6%**, consistent with its report and our replay.\n\n## What the model actually changes\n\nThe original English quadgram table contains **7,266,795** counted windows. The revised table has the same total and **68,083** distinct four-character windows. Our independent reconstruction exactly matches its scores by making only these substitutions inside each original four-letter window: **K and Q → C, V → U, Z → S**, then combining counts for windows that become identical.\n\nThe source describes the model as handling multi-character rune transliterations such as `TH`, `EO` and `NG`. Its implementation processes the four original Latin letters individually, and every resulting window remains four characters long. Thus the measured improvement is **an alias-collapse result**, not evidence that extra rune-unit expansion improved scoring. This does not invalidate the measured scores; it makes the operation precise enough to compare with a genuinely rune-unit-aware model later.\n\n## How we checked it\n\nThe bundled source script recovered the same five scored texts and generated the same **200** null decodes with seed **42**. It reproduced every saved page score, null summary and gate result. A separate checker rebuilt both quadgram tables, parsed the *A Koan* runes independently from the pinned transcription, reran the random keys and rescored all **205** texts without importing the source scorer.\n\nThis is a calibration of an English-language scoring instrument, **not a test of an unsolved-page cipher**. The null comes from one page and one set of 200 keys. A 0.0015 difference in the two sampled standard deviations does not establish that the revised model is generally noisier; it does mean this test did **not demonstrate the promised tightening**. Other languages and scoring registers need their own calibrated controls.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nFrom the repository root, using Python 3:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/rune-matched-scorer-calibration/run.py\npython experiments/records/rune-matched-scorer-calibration/check.py\npython experiments/records/rune-matched-scorer-calibration/plot.py\n```\n\nThe [measured data](experiments/records/rune-matched-scorer-calibration/results.json), [five scored texts](experiments/records/rune-matched-scorer-calibration/solved_texts.json), original executable, manuscript transcription and quadgram table are bundled from the pinned MIT-licensed source.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/rune-matched-scorer-calibration/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "3c0aea216f34a7a8e86c8e442aecf6f9b4028128692a0a5477a349ce27e2d407",

  }
}

  "article": "## Question and result\n\nA candidate can look convincing simply because we tried many keys and kept the best output. Comparing that winner with one randomly chosen wrong key would ignore the selection step. Here, each control repeats the **whole declared search** and keeps its best score, just as the real search would.\n\nThe best control scores rise as the nested dictionary grows from one to 256 keys, but none crosses the fixed −5.5 acceptance threshold in this grid. Searches of encrypted known text also fail that threshold when the true key is absent. Appending the true key makes every such control recover exactly and pass. This shows that the scorer can recognize the known answer **when this search includes it**; it does not establish a false-positive rate for larger or different searches.\n\n## Three conditions, kept separate\n\n| Condition | Ciphertext | Keys searched | What it checks |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| Null | Reproducible uniform pseudorandom rune indices | A declared wrong-key dictionary | The best score selected from the whole dictionary under this null generator. |\n| Positive, key absent | A known rune prefix encrypted by addition modulo 29 | The same dictionary, excluding its true seed | What a search reports when its intended answer is outside its bounds. |\n| Positive, key included | The same positive ciphertext | That dictionary plus its true key | Whether inclusion recovers the known answer and whether it wins the scoring comparison. |\n\nThe included condition has **one more candidate** than the stated wrong-key budget. At budget 256 it compares 257 candidates. Its known key is not secretly inserted into the other conditions, and its exact-recovery check is separate from score acceptance.\n\n## Inputs and bounds\n\nAll nine known-reading traces contribute their first 240 output rune indices, or their full length when shorter. Their lengths range from 85 to 240 runes. These are existing trace outputs, not edited English converted back into runes. No section is removed because of a poor score or unusual content.\n\nFor each section, 32 replicates generate a null ciphertext and a positive ciphertext of that section's length. Each null uses a fresh, recorded Python pseudorandom-generator seed and uniform draws from indices 0–28. Each positive uses the known prefix and a recorded derived key. The paired controls share length and search settings; they do not share ciphertext.\n\nThe candidate keys use SHA-256 over a fixed ASCII seed label and a four-byte big-endian counter, with digest bytes reduced modulo 29. Because 256 is not divisible by 29, this reduction is biased. It is an explicit fixture, not a uniform-pad claim. Candidate seeds are 0–255; positive seeds are 100000–100031 and therefore absent from that dictionary.\n\nFor every candidate, subtract its key from the ciphertext modulo 29, transliterate with the canonical rune labels, and average the English quadgram log scores. The unseen-quadgram count is 0.01 and the threshold is −5.5, inherited unchanged from the [scorer controls](#/experiments/english-scorer-controls). There are no offsets, alternate signs, skip rules or word-boundary adjustments.\n\n## Nested search budgets\n\nEvery search retains all 256 individual candidate scores and examines dictionary prefixes of 1, 4, 16, 64 and 256 keys. A larger budget contains every candidate in the smaller one. Its maximum therefore cannot decrease. Ties use the smallest seed ID, including when comparing an appended true key.\n\nThe figures preserve all nine source sections. At each budget, a dot is the median of the 32 best scores and the vertical line is their full observed range. Neither is a confidence interval. All panels share a score scale. The positive included condition has a constant score within a section because exact decryption returns the same known rune prefix despite different encryption keys.\n\n| Wrong-key budget | Null accepted | Positive accepted, true key absent | Positive exact and accepted, true key included |\n| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |\n| 1 | 0/288 | 0/288 | 288/288 (2 candidates) |\n| 4 | 0/288 | 0/288 | 288/288 (5 candidates) |\n| 16 | 0/288 | 0/288 | 288/288 (17 candidates) |\n| 64 | 0/288 | 0/288 | 288/288 (65 candidates) |\n| 256 | 0/288 | 0/288 | 288/288 (257 candidates) |\n\nThese are counts over the fixed grid, not independent-trial accuracy estimates. The full CSV keeps each section separate across all 135 section/budget/condition combinations. The JSON retains all 147,456 wrong-key scores, 288 true-key controls, ciphertexts, seeds, candidate hashes and search winners.\n\n## What a zero count means\n\nWe observed no threshold exceedances among these null searches. That does not prove the threshold is safe for a million-key search, a beam decoder, several language models, or repeated human choices about which output to keep. Such procedures offer different opportunities to find a high-scoring candidate and need their own controls.\n\nThe sections share source material, the dictionary is reused, and budgets are nested. Repetition does not turn this into 288 independent texts drawn from all possible plaintext. The null generator is also a chosen model, not an established description of the manuscript. We do not estimate a probability that a manuscript candidate is correct, pool the scores into an anomaly verdict, or infer a cipher family.\n\nThe [decoder alignment controls](#/experiments/decoder-skip-controls) demonstrate a complementary limitation: even a correct key can fail under an unsuitable decoder, and an incorrect rune sequence can pass a language score. Here the positive controls validate only ordinary modular addition and this declared dictionary search.\n\n## Reproduce and inspect\n\nExtract the experiment ZIP with its folder structure intact. Python 3 and its standard library are sufficient; there are no network requests, API calls or paid services.\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/search-maximum-controls/run.py --check\npython scripts/check_search_maximum_controls.py experiments/records/search-maximum-controls/results.json --receipt my-search-audit.json\npython experiments/records/search-maximum-controls/plot.py\n```\n\nThe independent checker imports no producer functions. It rebuilds the source prefixes, null ciphertexts and derived keys, checks every candidate hash, recalculates scores using counted quadgrams, and reconstructs every winner and tie decision. It also checks monotonic maxima and the additional candidate count when the true key is appended. All 288 paired searches passed; human review remains pending.\n\nThe practical lesson is to compare a selected result with controls that undergo the same selection. See [search space and bounds](#/wiki/search-space) and [null models](#/wiki/null-models). A different dictionary, decoder, scoring rule or adaptive workflow should be a documented variant, with the complete search repeated in its controls.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/search-maximum-controls/article.md",

  "reader_note": "The three streams really contain 1,433 runes apiece, but the tested arithmetic alignment does not stand out.",
  "reader_limit": "The comparison is conditional on the already-chosen sections, F rules, operations and score.",
  "scope_summary": "Three 1,433-rune streams · twelve operations · 999 controls.",
  "article": "# Do the three 1,433-rune sections align?\n\n**Result:** No distinctive printed-order arithmetic reading appears in this bounded test. The best of **12 fixed outputs** has an index of coincidence of **0.034813**. When the same 12-way choice is repeated after independent circular shifts, **465 of 999** trials score at least as high. The reported equal lengths are real; they do not, by themselves, choose an alignment or arithmetic operation.\n\n![The observed best score nearly coincides with the median of selected shifted controls.](experiments/records/section-1433-pairing/comparison.svg)\n\nThe [section-count source](#/wiki/section-rune-counts) identifies three streams of 1,433 runes. We rebuilt each directly from the archived page text, using its explicit section breaks:\n\n| Stream | Construction | F rune |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| Koan 2 + Spirals | LP1-14–15, then LP2-03–07 | Omit all 31 |\n| Cuneiform | Second piece of LP2-33 through first piece of LP2-39 | Omit all 35 |\n| Wing and Tree | LP2-27–32 | Retain all 52 |\n\nFor each of the **three pairings**, the test adds or subtracts corresponding zero-based rune indices modulo 29, with the second stream either forward or reversed. It measures the equal-rune-pair rate over the complete output (index of coincidence, or IoC). This yields four operations per pairing, 12 outputs in all; the largest score is the test statistic.\n\n| Printed-order pairing | Best of four IoC |\n| --- | ---: |\n| Koan 2 + Spirals / Cuneiform | **0.034813** |\n| Koan 2 + Spirals / Wing and Tree | 0.034618 |\n| Cuneiform / Wing and Tree | 0.034524 |\n\nThe observed winner is reverse-subtraction of Cuneiform against Koan 2 + Spirals. The median **best-of-12** control score is **0.034799**, nearly the same. Each control trial draws a nonzero circular shift independently for each pair and **repeats the entire 12-output choice**. The saved report includes the 12 printed-order scores and all 999 selected control scores; an independent script recounts them.\n\nThis comparison is deliberately narrow. Its controls condition on the three previously noticed equal-length streams, the F-removal decisions, this operation family and IoC as the success measure. **466/1,000** is the add-one tail fraction for this conditional setup, *not* the chance of discovering the equality or a probability that the manuscript has no related cipher. Other transformations or a specific plaintext prediction would require a separately fixed test.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nFrom the repository root, run `python experiments/records/section-1433-pairing/run.py --check`, then `python experiments/records/section-1433-pairing/check.py`. Both use the Python standard library. The [plan](experiments/records/section-1433-pairing/plan.json) declares all 12 candidates and the control rule; [results](experiments/records/section-1433-pairing/results.json) save the input hashes and scores. The related [1,894-rune pairing](#/experiments/section-1894-pairing) uses the same arithmetic family on a separate reported equality.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/section-1433-pairing/article.md",

  "article": "# The 1,814-rune section pairing\n\n**Result.** The printed-order pairing scores above the median of the shift controls, but it is not isolated: **107 of 1,813 nonzero circular shifts** score at least as high after the same four-way choice. That is a conditional rank of **108/1,814 (5.95%)** when the printed alignment is included. It does not yield a reading or establish a key.\n\n![The printed pairing scores above the shift median but is matched or exceeded by 107 shifted pairings.](experiments/records/section-1814-pairing/comparison.svg)\n\nThis is a variant of the [1,894-rune pairing](#/experiments/section-1894-pairing). Only the input streams change. The published section counts give **753 + 747 + 314 = 1,814** runes for Koan 1, Loss of Divinity and Koan 2 after removing every F. Sign Post and Spirals give **695 + 1,119 = 1,814** under the same omission. We reconstructed those streams in printed order from LP1-06–15 and LP2-00–07; the first stream uses the *runes*, not the known English reading.\n\nAt each position, we add or subtract the two zero-based rune indices modulo 29. We also try the same operations with the second stream reversed. The complete output is scored by its index of coincidence (IoC), and the highest of the four scores is kept. The best printed-order variant is **reverse, add**: 114,642 ordered equal-rune pairs, or IoC **0.034859**. The median best-of-four score among shifted controls is **113,934**.\n\nThe control circularly shifts the second stream through *every* other alignment, applying all four operations and selecting the best each time. It accounts for choosing among those four operations **at this fixed pair of sections**. It does not account for choosing this equality from the source sheet, trying other section combinations or judging candidate plaintext after inspection. The modest upper-tail position is therefore a reason to specify a predictive decoding rule, not evidence that the pairing solves an LP2 page.\n\nRun `python experiments/records/section-1814-pairing/run.py --check` and `python experiments/records/section-1814-pairing/check.py` from the repository root. The [plan](experiments/records/section-1814-pairing/plan.json) freezes the four operations and control; the [result file](experiments/records/section-1814-pairing/results.json) includes all 1,814 shift scores. The independent checker rebuilds the streams and selected scores from the archived transcriptions.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/section-1814-pairing/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "ec10fd38d47a1c14293de56586d4d5e8efd27eb46377bc366018609cad2974e2",

  }

  "article": "# Does the 1,894-rune count give a useful alignment?\n\n**Result.** No unusual alignment appears under four fixed arithmetic readings. The best printed-order output has an index of coincidence of **0.034549**. Of the 1,893 nonzero circular shifts used as controls, **1,410 score at least as high** after the same four-way choice. This tests a proposed use of the equal length, not whether the section-count equality itself is correct.\n\n![The observed pairing lies within the range of shifted pairings; 1,410 of 1,893 shifts score at least as high.](experiments/records/section-1894-pairing/comparison.svg)\n\nThe published [section-count sheet](#/wiki/section-rune-counts) gives **1,894** runes on each side: Koan 1, Loss of Divinity, Koan 2 and Instruction after removing every F; and the Möbius section after its nine-rune heading with F retained. The first stream uses solved LP1 page *runes*, not the English reading. We rebuilt both streams directly from the archived page transcriptions, retaining their printed order and the explicit section breaks on LP1-16 and LP2-15.\n\nFor each aligned pair of rune indices `A` and `B`, the test forms `(B + A) mod 29` or `(B − A) mod 29`, with `B` either forward or reversed. Each complete output receives a whole-stream equal-rune-pair score, reported as index of coincidence (IoC); the **highest of the four** is the chosen score. We repeat that whole selection for every circular shift of `B`, so the control includes the choice among the four operations.\n\n| Printed-order operation | Equal-rune pairs | IoC |\n| --- | ---: | ---: |\n| Add | 123,206 | 0.034364 |\n| Subtract | 123,468 | 0.034437 |\n| Reverse, add | **123,870** | **0.034549** |\n| Reverse, subtract | 123,266 | 0.034381 |\n\nThe observed best score is **below the median shifted best score** of 124,096. Its rank is ordinary under this narrow comparison; the count match alone does not choose an operation or recover readable text. The [full result](experiments/records/section-1894-pairing/results.json) saves all 1,894 best-of-four scores, and the [plan](experiments/records/section-1894-pairing/plan.json) fixes the operations and exclusions.\n\nRun `python experiments/records/section-1894-pairing/run.py --check` and `python experiments/records/section-1894-pairing/check.py` from the repository root. The second program independently rebuilds the section streams and checks the observed variants and selected shifts. This control conditions on a previously noticed equality and one score. It does not cover every section pairing, every cipher operation, or a full language-based reading test.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/section-1894-pairing/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "9102af6a265c08f93d9a60e5f6cd14fda76e2564375887854e6517675d8251c8",

    "id": "measurement",
    "label": "Manuscript measurement",
    "description": "Measures a stated feature or statistical comparison; it does not test a complete decoding rule."
  }

  "scope_summary": "LP2-00–55 · nine section groups · 308-rune ending versus 2,701 equal-length windows.",
  "article": "# Do the final LP2 pages have different rune statistics?\n\nThe last two pages, LP2-54–55, have **308 runes**. We compared their rune collision rate and adjacent repeats with the preceding LP2-40–53 section. A direct comparison of all 3,008 earlier runes with 308 ending runes would conceal how much these measures fluctuate at the shorter length, so the main reference is **every 308-rune window** of the earlier section.\n\n**Both ending values fall inside the middle 95% of those earlier windows.** This is a useful check against a conspicuous simple change in these two measures. It neither proves the sections use the same construction nor rules out different keys, transforms or page-specific instructions.\n\n![Two horizontal scales show the final pages' collision and doublet rates inside the central range of equal-length windows from pages 40–53.](experiments/records/sectionwise-rune-profile/comparison.svg)\n\n| Measure | LP2-54–55 | Middle 95% of LP2-40–53 windows | Earlier windows at least as high |\n| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |\n| Rune index of coincidence | 0.03382 | 0.03302–0.03655 | 1,892 of 2,701 |\n| Equal adjacent runes, within pages | 3 / 306 = 0.98% | 0.33–1.63% | 759 of 2,701 |\n\n*Index of coincidence* (IoC) is the chance that two rune positions contain the same symbol. Its near-uniform reference for a 29-rune alphabet is 1/29 ≈ 0.03448. A *doublet* is two equal runes adjacent after non-runes are removed within one page; page joins do not count. The 2,701 reference windows overlap heavily, so “windows at least as high” is a descriptive position among windows, **not a p-value** or 2,701 independent trials. The doublet count of three is also small enough that the rate is unstable.\n\n## Section overview\n\nThe section boundaries below follow the artwork grouping used for this comparison. They are not independently established cipher boundaries. LP2-50 contains no runes and contributes nothing to the rune measures.\n\n| Pages | Runes | IoC | Doublets / within-page pairs |\n| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |\n| 00–02 | 729 | 0.03408 | 4 / 726 |\n| 03–07 | 1,145 | 0.03463 | 6 / 1,140 |\n| 08–14 | 1,729 | 0.03446 | 9 / 1,722 |\n| 15–22 | 1,903 | 0.03450 | 10 / 1,895 |\n| 23–26 | 1,021 | 0.03427 | 11 / 1,017 |\n| 27–32 | 1,433 | 0.03419 | 13 / 1,427 |\n| 33–39 | 1,680 | 0.03436 | 12 / 1,673 |\n| 40–53 | 3,008 | 0.03454 | 18 / 2,995 |\n| 54–55 | 308 | 0.03382 | 3 / 306 |\n\nThese are measurements of the archived rune transcription, not a classification of cipher types. The page ranges were chosen for their visible section organization; selecting another split after seeing these numbers would require its own declared test. The window comparison conditions on the composition and order of the earlier section. It does not simulate a cipher or account for the many possible ways to divide the manuscript.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nFrom the repository root, using Python 3.12 and its standard library:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/sectionwise-rune-profile/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/sectionwise-rune-profile/check.py\n```\n\nThe [plan](experiments/records/sectionwise-rune-profile/plan.json) fixes the group boundaries, measures and equal-length comparison; [results](experiments/records/sectionwise-rune-profile/results.json) contain exact counts and input hashes. `run.py` without `--check` regenerates that JSON; `plot.py` redraws the figure. The independent checker uses direct rune-pair enumeration instead of the producer's frequency counter. For the complete 86-doublet source-location ledger and separator sensitivity, see [doublets](#/wiki/doublets) and [doublet boundaries](#/experiments/doublet-boundaries).\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/sectionwise-rune-profile/article.md",

  "article": "# Does matching the opening text identify a seed?\n\nA short readable opening can have several explanations. This experiment plants a known 95-rune passage under two fixed keystream generators, searches a finite seed dictionary, and asks whether seeds that reproduce the opening also predict the remaining text. No candidate is selected by looking at that remaining text.\n\nA **crib** is an assumed exact plaintext sequence at an exact position. Here the crib is supplied as part of the control. It is not guessed from the ciphertext or inferred from a language score. The **withheld suffix** is everything after the crib: the part reserved for checking a prediction.\n\nWith two crib runes, every tested search retains several seeds. Only the true generating pairs recover the complete passage. At four or more crib runes, those generating pairs are the only survivors in the searches that include them; the other controls retain none. This is a result for these fixtures and dictionaries, not a general four-rune requirement.\n\n## What is searched?\n\nThe plaintext is the 95 output rune indices from the known reading of LP2-57. New ciphertexts are generated from it. This is not a new attempt to decrypt the original LP2-57 image, and it supplies no claim about the unsolved pages.\n\nThe two generators use SHA-256 and SHA-512. Each hashes the ASCII domain separator `liberpedia-seed-control:v1:`, followed by a four-byte unsigned big-endian seed and a four-byte unsigned big-endian counter starting at zero. Digest bytes of 232 or greater are discarded; the remaining bytes are reduced modulo 29. Digests are concatenated until 95 indices are available. There are no skips, offsets, resets or alternate signs.\n\nEach generator plants seeds 17, 4095 and 4096. Each search tests seeds **0 through 4095**, inclusive, under one generator. Seed 4096 is deliberately absent from both search dictionaries even though it is a valid generator input. Thus an unsuccessful search can simply mean the needed seed is outside its bounds.\n\nEncryption is `cipher[i] = (plain[i] + key[i]) mod 29`. A seed survives when it reproduces every assumed crib rune at the start. Every survivor is retained; there is no English score, best-candidate ranking or phrase selection. Its complete decoded sequence is then compared with the known plaintext, keeping full-passage equality and withheld-suffix equality separate.\n\n## Results\n\nThe figure reports the range of candidate counts across the searches in each control group. These ranges are not confidence intervals. The incorrect-crib group changes only the first rune by adding one modulo 29, leaving the rest of the assumed opening unchanged. It includes both matching and mismatched search generators.\n\n| Control | Searches per crib length | Survivors with 2 crib runes | Survivors with 4, 8, 16 or 32 crib runes |\n| --- | ---: | --- | --- |\n| Correct crib; generating pair included | 4 | 4, 6, 11, 8 | Exactly 1 per search |\n| Correct crib; matching generator but seed outside range | 2 | 5, 4 | 0 |\n| Correct crib; wrong generator | 6 | 8, 5, 10, 6, 8, 2 | 0 |\n| Incorrect first crib rune | 12 | 6, 5, 2, 7, 4, 3, 8, 6, 7, 4, 4, 6 | 0 |\n\nAt length two, the four included-pair searches contain 29 survivors in total. Four are the true generating pairs; the other 25 fail to predict the complete 93-rune withheld suffix. All survivors in the other three control groups also fail that complete suffix test. They may agree with individual withheld runes, which is why the full report preserves both exact equality and the number of correct positions.\n\nFor all longer tested cribs, each included-pair search retains exactly the true seed, which recovers all 95 runes. An incorrect first crib rune prevents full-passage equality by construction; the independently evaluated suffix test is a separate check.\n\nThe complete summary retains all **120 cells**, including zero-survivor cases. The full JSON also stores every searched keystream, every planted ciphertext and every surviving candidate's decoded sequence. A generating-pair identity and an exact finite-stream match are conceptually different; no alternative pair recovers the whole passage in these controls.\n\n## What an empty search establishes\n\nAn empty result excludes only the tested generator/seed pairs under the exact crib and alignment. It does not exclude seeds outside the dictionary, other generators, another seed encoding, a different crib, an unknown offset or a different cipher mechanism. The two omitted-seed fixtures demonstrate this directly: their ciphertexts are generated by a tested generator, yet the bounded correct-crib searches retain no seed once the crib reaches four runes.\n\nThese cells reuse one plaintext and fixed dictionaries. They are dependent controls, not independent samples from a population of ciphers. Short prefixes can match accidentally; no probability that an LP proposal is correct follows from these counts. Random-looking ciphertext also does not establish an independent one-time pad.\n\n## Reproduce and inspect\n\nExtract this experiment's ZIP with folders intact, or use the repository. Python 3 and its standard library are sufficient; no additional corpus, original-image download, API or model is needed.\n\n```sh\npython experiments/records/seed-crib-controls/run.py --check\n```\n\nThe command reconstructs the result, independently checks every stream and survivor, and compares the complete summary and figure. Use `--output seed-replay` instead to retain newly generated reports in a new directory. The plot can also be regenerated with `python experiments/records/seed-crib-controls/plot.py`.\n\nThe protocol was committed before candidate generation. The checker imports no producer code: it separately packs seed/counter bytes, uses division to implement rejection conversion and checks compatibility by directly encrypting the assumed crib. Both implementations share Python's hash primitives. Boundary and exhaustive toy controls test byte order, the 231/232 cutoff and the difference between prefix, suffix and whole-text agreement. Human review remains pending.\n\n## Related explanations\n\nRead [search spaces and bounds](#/wiki/search-space) for interpreting an empty search, [one-time pads and short seeds](#/wiki/one-time-pad) for the identification limits, and [search-maximum controls](#/experiments/search-maximum-controls) for the different problem of selecting the highest language score.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/seed-crib-controls/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "cc328de8bb18f1b8d7f3d9178391996dd3cf6577898dc92babc12183d433b8da",

  }

  "sources": [
    {

  "article": "# Selected phrase and MYRMELEONTIDAE word sums\n\nThis variant changes the baseline's candidate list to five supplied words: PROVE, WORTHIER, FIND, TRUTHS and MYRMELEONTIDAE. The first four were proposed against totals 131, 151, 151 and 131; the last against 809. It checks those selected matches without claiming that the resulting phrase or name is recovered plaintext.\n\n## What changes from the baseline?\n\nThe [baseline word-sum audit](#/experiments/mixed-square-word-sums) tests sixteen other supplied word-and-total pairs, including FIND. This variant retains the same 29-label alphabet, V-to-U normalization, exhaustive segmentation procedure and prime-value summation. Only the candidate list and proposed targets change. FIND is intentionally retained as a shared check.\n\nThe candidate list was fixed before enumeration, but the supplied words were already selected for their claimed numerical matches. This is an exploratory audit, not an unbiased measure of how frequently words match these targets.\n\n## All ten segmentations\n\nEvery segmentation is retained below. A slash separates rune labels; adjacent Latin letters inside one label belong to a single rune.\n\n| Candidate | Rune labels | Sum | Proposed target matched? |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| PROVE | P / R / O / U / E | 131 | Yes |\n| WORTHIER | W / O / R / TH / I / E / R | 151 | Yes |\n| WORTHIER | W / O / R / T / H / I / E / R | 228 | No |\n| FIND | F / I / N / D | 151 | Yes |\n| TRUTHS | T / R / U / TH / S | 131 | Yes |\n| TRUTHS | T / R / U / T / H / S | 208 | No |\n| MYRMELEONTIDAE | M / Y / R / M / E / L / EO / N / T / I / D / A / E | 809 | Yes |\n| MYRMELEONTIDAE | M / Y / R / M / E / L / EO / N / T / I / D / AE | 746 | No |\n| MYRMELEONTIDAE | M / Y / R / M / E / L / E / O / N / T / I / D / A / E | 842 | No |\n| MYRMELEONTIDAE | M / Y / R / M / E / L / E / O / N / T / I / D / AE | 779 | No |\n\nAll five targets are achievable, each by one segmentation. PROVE and FIND each have only one segmentation under the declared rules. WORTHIER and TRUTHS each have two; MYRMELEONTIDAE has four.\n\n## The 809 match requires a particular segmentation\n\nMYRMELEONTIDAE gives 809 when EO is combined but the final A and E are separate. Combining both EO and AE gives 746. Separating both pairs gives 842; combining only the final AE gives 779. These alternatives differ because a two-letter rune's prime value is not the sum of its two separate letters' values.\n\nA converter that always consumes the longest available label would choose EO and AE and return 746. A converter that always treats each Latin letter separately would return 842. The proposed 809 result is therefore possible within the exhaustive search, but it is not determined by the spelling alone. No evidence here selects that segmentation as the manuscript's intended representation.\n\n## What the phrase match establishes\n\nThe matching totals for PROVE WORTHIER FIND TRUTHS are 131, 151, 151 and 131. That verifies four arithmetic assignments. It does not recover their order, grammar or intended meaning from the square. Choosing words for their fitting totals and then observing that those totals are prime is not a second independent test: the target numbers already supplied that property.\n\nThe [mixed-square guide](#/wiki/magic-squares) distinguishes LP1-05's 1033 square, LP1-16's 3301 square and the separate LP2-15 panel. This variant associates the first four targets with LP1-05 and 809 with LP1-16; it does not move the red 3299 from LP2-15 into either square. A claimed thematic relation of a word to insect imagery would require separate evidence and is not tested here.\n\n## Reproduce and inspect\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/selected-phrase-word-sums/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/selected-phrase-word-sums/check.py\n```\n\nThe runner is byte-identical to the baseline runner and reads this variant's plan. Without `--check`, it prints the complete JSON report. The independent checker enumerates every cut/no-cut choice between Latin letters, rejects pieces absent from the alphabet, and verifies all retained segmentations and totals. Both commands passed in the extracted reproduction bundle. Python's standard library is sufficient; no dictionary download or hosted AI is involved.\n\n## Limits and next variants\n\nNo alternative words, synonyms or dictionary entries were searched. No cipher was applied to the manuscript, and no null model estimates the surprise of the selected words. The finding neither proves an intended phrase nor shows that these are the only fitting words.\n\nA broader word search must pin its vocabulary, normalization and segmentation policy, then retain all matches. A fixed longest-label policy would be a different variant. A cipher test using these candidates must specify the target pages, transform, key advancement and success criterion. The [rune-length bounds](#/wiki/prime-sums?section=length-bounds) can rule out impossible lengths before a dictionary search starts.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/selected-phrase-word-sums/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "fa37d2e9e709b8f1e1685666ad2a2d067aaeacd6de523abd176c745921a833cc",

  "id": "semantic-seed-screen-gate-audit",

  "reader_question": "Did this seed search actually let promising answers through to its final check?",

  "article": "## Finding\n\nThe published semantic-seed sweep tried **4,274 combinations** of candidate seeds, generators and decoders. Its saved screening scores can be reproduced. But **none of those candidates could reach the stated full hit test**, even if one decrypted the page perfectly.\n\n![The source sweep, a perfectly recovered planted key, and the unreachable promotion rule.](experiments/records/semantic-seed-screen-gate-audit/gate.svg)\n\nThe code promotes a candidate only if its *screen score is at least +5*. That score is an average of log-probabilities; it cannot exceed **0**. The best actual score was **−6.58**. More decisively, a planted key recovered **all 120 test runes** and scored **−4.35**. The screen discarded it too. The separate published control called the later hit test directly, bypassing this screen.\n\nThis changes the interpretation of the reported zero survivors. It is a consequence of the promotion rule, **not evidence that these seeds and generators failed the full test**. The 4,274 saved scores still describe what the source code produced; they do not close the method family.\n\n## What was replayed\n\nThe source's seed builder regenerated all **323** committed seeds exactly. The Py2.7 random-generator self-test passed, all seven generator functions ran, and the original sweep reproduced **4,274 rows** against the source's 12,956-rune LP2 transcription. The row count is lower than 323 × 7 × 2 because **31 phrase strings** are used with only three generators. The reproduced best score, −6.5781, matches the published summary.\n\nThe nine-register language model used by the later hit test is absent from the pinned repository, as are three exact training corpora needed to rebuild it. We therefore did **not** rerun that test or replace it with a different scorer. The pinned `control.json` is retained as a source artifact, not treated as an independently reproduced control result.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nFrom the repository root, Python 3 with NumPy runs the fast audit in about a second:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/semantic-seed-screen-gate-audit/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/semantic-seed-screen-gate-audit/check.py\n```\n\nTo rerun all 4,274 upstream screening rows in a temporary copy, use `python experiments/records/semantic-seed-screen-gate-audit/run.py --replay`. This takes roughly three minutes. The [saved rows](experiments/records/semantic-seed-screen-gate-audit/rows.jsonl) and [machine-readable result](experiments/records/semantic-seed-screen-gate-audit/results.json) are bundled with the pinned source and its MIT license. The full source hit test would require its original model and exact corpus bytes, then a corrected, predeclared promotion rule and an end-to-end planted control.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/semantic-seed-screen-gate-audit/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "856f17c04041a57ce798848f670281e8198c8d2a8012cf6e4216f9a21c2d0d91",

  "reader_note": "An exact two-rune lag-13 recurrence is ordinary under page shuffling; the source did not specify its original windows or motif.",
  "reader_limit": "This is a narrow new test of one interpretation, not a replay of the reported attempt.",
  "scope_summary": "LP2-00–55 · 12,186 15-rune windows · 499 page shuffles · 27-lag search control.",
  "article": "# Do short spans repeat at lag 13?\n\nA reported idea describes repeated rune patterns in 10–15-rune windows at lag 13, perhaps in connection with an interrupted cipher stream. It does not supply the original windows, positions, or a rule for what counts as a repeat. This record tests **one precise interpretation**: a 15-rune span whose first two runes match the two runes 13 positions later.\n\n**We found 17 such spans in LP2-00–55.** The exact expectation from independently shuffling the runes within each page is 14.1; 499 full page-shuffle runs commonly produced 7–22. The observed count is within that range. This test does not substantiate an unusual lag-13 excess under this rule, and it does not reproduce or refute a different pattern the original author might have meant.\n\n![Observed count of 17 repeated two-rune patterns at lag 13, within the middle 95 percent of page-shuffle counts from 7 to 22.](experiments/records/short-window-lag13/comparison.svg)\n\nFor a span `C₀ … C₁₄`, the test requires **C₀ = C₁₃ and C₁ = C₁₄**. There are 12,186 eligible within-page 15-rune windows in the archived transcription. A 10–13-rune window has no rune pair 13 positions apart; a 14-rune window has one such pair; a 15-rune window has only two. Thus a short attractive-looking example gives little independent evidence on its own. We count *all* eligible windows, not a hand-picked example.\n\n| Check | Result |\n| --- | ---: |\n| Repeated two-rune spans at lag 13 | 17 |\n| Exact expectation under fixed page counts | 14.12 |\n| Middle 95% of 499 page shuffles | 7–22 |\n| Shuffles with at least 17 | 111 of 499 |\n\nThe claim mentioned lag 13 and other potentially important lags. To show the cost of selecting a lag after inspecting the manuscript, the [plan](experiments/records/short-window-lag13/plan.json) also scans **all lags 2–28** for the same repeated-two-rune rule. Lag 13 is not the highest: its observed-to-expected ratio is 1.20, while lag 5 gives the largest ratio, 1.91. When every shuffled manuscript gets the same best-of-27 search, **30 of 499** shuffles reach or exceed that best observed ratio. Even this control only covers those 27 exact-pattern tests; it does not adjust for trying other motif definitions, page ranges, window rules or marker choices.\n\nShuffling retains each page's rune counts and length but destroys its original order. The result is conditional on that reference, the archived transcription, and the exact two-rune definition. No key sequence, F-skip rule, collision skip or I/M marker is tested here. Those would require complete transition and reset rules, plus a predicted output distinct from the statistic used to select them. See the [doublet ledger](#/wiki/doublets) and [short-lag equality profile](#/experiments/doublet-lag-profile) for related but different events.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nUsing Python 3.12 and its standard library from the repository root:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/short-window-lag13/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/short-window-lag13/check.py\n```\n\nThe producer repeats the seeded 499-shuffle comparison and checks it against [saved results](experiments/records/short-window-lag13/results.json). The independent checker parses the archive separately and verifies every observed count through direct two-position slice comparison. The figure is regenerated with `python experiments/records/short-window-lag13/plot.py`. Neither checker can recover the unspecified original windows from the screenshot.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/short-window-lag13/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "24a860799e143eea94b2cea0a6fee21ce5f0860b6d78ca3a2152c6476b88ffe5",

    "description": "Measures a stated feature or statistical comparison; it does not test a complete decoding rule."
  }
}

    "procedure": "For each rune type separately, delete every occurrence while preserving surviving order and page boundaries; recount equal adjacent rune pairs, destroyed pairs, newly bridged pairs, surviving edges and fixed-count shuffle expectation.",
    "parameters": "Exactly 29 fixed global deletion rules. No individual position selection, no threshold optimization, no plaintext scoring, no key or subsequent decoder.",
    "exclusions": "Multi-type or position-specific deletion; word-boundary-dependent counting; changed cipher alignment after deletion; alternative transcriptions; LP2-56–57; a claim of general null impossibility."

  "outcome": "not-supported",
  "finding": "No complete one-rune-type deletion reduces the 86 original adjacent equal-rune pairs. The resulting counts range from 92 to 109; the exact bridge identity explains each change. Fixed-count shuffle expectations for the retained streams range from 437.08 to 440.80 pairs.",
  "limitations": "This finite result only addresses raw within-page doublet counts after one globally deleted rune type. The shuffle expectation is descriptive and does not model a plaintext language. Deletion before another transform may change key alignment and is outside scope.",
  "next_steps": "For a broader null claim, predeclare the symbol or positional rule, deletion budget and order relative to any cipher; use known-reading controls and matched searches before evaluating LP2 output.",

  "visuals": [
    {
      "path": "experiments/records/single-rune-null-doublets/single-rune-null-doublets.svg",
      "caption": "All 29 fixed single-rune-type deletions increase the within-page adjacent equal-pair count above the original 86."
    }
  ],
  "article": "# Does removing one rune type reduce LP2’s adjacent repeats?\n\nNo, under the fixed rule tested here. For each of the 29 rune types, remove **every occurrence of that type** from LP2-00–55 and recount equal adjacent runes within pages. The archived stream has **86 doublets**. Every one-type deletion leaves **92 to 109**, so none reduces the raw count. This closes a small, explicit class of null-removal suggestions; it does not test arbitrary null positions or whether deletion before a later cipher could help.\n\n![Adjacent equal-rune counts for every fixed one-type deletion](experiments/records/single-rune-null-doublets/single-rune-null-doublets.svg)\n\n## What was fixed\n\nThe inputs are the 56 archived LP2-00–55 page texts and the stored 29-rune alphabet. Headings are included. Within each page, remove non-runes as in the [published doublet census](#/wiki/doublets); never count a pair across pages. For each rune type, delete all its occurrences, leave all surviving runes in order, and count adjacent equal pairs again. The rule has exactly **29 configurations**, not a search over individual positions. The [plan](experiments/records/single-rune-null-doublets/plan.json) and source hashes make the corpus and comparison explicit.\n\n| Result | Value |\n| --- | ---: |\n| Original adjacent equal pairs | 86 of 12,901 within-page edges |\n| Lowest after a one-type deletion | 92 (G, W, S or NG) |\n| Highest after a one-type deletion | 109 (R) |\n| Fixed-count shuffle expectation after deletion | 437.08–440.80 pairs, depending on type |\n\nDeleting a type can destroy an existing pair of that rune, but it can also bring two formerly separated surviving runes together. For G, five old G–G pairs disappear while 11 new equal pairs form across deleted runs, giving **86 − 5 + 11 = 92**. For R, two old pairs disappear and 25 new bridges form, giving **109**. The [complete result](experiments/records/single-rune-null-doublets/results.json) records the removed symbols, destroyed pairs, new bridges, surviving edges, rate and reference expectation for every type. Its exact bridge accounting is checked independently.\n\nThe fixed-count shuffle expectation is calculated separately from each **retained** page’s rune frequencies. The observed-to-expected ratio stays between **0.209 and 0.248** across the 29 deletions. That comparison says the low-adjacency feature is still visible after this transformation relative to a within-page shuffle of the retained symbols. It is **not** a probability that a null model is false, and a shuffled stream is not a plaintext-language model.\n\n## What this does and does not close\n\nIf the proposal is specifically “one rune type is padding, and deleting all of it will remove the low-doublet feature from the raw LP2 stream,” these 29 exhaustive cases do not support it. A different claim could delete only selected positions, delete several rune types, preserve word boundaries differently, or delete before applying a cipher whose alignment then changes. Those have much larger search spaces and need separate bounds and controls. A readable fragment after hand-selecting deleted positions would not be comparable with this fixed sweep.\n\nThis record measures a ciphertext statistic. It does not recover plaintext, identify a null symbol, or rule out nulls in general. The [null-removal guide](#/wiki/method-nulls) explains the larger family and the order-of-operations issue; the [doublet guide](#/wiki/doublets) defines the 86-pair baseline.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nFrom the repository root or extracted [experiment ZIP](downloads/experiments/single-rune-null-doublets.zip), using Python 3 standard library:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/single-rune-null-doublets/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/single-rune-null-doublets/check.py\n```\n\nThe producer checks every input hash and reproduces the report and SVG. The separate checker extracts rune streams through a different parser, verifies the destroyed-pair and bridge identity for all 29 cases, and recalculates every edge count and exact fixed-count shuffle expectation. Both compare the same declared source files; neither re-reads the manuscript images.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/single-rune-null-doublets/article.md",

  "related": [],
  "visuals": [
    {
      "path": "experiments/records/spiral-branches-paired-subtraction/score-controls.svg",
      "caption": "Observed best-of-five equal-pair count against exhaustive circular shifts and page-conditioned shuffles; each box shows the middle half, with median and full range."
    }
  ],
  "article": "## What is being tested?\n\nThe Spirals and Branches text, followed by the nine-rune heading before the Möbius number panel, contains 2,883 runes. Spiral Branches also has 2,883 runes after its 125 F runes are removed. A source discussion suggested pairing the streams, reversing Branches like a musical retrograde, or applying Atbash before modular subtraction. We test five *specified* ways to do that pairing and ask whether the best output has unusually high whole-stream index of coincidence (IoC) relative to two controls.\n\nThis is a new computation of suggestions in that discussion, not a replay of a reported successful decryption. The two long runic strings pasted in the supplied source thread match the archived Spirals and Branches-plus-heading transcriptions exactly: 1,145 and 1,738 runes, respectively. Their hashes are fixed in the [plan](experiments/records/spiral-branches-paired-subtraction/plan.json). The second 2,883-rune stream is rebuilt from LP2-40–53 after removing every F; the discussion did not supply a complete scored sweep of it.\n\n## Inputs and five variants\n\nUse zero-based positions in the 29-rune alphabet. Let **A** be the 1,145 Spirals runes, then the 1,729 Branches runes, then the nine-rune pre-Möbius heading. Let **B** be the 3,008 Spiral Branches runes after deleting its 125 F runes. Retain all other headings. Punctuation, page breaks and the number panel are not rune positions. At every aligned position output `(B − A) mod 29`.\n\n| Variant | What changes in A |\n| --- | --- |\n| Direct | Nothing; printed order. |\n| Reverse Branches | Reverse its 1,729 runes; leave the nine-rune heading at the end. |\n| Reverse tail | Reverse Branches and the heading together as one 1,738-rune block. |\n| Atbash Branches | Replace each Branches index `x` by `28 − x`; leave the heading unchanged. |\n| Atbash tail | Atbash the entire Branches-plus-heading block. |\n\nThe two reverse and two Atbash treatments make the thread's “Branches” versus “Branches + Table” boundary ambiguity explicit. A head-of-Spirals-to-tail-of-Branches pairing is covered by reversal of the relevant tail. We do not search starts, other page ranges, arbitrary offsets, keys, multiplication, XOR, or different F handling.\n\n## Score and controls\n\nFor each complete output, count ordered pairs of identical runes and divide by `2,883 × 2,882 = 8,308,806`. This is whole-stream IoC, not a language score. The chosen statistic is the **largest** of the five variant scores. Each control repeats all five variants and takes its own maximum:\n\n1. **Every nonzero circular shift of B:** 2,882 comparisons preserve its rune sequence and frequencies but change its alignment with A. The observed unshifted alignment is the remaining position.\n2. **999 within-page shuffles of B:** each LP2-40–53 non-F page chunk is independently shuffled, preserving its size and rune counts. These disrupt local order while retaining page-level composition. The pseudorandom seed is recorded in the plan.\n\nThese controls ask whether the observed *alignment* stands out under their respective assumptions. They do not estimate how rarely a researcher might discover some equal-length sections and some promising operation after searching many alternatives.\n\n## Result\n\n| Variant | Ordered equal-rune pairs | IoC |\n| --- | ---: | ---: |\n| Direct | 286,654 | 0.034500 |\n| Reverse Branches | 286,132 | 0.034437 |\n| Reverse tail | **287,504** | **0.034602** |\n| Atbash Branches | 286,138 | 0.034438 |\n| Atbash tail | 286,280 | 0.034455 |\n\nReverse tail is the best of the five on this measure. But 921 of the 2,882 nonzero circular shifts reach at least its score; including the observed alignment gives **922/2,883 ≈ 0.320**. Similarly, 341 of 999 within-page shuffles reach it; the usual add-one estimate is **342/1,000 = 0.342**. The selected score is ordinary under both comparisons. Neither number is a probability that the full historical idea is correct or incorrect.\n\n![Two horizontal box plots show the best-of-five score inside both control distributions.](experiments/records/spiral-branches-paired-subtraction/score-controls.svg)\n\nThe boxes span each control's middle half, their central lines mark medians, and the whiskers reach the saved minimum and maximum. The dashed line is the observed 287,504. The figure displays the distribution of the **maximum over five** for every control input, not the distribution of a single selected variant. [Download the figure](experiments/records/spiral-branches-paired-subtraction/score-controls.svg), [all candidate streams and source coordinates](experiments/records/spiral-branches-paired-subtraction/candidate-streams.json), or [the complete results and control scores](experiments/records/spiral-branches-paired-subtraction/results.json).\n\n## Reproduce and interpret\n\nFrom a full checkout or the [experiment ZIP](downloads/experiments/spiral-branches-paired-subtraction.zip), run:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/spiral-branches-paired-subtraction/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/spiral-branches-paired-subtraction/check.py\npython experiments/records/spiral-branches-paired-subtraction/plot.py --check\n```\n\nThe first command rebuilds all five outputs, 2,882 shifted maxima and 999 shuffled maxima. The independent checker verifies each stored source coordinate against the archived text, all 14,415 output runes by re-encryption, every observed score through direct rune-pair comparison, sampled controls and both complete tail counts. The [source-bound section-count guide](#/wiki/section-rune-counts) checks the 2,883 construction separately. The [reported-attempt entry](#/wiki/reported-attempts?section=spirals-branches-2883-alignment) identifies the supplied discussion without republishing its full transcript.\n\nThis result does **not support an unusual IoC peak** for the five subtraction variants and exact representation above. It does not test n-gram scores, additions, multiplication, XOR, periodic IoC, alternative page spans, partial readings or different interruption rules. Even a high whole-stream IoC would need a complete, stable reading and a prediction on text not used to choose its operation. Keep a later variant as a separate test with its own search scope and controls.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/spiral-branches-paired-subtraction/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "19680051604ba6b46a7ae57c6eecb65681b37fd3389398540dc6a7268b140c5f",

  "article": "# Does 331 / 133 point uniquely to STUDY HERE?\n\n**Result.** On the archived 464-word solved LP1 sequence, forward word **331** is STUDY and reverse word **133** is HERE. The reverse position is forward word 332, so the two directions pick adjacent words. The phrase appears at **five** positions in this already-decoded text, not only at the reported 331 / 133 split. At the selected cut, the final 133 cipher words have the reported Gematria Primus (GP) sum **26,893**. The first 331 sum to **72,065**, which is **102 above** the reported 71,963.\n\n![A line marks the five locations of STUDY HERE in the 464-word reading; the chosen 331/133 split is highlighted with the two measured GP block sums below.](experiments/records/study-here-bidirectional-pointer/pointer-locations.svg)\n\n| Forward STUDY word | Reverse HERE word | First block GP sum | Remaining block GP sum |\n| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |\n| 196 | 268 | 42,503 | 56,455 |\n| 227 | 237 | 48,700 | 50,258 |\n| 262 | 202 | 56,114 | 42,844 |\n| 293 | 171 | 62,910 | 36,048 |\n| **331** | **133** | **72,065** | **26,893** |\n\nThe source conversation links the selected split to two purported prime sums, 71,963 and 26,893. Only the latter reproduces from this archive's nine-page ciphertext transcription. The reporter's exact 464-word input list was not supplied, so the 102-point difference is an **unresolved source discrepancy**; it does not prove the original calculation was impossible on another transcription.\n\nThe pointer arithmetic is less selective than it first looks: for any cut after forward word *k* in a 464-word list, reverse word *(464 − k)* is automatically the next forward word. The audit therefore checks every adjacent STUDY HERE occurrence and every one of the 463 possible cuts. Thirteen cuts have prime GP sums on both sides, while the selected 331 cut has a prime on only the final side. These are descriptive counts, **not a probability**: the positions, phrase and number links were discussed after the solved text was available.\n\nThe [plan](experiments/records/study-here-bidirectional-pointer/plan.json) fixes the four-section word order and counting rule. The [result](experiments/records/study-here-bidirectional-pointer/results.json) records input hashes, all five phrase locations and the prime-cut count. Reproduce it from the repository root with `python experiments/records/study-here-bidirectional-pointer/run.py --check`; the underlying independent word/token audit is `python scripts/audit_464_pointer.py --check`. This tests the reported **LP1 pointer**, not whether it specifies an LP2 decryption.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/study-here-bidirectional-pointer/article.md",

      "path": "experiments/records/target-sized-languages/comparison.svg",
      "caption": "Identical axes and styling for all eight languages. Blue ranges are observed reference-sample distances; diamonds are manuscript distances. Ranges are not confidence limits."

  "article": "## Why match the number of tokens?\n\nThe [aligned-language baseline](#/experiments/parallel-languages) compares the manuscript with much longer reference texts. This control asks a narrower question: how do those reference languages behave when each sample contains exactly **2,896 tokens**, the size of the unsolved rune-token target?\n\nEvery complete reference sample is nearest to its own language profile. However, **the manuscript is farther from every language profile than any of that language's reference samples are**. English is still the nearest of the eight candidates, but nearest does not mean that its profile closely explains the manuscript. These are observed distances, not probabilities or statistical rejection thresholds.\n\n## What is held fixed\n\nThe languages, translations, development profiles, three common representations and total-variation distance are inherited from the baseline. There is no fitted classifier or new language selection. Each evaluation translation is tokenized sentence by sentence, then divided in original order into disjoint blocks of 2,896 tokens. Every complete block is retained; the final incomplete remainder is counted and reported but not scored as an equal-size sample.\n\nThis produces seven blocks each for English and German, eight each for French, Italian, Portuguese, Spanish and Welsh, and five for Finnish. The three representations reuse the same texts. The resulting 177 profile checks are **not 177 independent trials**, and they are not pooled into a claimed general classification accuracy.\n\nEqual token counts do not preserve identical translated passages: different languages use different numbers of words for the same content. This control addresses size. The [aligned-block variant](#/experiments/parallel-language-blocks) separately preserves sentence ranges across languages. Neither controls for the difference between translated web material and Liber Primus's style.\n\n## Reading the distances\n\nEach sample is compared with all eight full development profiles using length bins 1 through 15 and 16+. Total variation is half the sum of the absolute differences in bin proportions. Zero means matching distributions; larger values mean greater separation. All distances are stored as exact rational numbers, and ties would be retained rather than broken by language order.\n\n| Language | Complete blocks per representation | Largest letter-control distance | Manuscript to letter profile |\n| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |\n| English | 7 | 0.0508 | 0.0831 |\n| Finnish | 5 | 0.0466 | 0.4051 |\n| French | 8 | 0.0514 | 0.1781 |\n| German | 7 | 0.0561 | 0.1665 |\n| Italian | 8 | 0.0436 | 0.2375 |\n| Portuguese | 8 | 0.0426 | 0.2114 |\n| Spanish | 8 | 0.0456 | 0.2230 |\n| Welsh | 8 | 0.0404 | 0.1650 |\n\n“Largest control distance” means the farthest observed sample from its own language's development profile. It is not a confidence limit. The manuscript lies beyond those observed ranges for all eight languages in all three representations, including GP-style grouping. That grouping is an orthographic sensitivity, not a validated conversion of each language into runes.\n\nWithin this corpus, all complete samples have a unique nearest profile matching their known language. The manuscript's nearest profile is English in all three representations. The report preserves every competing distance and the margin over the nearest competing language, so this statement can be checked without relying on a winner-only table.\n\n## A Unicode exception found before scoring\n\nThe original follow-up plan assumed that all three representations would preserve token boundaries. The implementation stopped when that check failed. Lowercasing the capital dotted I in “İzmir” creates an i followed by a combining dot; the inherited raw-letter tokenizer treats the mark as a separator. Accent folding removes it, joining the word. Three source sentences are affected.\n\nAn amendment was committed after inspecting that tokenization issue and before inspecting follow-up scores. The baseline tokenizer was not silently changed. Each representation is partitioned independently, its endpoint ledger is retained, and the report states whether boundaries agree. Folded letters and GP grouping do share boundaries. The original plan remains available alongside the amendment.\n\n## What this does not establish\n\nThe control does not identify the manuscript's language, eliminate the eight languages, or estimate a posterior probability. The sample ranges are small, adjacent blocks can share a source article, and both reference splits come from the same benchmark. The manuscript has different genre, spelling, unit and boundary uncertainties. Even its closest reference profile can therefore be a poor match for reasons other than language.\n\nThe [known-reading control](#/experiments/known-reading-languages) supplies a complementary warning: some short, established English sections rank nearest to other language profiles. The [cipher-invariants guide](#/wiki/cipher-invariants) explains which transformations preserve lengths and which change the assumptions behind this comparison.\n\n## Reproduce and inspect\n\nPython 3's standard library is sufficient; no API or model is involved. From the repository or extracted reproduction bundle, choose new output filenames:\n\n```sh\npython scripts/run_target_sized_languages.py --output my-language-controls.json\npython scripts/check_target_sized_languages.py my-language-controls.json --receipt my-language-audit.json\npython -m unittest discover -s scripts -p test_target_sized_languages.py\n```\n\nThe independent checker imports neither the producer nor the baseline tokenizer. It reconstructs words with a regex tokenizer, calculates distances from integer histogram counts, and checks all sample boundaries, remainders, 177 profiles, competing distances, margins and summary decisions. Its saved receipt records the report and checker hashes. Computational verification has passed; human review remains pending.\n\nFLORES translations and this derived account are provided under CC BY-SA 4.0. The baseline's source attribution is included with the reproduction files.\n",
