  "article": "## What was tested\n\nThe proposed 27 × 27 reading can be reproduced **when its selected cells and key nodes are supplied**. This experiment checks that arithmetic, the map itself, and the additional rules for predicting properties of the next block. It does not find the route from the manuscript without those selections.\n\nThe source is pinned to commit `d5eed3f10428372c7202ceebc65cc3bdead0819d`. Later edits to that repository are outside this result. The downloadable input records the coordinates, keys, source-file hashes and proposed output rune indices. No language model or language scorer chooses words in this replay.\n\n## Results at a glance\n\n| Check | Result | What it establishes |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| Map compared with archived LP2-00–02 | 729 of 729 cells agree | The selected matrix uses our transcription in page order |\n| Main reading | 17 blocks, 61 rune subtractions reproduce | Correct arithmetic for supplied choices |\n| Alternative SOON block | 4 further subtractions reproduce | A second supplied route produces the same word |\n| Next-key signature | 16 of 16 transitions match | Fit to the recorded route |\n| Next axis and boundary role | Each matches 16 of 16 | Further fit to the same route, not independent discoveries |\n| Ciphertext coverage | 54 distinct cells of 729, about 7.4% | The proposed reading is a selection, with reused cells |\n| Same SOON key from three nodes | Horizontal / diagonal / diagonal | Key equality does not settle the node choice |\n\n**Outcome: inconclusive as a decryption claim.** Successful arithmetic is a real result. The supplied rules do not yet uniquely select and read the full matrix, and this experiment does not establish whether the proposed passage was intended.\n\n[Open the full-size coverage map](exports/figures/totient-map-coverage.svg) · [Open the node-choice diagram](exports/figures/totient-map-node-choice.svg)\n\n## How the map is made\n\nRead [LP2-00](#/page/lp2-00), [LP2-01](#/page/lp2-01) and [LP2-02](#/page/lp2-02) in that order. Keep every rune, including the heading, remove punctuation and spacing, and fill rows of 27 from left to right. Coordinates start at (1,1). This gives exactly 729 cells; the repository's displayed map agrees cell by cell. It is a rearrangement of the text, not the original page layout.\n\nThe coverage figure highlights only ciphertext cells used in the primary route. Keys and navigation landmarks can use other cells. There are 61 output positions but only 54 distinct ciphertext cells because several are read more than once. Reuse is not automatically an error in a geometric cipher; it needs an explicit rule, just as skipping cells does.\n\nFor the functions themselves, see [Euler’s totient](#/wiki/totient) and [the Möbius function](#/wiki/mobius-function).\n\n## A complete arithmetic example: WEATHER\n\nThe node at row 14, columns 4–6 is X–OE–X, with indices 14,22,14. Replace the middle index by its totient: φ(22)=10, giving X–I–X. Apply μ(φ(k)) to each derived key index. The signature is (1,0,1), whose sum modulo 3 is 2. Rotate the key left twice to get X–X–I and repeat it.\n\n| Cipher cell | Cipher index | Key index | Difference modulo 29 | Output |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| (14,14) | NG = 21 | X = 14 | 7 | W |\n| (14,15) | P = 13 | X = 14 | 28 | EA |\n| (14,16) | EO = 12 | I = 10 | 2 | TH |\n| (14,17) | O = 3 | X = 14 | 18 | E |\n| (14,18) | E = 18 | X = 14 | 4 | R |\n\nFive output runes spell WEATHER. This calculation does not itself explain why those five cells are chosen, why the block stops there, or which block follows. The opening block also crosses a row boundary, whereas later selections include vertical and diagonal segments. TURNS uses its three node indices directly rather than transforming the center. Those choices are preserved in the replay instead of silently replacing them with a uniform rule.\n\nThe output trace retains rune tokens such as TH and EA. Spaces and punctuation in the proposed English reading are editorial interpretations, not separate decoded symbols.\n\n## What the transition rules add\n\nThe source provides more than word examples. It predicts a next-key signature using Möbius values of current block coordinates. It switches between direct and half-turned positions at cumulative phase totals 7 and 14. A quarter-turn calculation updates the outer signature state. A separate formula involving the current beginning, end and original node center predicts horizontal, vertical or diagonal; another predicts whether the next block's leftmost cell is its beginning or end.\n\nWe recomputed all 16 primary transitions, treating OF and THE separately and using the primary SOON route. All three checks match. The starting state, block boundaries, node centers and phase thresholds are inputs. The source states that the thresholds were identified from this route. Consequently, **16 matches are an in-sample fit, not 16 held-out predictions**. The signature, axis and boundary checks also share inputs and must not be multiplied as independent probabilities.\n\n### How many keys share a signature?\n\nA signature constrains a key without identifying its runes. For example, (0,0,0) is shared by 4,096 ordered triples of positive rune indices; (1,0,1) by 1,296. These counts enumerate indices 1–28 only. They exclude F=0, for which the standard positive-integer totient is not defined here. They are not counts of reachable nodes: geometric restrictions can reduce the candidates considerably.\n\nFor each derived key index k, compute μ(φ(k)). Among indices 1–28, 16 give zero, 3 give −1, and 9 give +1. An ordered key with signature (0,0,0) can independently select any of the 16 zero-class indices in each slot: 16 × 16 × 16 = 4,096. Repeated indices are allowed in this algebraic count. The signature (1,0,1) similarly gives 9 × 16 × 9 = 1,296.\n\n[Inspect the signature-class diagram](exports/figures/totient-signature-classes.svg). These are derived key triples before phase rotation; equal outer signature values do not require equal outer rune indices. They do not enumerate manuscript locations, enforce mirror-node geometry, or measure how many alternatives survive the complete proposed traversal. Therefore they cannot be used as the denominator of a chance probability for the reading.\n\n### Check one transition by hand: WEATHER → TURNS\n\nWEATHER occupies absolute positions 365–369, where position is `27 × (row − 1) + column`. Its original key-node center is (14,5), position 356, and contains OE with rune index 22. The cumulative phase total before this transition is 2, so the direct-position mode with offset 1 applies.\n\n| Quantity | Calculation | Result |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| Next phase | `(1 + μ(365) + μ(366) + μ(367) + μ(368) + μ(369)) mod 3` = `(1 + 1 − 1 − 1 + 0 + 0) mod 3` | 0 |\n| Next outer state | Quarter-turned positions are 365, 392, 419, 446, 473; minimum 365 has μ = 1. Update `(1 + 1) mod 2`. | 0 |\n| Next signature | Phase 0 and outer state 0 force the middle component to 0. | (0,0,0) |\n| Next axis | `μ(365 + 356) + μ(gcd(473,361))` = `μ(721) + μ(1)` = 1 + 1 | Positive: vertical |\n| Next boundary role | Three-quarter-turned endpoint has position 257. `(μ(257) + φ(22)) mod 2` = `(−1 + 10) mod 2` | 1: beginning |\n\nFor a vertical block, the minimum quarter-turned position corresponds to its bottommost cell. Calling that cell the beginning therefore predicts upward reading. The supplied TURNS block does read upward, from (14,19) to (10,19), and its key has signature (0,0,0). These properties agree; the calculation still does not choose column 19, the block's starting row, its length, or the exact key.\n\nEvery transition now has the same level of detail in the report's `calculation` object: coordinates, transformed positions, individual Möbius values, cumulative state, gcd arguments and boundary selection. The independent checker reconstructs these entries by rotating coordinates directly instead of using the replay's formulas for rotated absolute positions.\n\n## A controlled ambiguity: three SOON nodes\n\nThe source documents L–C–EA, L–I–EA and L–EO–EA. Their center indices 5, 10 and 12 all have totient 4. All therefore derive L–R–EA, align to EA–L–R, and turn the same X–D–W–H ciphertext into SOON.\n\nHowever, the next-axis formula also uses the original center's **position**. With the documented centers (25,7), (20,15) and (25,14), the scores are respectively 0, −1 and −1: horizontal, diagonal, diagonal. The published transition fit chooses (25,7), which agrees with THEN's horizontal block. The source explicitly identifies that choice.\n\nThis is a bounded example of a selection that affects the result. It does not prove that any desired sentence can be produced, or that all three choices satisfy every proposed navigation condition. It shows why a full decoder needs a rule selecting the original node before the next block is inspected.\n\n## Are three-rune mirrors unusual by themselves?\n\nWe counted equal outer runes around any center, along rows, columns and the two diagonals, at every in-bounds radius from 1 to 13. Each unoriented triple is counted once. The map has **507** such mirrors.\n\nAs a control, we shuffled the same 729 rune indices 99 times using seed 3301. This preserves rune frequencies but removes their original positions. Mirror counts ranged from **458 to 568**. The observed count is inside that range.\n\nThis control is deliberately narrow. It tests the abundance of this simple geometric pattern, not the quality of the proposed English, the complete traversal, or the combined transition rules. It supplies no chance probability for the selected reading. Testing that stronger claim would require a completely specified search procedure, the same search budget on controls, and a scoring rule chosen before inspecting the results.\n\n## How to reproduce\n\nDownload this experiment's bundle and extract it without changing its folder structure. Python 3 and its standard library are sufficient; no network, API or model is required.\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/totient-map-route/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/totient-map-route/check.py\npython experiments/records/totient-map-route/signature_figure.py\n```\n\nThe first command rebuilds the report and coverage image in memory and compares them with the saved versions. It checks all selected key nodes and subtractions, recomputes transition matches, enumerates signature classes, and repeats the mirror controls. Running without `--check` writes the report and coverage image. The explanatory node-choice diagram is an authored illustration of the reported three-node comparison.\n\nThe second command independently derives totients through prime factorization, checks all 65 recorded rune subtractions and node-derived keys, and compares totients with coprime counting for 1–729. It also independently verifies all 16 transition calculation records, all 18 key-node midpoints, and rotation identities for all 729 cells. It does not independently rediscover the route or certify the author's navigation choices. The JSON report includes all rune traces, transition inputs/results, the 99 control counts, reused cells, and phase-rotation ablations. Those ablations deliberately change the phase rule; they are sensitivity checks, not alternatives permitted by the fixed phase formula.\n\nThe third command independently calculates totients by counting coprimes and Möbius values by factorization, checks all six reported signature-class counts, and verifies the saved diagram. Add `--write` only to regenerate that diagram. It does not search for map nodes or produce plaintext.\n\n## What would strengthen the claim\n\nA useful next variant would freeze a deterministic procedure for choosing the initial node, subsequent anchors, node transformations, distance expressions, block lengths, directions, stopping condition and tie-breaking. It should specify how to handle zero-valued runes and every branch that remains possible.\n\nRun that fixed procedure on an unseen continuation before adjusting it. Report all outputs, not only readable ones. If alternatives remain, bound the enumeration and apply an explicit score to every candidate and to matched controls. This is the distinction between a reproducible selected reading and a decoder capable of making a new prediction. See [search space and bounds](#/wiki/search-space) and [planning a first experiment](#/wiki/first-experiment).\n\nThe numerical and thematic correspondences in the source's “Strongest Plaintext Evidence” discussion are not assigned significance here. Nor does this test rule out other 27 × 27, totient or geometric methods. Revisions that change node selection or traversal belong as related variants in this experiment family, with their changed choices stated explicitly.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/totient-map-route/article.md",

  }

  "visuals": [
    {
      "path": "experiments/records/transcription-correction-sensitivity/correction-effects.svg",
      "caption": "Eight stored corrections compared by mark edits, ordered runes, and normalized rune tokens. This summarizes the tested data layers; it is not a new image reading."
    }
  ],
  "article": "# Do the stored transcription corrections change the published LP2 word-length statistics?\n\nFor the **seven currently stored LP2 reviewed-text layers**, no. Applying them all leaves the ordered rune stream, rune-token sequence, 2,896-token length distribution, and whole-stream IoC pair counts unchanged under the site's published counting rule. The one LP1 reviewed layer is a useful positive control: LP1-10 swaps two neighboring runes, changing six ordered-bigram type counts, while retaining its rune multiset and token-length sequence.\n\nThis is a sensitivity measurement of the stored layers, **not** a fresh verification of the manuscript images. It says nothing about corrections not yet recorded. A method that treats every punctuation mark as a key reset can change even when this particular word-length statistic does not.\n\n![Per-page correction effects: mark edits, rune order, and rune-token sequence](experiments/records/transcription-correction-sensitivity/correction-effects.svg)\n\n## Inputs and rules\n\nUse the archived `raw` and separate `reviewed_text` in the eight page records: LP1-10; LP2-05, 07, 11, 15, 35, 37 and 38. These are the only eight records with a distinct reviewed layer in the current [75-page inventory](#/wiki/transcription-checking?section=coverage). Every input page record and the 29-rune alphabet are pinned by SHA-256 in `plan.json`.\n\nFor word lengths, concatenate LP2-00 through LP2-55 in order, remove slash and CR/LF row wraps, keep headings, and identify runs of the 29 runes with optional internal apostrophes. Other punctuation separates tokens. Count runes, not Latin transliteration letters. This is the same rule used by the [word-length census](#/wiki/word-lengths). No alternative punctuation policy or page-local tokenization is included in the main comparison.\n\nThe seven LP2 corrections consist of added or removed notation marks, with no rune substitution. The LP1-10 correction swaps the runes at zero-based rune indices 116 and 117; it is outside the LP2 corpus. The independent checker reconstructs all seven LP2 reviewed strings from the documented edit offsets and checks the LP1 adjacent swap separately.\n\n## Measured effect\n\n| Page | Stored change | Ordered runes | Rune-token sequence | Token count |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- | ---: |\n| LP1-10 | Adjacent rune swap | Changed | Changed | 40 → 40 |\n| LP2-05 | Add `-` | Same | Same | 59 → 59 |\n| LP2-07 | Add `.` | Same | Same | 50 → 50 |\n| LP2-11 | Add `-` | Same | Same | 55 → 55 |\n| LP2-15 | Add `.` | Same | Same | 37 → 37 |\n| LP2-35 | Add an apostrophe | Same | Same after omitting the apostrophe | 61 → 61 |\n| LP2-37 | Remove three `-` and one `.` | Same | Same | 53 → 53 |\n| LP2-38 | Add `.` | Same | Same | 47 → 47 |\n\nAcross LP2-00–55, both versions contain **12,956 runes**, **2,896 rune tokens**, and a maximum token length of **14**. Their complete token-length histograms match. Their whole-stream IoC numerator and denominator are **5,787,026 / 167,844,980** in both versions. The ordered rune stream and normalized token sequence have matching SHA-256 values. LP2-35's literal token text contains an extra apostrophe; the apostrophe is not a rune, and its normalized rune token is unchanged.\n\nLP1-10 demonstrates that the audit can register a real ordered-rune difference: the two-rune exchange changes six ordered-bigram type counts. Because it is a swap, its rune count, multiset and whole-page IoC remain unchanged. Its word lengths remain 40 tokens with the same length sequence, even though the token containing the swapped symbols has different rune order.\n\n## What follows—and what does not\n\nFor these exact stored LP2 corrections, recomputing the site's joined-page word-length histogram will not change the result. A rune-only frequency or IoC calculation also receives the same symbols in the same order. This is stronger than merely saying that punctuation changes *might* affect word lengths: it measures the actual published corrections under a declared tokenizer.\n\nIt does **not** prove that punctuation is irrelevant. A period, hyphen or apostrophe can drive a reset or extraction rule that this experiment does not run. Different tokenization, image-derived separators, or a newly corrected rune can change later measurements. Nor does matching a reviewed layer establish that the image was transcribed correctly everywhere. See [the transcription guide](#/wiki/transcription-checking) for the distinction between archived text, reviewed correction and original-image evidence.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nFrom the repository root or extracted experiment ZIP, with Python 3 and no packages:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/transcription-correction-sensitivity/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/transcription-correction-sensitivity/check.py\n```\n\nThe first command recomputes every page and the complete LP2 corpus, then compares `results.json` and the SVG. The second independently reconstructs the reviewed strings and scans rune tokens with a separate parser. `run.py` without flags prints a compact summary. The full machine-readable result includes per-page histograms, correction fields, hashes and the exact IoC pair counts.\n\nThe next variants should test a *specified* punctuation-sensitive key clock or tokenization policy, then add newly image-reviewed disputed marks one at a time. Retain this archived-versus-reviewed baseline so any changed conclusion can be attributed to the exact edit that caused it.\n\nFor a more specific statistic on the same seven LP2 reviewed layers, the [doublet boundary audit](#/experiments/doublet-boundaries) checks all 86 equal-rune pairs and whether any stored mark edit changes the intervening-separator class.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/transcription-correction-sensitivity/article.md",

Display ends at 649, with the remaining probability retained in JSON. This is a specific model comparison, not a plaintext-language probability."

  "article": "## What was tested\n\nThe archived LP2-00–55 text has **86 adjacent equal-rune pairs across 12,901 within-page edges**. Independent uniform additive keys modulo 29 would produce about **444.86 matches on average**. The exact probability of 86 or fewer under that model is approximately **1.0708 × 10⁻⁹⁸**.\n\nThis is a strong disagreement with one precisely defined model. It does not rule out encryption, random choices in other constructions, or any particular plaintext language. The low count and an earlier statement of this model were known before the replication. The probability is conditional on the model and is not adjusted for the historical search across manuscript features.\n\n## The model in ordinary terms\n\nFor every plaintext rune, independently choose a key uniformly from 0 through 28 and add it modulo 29. The plaintext may be any fixed sequence. Each resulting ciphertext rune is uniform, and different positions are independent. Keep the observed page lengths fixed.\n\nThe prediction concerns fresh, independent uniform symbols. A shuffle that preserves the manuscript's observed rune counts asks a different question. So does a generator that forbids repeats, uses nonuniform keys, reuses key values dependently, or changes its output according to the plaintext.\n\nThe [EA running-sum control](#/experiments/ea-frequency-control) examines an especially different equation: nonzero multiplicative keys and an EA offset make repeats depend on plaintext EA frequency. Its required EA count should not be tested with this record's independent-uniform-additive-key tail.\n\nThe [short-lag profile](#/experiments/doublet-lag-profile) uses that different, fixed-count page-shuffle reference. It shows the deficit at adjacent positions but not at rune distances two through five. Its bands must not be read as the exact uniform-key probability computed here.\n\n## Why overlapping pairs still give a binomial law here\n\nAdjacent comparisons share positions: the first pair of ABC uses A and B, and the next uses B and C. Shared positions do not automatically make these match indicators dependent under this particular uniform model.\n\nWithin one page, replace the ciphertext sequence by its first rune and the successive differences modulo 29. This transformation is reversible: start at the first rune and add each difference to recover the page. A reversible transformation of the uniformly distributed full sequence remains uniform over all such coordinate tuples. The differences are therefore independent uniform residues. A pair matches exactly when its difference is zero, which has probability 1/29.\n\nApply this separately to each page. There are 12,956 runes on 55 nonempty pages, hence **12,956 − 55 = 12,901 differences**. LP2-50 has no alphabet runes and adds no edge. Their zero count has the binomial distribution with 12,901 trials and success probability 1/29.\n\nUniformity matters. For independent binary symbols with probabilities 3/4 and 1/4, one pair matches with probability 5/8. Both overlapping pairs match with probability 7/16, which is different from (5/8)² = 25/64. The corresponding independence argument fails for that nonuniform model.\n\n## Reading the figure and the probability\n\nThe bars show probabilities for ten-count intervals under the uniform model. The observed count is far to the left of the main mass; its tiny probability cannot be resolved at this linear plotting scale. Values 650 and above are retained in one overflow bin in the JSON but omitted from the displayed range. The exact lower tail includes every count from zero through 86, not just the probability of exactly 86.\n\nThe numerator is the integer sum `Σ comb(E,j) × 28^(E−j)` for j from 0 through D, and the denominator is `29^E`, with E = 12,901 and D = 86. The script uses exact integers for that sum and 80-digit decimal arithmetic to render the ratio. It records hashes of both exact integers and supplies their reconstruction formulas. No normal approximation is used.\n\nThe separate checker reconstructs the same integer masses using a recurrence. It verifies the entire set of plotting bins against exact integer totals, independently recounts all 56 source files with regular expressions, and exhausts twelve small uniform-alphabet/page-length cases. Those controls include overlapping edges, multiple pages, empty pages and single-rune pages. They check the calculation and boundary handling; they do not authenticate the underlying handwriting.\n\n## What remains possible\n\nThe model assigns this event a very small but nonzero probability. That is statistical evidence against the model, not a mathematical impossibility certificate. It neither selects an alternative model nor explains the suppression.\n\nIn particular, the [multiplicative running-sum model](#/wiki/doublets?section=ea-constraint) has a different equation. There, with nonzero keys modulo 29, a repeat can be determined by a particular plaintext rune. Uniform selection of its nonzero keys does not imply a repeat probability of 1/29. This experiment must not be used to reject that construction.\n\n## Reproduce the comparison\n\nDownload this experiment's bundle and preserve its folders. Python 3 standard library only; no network, API, or model is required.\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/uniform-additive-doublets/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/uniform-additive-doublets/check.py\npython experiments/records/uniform-additive-doublets/plot.py --check\n```\n\nThe first verifies the input hashes, per-page counts, exact tail and saved bins. The second uses the independent recurrence and controls. The third checks the chart against the saved probabilities. To regenerate, run the producer with `--write` and the plotter without `--check`.\n\nThe [committed plan](experiments/plans/uniform-additive-doublets.md) was fixed before these new calculations, after the prior count and claim were known. This is computationally checked replication; human review is pending. See [doublet definitions](#/wiki/doublets), [null-model selection](#/wiki/null-models), and [what a scoped exclusion means](#/wiki/first-experiment?section=exclusions).\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/uniform-additive-doublets/article.md",

  "article": "# Eleven-rune windows in the Wing and Tree section\n\nAcross six pages, **seven windows sum to 563 and ten sum to 569**. This record supports recurrence under the rules below, not statistical significance, intent or decipherment.\n\n## What changed from the grid experiment?\n\nThe baseline rearranges LP2-32 into an 11×11 grid and selects a row, column and perimeter. This variant expands the input to LP2-27–32 and selects every consecutive eleven-rune window within each page. It retains prime values and fixed targets 563 and 569. It does not test the perimeter target 1136. The family comparison lists every changed scope field.\n\n## Complete counting rules\n\nRead the archived text in order, including headings. Keep only the 29 alphabet runes. Remove punctuation and line markers, but start a fresh stream at each page. Sum runes 1–11, then 2–12, continuing to the last complete window. A page with N runes contributes N−10 windows. Do not reverse, pad, wrap or cross a page boundary.\n\n| Page | Runes | Windows | Sum 563 | Sum 569 |\n| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |\n| LP2-27 | 234 | 224 | 0 | 2 |\n| LP2-28 | 269 | 259 | 2 | 2 |\n| LP2-29 | 277 | 267 | 1 | 2 |\n| LP2-30 | 263 | 253 | 0 | 1 |\n| LP2-31 | 269 | 259 | 3 | 3 |\n| LP2-32 | 121 | 111 | 1 | 0 |\n| Total | 1433 | 1373 | 7 | 10 |\n\nAll window sums total 784505, giving a mean of approximately 571.38. The ledger retains all 1373 windows, including nonmatches. Each includes its rune sequence, sum, one-based rune interval and zero-based source character offsets.\n\n## Why the 569 column is not counted on LP2-32\n\nThe first grid column selects positions 1, 12, 23, …, 111. Those positions sum to 569, but are not consecutive. The first grid row uses positions 1–11 and is counted here. A column and a sliding window use different selection rules.\n\n## Limits\n\nBoth the targets and section were chosen after the original correspondence was noticed. Adjacent windows share ten runes. Counts cannot be treated as independent trials or p-values. There is no shuffled corpus or adjustment for other targets, lengths and layouts searched. This record does not resolve image-only claims about unspecified row alignments.\n\n## Reproduce and independently check\n\nExtract the experiment ZIP with folders intact, or use the repository. No external packages, images, network requests or AI calls are needed.\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/wing-tree-eleven-rune-windows/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/wing-tree-eleven-rune-windows/check.py\n```\n\nThe first command runs the shared census implementation and compares the saved report. The independent checker reads page JSON, constructs intervals by their ending position and sums each directly. It verifies every sequence, coordinate and total without importing the census implementation. Both text representations derive from the same archive: agreement is a computational check, not an independent visual review of the manuscript.\n",

  "reader_question": "If we try many rune distances and formulas, does the strongest pattern still stand out?",
  "reader_note": "The top result is a repeated rune after five positions, not the proposed six-position formula. Both exceed this shuffle baseline, but neither identifies a cipher or yields plaintext.",
  "reader_limit": "Other word boundaries, earlier exploratory choices, and realistic encryption models were not tested. A shuffled word is only one reference for ordinary sequence structure.",
  "scope_summary": "LP2-00–55 · 12 distances · 841 formulas each · 999 complete shuffled-word controls.",
  "visuals": [
    {
      "path": "experiments/records/word-internal-affine-all-lags/selection-null.svg",
      "caption": "Full-search maxima from 999 word shuffles. Lines mark the strongest actual relation and the previously proposed lag-six rule."
    }
  ],
  "record_type": {
    "id": "measurement",
    "label": "Manuscript measurement",
    "description": "Measures a stated feature or statistical comparison; it does not test a complete decoding rule."
  },
  "article": "# Affine relations across twelve rune distances\n\n## Finding\n\nAcross **12 distances and 841 formulas per distance**, the strongest excess is a **same-rune repeat five positions later**: 102 matches versus 60.6 expected after shuffling runes within each visible word. Only **4 of 999** shuffled-word searches found a result at least this strong (**p = 0.005**, including the one-count Monte Carlo correction). The earlier six-rune rule ranked below this repeat; 23 shuffled searches reached its score somewhere in the full search.\n\n![Histogram of the strongest score in each shuffled-word search, with markers for the actual maximum and the proposed six-rune rule.](experiments/records/word-internal-affine-all-lags/selection-null.svg)\n\nThe test finds word-internal structure that this shuffle does not explain. **It does not identify the encryption algorithm.** A shuffle breaks ordinary sequence patterns too, so an elevated count alone cannot distinguish a cipher rule from other structure in the manuscript.\n\n## Why scan the full range?\n\nThe [earlier lag-six measurement](#/experiments/word-internal-affine-lags) compared the proposed rule c′ = 24 − 2c (mod 29) against all 841 affine maps **at distance six**. That comparison did not account for choosing the distance after exploration. Here every shuffle must compete over the same 12 distances and 841 maps as the actual transcription. The proposed rule has 77 matches against a shuffle mean of 44.8; its standardized score is 4.763. The complete-search reference reaches at least that score in **23 of 999** trials (corrected tail 0.024). This is a comparison to a wider search, not a fresh independent test of the original idea.\n\nThe largest observed score, 5.272, comes from the identity relation at distance five: the rune repeats. It is 102 matches against an exact within-word shuffle expectation of 60.6. Four controls have a maximum score at least this high after repeating the **entire** search. That 4/999 count belongs to the strongest relation, not specifically to the original six-rune formula.\n\n## How the comparison works\n\nUse the archived rune order on LP2-00–55. A hyphen or full stop ends a word; a slash or line break does not. Each page remains separate. For each distance from 1 through 12, count rune pairs that stay within a visible word. Try all maps c′ = ac + b (mod 29), with a and b each 0–28. These are pattern measurements, including noninvertible maps, rather than candidate decryption keys.\n\nFor each map and distance, calculate its expected count under independent random order inside each word, keeping that word's exact rune counts. Divide the excess count by the square root of expected count plus one. Select the largest of the **10,092** scores. The denominator is a ranking scale, not a claim that scores follow a normal distribution; the full selection is calibrated by 999 seeded shuffles that repeat the same scan. The [frozen plan](experiments/records/word-internal-affine-all-lags/plan.json) records this score, search range, word rule, seed, stopping rule, and threshold before the run.\n\n## What remains open\n\nThe word rule follows the archived transcription, which has disputed separators. Other segmentations, page subsets, relations, and prior exploratory choices were not included in the selection control. The shuffled words preserve local rune counts and word lengths but are not simulated ciphertext. The high same-rune count at distance five should be tested on held-out material or against a more realistic generative control before treating it as a mechanism. Neither result supplies a key, plaintext, or explanation for missing adjacent doublets.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nFrom the repository root with Python 3.12 and the standard library:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/word-internal-affine-all-lags/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/word-internal-affine-all-lags/check.py\n```\n\nThe first command reruns all 999 complete searches and compares the full [saved result](experiments/records/word-internal-affine-all-lags/results.json) and chart byte for byte. The second independently checks the word and pair counts, the earlier 77-match rule, the exact shuffle expectation on a small exhaustive example, and the saved tail arithmetic. Input hashes and exact bounds are in the plan and download bundle. The run reached its planned 999 trials; the score, range, and stopping rule were not changed after seeing the result.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/word-internal-affine-all-lags/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "a0bc4d3aff8a4d0679b0a5b06af4281acd691f3423b52cbb7c4253edc5ac7a00"
}

  "record_type": {
    "id": "measurement",
    "label": "Manuscript measurement",
    "description": "Measures a stated feature or statistical comparison; it does not test a complete decoding rule."
  },
  "reader_note": "The excess is worth investigating, but it does not reveal the encryption method. The proposed 80 matches and zero matches across word gaps did not reproduce under this word rule; we counted 77 inside words and 389 across gaps.",
  "reader_limit": "We do not know whether this pattern is part of the encryption. The lag and formula were selected after exploration; other lags and word rules were not included in this comparison.",
  "scope_summary": "LP2-00–55 · rune pairs six places apart inside visible words · 1,267 pairs · 2,000 within-word shuffles.",
  "article": "## Finding\n\nThe relation **c′ = 24 − 2c (mod 29)** appears **77 times in 1,267 eligible pairs**, compared with **44.8 expected** when runes are shuffled within each word. It ranks first among 841 affine maps at lag six; only **3 of 2,000 shuffles** reached 77 matches after choosing their best map.\n\n![Observed lag-six count compared with fixed-map and best-of-841 word-shuffle means.](experiments/records/word-internal-affine-lags/comparison.svg)\n\nThis is a reproducible pattern in the archived transcription. It is **not a recovered encryption rule**. The formula and lag were supplied after exploration; the 841-map comparison does not account for trying other lags, word rules, page subsets, or formula families. The simple 1-in-29 reference would predict 43.7 matches, but it ignores each word's rune composition, so the within-word shuffle is the more relevant comparison here.\n\n## What counts as a word\n\nWe split at printed hyphens and full stops, join text across slashes and line breaks, and never connect different pages. This follows the archived transcription's visible separators; it does not settle disputed breaks in the source images. Splitting at **every** non-rune character instead leaves 965 opportunities and 58 matches. That choice would incorrectly turn layout wraps into word breaks. The supplied figure of **80 against 45.7** was not reproduced under either explicit rule and may use a different page range or transcription. The report keeps the rules and exact inputs visible so a differing count can be traced.\n\nAt the same six-rune distance, **389 of 11,359** pairs *crossing* a word gap also satisfy the formula. Thus “zero across word gaps” is false if it means all lag-six pairs whose ends lie in different words. A more specific boundary test would need its own definition.\n\n## What the comparison does and does not show\n\nThe formula's count is elevated relative to a fixed-map word shuffle, and it remains unusual against the **best of 841 maps at this one lag**. The report also records the same formula at lags 1–12 and counts on each page, so readers can check whether a few long words or pages dominate it. These are exploratory diagnostics; they do not establish that preventing doublets *causes* the lag-six relation. A causal proposal needs a fully specified generator that predicts both the missing adjacent repeats and the excess lag-six pairs, plus a held-out test.\n\nFor the adjacent-repeat baseline, see [equal rune pairs at lags one through five](#/experiments/doublet-lag-profile) and [doublet placement](#/experiments/doublet-placement). Those records measure different events and cannot by themselves confirm the proposed link.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nWith Python 3.12 and no extra packages, from the repository root:\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/word-internal-affine-lags/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/word-internal-affine-lags/check.py\n```\n\nThe first command rebuilds every count, the 2,000 seeded shuffles, and the figure in memory, then compares them with the saved outputs. The second independently scans the transcription to verify the 77 internal and 389 crossing-gap matches. The [machine-readable result](experiments/records/word-internal-affine-lags/results.json) includes page counts, all lag counts, selection-control ranks, and input hashes.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/word-internal-affine-lags/article.md",
  "script_sha256": "62d2be8191dc393072f57d4411afe684bd96ab8b05bec69e8746a3e79d8dc7f5"
}

  "visuals": [

      "caption": "Exact repetition and anagram repetition test different assumptions. The examples illustrate logical implications, not manuscript plaintext."

  "article": "# What do the missing word repetitions constrain?\n\n**Every selected ciphertext token is distinct:** 1,589 tokens when apostrophes are boundaries, or 1,591 when apostrophes are transparent. Allowing anagrams adds four pairs of four-rune tokens, but no pairs of five or more runes. These are constraints on particular word-local models, not a proof that every word-based cipher is impossible.\n\n## Exactly which tokens are counted?\n\nRead archived LP2-00–55 one page at a time, retaining headings. Slashes and CR/LF line wraps do not break a token. Other nonrune characters are boundaries. Run the analysis twice: once with apostrophes as boundaries, once with apostrophes ignored. No Latin expansion is used: TH and NG each count as one rune.\n\nDrop the first and last nonempty token of each page before comparing. Those units may be fragments at page edges. This deliberately omits some complete words too; it avoids assuming that the printed page edges are word boundaries. Do not join pages. Keep only the remaining tokens containing at least four ciphertext runes.\n\n| Apostrophe policy | Selected tokens | Distinct exact tokens | Equal pairs | Anagram pairs, length ≥4 | Anagram pairs, length ≥5 |\n| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |\n| Boundary | 1589 | 1589 | 0 | 4 | 0 |\n| Transparent | 1591 | 1591 | 0 | 4 | 0 |\n\nA pair means two distinct token occurrences, even if they are on the same page. A group of k equal signatures contributes k(k−1)/2 pairs. The ledger identifies every selected token, its original page-local token index and each rune's source offset, plus all collision groups.\n\n## Model 1: a deterministic cipher reset for each word\n\nSuppose each printed ciphertext token comes from one plaintext unit through the same deterministic function F, with identical key and reset context:\n\n```text\nciphertext unit = F(plaintext unit)\n```\n\nEqual inputs to the same function produce equal outputs. Therefore, if two ciphertext units differ, their plaintext units cannot have been equal under that model. Since all selected ciphertext tokens differ, their corresponding plaintext units must differ wherever the same F applies.\n\nThe function may contain a complicated composition, deterministic padding, fractionation or hashing. None of that changes the equal-input implication. F need not be invertible, and plaintext length need not equal ciphertext length. The four-rune cutoff is a selection rule on the observed ciphertext only.\n\nThis does **not** prove the unknown plaintext repeats. It supplies a necessary condition for this model, rather than a general exclusion of deterministic word ciphers.\n\n## Model 2: a shared symbol map plus word-local shuffling\n\nA different proposal applies the same symbol map to every word, then independently rearranges each word's output. Identical plaintext words may now give different ordered ciphertext, but they must give the same multiset of ciphertext symbols: they must be anagrams.\n\nFor example, A B A mapped to 2 5 2 can be rearranged into 2 2 5 or 5 2 2. The order changes, but the two 2s and one 5 remain. This implication does not require an injective symbol map; each input rune only needs one fixed output rune.\n\nThere are no selected anagram pairs of length five or more. Thus no two such tokens can encode the same plaintext rune word under this shared-map-and-shuffle model. Among length-four-or-longer selected tokens, at most four occurrence pairs can represent repeated plaintext words. An anagram match is only necessary, not proof that a pair encodes the same word.\n\nUnlike Model 1, this model preserves rune length. Padding, fractionation, or a different substitution for each word changes its assumptions.\n\n## The four anagram pairs\n\nBoth apostrophe policies produce these same pairs. Spaces below separate rune labels; NG, EA, TH, OE and AE each denote one rune. Token indices are zero-based in the original per-page token list, before removing edge tokens.\n\n| First occurrence | Second occurrence |\n| --- | --- |\n| [LP2-42](#/page/lp2-42), token 4: **F A NG E** | [LP2-53](#/page/lp2-53), token 16: **E F A NG** |\n| [LP2-12](#/page/lp2-12), token 40: **EA TH W Y** | [LP2-46](#/page/lp2-46), token 59: **Y EA TH W** |\n| [LP2-10](#/page/lp2-10), token 60: **S N OE X** | [LP2-12](#/page/lp2-12), token 33: **OE S N X** |\n| [LP2-09](#/page/lp2-09), token 17: **J Y T AE** | [LP2-49](#/page/lp2-49), token 9: **T Y AE J** |\n\nThese are ciphertext comparisons, not proposed readings. The resemblance of a label sequence to a familiar word is not evidence of plaintext.\n\n## What changing context does\n\nAn algorithm can be deterministic while its output depends on position, carried state, a different key, or a nonce. Those inputs belong to the effective context. If they differ, equal plaintext words need not give equal ciphertext. A Vigenère key continuing between words is not automatically a reset-per-word cipher.\n\nLikewise, allowing a different symbol map for each word can destroy the anagram relationship. Two copies of A B A could map to 0 1 0 and 2 3 2; their multiplicity patterns agree, but their named-symbol multisets differ. This experiment does not test that more flexible model.\n\n## Reproduce and independently check\n\nDownload and extract the experiment ZIP with folders intact. Python 3's standard library is enough; no packages, network requests or AI calls are required.\n\n```text\npython experiments/records/word-reset-repetition/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/word-reset-repetition/check.py\n```\n\nThe main script scans characters and groups sorted rune sequences. The independent checker reads page JSON, tokenizes with a regular expression, and compares 29-component count vectors. It verifies source positions and every collision group, and checks the anagram implication over 4,374 small mapping/permutation cases, including noninjective maps.\n\nBoth input formats share their archival source; this is not a second visual transcription audit. The supplied closure archive reports the same observations in C31 and C33. This record freshly reproduces them and explains the elementary implications. It does not rerun or claim verification of the archive's Lean project.\n\n## Scope of the conclusion\n\nThe counting is exact for these token rules. No English frequency model, likelihood, p-value, or assumption that a particular word must appear is used. Changed boundaries, page-edge inclusion, a corrected transcription, different contexts, or a different output construction require an explicitly recorded retest. The word-length article uses a different boundary convention for a different purpose; its total should not be substituted for the counts here.\n",
  "article_path": "experiments/records/word-reset-repetition/article.md",

  "article": "# How many words fit the selected magic-square totals?\n\nThe proposed phrase **PROVE WORTHIER FIND TRUTHS** fits the LP1 square values 131, 151, 151, 131. That arithmetic is already [checked word by word](#/experiments/selected-phrase-word-sums). It leaves a different question: how many *other* words would also fit those values if a solver searched a large list and chose a pleasing phrase afterward?\n\nThis control counts candidates in a [preserved revision of the Liber Primus Crib Assist word list](https://github.com/mortlach/Liber-Primus-Crib-Assist/tree/9c10cafce02e512840cc9e173127930594a56281/data/1_grams-full). The supplied discussion linked an older `data/1_grams` path and mentioned a separate `worddata.csv`. Those exact historical bytes are unavailable in the supplied transcript. This is therefore a **pinned-corpus control**, not a reconstruction of every historical search or its dictionary.\n\n## What the census found\n\nThe sixteen preserved CSVs contain **138,466 distinct word rows**. Every stored GP total agrees with summing its stored rune values after accounting for one source-font difference: the corpus writes J as `ᛂ`, while this site's manuscript alphabet writes J as `ᛄ`; both carry value 37. The source glyph occurs in 2,217 rows. That mapping is declared in the plan, not silently normalized.\n\n| Phrase slot | Target GP total | Stored rune length | Matching corpus words |\n| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |\n| PROVE | 131 | 5 | 38 |\n| WORTHIER | 151 | 7 | 15 |\n| FIND | 151 | 4 | 10 |\n| TRUTHS | 131 | 5 | 38 |\n\nAll four proposed words occur in the preserved corpus. At the four fixed totals **and** rune lengths, there are **38 × 15 × 10 × 38 = 216,600 ordered word combinations**. If the first and fourth words must differ, there are **210,900**. These are combinations of dictionary entries, not 216,600 grammatical sentences. They have not been scored for meaning, syntax or relation to the manuscript.\n\nIf rune length is discarded, 105 corpus words have GP 131 and 133 have GP 151, giving 195,021,225 ordered combinations for the same four total slots. This illustrates why a claim must state its length constraint before a phrase is chosen. The corpus has only one row with GP 809, **DETECTABILITY** at 13 runes. The proposed **MYRMELEONTIDAE** is absent from this corpus; absence from a bounded word list is not evidence against that separately verified arithmetic assignment.\n\n![Three histograms of corpus word counts by GP sum for four-, five-, and seven-rune words, highlighting the selected 131 and 151 totals.](experiments/records/word-sum-corpus-control/candidate-space.svg)\n\nThe graph shows GP totals 80–220 so the selected values remain legible. The downloadable result keeps the complete count distribution for every rune length and observed total. Neither the displayed interval nor the source frequency column is used to select candidate words.\n\n## What was counted\n\nThe [plan](experiments/records/word-sum-corpus-control/plan.json) fixes the four word slots, totals and rune lengths. Each distinct CSV row counts once, including rows in the `2a1` and `3a1` files. The script checks the SHA-256 of all sixteen CSVs, the source manifest, its GPL-3.0 license and the manuscript alphabet before reading them. It validates every row's printed GP sum against the stored rune sequence. The opaque source count and flag columns are retained in the output but are not interpreted as independent evidence about language or author intent.\n\nThe ordered product lets any word fitting one slot combine with any word fitting the others. It does not test whether a coherent four-word sentence is common. Conversely, finding many alternatives does not prove the proposed phrase accidental. A sentence-level test would need a predeclared grammar or language score, the original vocabulary and all candidate phrases retained, plus matched square-value controls.\n\n## Reproduce\n\nFrom the repository root or the standalone experiment ZIP, run:\n\n```sh\npython experiments/records/word-sum-corpus-control/run.py --check\npython experiments/records/word-sum-corpus-control/check.py\n```\n\nThe runner checks the saved JSON and SVG byte for byte. The separate checker reads the preserved CSVs afresh, verifies each stored GP value and recomputes the target counts and products without importing the runner. Both use Python's standard library and require no network or AI model. The CSVs are redistributed unchanged with their source revision, per-file hashes, attribution and GPL-3.0 text in the experiment bundle.\n\n## Limits and next test\n\nThis corpus is a surviving version of the linked tool's word data, not proven identical to the forum attachment called `worddata.csv`. It ends at 14 stored runes and its vocabulary is neither all English nor an unbiased sample of possible keys. The result measures **candidate freedom under one explicit list**. It does not reconstruct how the phrase was selected, apply a word to LP2, or judge any unsolved reading.\n\nThe next defensible variant is to recover the historical CSV or document that it is lost, then fix a phrase-generation and scoring procedure before seeing its winners. A separate cipher test must specify which selected word maps to which target, exactly how the word acts as a key, and what held-out output would count as success.\n",
